These are the names of Ishmael's sons, listed in the order of their birth: Nebaioth was Ishmael's firstborn, then came Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah.
These were the sons of Ishmael, and these are the names of the twelve tribal rulers, listed by their villages and camps.
Ishmael lived a hundred and thirty-seven years in all. Then he breathed his last and died, and he joined his ancestors.
His descendants settled in the area from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt, on the way to Assyria. They lived at odds with all their relatives.
This is the family line of Abraham's son Isaac. Abraham was the father of Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah. She was the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan Aram, and the sister of Laban the Aramean.
Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she could not have children. The LORD answered his prayer, and his wife Rebekah became pregnant.
The babies pushed against each other inside her, and she said, "Why is this happening to me?" So she went to ask the LORD.
The LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will come from you and be separated. One people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger."
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twin boys in her womb.
The first to come out was red, and his whole body was covered with hair like a hairy coat. So they named him Esau.
After this, his brother came out, holding on to Esau's heel with his hand. So he was named Jacob, which means "he grabs the heel". Isaac was sixty years old when Rebekah gave birth to them.
The boys grew up. Esau became a skilled hunter who loved the open country, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home among the tents.
Isaac loved Esau because he liked to eat the wild meat Esau hunted, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Once when Jacob was cooking some stew, Esau came in from the open country, very hungry.
Esau said to Jacob, "Quick, let me have some of that red stew! I am starving!" That is why he was also called Edom, which means "red".
Jacob replied, "First sell me your rights as the firstborn son."
"Look, I am about to die," Esau said. "What good are these rights to me?"
But Jacob said, "Make a solemn promise to me first." So Esau made the promise, and sold his rights as the firstborn to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau some bread and some lentil stew. He ate and drank, and then got up and left. So Esau showed that he did not care about his rights as the firstborn son.
Now there was a famine in the land, besides the earlier famine in Abraham's time. So Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, in Gerar.
The LORD appeared to Isaac and said, "Do not go down to Egypt. Live in the land where I tell you to live.
Stay in this land for a while, and I will be with you and bless you. I will give all these lands to you and your descendants, and I will keep the promise I made to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as many as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands. Through your descendants all nations on earth will be blessed,
because Abraham obeyed me. He did everything I asked him to do. He kept my commands, my rules and my laws."
So Isaac stayed in Gerar.

When the men of that place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister." He was afraid to say, "She is my wife." He thought, "The men of this place might kill me because of Rebekah, since she is so beautiful."
When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from a window and saw Isaac hugging and kissing his wife Rebekah.
So Abimelech called for Isaac and said, "She is really your wife! Why did you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac answered him, "Because I thought I might be killed because of her."
Then Abimelech said, "What have you done to us? One of the men might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us."
So Abimelech gave orders to all the people: "Anyone who harms this man or his wife will be put to death."
Isaac planted crops in that land, and the same year he harvested a hundred times as much as he had planted, because the LORD blessed him.
Isaac became rich. His wealth kept growing until he was very rich indeed.
He had so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines became jealous of him.
So the Philistines filled up all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the time of his father Abraham. They filled them with earth.
Then Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us. You have become far too powerful for us."
So Isaac moved away from there. He set up his tents in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.
Isaac dug out again the wells that had been dug in the time of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had filled up after Abraham died. He gave them the same names his father had given them.
Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh, flowing water there.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarrelled with Isaac's herdsmen and said, "The water is ours!" So Isaac named the well Esek, which means "argument", because they argued with him.
Then they dug another well, but they quarrelled over that one too. So he named it Sitnah, which means "enemy".
He moved on from there and dug another well, and no one quarrelled over it. He named it Rehoboth, which means "open space". He said, "Now the LORD has given us room, and we will do well in the land."
From there he went up to Beersheba.

That night the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, because I am with you. I will bless you and give you many descendants for the sake of my servant Abraham."
Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. He set up his tent there, and his servants dug a well there.
Meanwhile, Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac asked them, "Why have you come to me, since you were hostile to me and sent me away?"
They answered, "We could see clearly that the LORD was with you. So we said, 'There should be a solemn agreement between us and you.' Let us make a covenant with you,
that you will not harm us, just as we did not harm you. We always treated you well and sent you away in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD."
Isaac then made a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
Early the next morning the men made solemn promises to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
That day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug. They said, "We have found water!"
He called it Shibah, which means "promise". To this day the name of the town has been Beersheba.
When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and also Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
These women made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, he called for Esau, his older son. "My son," he said. "Here I am," Esau answered.
Isaac said, "I am now an old man, and I do not know when I will die.
So get your weapons, your bow and arrows, and go out into the open country to hunt some wild animals for me.
Cook me the kind of tasty food I like and bring it to me to eat. Then I will give you my blessing before I die."
Now Rebekah was listening while Isaac spoke to his son Esau. When Esau left for the open country to hunt for wild meat and bring it back,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "Listen! I heard your father say to your brother Esau,
'Bring me some wild meat and cook me some tasty food to eat. Then I will bless you in front of the LORD before I die.'
Now, my son, listen carefully and do what I tell you.
Go out to the flock and bring me two of the best young goats. I will cook some tasty food for your father, just the way he likes it.
Then take it to your father to eat, so that he will give you his blessing before he dies."
Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, "But my brother Esau is a hairy man, and my skin is smooth.
What if my father touches me? He will see that I am tricking him, and I would bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing."
His mother said to him, "My son, let the curse fall on me. Just do what I say. Go and get the goats for me."
So he went and got them and brought them to his mother, and she cooked some tasty food, just the way his father liked it.
Then Rebekah took the best clothes of Esau, her older son, which she had in the house, and put them on her younger son Jacob.
She also covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the goatskins.
Then she handed her son Jacob the tasty food and the bread she had made.
He went to his father and said, "My father." "Yes, my son," he answered. "Who is it?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my wild meat, so that you can give me your blessing."
Isaac asked his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" He replied, "The LORD your God gave me success."
Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Come near so that I can touch you, my son, to know whether you really are my son Esau or not."
Jacob went close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
He did not recognise him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau. So he got ready to bless him.
"Are you really my son Esau?" he asked. "I am," he replied.
Then Isaac said, "Bring me some of your wild meat to eat, my son, so that I can give you my blessing." Jacob brought it to him, and he ate. Then he brought him some wine, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come here, my son, and kiss me."
So he went to him and kissed him. When Isaac smelled the smell of his clothes, he blessed him and said, "The smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
May God give you dew from the sky and rich soil on the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine.

May nations serve you and peoples bow down to you. Be the master over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. May those who curse you be cursed, and may those who bless you be blessed."
Isaac had just finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had hardly left his father's presence, when his brother Esau came in from hunting.
He too cooked some tasty food and brought it to his father. Then he said to him, "My father, please sit up and eat some of my wild meat, so that you can give me your blessing."
His father Isaac asked him, "Who are you?" "I am your son," he answered, "your firstborn, Esau."
Isaac began to shake all over and said, "Then who was it that hunted wild meat and brought it to me? I ate it just before you came, and I blessed him. And he will be blessed!"
When Esau heard his father's words, he cried out loudly and bitterly. He said to his father, "Bless me too, my father!"
But Isaac said, "Your brother came and tricked me, and he has taken your blessing."

Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? He has cheated me two times now. He took my rights as the firstborn, and now he has taken my blessing!" Then he asked, "Have you not kept back any blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "I have made him master over you, and I have made all his relatives his servants. I have given him plenty of grain and new wine. So what can I possibly do for you, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, my father!" And Esau wept loudly.
His father Isaac answered him, "You will live far away from the rich soil of the earth, far from the dew of the sky above.
You will live by the sword, and you will serve your brother. But when you grow restless, you will throw his heavy load off your neck."
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are near. Then I will kill my brother Jacob."
When Rebekah was told what her older son Esau had said, she sent for her younger son Jacob. She said to him, "Your brother Esau is comforting himself with the thought of killing you.
Now then, my son, do what I say. Run away at once to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him for a while, until your brother's fury calms down.
When your brother is no longer angry with you and has forgotten what you did to him, I will send word for you to come back from there. Why should I lose both of you in one day?"

Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am sick and tired of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the women of this land, a Hittite woman like these, my life will not be worth living."
So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. Then he commanded him, "Do not marry a Canaanite woman.
Go at once to Paddan Aram, to the house of your mother's father Bethuel. Choose a wife for yourself there, from among the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you and give you many children, until you become a whole community of peoples.
May he give you and your descendants the blessing he gave to Abraham, so that you will own the land where you now live as a stranger, the land God gave to Abraham."
Then Isaac sent Jacob on his way, and he went to Paddan Aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean. Laban was the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Esau found out that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan Aram to find a wife there. He also heard that when Isaac blessed him, he commanded him, "Do not marry a Canaanite woman."
And he learned that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and had gone to Paddan Aram.
Then Esau realised how much his father Isaac disliked the Canaanite women.
So Esau went to Ishmael, Abraham's son, and married his daughter Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth. She was added to the wives he already had.
Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.
When he came to a certain place, he stopped for the night because the sun had set. He took one of the stones there, put it under his head as a pillow, and lay down to sleep.
He had a dream. He saw a stairway standing on the earth, with its top reaching up to heaven, and the angels of God were going up and coming down on it.
There above it stood the LORD, and he said, "I am the LORD, the God of your grandfather Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land you are lying on.

Your descendants will be as many as the dust of the earth. They will spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. All the families on earth will be blessed through you and your descendants.
I am with you, and I will look after you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done everything I have promised you."
When Jacob woke up from his sleep, he thought, "The LORD is surely in this place, and I did not know it."
He was afraid and said, "How amazing and frightening this place is! This is none other than the house of God. This is the gate of heaven."
Early the next morning Jacob took the stone he had put under his head and set it up as a pillar, and he poured oil on top of it.
He named that place Bethel, which means "house of God", although the town used to be called Luz.
Then Jacob made a solemn promise. He said, "If God will be with me and look after me on this journey, and give me food to eat and clothes to wear,
so that I come back safely to my father's home, then the LORD will be my God.
This stone that I have set up as a pillar will be God's house, and of everything you give me I will give you a tenth."
Then Jacob continued on his journey and came to the land of the eastern peoples.
There he saw a well in the open country, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks were given water from that well. The stone over the mouth of the well was large.

When all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone away from the mouth of the well and give water to the sheep. Then they would put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
Jacob asked the shepherds, "My friends, where are you from?" "We are from Haran," they replied.
He said to them, "Do you know Laban, Nahor's grandson?" "Yes, we know him," they answered.
Then Jacob asked them, "Is he well?" "Yes, he is well," they said. "And here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
"Look," he said, "it is still the middle of the day. It is not time for the flocks to be gathered. Give the sheep water and take them back to the fields."
"We cannot," they replied, "until all the flocks are gathered and the stone has been rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we will give the sheep water."
While he was still talking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, because she was a shepherd.
When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his uncle Laban, with Laban's sheep, he went over and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and gave water to his uncle's sheep.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and began to weep loudly.
He told Rachel that he was a relative of her father, the son of Rebekah. So she ran and told her father.
As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he hurried to meet him. He hugged him and kissed him and brought him to his home. There Jacob told him all that had happened.
Then Laban said to him, "You really are my own flesh and blood." Jacob stayed with him for a whole month.
Then Laban said to him, "Just because you are my relative, you should not work for me for nothing. Tell me what your pay should be."
Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older one was Leah, and the name of the younger one was Rachel.
Leah had gentle eyes, but Rachel had a lovely figure and was beautiful.
Jacob was in love with Rachel. So he said, "I will work for you for seven years in return for your younger daughter Rachel."
Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than to some other man. Stay here with me."
So Jacob worked for seven years to get Rachel, but they seemed like only a few days to him because he loved her so much.
Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife. My time is finished, and I want to sleep with her."
So Laban brought together all the people of the place and gave a feast.
But when evening came, he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her.
Laban gave his slave woman Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
When morning came, there was Leah! So Jacob said to Laban, "What have you done to me? I worked for you to get Rachel, did I not? Why have you tricked me?"
Laban replied, "It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older one.
Finish this daughter's wedding week. Then we will give you the younger one too, in return for another seven years of work."
And Jacob did so. He finished the week with Leah, and then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.
Laban gave his slave woman Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob slept with Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. And he worked for Laban for another seven years.
When the LORD saw that Leah was not loved, he made it possible for her to have children, but Rachel could not have children.
Leah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben, because she said, "The LORD has seen my trouble. Surely my husband will love me now."
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. She said, "Because the LORD heard that I am not loved, he has given me this son too." So she named him Simeon, which sounds like "heard".

Again she became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She said, "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have given him three sons." So he was named Levi, which sounds like "attached".
She became pregnant once more and gave birth to a son. She said, "This time I will praise the LORD." So she named him Judah, which sounds like "praise". Then she stopped having children for a while.
When Rachel saw that she was not having any children for Jacob, she became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob became angry with her and said, "Am I God? He is the one who has kept you from having children."
Then she said, "Here is my slave woman Bilhah. Sleep with her, so that she can have children for me. Then I too can have a family through her."
So she gave him her slave woman Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah became pregnant and gave Jacob a son.
Then Rachel said, "God has judged in my favour. He has listened to me and given me a son." So she named him Dan, which means "he judged".
Rachel's slave woman Bilhah became pregnant again and gave Jacob a second son.
Then Rachel said, "I have had a great struggle with my sister, and I have won." So she named him Naphtali, which means "my struggle".
When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she took her slave woman Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah's slave woman Zilpah gave Jacob a son.
Then Leah said, "What good fortune!" So she named him Gad, which means "good fortune".
Leah's slave woman Zilpah gave Jacob a second son.
Then Leah said, "How happy I am! The women will call me happy." So she named him Asher, which means "happy".

During the wheat harvest, Reuben went out into the fields and found some mandrake plants, which were believed to help women have children. He brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

But Leah said to her, "Was it not enough that you took away my husband? Will you take my son's mandrakes too?" "Very well," Rachel said, "he can sleep with you tonight in return for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the fields that evening, Leah went out to meet him. "You must sleep with me tonight," she said. "I have paid for you with my son's mandrakes." So he slept with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she became pregnant and gave Jacob a fifth son.
Then Leah said, "God has rewarded me for giving my slave woman to my husband." So she named him Issachar, which sounds like "reward".
Leah became pregnant again and gave Jacob a sixth son.
Then Leah said, "God has given me a precious gift. This time my husband will honour me, because I have given him six sons." So she named him Zebulun, which sounds like "honour".
Some time later she gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and made it possible for her to have children.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She said, "God has taken away my shame."
She named him Joseph, which means "may he add", and said, "May the LORD add another son to me."
After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Let me go, so that I can go back to my own home and country.
Give me my wives and children, for whom I have worked for you, and I will be on my way. You know how much work I have done for you."
But Laban said to him, "If you are pleased with me, please stay. I have learned by signs that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
He added, "Tell me what you want to be paid, and I will pay it."
Jacob said to him, "You know how I have worked for you, and how well your livestock has done under my care.
You had very little before I came, and it has grown into a great deal. The LORD has blessed you wherever I have gone. But now, when can I do something for my own family?"
"What shall I give you?" Laban asked. "Do not give me anything," Jacob replied. "But if you will do this one thing for me, I will go on looking after your flocks and caring for them.
Let me go through all your flocks today and take out every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-coloured lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. They will be my pay.

In the future my honesty will speak for me. Whenever you check on the animals you have paid me, any goat that is not speckled or spotted, and any lamb that is not dark-coloured, will count as stolen if it is found with me."
"Agreed," said Laban. "Let it be as you have said."

But that same day Laban removed all the male goats that had stripes or spots, all the speckled or spotted female goats, all that had white on them, and all the dark-coloured lambs. He put them in the care of his sons.
Then he put a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob went on looking after the rest of Laban's flocks.
Jacob took fresh-cut branches from poplar, almond and plane trees. He peeled white stripes on them by stripping off the bark and showing the white wood underneath.
Then he put the peeled branches in all the water troughs, so that they were right in front of the flocks when they came to drink. The animals mated when they came to drink.
They mated in front of the branches, and they gave birth to young that were striped or speckled or spotted.

Jacob set apart the young animals of the flock by themselves. He made the rest face the striped and dark-coloured animals that belonged to Laban. So he built up his own flocks and kept them separate from Laban's animals.
Whenever the stronger animals were mating, Jacob put the branches in the troughs in front of them, so that they would mate near the branches.
But if the animals were weak, he did not put the branches there. So the weak animals went to Laban, and the strong ones to Jacob.
In this way Jacob became very rich. He had large flocks, male and female servants, and camels and donkeys.
Jacob heard that Laban's sons were saying, "Jacob has taken everything our father owned. He has got all this wealth from what belonged to our father."
And Jacob noticed that Laban was no longer as friendly towards him as he had been before.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Go back to the land of your ancestors and to your relatives, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent word to Rachel and Leah to come out to the fields where his flocks were.
He said to them, "I can see that your father is not as friendly towards me as he was before. But the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have worked for your father as hard as I could.
Yet your father has cheated me by changing my pay ten times. But God has not let him harm me.

If he said, 'The speckled ones will be your pay', then all the flocks gave birth to speckled young. And if he said, 'The striped ones will be your pay', then all the flocks gave birth to striped young.
So God has taken away your father's livestock and given it to me.
Once, during the mating season, I had a dream. I looked up and saw that the male goats mating with the flock were striped, speckled or spotted.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' I answered, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Look up and see that all the male goats mating with the flock are striped, speckled or spotted, because I have seen everything Laban has been doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you poured oil on a pillar and where you made a solemn promise to me. Now get ready to leave this land at once and go back to the land where you were born.'"
Then Rachel and Leah replied, "Do we still have any share in the inheritance of our father's estate?
Does he not treat us like foreigners? Not only has he sold us, but he has used up all the money that was paid for us.
Surely all the wealth that God took away from our father belongs to us and our children. So do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob got ready and put his children and his wives on camels.
He drove all his livestock ahead of him, with all the goods he had gathered in Paddan Aram, and set out to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
While Laban had gone to cut the wool from his sheep, Rachel stole her father's household idols.
Jacob also tricked Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away.
So he ran away with everything he had. He crossed the Euphrates River and headed for the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had run away.
He took his relatives with him and chased Jacob for seven days. He caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
Then God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream at night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."
Jacob had set up his tent in the hill country of Gilead when Laban caught up with him. Laban and his relatives set up camp there too.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have tricked me, and you have carried off my daughters like prisoners of war.
Why did you run away secretly and trick me? Why did you not tell me? I would have sent you off with joy and singing, with the music of tambourines and harps.
You did not even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye. You have done a foolish thing.
I have the power to harm you. But last night the God of your father said to me, 'Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.'
Now you have gone off because you longed so much to go back to your father's home. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid. I thought you would take your daughters away from me by force.

But if you find anyone who has your gods, that person will not live. Here, in front of our relatives, look for yourself and see if there is anything of yours with me, and if so, take it." Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the gods.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent, and into Leah's tent, and into the tent of the two slave women, but he found nothing. After he came out of Leah's tent, he went into Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the household idols and put them inside her camel's saddle, and she was sitting on them. Laban searched through everything in the tent but found nothing.
Rachel said to her father, "Please do not be angry, sir, that I cannot stand up in front of you. I am having my monthly period." So he searched but could not find the household idols.
Then Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. "What wrong have I done?" he asked Laban. "What sin have I committed, that you have chased after me so fiercely?
Now that you have searched through all my goods, what have you found that belongs to your household? Put it here in front of your relatives and mine, and let them judge between the two of us.
I have been with you for twenty years now. Your sheep and goats have not lost their young, and I have not eaten any rams from your flocks.
I did not bring you animals torn apart by wild beasts. I paid for the loss myself. And you made me pay for whatever was stolen, whether by day or by night.
This is how it was for me: the heat wore me out in the daytime and the cold at night, and I could not sleep.
For twenty years I have been in your household. I worked for you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flocks, and you changed my pay ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham, the God whom Isaac fears, had not been with me, you would surely have sent me away with nothing. But God has seen my trouble and my hard work, and last night he warned you."

Laban answered Jacob, "The women are my daughters, the children are my children, and the flocks are my flocks. Everything you see is mine. But what can I do today about these daughters of mine, or about the children they have had?
Come now, let's make a covenant, you and I. Let it be a witness between us."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
He said to his relatives, "Gather some stones." So they took stones and piled them in a heap, and they ate there beside the heap.
Laban called it Jegar Sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed. Both names mean "heap of witness".
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between you and me today." That is why it was called Galeed.
It was also called Mizpah, which means "watchtower", because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are apart from each other.
If you treat my daughters badly, or if you marry other wives besides my daughters, remember that even though no one else is with us, God is a witness between you and me."
Laban also said to Jacob, "Here is this heap, and here is this pillar I have set up between you and me.
This heap is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not go past this heap to harm you, and that you will not go past this heap and pillar to harm me.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob made a solemn promise in the name of the God whom his father Isaac feared.
Jacob offered a sacrifice there in the hill country and invited his relatives to a meal. After they had eaten, they spent the night there.
Early the next morning Laban kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then he left and went back home.
Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's camp!" So he named that place Mahanaim, which means "two camps".
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He told them, "This is what you must say to my master Esau: 'Your servant Jacob says, I have been staying with Laban and have remained there until now.
I have cattle and donkeys, sheep and goats, and male and female servants. Now I am sending this message to my master, hoping that you will be kind to me.'"
When the messengers came back to Jacob, they said, "We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you, with four hundred men."
Jacob was very afraid and worried. So he divided the people who were with him into two groups, and the flocks and herds and camels as well.
He thought, "If Esau comes and attacks one group, the group that is left may escape."
Then Jacob prayed, "O God of my grandfather Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O LORD, you told me, 'Go back to your country and your relatives, and I will make you do well.'
I am not worthy of all the kindness and faithfulness you have shown your servant. When I crossed this Jordan River, I had only my walking stick. But now I have become two camps.
Please save me from the hand of my brother Esau. I am afraid that he will come and attack me, and the mothers with their children too.
But you have said, 'I will surely make you do well, and I will make your descendants like the sand of the sea, which is too much to count.'"
Jacob spent the night there. Then from what he had with him he chose a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred female sheep and twenty rams,
thirty female camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, and twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He put each herd in the care of one of his servants and said to them, "Go on ahead of me, and keep some space between the herds."
He told the servant in front, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks, 'Who is your master? Where are you going? Who owns all these animals in front of you?'
then you must say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift sent to my master Esau, and Jacob himself is coming behind us.'"
He gave the same instructions to the second servant, the third, and all the others who followed the herds. He said, "You must say the same thing to Esau when you meet him.
And be sure to say, 'Your servant Jacob is coming behind us.'" Jacob thought, "I will calm him down with these gifts I am sending on ahead. Later, when I see him, perhaps he will welcome me."
So Jacob's gifts went on ahead of him, but he himself spent the night in the camp.
That night Jacob got up and took his two wives, his two slave women and his eleven sons, and crossed the river Jabbok at the shallow place.
After he had sent them across the stream, he sent over everything he owned.
So Jacob was left alone. Then a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not win, he touched the socket of Jacob's hip, and Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with the man.
Then the man said, "Let me go, because it is daybreak." But Jacob replied, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
The man asked him, "What is your name?" "Jacob," he answered.
Then the man said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, which means 'he struggles with God', because you have struggled with God and with people, and you have won."
Jacob said, "Please tell me your name." But he replied, "Why do you ask my name?" Then he blessed him there.
So Jacob named the place Peniel, which means "face of God". He said, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared."
The sun rose above him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping because of his hip.
That is why, to this day, the people of Israel do not eat the muscle attached to the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob's hip was touched near that muscle.
Jacob looked up, and there was Esau coming with his four hundred men. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel and the two slave women.
He put the slave women and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the back.
He himself went on ahead of them, and he bowed down to the ground seven times as he came near his brother.
But Esau ran to meet Jacob and hugged him. He threw his arms around his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
Then Esau looked up and saw the women and children. "Who are these with you?" he asked. Jacob answered, "They are the children God has kindly given your servant."
Then the slave women and their children came near and bowed down.
Next, Leah and her children came and bowed down. Last of all came Joseph and Rachel, and they too bowed down.
Esau asked, "What do you mean by all these herds I met?" "They are to win your favour, my master," Jacob said.
But Esau said, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have for yourself."
"No, please," said Jacob. "If you are pleased with me, accept this gift from me. To see your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have welcomed me so kindly.
Please accept the gift that was brought to you, because God has been kind to me, and I have everything I need." Because Jacob kept on asking him, Esau accepted it.
Then Esau said, "Let's be on our way. I will go with you."

But Jacob said to him, "My master knows that the children are weak, and that I have to take care of the sheep and cattle that are feeding their young. If they are driven hard for even one day, all the animals will die.
So let my master go on ahead of his servant, while I move along slowly at the pace of the flocks and herds in front of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my master in Seir."
Esau said, "Then let me leave some of my men with you." "Why do that?" Jacob asked. "It is enough that my master is pleased with me."
So that day Esau started back on his way to Seir.
But Jacob went to Succoth. There he built a house for himself and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth, which means "shelters".
After Jacob came from Paddan Aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in Canaan and set up camp near the city.
For a hundred pieces of silver, he bought the piece of land where he had put up his tent. He bought it from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem.
There he set up an altar and called it El Elohe Israel, which means "God, the God of Israel".
One day Dinah, the daughter Leah had given Jacob, went out to visit the young women of the land.
Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, who ruled that area, saw her. He took her and forced her to sleep with him, and he disgraced her.
But his heart was drawn to Dinah, Jacob's daughter. He loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, "Get me this girl as my wife."
Jacob heard that his daughter Dinah had been disgraced. But his sons were out in the fields with his livestock, so he said nothing about it until they came home.
Then Shechem's father Hamor went out to talk with Jacob.

Meanwhile, Jacob's sons had come in from the fields as soon as they heard what had happened. They were shocked and furious, because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by sleeping with Jacob's daughter. Such a thing should never be done.
But Hamor said to them, "My son Shechem has his heart set on your daughter. Please let him marry her.
Let our families marry each other. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You can live among us, and the land will be open to you. Live in it, trade in it, and buy property in it."
Then Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "Please be kind to me, and I will give you whatever you ask.
Make the bride price and the gift as great as you like, and I will pay whatever you ask me. Only let me marry the girl."
Because Shechem had disgraced their sister Dinah, Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor with a trick.
They said to them, "We cannot do such a thing. We cannot give our sister to a man who is not circumcised. That would be a disgrace to us.
We will agree to it on one condition only: that you become like us by circumcising all your males.
Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We will live among you and become one people with you.
But if you will not agree to be circumcised, we will take our sister and go."
Their offer seemed good to Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man did not waste any time doing what they said, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter. And he was the most respected member of his father's family.
So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city to speak to the men of their city.
They said, "These men are friendly towards us. Let them live in our land and trade in it. The land has plenty of room for them. We can marry their daughters, and they can marry ours.
But the men will agree to live with us as one people only on one condition: that every male among us is circumcised, as they are.
Will not their livestock, their property and all their other animals become ours? So let's agree to their condition, and they will settle among us."
All the men who went out of the city gate agreed with Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male in the city was circumcised.

Three days later, while all of them were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, who were Dinah's brothers, took their swords. They attacked the city, which was not expecting it, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem's house and left.
Then the other sons of Jacob came upon the dead bodies and looted the city where their sister had been disgraced.
They took their sheep, cattle and donkeys, and everything else of theirs in the city and in the fields.
They carried off all their wealth and all their women and children, and took everything in their houses.

Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me. You have made me hated by the people living in this land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. We are only a few, and if they join together against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed."
But they replied, "Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?"
Then God said to Jacob, "Get ready and go up to Bethel, and live there. Build an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you were running away from your brother Esau."
So Jacob said to his household and to everyone who was with him, "Get rid of the foreign gods you have with you. Make yourselves clean, and change your clothes.
Then come, let's go up to Bethel. There I will build an altar to God, who answered me when I was in trouble and who has been with me everywhere I have gone."
So they gave Jacob all the foreign gods they had, and the earrings they were wearing, and Jacob buried them under the oak tree near Shechem.
Then they set out, and a great fear from God fell on the towns all around them, so that no one chased after Jacob's sons.
Jacob and all the people with him came to Luz, which is Bethel, in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar, and he called the place El Bethel, which means "God of Bethel", because it was there that God had shown himself to him when he was running away from his brother.
Then Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was buried under the oak tree below Bethel. So it was named Allon Bakuth, which means "oak of weeping".
After Jacob came back from Paddan Aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
God said to him, "Your name is Jacob, but you will no longer be called Jacob. Your name will be Israel." So he named him Israel.
And God said to him, "I am God Almighty. Have many children and increase in number. A nation, and a whole community of nations, will come from you, and kings will be among your descendants.
The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac I also give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you."
Then God went up from him at the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a stone pillar at the place where God had spoken with him. He poured out a drink offering on it, and he also poured oil on it.
Jacob called the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
Then they moved on from Bethel. While they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and she had great difficulty.
While she was having this great difficulty, the woman helping her said to her, "Do not be afraid. You have another son."
As she breathed her last, because she was dying, she named her son Ben-Oni, which means "son of my trouble". But his father named him Benjamin, which means "son of my right hand".
So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave, and to this day that pillar marks Rachel's grave.
Israel moved on again and set up his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
While Israel was living in that area, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father's secondary wife, and Israel heard about it. Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah were Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Rachel's slave woman Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Leah's slave woman Zilpah were Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan Aram.
Jacob came home to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath Arba, which is Hebron. Abraham and Isaac had both lived there as strangers.
Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years.
Then he breathed his last and died, and he joined his ancestors, old and full of years. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
This is the family line of Esau, who is also called Edom.
Esau married women from among the Canaanites: Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite.
He also married Basemath, Ishmael's daughter and the sister of Nebaioth.
Adah gave Esau a son named Eliphaz, and Basemath had Reuel.
Oholibamah had Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were the sons of Esau, who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters and all the members of his household, as well as his livestock and all his other animals and all the goods he had gained in Canaan. He moved to a land some distance away from his brother Jacob.
They owned too much to stay together. The land where they were living could not support them both, because they had so much livestock.
So Esau, who is also called Edom, settled in the hill country of Seir.
This is the family line of Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, the son of Esau's wife Adah, and Reuel, the son of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz.
Esau's son Eliphaz also had a secondary wife named Timna, and she gave birth to Amalek. These were the grandsons of Esau's wife Adah.
The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the grandsons of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, whom she gave to Esau, were Jeush, Jalam and Korah.
These were the clan leaders among Esau's descendants. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, were the leaders Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,
Korah, Gatam and Amalek. These were the leaders who came from Eliphaz in Edom. They were grandsons of Adah.
The sons of Esau's son Reuel were the leaders Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the leaders who came from Reuel in Edom. They were grandsons of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah were the leaders Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were the leaders who came from Esau's wife Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah.
These were the sons of Esau, who is Edom, and these were their leaders.
These were the sons of Seir the Horite, who were living in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These sons of Seir in Edom were the Horite leaders.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Homam. Timna was Lotan's sister.
The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam.
The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found the hot springs in the desert while he was looking after the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
The children of Anah were Dishon and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah.
The sons of Dishon were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Keran.
The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan.
The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran.
These were the Horite leaders: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These were the Horite leaders, listed by their clans in the land of Seir.
These were the kings who ruled in Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites:
Bela son of Beor became king of Edom. His city was named Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah became king after him.
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king after him.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad became king after him. Hadad was the one who defeated Midian in the country of Moab. His city was named Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king after him.
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the river became king after him.
When Shaul died, Baal-Hanan son of Akbor became king after him.
When Baal-Hanan son of Akbor died, Hadar became king after him. His city was named Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel. She was the daughter of Matred and the granddaughter of Me-Zahab.
These were the leaders who came from Esau, listed by their clans and their places, by name: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
Magdiel and Iram. These were the leaders of Edom, listed by where they lived in the land they owned. This is the family line of Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites.
Jacob lived in the land of Canaan, where his father had lived as a stranger.

This is the story of Jacob's family. Joseph, a young man of seventeen, was looking after the flocks with his brothers, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. Joseph brought their father bad reports about them.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than any of his other sons, because he had been born to him in his old age. So he made him a beautiful robe with long sleeves.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not say a kind word to him.
Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more.
He said to them, "Listen to this dream I had.
We were tying up bundles of grain out in the field. Suddenly my bundle stood up straight, and your bundles gathered around mine and bowed down to it."
His brothers said to him, "Do you really think you will be king over us? Will you really rule over us?" And they hated him all the more because of his dream and what he had said.
Then he had another dream, and he told it to his brothers. "Listen," he said, "I had another dream, and this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."

When he told his father as well as his brothers, his father scolded him and said, "What is this dream you had? Will your mother and I and your brothers really come and bow down to the ground in front of you?"
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept thinking about what Joseph had said.
Some time later his brothers went to look after their father's flocks near Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, "As you know, your brothers are looking after the flocks near Shechem. Come, I am going to send you to them." "Very well," Joseph replied.
So he said to him, "Go and see if all is well with your brothers and with the flocks, and come back and tell me." Then he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. When Joseph arrived at Shechem,
a man found him wandering around in the fields. The man asked him, "What are you looking for?"
He replied, "I am looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are looking after their flocks?"
"They have moved on from here," the man answered. "I heard them say, 'Let's go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them near Dothan.
They saw him in the distance, and before he reached them, they made a plan to kill him.
"Here comes that dreamer!" they said to each other.
"Come now, let's kill him and throw him into one of these dry wells. We can say that a wild animal ate him. Then we will see what becomes of his dreams."
When Reuben heard this, he tried to save Joseph from them. "Let's not take his life," he said.
"Do not kill him," Reuben said. "Throw him into this well here in the desert, but do not lay a hand on him." Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from them and take him back to his father.
So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the beautiful robe he was wearing.
Then they took him and threw him into the well. The well was empty. There was no water in it.

As they sat down to eat their meal, they looked up and saw a group of Ishmaelite traders coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, healing balm and myrrh, and they were on their way to take them down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, "What will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his death?
Come, let's sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay our hands on him. After all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood." His brothers agreed.
So when the Midianite traders came by, the brothers pulled Joseph up out of the well and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. And the traders took Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben came back to the well and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes in grief.
He went back to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone! What am I going to do now?"
Then they took Joseph's robe, killed a goat and dipped the robe in its blood.
They took the beautiful robe back to their father and said, "We found this. Look at it carefully and see if it is your son's robe."
He recognised it and said, "It is my son's robe! A wild animal has eaten him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces."
Then Jacob tore his clothes, put on rough cloth to show his sorrow, and mourned for his son for a long time.
All his sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. "No," he said, "I will go down to the grave mourning for my son." And his father wept for him.
Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, the captain of the guard.
At that time Judah left his brothers and went down to stay with a man from Adullam named Hirah.
There Judah met the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He married her and slept with her.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, who was named Er.
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a son, and she named him Onan.
She gave birth to yet another son and named him Shelah. He was born at Kezib.
Judah chose a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Judah's firstborn, Er, was wicked in the LORD's eyes, so the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Sleep with your brother's wife and do your duty as her brother-in-law. Give your brother children who will carry on his name."

But Onan knew that the children would not be counted as his. So whenever he slept with his brother's wife, he made sure she could not become pregnant, so that he would not give children to his brother.
What he did was wicked in the LORD's eyes, so the LORD put him to death too.

Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up." He thought, "He might die too, just like his brothers." So Tamar went to live in her father's house.

After a long time Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up to Timnah, to the men who were cutting the wool from his sheep. His friend Hirah the Adullamite went with him.
Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is on his way to Timnah to cut the wool from his sheep."

So she took off her widow's clothes and covered herself with a veil to hide who she was. Then she sat down at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. She did this because she saw that Shelah had grown up, but she had not been given to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
Not realising that she was his daughter-in-law, he went over to her by the roadside and said, "Come, let me sleep with you." "What will you give me to sleep with you?" she asked.
"I will send you a young goat from my flock," he said. "Will you give me something as a pledge until you send it?" she asked.
He said, "What pledge should I give you?" "Your seal and its cord, and the walking stick in your hand," she answered. So he gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
After she left, she took off her veil and put on her widow's clothes again.
Meanwhile, Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to get back his pledge from the woman, but he could not find her.
He asked the men who lived there, "Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?" "There has never been any shrine prostitute here," they said.
So he went back to Judah and said, "I did not find her. Besides, the men who live there said, 'There has never been any shrine prostitute here.'"
Then Judah said, "Let her keep what she has, or we will become a laughing stock. After all, I did send her this young goat, but you could not find her."
About three months later Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar has acted like a prostitute, and as a result she is now pregnant." Judah said, "Bring her out and have her burned to death!"

As she was being brought out, she sent a message to her father-in-law. "I am pregnant by the man who owns these," she said. And she added, "See if you recognise whose seal and cord and walking stick these are."
Judah recognised them and said, "She is more in the right than I am, because I would not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not sleep with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twin boys in her womb.
As she was giving birth, one of them put out his hand. So the woman helping her took a red thread and tied it on his wrist and said, "This one came out first."
But when he pulled his hand back, his brother came out. She said, "So this is how you have broken out!" And he was named Perez, which means "breaking out".
Then his brother, who had the red thread on his wrist, came out. And he was named Zerah, which means "bright red".
Now Joseph had been taken down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian who was one of Pharaoh's officials and the captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and everything went well for him. He lived in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD made everything he did succeed.
Joseph pleased his master and became his personal servant. Potiphar put him in charge of his household, and he trusted him with everything he owned.

From the time Potiphar put him in charge of his household and of everything he owned, the LORD blessed the household of the Egyptian because of Joseph. The LORD's blessing was on everything Potiphar had, both in the house and in the fields.
So Potiphar left everything he had in Joseph's care. With Joseph in charge, he did not worry about anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was strong and handsome.
After a while, his master's wife noticed Joseph and said, "Come to bed with me!"
But he refused. He said to her, "With me in charge, my master does not worry about anything in the house. He has trusted me with everything he owns.
No one in this house is greater than I am. My master has kept nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a wicked thing and sin against God?"
She kept on asking Joseph day after day, but he refused to go to bed with her or even be with her.
One day he went into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants were inside.
She grabbed him by his cloak and said, "Come to bed with me!" But he left his cloak in her hand and ran out of the house.
When she saw that he had left his cloak in her hand and had run out of the house,
she called her household servants. "Look," she said to them, "this Hebrew has been brought here to make fools of us! He came in here to sleep with me, but I screamed.
When he heard me scream for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house."
She kept his cloak beside her until his master came home.
Then she told him the same story: "That Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make a fool of me.
But as soon as I screamed for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house."
When his master heard the story his wife told him, saying, "This is how your slave treated me", he became furious.
Joseph's master took him and put him in prison, the place where the king's prisoners were kept. So Joseph stayed there in prison.
But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him kindness. He made the prison warden like him.
So the warden put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners in the prison, and Joseph was responsible for everything that was done there.
The warden did not need to check on anything that Joseph was in charge of, because the LORD was with Joseph and made everything he did succeed.
Some time later, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt did something wrong against their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officials, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the same prison where Joseph was being kept.
The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and he looked after them. They stayed in custody for some time.
One night the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were being held in prison, both had dreams. Each dream was different, and each had its own meaning.
When Joseph came to them the next morning, he saw that they were upset.
So he asked Pharaoh's officials who were in custody with him in his master's house, "Why do you look so sad today?"
"We both had dreams," they answered, "but there is no one to tell us what they mean." Then Joseph said to them, "Is it not God who explains dreams? Please tell me your dreams."
So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream. He said to him, "In my dream I saw a vine in front of me.
On the vine were three branches. As soon as it budded, it blossomed, and its bunches of grapes became ripe.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, squeezed them into Pharaoh's cup and put the cup in his hand."
Joseph said to him, "This is what it means. The three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you back your job. You will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, just as you used to do when you were his cupbearer.
But when everything is going well for you, remember me and show me kindness. Mention me to Pharaoh and get me out of this prison.
I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing to deserve being put in this dungeon."
When the chief baker saw that Joseph had given a good meaning, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream. On my head there were three baskets of bread.
In the top basket were all kinds of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head."
Joseph said, "This is what it means. The three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang your body on a pole. And the birds will eat your flesh."
Three days later it was Pharaoh's birthday, and he gave a feast for all his officials. In front of them all, he lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He gave the chief cupbearer back his job, so that he once again put the cup into Pharaoh's hand.
But he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had said in explaining their dreams.
But the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph. He forgot all about him.
Two whole years later, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing beside the River Nile,
when out of the river came seven cows, healthy and fat, and they ate the grass among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up out of the Nile, ugly and thin. They stood beside the other cows on the bank of the river.
Then the ugly, thin cows ate up the seven healthy, fat cows. And Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep again and had a second dream. Seven heads of grain, full and good, were growing on one stalk.
After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted. They were thin and dried up by the hot east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven full, healthy heads. Then Pharaoh woke up, and he realised it had been a dream.
In the morning he was worried, so he sent for all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could tell him what they meant.
Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "Today I am reminded of my failures.
Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard.
One night each of us had a dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
A young Hebrew man was there with us. He was a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he explained them to us. He told each of us what our dream meant.
And things turned out exactly as he said they would. I was given back my job, and the baker was hanged."
So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and he was quickly brought out of the dungeon. When he had shaved and changed his clothes, he came to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I had a dream, and no one can tell me what it means. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can explain it."
"I cannot do it," Joseph replied to Pharaoh, "but God will give Pharaoh the answer he needs."
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile,
when out of the river came seven cows, fat and healthy, and they ate the grass among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up. They were weak, very ugly and thin. I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt.
The thin, ugly cows ate up the seven fat cows that came up first.
But even after they had eaten them, no one could tell that they had done so. They still looked just as ugly as before. Then I woke up.
In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, full and good, growing on one stalk.
After them, seven other heads sprouted, withered and thin and dried up by the east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads. I told this to the magicians, but none of them could explain it to me."
Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The two dreams of Pharaoh mean the same thing. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. It is one and the same dream.
The seven thin, ugly cows that came up afterwards are seven years, and so are the seven worthless heads of grain dried up by the east wind. They are seven years of famine.
It is just as I said to Pharaoh. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Seven years of great plenty are coming throughout the land of Egypt.
But after them, seven years of famine will follow. Then all the plenty in Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will ruin the land.
The good years will not be remembered, because the famine that follows will be so terrible.
The dream was given to Pharaoh in two forms because God has firmly decided this, and God will do it soon.
So now Pharaoh should look for a wise man with good understanding and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh should appoint officials over the land to collect a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of plenty.
They should collect all the food of these good years that are coming and store up the grain under the authority of Pharaoh. It should be kept in the cities for food.
This food will be held in reserve for the country, to be used during the seven years of famine that will come on Egypt. Then the country will not be ruined by the famine."
The plan seemed good to Pharaoh and to all his officials.
So Pharaoh asked them, "Can we find anyone like this man, who has the Spirit of God in him?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is no one as wise and understanding as you.
You will be in charge of my palace, and all my people will obey your orders. Only I, because I sit on the throne, will be greater than you."
So Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I now put you in charge of the whole land of Egypt."
Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his finger and put it on Joseph's finger. He dressed him in robes of fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in a chariot as his second-in-command, and people shouted in front of him, "Make way!" So Pharaoh put him in charge of the whole land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but without your permission no one will lift a hand or foot in all Egypt."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-Paneah. He also gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph travelled throughout the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he began serving Pharaoh king of Egypt. He went out from Pharaoh's presence and travelled all over Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty, the land produced huge harvests.
Joseph collected all the food produced in Egypt during those seven years and stored it in the cities. In each city he stored the food grown in the fields around it.
Joseph stored up huge amounts of grain, like the sand of the sea. There was so much that he stopped keeping records, because it was more than could be measured.
Before the years of famine came, Joseph had two sons by Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh, which sounds like "forget", because he said, "God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's family."
He named the second son Ephraim, which sounds like "fruitful", because he said, "God has made me fruitful in the land where I have suffered."
The seven years of plenty in Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the other lands, but in the whole land of Egypt there was food.
When all Egypt began to feel the famine, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. Then Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph and do what he tells you."
When the famine had spread over the whole country, Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, because the famine was terrible throughout Egypt.
And people from all over the world came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was terrible everywhere.
When Jacob learned that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you just keep looking at each other?"
He went on, "I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we can stay alive and not die."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Joseph's brother Benjamin with the others, because he was afraid that something bad might happen to him.
So the sons of Israel were among the many people who went to buy grain, because the famine had reached the land of Canaan too.
Now Joseph was the governor of the land, the one who sold grain to all its people. So when Joseph's brothers arrived, they bowed down to him with their faces to the ground.

As soon as Joseph saw his brothers, he recognised them. But he pretended to be a stranger and spoke harshly to them. "Where do you come from?" he asked. "From the land of Canaan," they replied, "to buy food."
Although Joseph recognised his brothers, they did not recognise him.
Then Joseph remembered his dreams about them, and he said to them, "You are spies! You have come to see where our land is weak."
"No, sir," they answered. "Your servants have come to buy food.
We are all the sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants are not spies."
"No!" he said to them. "You have come to see where our land is weak."
But they replied, "Your servants were twelve brothers, the sons of one man who lives in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no longer alive."
Joseph said to them, "It is just as I told you. You are spies!
And this is how you will be tested. As surely as Pharaoh lives, you will not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.

Send one of you to get your brother. The rest of you will be kept in prison, so that your words can be tested to see if you are telling the truth. If you are not, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!"
And he put them all in prison for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, because I respect God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers stay here in prison, while the rest of you go and take grain back for your starving families.
But you must bring your youngest brother to me. Then your words will be proved true, and you will not die." So they agreed to do this.

They said to each other, "We are surely being punished because of our brother. We saw how upset he was when he begged us to spare him, but we would not listen. That is why this trouble has come on us."
Reuben answered them, "Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen! Now we must pay for his blood."
They did not know that Joseph could understand them, because he was using an interpreter.
He turned away from them and began to weep. Then he came back and spoke to them again. He had Simeon taken from them and tied up in front of their eyes.
Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to put each man's silver back in his sack, and to give them supplies for their journey. After this was done for them,
they loaded their grain on their donkeys and left.
At the place where they stopped for the night, one of them opened his sack to get food for his donkey, and he saw his silver in the top of his sack.

"My silver has been given back," he said to his brothers. "Here it is in my sack!" Their hearts sank, and they turned to each other, shaking with fear. They said, "What is this that God has done to us?"
When they came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they told him everything that had happened to them. They said,
"The man who is lord over the land spoke harshly to us and treated us as though we were spying on the country.
But we said to him, 'We are honest men. We are not spies.
We were twelve brothers, sons of one father. One is no longer alive, and the youngest is now with our father in Canaan.'
Then the man who is lord over the land said to us, 'This is how I will know whether you are honest men: leave one of your brothers here with me, and take food for your starving families and go.
But bring your youngest brother to me, so that I will know that you are not spies but honest men. Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.'"
As they were emptying their sacks, there in each man's sack was his bag of silver! When they and their father saw the bags of silver, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You have taken my children from me. Joseph is gone, and Simeon is gone, and now you want to take Benjamin. Everything is against me!"
Then Reuben said to his father, "You may put both of my sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my care, and I will bring him back."

But Jacob said, "My son will not go down there with you. His brother is dead, and he is the only one left. If anything happens to him on the journey you are taking, you will send me, a grey-haired old man, to the grave in sorrow."
The famine was still terrible in the land.
When they had eaten all the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go back and buy us a little more food."
But Judah said to him, "The man strongly warned us, 'You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you.'
If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down, because the man said to us, 'You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel asked, "Why did you bring this trouble on me by telling the man you had another brother?"

They replied, "The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family. He asked us, 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' We simply answered his questions. How could we possibly know he would say, 'Bring your brother down here'?"
Then Judah said to his father Israel, "Send the boy with me, and we will go at once, so that we and you and our children can live and not die.

I myself promise to keep him safe. You can hold me personally responsible for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him here in front of you, I will bear the blame in front of you for the rest of my life.
If we had not wasted so much time, we could have gone and come back twice by now."

Then their father Israel said to them, "If it must be, then do this. Put some of the best things from our land in your bags and take them down to the man as a gift: a little healing balm and a little honey, some spices and myrrh, some pistachio nuts and almonds.
Take twice the amount of silver with you, because you must give back the silver that was put back in the tops of your sacks. Perhaps it was a mistake.
Take your brother too, and go back to the man at once.
And may God Almighty make the man kind to you, so that he will let your other brother and Benjamin come back with you. As for me, if I lose my children, then I lose them."
So the men took the gifts and twice the amount of silver, and Benjamin too. They hurried down to Egypt and stood in front of Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the man in charge of his house, "Take these men to my house. Kill an animal and prepare a meal, because they are going to eat with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph told him and took the men to Joseph's house.

Now the men were frightened when they were taken to his house. They thought, "We were brought here because of the silver that was put back in our sacks the first time. He wants to attack us and overpower us, and take us as slaves and take our donkeys."
So they went up to the man in charge of Joseph's house and spoke to him at the entrance to the house.
"Please, sir," they said, "we came down here the first time to buy food.
But at the place where we stopped for the night, we opened our sacks, and each of us found his silver, the exact amount, in the top of his sack. So we have brought it back with us.
We have also brought more silver with us to buy food. We do not know who put our silver in our sacks."
