"It is all right," he said. "Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, must have put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your silver." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The man took the men into Joseph's house. He gave them water to wash their feet and food for their donkeys.
They got their gifts ready for Joseph's arrival at noon, because they had heard that they were going to eat there.
When Joseph came home, they brought him the gifts they had carried into the house, and they bowed down to the ground in front of him.
He asked them how they were, and then he said, "How is your old father you told me about? Is he still alive?"
They replied, "Your servant our father is still alive and well." And they bowed down low to show him honour.
As Joseph looked around and saw his brother Benjamin, his own mother's son, he asked, "Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about?" And he said, "May God be kind to you, my son."
Joseph was so deeply moved at the sight of his brother that he hurried out, looking for a place to weep. He went into his private room and wept there.
After he had washed his face, he came out. Controlling himself, he said, "Serve the food."
They served him by himself, the brothers by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves. Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews, because they thought that was disgraceful.
The brothers had been seated in front of him in the order of their ages, from the firstborn to the youngest, and they looked at each other in amazement.
Portions of food were taken to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as anyone else's. So they feasted and drank freely with him.
Then Joseph gave these orders to the man in charge of his house: "Fill the men's sacks with as much food as they can carry, and put each man's silver in the top of his sack.
Then put my cup, the silver one, in the top of the youngest one's sack, along with the silver for his grain." And he did as Joseph said.
As soon as it was light the next morning, the men were sent on their way with their donkeys.
They had not gone far from the city when Joseph said to the man in charge of his house, "Go after those men at once. When you catch up with them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid good with evil?
Is this not the cup my master drinks from and also uses to find out hidden things? You have done a wicked thing.'"
When he caught up with them, he repeated these words to them.
But they said to him, "Why does my master say such things? Your servants would never do anything like that!
We even brought back to you from the land of Canaan the silver we found in the tops of our sacks. So why would we steal silver or gold from your master's house?
If any of your servants is found to have it, he will die, and the rest of us will become my master's slaves."
"Very well, then," he said, "let it be as you say. Whoever is found to have it will become my slave, but the rest of you will be free from blame."
Each of them quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it.
Then the man searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
At this, they tore their clothes in grief. Then they all loaded their donkeys and went back to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, and he was still there. They threw themselves to the ground in front of him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this you have done? Did you not know that a man like me can find out hidden things?"

"What can we say to my master?" Judah replied. "What can we say? How can we prove we are innocent? God has uncovered your servants' guilt. We are now my master's slaves, we ourselves and the one who was found to have the cup."
But Joseph said, "I would never do such a thing! Only the man who was found to have the cup will become my slave. The rest of you, go back to your father in peace."
Then Judah went up to him and said, "Please, my master, let your servant speak a word to you. Do not be angry with your servant, even though you are as powerful as Pharaoh himself.
My master asked his servants, 'Do you have a father or a brother?'
And we answered, 'We have an old father, and there is a young son born to him in his old age. His brother is dead, and he is the only one of his mother's sons left, and his father loves him.'
Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me so that I can see him for myself.'
And we said to my master, 'The boy cannot leave his father. If he leaves him, his father will die.'
But you told your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you will not see my face again.'
When we went back to your servant my father, we told him what my master had said.
Then our father said, 'Go back and buy a little more food.'
But we said, 'We cannot go down. We will go only if our youngest brother is with us. We cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'
Your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife Rachel gave me two sons.
One of them went away from me, and I said, "He has surely been torn to pieces." And I have not seen him since.
If you take this one from me too and something bad happens to him, you will send me, a grey-haired old man, to the grave in misery.'
So now, if I go back to your servant my father and the boy is not with us, and since my father's life is so closely bound up with the boy's life,
when he sees that the boy is not there, he will die. Your servants will send our father, your grey-haired servant, to the grave in sorrow.
Your servant promised my father to keep the boy safe. I said, 'If I do not bring him back to you, I will bear the blame in front of you, my father, for the rest of my life.'
So now, please let your servant stay here as my master's slave instead of the boy, and let the boy go back with his brothers.
How can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I could not bear to see the misery that would come on my father."
Then Joseph could no longer control his feelings in front of all his servants, and he cried out, "Make everyone leave me!" So there was no one with Joseph when he told his brothers who he was.
He wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and even Pharaoh's household heard about it.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, because they were terrified at being in front of him.
Then Joseph said to his brothers, "Come close to me." When they had done so, he said, "I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into Egypt.
But now, do not be upset, and do not be angry with yourselves for selling me here, because it was to save lives that God sent me ahead of you.
For two years now there has been famine in the land, and for the next five years there will be no ploughing and no harvesting.
But God sent me ahead of you to keep your family alive on the earth and to save your lives in a great rescue.
So then, it was not you who sent me here, but God. He made me an adviser to Pharaoh, lord of his whole household and ruler of all Egypt.
Now hurry back to my father and say to him, 'This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me, and do not delay.
You will live in the region of Goshen and be near me, you, your children and grandchildren, your flocks and herds, and everything you have.
I will provide for you there, because five years of famine are still to come. Otherwise you and your household and all who belong to you will become poor.'
You can see for yourselves, and so can my brother Benjamin, that it is really I who am speaking to you.
Tell my father about all the honour I have been given in Egypt and about everything you have seen. And bring my father down here quickly."
Then he threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin hugged him, weeping.
And he kissed all his brothers and wept over them. After that his brothers talked with him.
When the news reached Pharaoh's palace that Joseph's brothers had come, Pharaoh and all his officials were pleased.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Tell your brothers, 'Do this: load your animals and go back to the land of Canaan.
Bring your father and your families back to me. I will give you the best land in Egypt, and you can enjoy the best food the land produces.'
You are also told to say to them, 'Do this: take some carts from Egypt for your children and your wives, and get your father and come.
Do not worry about your belongings, because the best of all Egypt will be yours.'"
So the sons of Israel did this. Joseph gave them carts, as Pharaoh had commanded, and he also gave them supplies for their journey.
He gave each of them a new set of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five sets of clothes.
And this is what he sent to his father: ten donkeys loaded with the best things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and other food for the journey.
Then he sent his brothers away, and as they were leaving, he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the way!"
So they went up out of Egypt and came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan.
They told him, "Joseph is still alive! In fact, he is ruler of all Egypt." Jacob was stunned. He did not believe them.
But when they told him everything Joseph had said to them, and when he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him back, the spirit of their father Jacob came back to life.
And Israel said, "I believe it now! My son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
So Israel set out with everything he had. When he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
God spoke to Israel in a vision at night and said, "Jacob! Jacob!" "Here I am," he replied.
"I am God, the God of your father," he said. "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, because I will make you into a great nation there.
I will go down to Egypt with you, and I will surely bring you back again. And Joseph's own hand will close your eyes when you die."
Then Jacob left Beersheba. The sons of Israel took their father Jacob, their children and their wives in the carts that Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They also took their livestock and the goods they had gained in Canaan. So Jacob and all his descendants went to Egypt.
He took with him to Egypt his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters. He took all his descendants with him.
These are the names of the sons of Israel, Jacob and his descendants, who went to Egypt: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn.
The sons of Reuben were Hanok, Pallu, Hezron and Karmi.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi were Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
The sons of Judah were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez and Zerah. But Er and Onan had died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar were Tola, Puah, Jashub and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun were Sered, Elon and Jahleel.
These were the sons Leah gave Jacob in Paddan Aram, besides his daughter Dinah. His sons and daughters by Leah numbered thirty-three in all.
The sons of Gad were Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli.
The sons of Asher were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah. Their sister was Serah. The sons of Beriah were Heber and Malkiel.
These were the children Jacob had by Zilpah, the slave woman Laban had given to his daughter Leah. They numbered sixteen in all.
The sons of Jacob's wife Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
In Egypt, Joseph had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Their mother was Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
The sons of Benjamin were Bela, Beker, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim and Ard.
These were the sons of Rachel who were born to Jacob. They numbered fourteen in all.
The son of Dan was Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali were Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem.
These were the sons Jacob had by Bilhah, the slave woman Laban had given to his daughter Rachel. They numbered seven in all.
All those who went to Egypt with Jacob, who were his own descendants, not counting his sons' wives, numbered sixty-six people.
With the two sons who had been born to Joseph in Egypt, the members of Jacob's family who went to Egypt numbered seventy in all.
Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When they arrived in the region of Goshen,
Joseph had his chariot made ready and went to Goshen to meet his father Israel. As soon as Joseph appeared in front of him, he threw his arms around his father and wept for a long time.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I am ready to die, since I have seen for myself that you are still alive."

Then Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and speak to Pharaoh. I will tell him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were living in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
The men are shepherds. They look after livestock, and they have brought along their flocks and herds and everything they own.'
When Pharaoh calls you in and asks, 'What is your work?'

you should answer, 'Your servants have looked after livestock ever since we were boys, just as our ancestors did.' Then you will be allowed to settle in the region of Goshen, because the Egyptians look down on all shepherds."
Joseph went and told Pharaoh, "My father and brothers have come from the land of Canaan, with their flocks and herds and everything they own. They are now in Goshen."
He chose five of his brothers and presented them to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked the brothers, "What is your work?" "Your servants are shepherds," they replied to Pharaoh, "just as our ancestors were."

They also said to him, "We have come to live here for a while, because the famine is terrible in Canaan and there is no grass for your servants' flocks. So now, please let your servants settle in Goshen."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you,

and the land of Egypt is open to you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best part of the land. Let them live in Goshen. And if you know of any among them who are especially skilled, put them in charge of my own livestock."
Then Joseph brought his father Jacob in and presented him to Pharaoh. And Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked him, "How old are you?"
Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The years of my travels are a hundred and thirty. My years have been few and hard, and they do not equal the years of the travels of my ancestors."
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and left his presence.
So Joseph settled his father and his brothers in Egypt and gave them property in the best part of the land, the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had ordered.
Joseph also provided his father and his brothers and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their children.
But there was no food anywhere in the land, because the famine was so terrible. The people of Egypt and Canaan were weak with hunger because of the famine.
Joseph collected all the money that could be found in Egypt and Canaan in payment for the grain they were buying, and he brought it to Pharaoh's palace.
When the money of the people of Egypt and Canaan was all gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die in front of your eyes? Our money is all used up."
"Then bring your livestock," Joseph said. "I will sell you food in exchange for your livestock, since your money is all gone."

So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and he gave them food in exchange for their horses, their sheep and goats, their cattle and their donkeys. And he brought them through that year with food in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year was over, they came to him the following year and said, "We cannot hide from our master the fact that our money is gone, and our livestock now belongs to you. There is nothing left for our master except our bodies and our land.

Why should we die in front of your eyes, we and our land as well? Buy us and our land in exchange for food, and we with our land will be slaves to Pharaoh. Give us seed so that we can live and not die, and so that the land does not become a desert."
So Joseph bought all the land in Egypt for Pharaoh. The Egyptians, one and all, sold their fields, because the famine was too much for them. The land became Pharaoh's,
and Joseph made the people slaves from one end of Egypt to the other.
But he did not buy the land of the priests, because they received a regular share of food from Pharaoh and had enough to live on from what Pharaoh gave them. That is why they did not sell their land.
Joseph said to the people, "Now that I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh, here is seed for you so that you can plant the ground.
But when the crops come in, give a fifth of them to Pharaoh. The other four-fifths you may keep as seed for the fields and as food for yourselves, your households and your children."
"You have saved our lives," they said. "Please be kind to us, our master, and we will be Pharaoh's slaves."
So Joseph made it a law about land in Egypt, still in force today, that a fifth of the harvest belongs to Pharaoh. Only the land of the priests did not become Pharaoh's.
The Israelites settled in Egypt in the region of Goshen. They gained property there and had many children and grew greatly in number.
Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen years, and he lived a hundred and forty-seven years in all.

When the time came near for Israel to die, he called for his son Joseph and said to him, "If you love me, put your hand under my thigh and promise that you will show me kindness and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt.
When I rest with my ancestors, carry me out of Egypt and bury me where they are buried." "I will do as you say," Joseph said.
"Promise me," Jacob said. Then Joseph promised him, and Israel bowed down in worship as he leaned on the top of his staff.
Some time later Joseph was told, "Your father is ill." So he took his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him.
When Jacob was told, "Your son Joseph has come to you", Israel gathered his strength and sat up on the bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there he blessed me.

He said to me, 'I am going to give you many children and increase your numbers. I will make you a community of peoples, and I will give this land to your descendants after you, to be theirs for ever.'
Now then, your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here will be counted as my own. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.
Any children born to you after them will be yours. In the land they inherit, they will be counted under the names of their brothers.

As I was coming back from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan while we were still on the way, a short distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem."
When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he asked, "Who are these?"
"They are the sons God has given me here," Joseph said to his father. Then Israel said, "Bring them to me so that I can bless them."
Now Israel's eyes were weak with old age, and he could hardly see. So Joseph brought his sons close to him, and his father kissed them and hugged them.
Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face again, and now God has even let me see your children."
Then Joseph took them from Israel's knees and bowed down with his face to the ground.
Joseph took them both, Ephraim on his right towards Israel's left hand, and Manasseh on his left towards Israel's right hand, and brought them close to him.

But Israel reached out his right hand and put it on Ephraim's head, though he was the younger, and he crossed his arms and put his left hand on Manasseh's head, even though Manasseh was the firstborn.
Then he blessed Joseph and said, "May the God whom my grandfather Abraham and my father Isaac served, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,

the angel who has rescued me from all harm, may he bless these boys. May they be called by my name and by the names of my grandfather Abraham and my father Isaac. And may they grow into a great many people on the earth."
When Joseph saw his father putting his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was not pleased. So he took hold of his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.
Joseph said to him, "No, my father, this one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."

But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will become great. But his younger brother will be greater than he is, and his descendants will become a whole group of nations."

He blessed them that day and said, "The people of Israel will use your names when they give a blessing. They will say, 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" So he put Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "I am about to die, but God will be with you and will take you back to the land of your ancestors.
And to you I give one more portion of land than to your brothers, the ridge of land I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow."
Then Jacob called for his sons and said, "Gather around, so that I can tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.
Gather together and listen, sons of Jacob. Listen to your father Israel.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength, the first sign of my power. You were first in honour and first in power.
But you are as wild as rushing water, and you will no longer be first, because you went up onto your father's bed. You disgraced my bed when you lay on it.
Simeon and Levi are brothers. Their swords are weapons of violence.
Let me not join in their secret plans. Let me not be part of their group, because in their anger they killed men, and they crippled oxen just as they pleased.
May their anger be cursed, because it is so fierce, and their fury, because it is so cruel! I will scatter them among the people of Jacob and spread them out among the people of Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies, and your father's sons will bow down to you.
You are a lion's cub, Judah. You come back from the hunt, my son. Like a lion he crouches and lies down. Like a lioness, who dares to wake him?
The royal sceptre will not leave Judah, nor the ruler's staff his descendants, until the one comes to whom it belongs. The nations will obey him.
He will tie his donkey to a vine, his young donkey to the best branch. He will wash his clothes in wine, his robes in the juice of grapes.
His eyes will be darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.
Zebulun will live by the seashore and become a harbour for ships. His border will reach as far as Sidon.
Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between two loads.
When he sees how good his resting place is and how pleasant his land is, he will bend his shoulder to carry the load and will be forced to work as a slave.
Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a snake by the road, a poisonous snake along the path, that bites the horse's heels so that its rider falls backwards.
I look to you to save me, LORD.
Gad will be attacked by a band of raiders, but he will attack them as they run away.
Asher's food will be rich. He will provide food fit for a king.
Naphtali is a deer running free that has beautiful young.
Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine near a spring, whose branches climb over a wall.
Archers attacked him fiercely. They shot at him and hated him.
But his bow stayed steady, and his strong arms stayed firm, because of the power of the Mighty One of Jacob, because of the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,

because of your father's God, who helps you, because of the Almighty, who blesses you. He blesses you with blessings from the sky above, blessings from the deep waters below, and blessings of many children and many animals.

Your father's blessings are greater than the blessings of the ancient mountains, greater than the riches of the age-old hills. May all these blessings rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the one who was set apart from his brothers.
Benjamin is a hungry wolf. In the morning he eats what he has caught, and in the evening he divides what he has taken."
These are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them when he blessed them. He gave each one the blessing that was right for him.
Then he gave them these instructions: "I am about to join my people who have died. Bury me with my ancestors in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre in Canaan. Abraham bought it, together with the field, from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
That is where Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried. Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried there, and there I buried Leah.
The field and the cave in it were bought from the Hittites."
When Jacob had finished giving instructions to his sons, he drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and joined his people who had died.
Joseph threw himself on his father's body. He wept over him and kissed him.
Then Joseph ordered the doctors who served him to prepare his father's body for burial. So the doctors embalmed Israel.
It took a full forty days, because that is how long it takes to embalm a body. And the Egyptians mourned for him for seventy days.
When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph said to Pharaoh's court, "If you are pleased with me, please speak to Pharaoh for me. Tell him,
'My father made me promise and said, "I am about to die. Bury me in the tomb I dug for myself in the land of Canaan." Now please let me go up and bury my father. Then I will come back.'"
Pharaoh said, "Go up and bury your father, as he made you promise."
So Joseph went up to bury his father. All Pharaoh's officials went with him: the leaders of his court and all the leaders of Egypt,
as well as all the members of Joseph's household, his brothers, and those belonging to his father's household. Only their children and their flocks and herds were left in Goshen.
Chariots and horsemen also went up with him. It was a very large group.
When they reached the threshing floor of Atad, near the Jordan, they cried loudly and bitterly. There Joseph held a time of mourning for his father for seven days.

When the Canaanites who lived there saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "The Egyptians are holding a time of deep mourning." That is why the place near the Jordan is called Abel Mizraim, which means "mourning of the Egyptians".
So Jacob's sons did for him what he had commanded them.
They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre. Abraham had bought it, together with the field, from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
After burying his father, Joseph went back to Egypt, together with his brothers and all the others who had gone with him to bury his father.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?"
So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, "Before your father died, he left these instructions:

'This is what you must say to Joseph: Please forgive your brothers for the wrong they did and for the sins they committed in treating you so badly.' So now, please forgive the sins of the servants of the God of your father." When their message came to him, Joseph wept.
Then his brothers came and threw themselves down in front of him. "We are your slaves," they said.
But Joseph said to them, "Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?
You planned to harm me, but God planned it for good. He did it to save many lives, as is happening now.
So then, do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your children." And he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph stayed in Egypt, along with all his father's family. He lived a hundred and ten years.
He lived to see the third generation of Ephraim's children. The children of Makir son of Manasseh were also placed on Joseph's knees when they were born.
Then Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die. But God will surely come to help you and take you up out of this land to the land he promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob."
And Joseph made the Israelites make a solemn promise. He said, "God will surely come to help you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place."
So Joseph died at the age of a hundred and ten. They embalmed his body and put it in a coffin in Egypt.
Exod: These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each one with his family:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
Jacob's family who came from him numbered seventy people in all. Joseph was already in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and so did all his brothers and all the people of that time.
But the people of Israel had many children. Their numbers grew and grew, and they became very strong. The land was filled with them.
Then a new king came to power in Egypt, who did not know about Joseph.
He said to his people, "Look, the people of Israel are more in number and stronger than we are.
Come, we must deal with them wisely, or they will grow even more. If war breaks out, they could join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the land."
So the Egyptians put slave masters over them to make their lives hard with heavy work. They built the store cities of Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh.
But the more the Egyptians made them suffer, the more they grew in number and spread out. So the Egyptians came to fear the people of Israel.
The Egyptians forced the people of Israel to work without mercy.
They made their lives bitter with hard work, making mortar and bricks, and doing all kinds of work in the fields. In all their work, the Egyptians showed them no mercy.
Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, the women who helped mothers give birth. One was named Shiphrah and the other Puah.
He said, "When you help the Hebrew women give birth and see them on the birthing stool, if the baby is a boy, kill him. But if it is a girl, let her live."
But the midwives feared God. They did not do what the king of Egypt told them. They let the baby boys live.
So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and asked them, "Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?"
The midwives answered Pharaoh, "The Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong, and they give birth before the midwife gets there."
So God was good to the midwives, and the people kept growing in number and became very strong.
And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: "Every Hebrew boy that is born, you must throw into the River Nile. But let every girl live."
Now a man from the tribe of Levi married a woman who was also from the tribe of Levi.
She became pregnant and had a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful baby, she hid him for three months.

When she could not hide him any longer, she got a basket made of reeds for him and covered it with tar so that water could not get in. She put the baby in it and set it among the tall grass at the edge of the river.
His sister stood some distance away to see what would happen to him.
Then Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river to wash, while her servant girls walked along the river bank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant to get it.
She opened it and saw the baby. He was crying, and she felt sorry for him. "This is one of the Hebrew babies," she said.
Then his sister asked Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and find one of the Hebrew women to feed the baby for you?"
"Yes, go," Pharaoh's daughter answered. So the girl went and got the baby's own mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this baby and feed him for me, and I will pay you." So the woman took the baby and fed him.
When the child grew older, she took him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, because she said, "I pulled him out of the water."
Years later, when Moses had grown up, he went out to visit his own people, the Hebrews, and saw how hard they had to work. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people.
Moses looked this way and that way, and when he saw that no one was watching, he killed the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.
The next day he went out and saw two Hebrew men fighting. He asked the one who was in the wrong, "Why are you hitting your fellow Hebrew?"
The man answered, "Who made you our ruler and judge? Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid. He thought, "People must know what I did."
When Pharaoh heard about it, he tried to kill Moses. But Moses ran away from Pharaoh and went to live in the land of Midian. There he sat down beside a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and fill the drinking troughs for their father's flock.
Some shepherds came and chased them away. But Moses stood up to help them, and he watered their flock.
When the girls went home to their father Reuel, he asked them, "Why are you back so early today?"
They answered, "An Egyptian saved us from the shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered the flock."
He asked his daughters, "Where is he? Why did you leave him there? Invite him to come and eat with us."
Moses agreed to stay with the man, who gave him his daughter Zipporah to be his wife.
She had a son, and Moses named him Gershom, because he said, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land."
After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The people of Israel groaned because they were slaves, and they cried out. Their cry for help because of their slavery went up to God.
God heard their groaning, and he remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
God looked at the people of Israel, and he understood what they were going through.
Moses was taking care of the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the desert and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in flames of fire from the middle of a bush. Moses looked and saw that the bush was on fire, but it did not burn up.
So Moses thought, "I will go over and look at this amazing sight. Why does the bush not burn up?"
When the LORD saw that Moses had come over to look, God called to him from the middle of the bush, "Moses! Moses!" And Moses said, "Here I am."
God said, "Do not come any closer. Take off your sandals, because the place where you are standing is holy ground."
Then he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.
The LORD said, "I have seen how my people in Egypt are suffering. I have heard them cry out because of their slave masters, and I know their pain.

So I have come down to save them from the Egyptians and to bring them out of that land into a good and wide land, a land flowing with milk and honey. It is the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
The cry of the people of Israel has reached me, and I have seen how cruelly the Egyptians are treating them.
So now go. I am sending you to Pharaoh, to bring my people, the people of Israel, out of Egypt."
But Moses said to God, "Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the people of Israel out of Egypt?"
God said, "I will be with you. And this will be the sign that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will all worship God on this mountain."
Moses said to God, "Suppose I go to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your ancestors has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' What should I tell them?"
God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM. This is what you must say to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"

God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever. This is the name people will remember me by for all time.

Go and gather the leaders of Israel together and tell them, 'The LORD, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, appeared to me. He said: I have been watching over you, and I have seen what has been done to you in Egypt.
And I have promised to bring you up out of your suffering in Egypt into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.'

The leaders of Israel will listen to you. Then you and the leaders must go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Please let us go on a three-day journey into the desert to offer sacrifices to the LORD our God.'
But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless a mighty hand forces him.
So I will reach out my hand and strike Egypt with all the amazing things I will do there. After that, he will let you go.
And I will make the Egyptians kind to my people, so that when you leave, you will not go empty-handed.

Every woman will ask her neighbour, and any woman living in her house, for things made of silver and gold, and for clothes. You will put them on your sons and daughters. And so you will take away the riches of the Egyptians."
Moses answered, "But what if they do not believe me or listen to me? What if they say, 'The LORD did not appear to you'?"
The LORD asked him, "What is that in your hand?" "A staff," Moses answered.
The LORD said, "Throw it on the ground." So Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake. Moses ran away from it.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Reach out your hand and take it by the tail." So Moses reached out and caught it, and it turned back into a staff in his hand.
"Do this," the LORD said, "so that they will believe that the LORD, the God of their ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
Then the LORD said, "Put your hand inside your coat." So Moses put his hand inside his coat. When he took it out, his hand had a skin disease. It was as white as snow.
"Now put your hand back inside your coat," God said. So Moses put his hand back inside his coat. When he took it out, it was healthy again, like the rest of his body.
Then the LORD said, "If they do not believe you or pay attention to the first sign, they may believe the second sign.

And if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to you, take some water from the River Nile and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the river will turn into blood on the ground."
Moses said to the LORD, "Please, Lord, I have never been good with words, not in the past, and not since you started speaking to me, your servant. I speak slowly, and my tongue is slow."
The LORD said to him, "Who gave people their mouths? Who makes them unable to speak or hear? Who makes them able to see, or makes them blind? Is it not I, the LORD?
So go now. I will help you speak, and I will teach you what to say."
But Moses said, "Please, Lord, send someone else."
Then the LORD became angry with Moses. He said, "What about your brother Aaron, the Levite? I know he can speak well. He is already on his way to meet you, and he will be glad when he sees you.
You will speak to him and tell him what to say. I will help both of you speak, and I will teach you what to do.
He will speak to the people for you. He will be like your mouth, and you will be like God to him.
And take this staff in your hand, so that you can do the signs with it."

Then Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, "Please let me go back to my own people in Egypt to see if any of them are still alive." Jethro said to Moses, "Go, and peace be with you."
The LORD had said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, because all the men who wanted to kill you are dead."
So Moses put his wife and sons on a donkey and started back to Egypt. And he took the staff of God in his hand.

The LORD said to Moses, "When you get back to Egypt, make sure you do in front of Pharaoh all the wonders I have given you the power to do. But I will make him stubborn, so that he will not let the people go.
Then say to Pharaoh, 'This is what the LORD says: Israel is my son, my firstborn son.
I told you, "Let my son go, so that he can worship me." But you refused to let him go. So now I will kill your firstborn son.'"
On the way, at a place where they stopped for the night, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him.
But Zipporah took a sharp stone, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched Moses' feet with it. Then she said, "You are a husband of blood to me."
So the LORD left him alone. At that time she said "husband of blood" because of the circumcision.
The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the desert to meet Moses." So Aaron went and met Moses at the mountain of God, and he kissed him.
Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say, and about all the signs the LORD had commanded him to do.
Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the leaders of the people of Israel.
Aaron told them everything the LORD had said to Moses. He also did the signs in front of the people,
and the people believed. When they heard that the LORD had come to help the people of Israel and had seen their suffering, they bowed down and worshipped.
After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Let my people go, so that they can hold a feast for me in the desert.'"
Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey him and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go."

Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go on a three-day journey into the desert to offer sacrifices to the LORD our God. If we do not, he may strike us with disease or with the sword."
But the king of Egypt said, "Moses and Aaron, why are you taking the people away from their work? Get back to work!"
Pharaoh said, "Look, there are now so many of your people in the land, and you are stopping them from working."
That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the slave masters and the foremen over the people.
He said, "Do not give the people straw for making bricks any more, like you did before. Let them go and gather their own straw.
But make them make the same number of bricks as before. Do not lower the number. They are lazy. That is why they are crying out, 'Let us go and offer sacrifices to our God.'
Make the work harder for them, so that they are kept busy and pay no attention to lies."
So the slave masters and the foremen went out and said to the people, "This is what Pharaoh says: 'I will not give you any more straw.
Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it. But your work will not be reduced at all.'"
So the people spread out all over Egypt to gather stubble to use for straw.
The slave masters kept pushing them, saying, "Finish your work for each day, just as you did when you had straw!"
Pharaoh's slave masters beat the Israelite foremen they had put in charge. They asked them, "Why have you not made the same number of bricks yesterday and today as you did before?"
Then the Israelite foremen went to Pharaoh and cried out, "Why are you treating your servants like this?
We are given no straw, yet we are told, 'Make bricks!' Your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people."
Pharaoh said, "You are lazy! Lazy! That is why you keep saying, 'Let us go and offer sacrifices to the LORD.'
Now get back to work! You will not be given any straw, but you must still make the full number of bricks."
The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when they were told, "You must not reduce the number of bricks you make each day."
When they left Pharaoh, they found Moses and Aaron waiting to meet them.
They said to them, "May the LORD look at what you have done and judge you! You have made Pharaoh and his officials hate us. You have put a sword in their hands to kill us!"
Moses went back to the LORD and said, "Lord, why have you brought trouble on this people? Why did you send me?
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has treated this people badly. And you have not saved your people at all!"
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Because of my mighty hand, he will let them go. Because of my mighty hand, he will drive them out of his land."
God also said to Moses, "I am the LORD.
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty. But I did not make myself known to them by my name, the LORD.
I also made my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as foreigners.
And I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel, whom the Egyptians are keeping as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.

So tell the people of Israel: 'I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the heavy work of the Egyptians. I will set you free from being their slaves. I will save you with my mighty arm and with great acts of judgment.
I will take you as my own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the heavy work of the Egyptians.
And I will bring you to the land I promised to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you as your own. I am the LORD.'"
Moses told this to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to him, because their spirits were crushed and their slavery was cruel.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
"Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel leave his country."
But Moses said to the LORD, "The people of Israel will not listen to me. So why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I speak so poorly?"
But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron about the people of Israel and Pharaoh king of Egypt. He commanded them to bring the people of Israel out of Egypt.
These were the heads of their families. The sons of Reuben, the firstborn son of Israel, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These were the families of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These were the families of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi, in the order of their birth: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived one hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Gershon, by their families, were Libni and Shimei.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived one hundred and thirty-three years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These were the families of the Levites, in the order of their birth.
Amram married Jochebed, his father's sister, and she had Aaron and Moses. Amram lived one hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she had Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These were the families of the Korahites.
Eleazar son of Aaron married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she had Phinehas. These were the heads of the Levite families, by their families.
It was this same Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, "Bring the people of Israel out of Egypt, group by group, like an army."
They were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing the people of Israel out of Egypt. It was this same Moses and Aaron.
Now when the LORD spoke to Moses in Egypt,
he said to him, "I am the LORD. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I tell you."
But Moses said to the LORD, "I speak so poorly. Why would Pharaoh listen to me?"
The LORD said to Moses, "Look, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.
You must say everything I command you, and your brother Aaron will tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel leave his land.
But I will make Pharaoh stubborn, and I will do many signs and wonders in Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will bring my hand down on Egypt, and with great acts of judgment I will bring my people, the people of Israel, out of Egypt, group by group.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I reach out my hand against Egypt and bring the people of Israel out from among them."
Moses and Aaron did just what the LORD commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Show me a miracle,' then say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh,' and it will become a snake."
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just what the LORD commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a snake.
Then Pharaoh called for his wise men and sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their secret arts.
Each one threw down his staff, and each staff became a snake. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
Yet Pharaoh's heart was stubborn, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is stubborn. He refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water. Wait for him on the bank of the Nile. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a snake.
Then say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to say to you: Let my people go, so that they can worship me in the desert. But until now you have not listened.
This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. With the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn into blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, and the river will stink. The Egyptians will not be able to drink its water.'"

The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over its rivers, its streams, its pools, and all its ponds, and they will turn into blood.' There will be blood everywhere in Egypt, even in the wooden buckets and stone jars."
Moses and Aaron did just what the LORD commanded. Aaron raised his staff in front of Pharaoh and his officials and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water in the river turned into blood.
The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water. There was blood everywhere in Egypt.
But the magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart stayed stubborn, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.
Pharaoh turned and went back into his palace, and he did not take even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug along the Nile to find water to drink, because they could not drink the water of the river.
Seven days passed after the LORD struck the Nile.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, so that they can worship me.
If you refuse to let them go, I will send a plague of frogs on your whole country.

The Nile will be full of frogs. They will come up into your palace, into your bedroom, and onto your bed. They will go into the houses of your officials and onto your people, and into your ovens and the bowls where you make bread.
The frogs will jump on you, on your people, and on all your officials.'"
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, the streams, and the pools, and make frogs come up onto the land of Egypt.'"
So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land.
But the magicians did the same thing with their secret arts. They also made frogs come up onto the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let the people go to offer sacrifices to the LORD."
Moses said to Pharaoh, "You may choose the time. When should I pray for you, your officials, and your people, so that the frogs leave you and your houses, and stay only in the Nile?"
"Tomorrow," Pharaoh said. Moses replied, "It will be as you say, so that you will know that there is no one like the LORD our God.
The frogs will leave you, your houses, your officials, and your people. They will stay only in the Nile."
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the frogs he had brought on Pharaoh.
And the LORD did what Moses asked. The frogs died in the houses, in the yards, and in the fields.
The people piled them up in heaps, and the whole land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that the trouble was over, he made his heart stubborn and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the ground, and the dust will turn into lice all over the land of Egypt.'"
They did this. Aaron stretched out his hand with the staff and struck the dust of the ground, and lice came on people and animals. All the dust in the whole land of Egypt turned into lice.
The magicians tried to make lice with their secret arts, but they could not. And the lice stayed on people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God!" But Pharaoh's heart was stubborn, and he would not listen, just as the LORD had said.

Then the LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning and stand in front of Pharaoh when he goes out to the water. Say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, so that they can worship me.

If you do not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies on you, your officials, your people, and into your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of flies, and so will the ground they stand on.
But on that day I will treat the land of Goshen differently, where my people live. There will be no swarms of flies there. Then you will know that I, the LORD, am in this land.
I will make a difference between my people and your people. This sign will happen tomorrow.'"
And the LORD did this. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh's palace and into the houses of his officials. All over Egypt the land was ruined by the flies.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, offer sacrifices to your God here in this land."

But Moses said, "That would not be right. The sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be disgusting to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are disgusting to them right in front of their eyes, will they not throw stones at us?
We must take a three-day journey into the desert and offer sacrifices to the LORD our God, as he commands us."
Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to offer sacrifices to the LORD your God in the desert, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me."

Moses answered, "As soon as I leave you, I will pray to the LORD. Tomorrow the flies will leave Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. But Pharaoh must not trick us again by refusing to let the people go to offer sacrifices to the LORD."
Then Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.
And the LORD did what Moses asked. The flies left Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. Not one fly was left.
But this time also Pharaoh made his heart stubborn and would not let the people go.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so that they can worship me.
If you refuse to let them go and keep holding on to them,
the hand of the LORD will bring a terrible disease on your animals in the fields: on your horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and goats.
But the LORD will treat the animals of Israel differently from the animals of Egypt. Not one animal that belongs to the people of Israel will die.'"
The LORD set a time and said, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land."
And the next day the LORD did it. All the animals of the Egyptians died, but not one animal of the people of Israel died.
Pharaoh sent people to look, and they found that not even one of the animals of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh's heart was still stubborn, and he would not let the people go.
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and let Moses throw it into the air in front of Pharaoh.
It will become fine dust over the whole land of Egypt. It will cause boils to break out into open sores on people and animals all over Egypt."
So they took soot from a furnace and stood in front of Pharaoh. Moses threw it into the air, and boils broke out into open sores on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand in front of Moses because of the boils, because the boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had told Moses.

Then the LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning, stand in front of Pharaoh, and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so that they can worship me.
This time I will send all my plagues against you, against your officials, and against your people, so that you will know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
By now I could have reached out my hand and struck you and your people with a disease that would have wiped you off the earth.
But I have let you live for this reason: to show you my power, and so that my name will be made known in all the earth.
You still set yourself up against my people and will not let them go.
So at this time tomorrow I will send the worst hailstorm that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it became a nation until now.

So give an order now to bring your animals and everything you have in the fields into shelter. The hail will fall on every person and animal that is left out in the field and not brought inside, and they will die.'"
Some of Pharaoh's officials feared the word of the LORD. They hurried to bring their slaves and their animals inside.
But those who ignored the word of the LORD left their slaves and their animals in the field.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that hail will fall all over Egypt, on people and animals, and on every plant growing in the fields of Egypt."
When Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning flashed down to the ground. So the LORD made hail fall on the land of Egypt.
The hail fell, and lightning flashed back and forth among the hail. It was the worst storm in all the land of Egypt since it had become a nation.
All over Egypt the hail struck everything in the fields, both people and animals. It beat down every plant in the fields and broke every tree.
The only place where there was no hail was the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel lived.
Then Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron. He said to them, "This time I have sinned. The LORD is right, and I and my people are wrong.
Pray to the LORD, because we have had enough of this thunder and hail. I will let you go. You do not have to stay any longer."

Moses answered him, "When I have gone out of the city, I will lift up my hands in prayer to the LORD. The thunder will stop, and there will be no more hail, so that you will know that the earth belongs to the LORD.
But I know that you and your officials still do not fear the LORD God."
The flax and the barley were destroyed, because the barley had formed its heads and the flax was in flower.
But the wheat and the spelt were not destroyed, because they ripen later.
Then Moses left Pharaoh and went out of the city. He lifted up his hands to the LORD. The thunder and the hail stopped, and the rain no longer poured down on the land.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, the hail, and the thunder had stopped, he sinned again. He and his officials made their hearts stubborn.
So Pharaoh's heart was stubborn, and he would not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh. I have made him and his officials stubborn so that I can do these signs of mine among them.
And I did this so that you can tell your children and grandchildren how hard I was on the Egyptians, and about the signs I did among them. Then you will know that I am the LORD."

So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said to him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself in front of me? Let my people go, so that they can worship me.
If you refuse to let them go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country.
They will cover the ground so that it cannot be seen. They will eat whatever little you have left after the hail, including every tree that is growing in your fields.

They will fill your houses, and the houses of all your officials and all the Egyptians. Neither your parents nor your grandparents have ever seen anything like it, from the day they settled in this land until now.'" Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's officials said to him, "How long will this man be a trap for us? Let the people go, so that they can worship the LORD their God. Do you not see yet that Egypt is ruined?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. He said to them, "Go, worship the LORD your God. But tell me who will be going."
Moses answered, "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters, and with our flocks and herds, because we are to hold a feast for the LORD."
Pharaoh said, "The LORD would really have to be with you if I let you go with your children! Clearly you are planning something evil.
No! Only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been asking for." Then Moses and Aaron were driven out of Pharaoh's presence.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over Egypt so that locusts will swarm over the land and eat every plant, everything the hail has left."
So Moses stretched out his staff over Egypt, and the LORD made an east wind blow across the land all that day and all that night. By morning the wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts came over the whole land of Egypt and settled down everywhere. There had never been so many locusts before, and there never will be again.

They covered the whole ground until it was black. They ate everything growing in the fields and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh quickly called for Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.
Now please forgive my sin just this once more, and pray to the LORD your God to take this deadly plague away from me."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.
Then the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind. It picked up the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea. Not one locust was left anywhere in Egypt.
But the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he would not let the people of Israel go.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that darkness will cover Egypt, darkness so thick that people can feel it."
So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and total darkness covered all of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one left his place for three days. But all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and said, "Go and worship the LORD. Even your children may go with you. Only leave your flocks and herds behind."
But Moses said, "You must also let us have animals for sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to the LORD our God.

Our animals must go with us too. Not one hoof is to be left behind. We have to use some of them to worship the LORD our God, and until we get there, we will not know which ones we need to worship the LORD."
But the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he would not let them go.
Pharaoh said to Moses, "Get out of my sight! Make sure you never see my face again! The day you see my face, you will die."
Moses replied, "Just as you say. I will never see your face again."
Then the LORD said to Moses, "I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that he will let you go from here. And when he does, he will drive you out completely.
Tell the people that every man and every woman must ask their Egyptian neighbours for things made of silver and gold."
The LORD made the Egyptians kind to the people. And Moses himself was highly respected in Egypt by Pharaoh's officials and by the people.
So Moses said, "This is what the LORD says: 'About midnight I will go through Egypt.

Every firstborn son in Egypt will die, from the firstborn son of Pharaoh, who sits on the throne, to the firstborn son of the slave woman who grinds grain at her millstone, and all the firstborn of the animals too.
There will be loud crying all over Egypt, worse than there has ever been or ever will be again.
But not even a dog will bark at any of the people of Israel or at their animals. Then you will know that the LORD makes a difference between Egypt and Israel.'
All these officials of yours will come to me and bow down in front of me, saying, 'Go, you and all the people who follow you!' After that I will leave." Then Moses left Pharaoh, burning with anger.
The LORD had said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I can do even more wonders in Egypt."
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders in front of Pharaoh, but the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he would not let the people of Israel leave his country.
The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron in Egypt. He said,
"This month is to be the beginning of months for you. It will be the first month of your year.
Tell the whole community of Israel that on the tenth day of this month, each man must take a lamb for his family, one lamb for each household.

If a household is too small to eat a whole lamb, they must share one with their nearest neighbour, according to the number of people. Work out how much lamb is needed by how much each person will eat.
The animal you choose must be a one-year-old male without anything wrong with it. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats.
Take care of it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then all the people of the community of Israel must kill their animals at sunset.
They must take some of the blood and put it on the sides and the top of the door frames of the houses where they eat the lambs.
That same night they must eat the meat roasted over the fire, along with bitter herbs and bread made without yeast.
Do not eat the meat raw or boiled in water. Roast the whole animal over the fire, its head, legs, and insides.
Do not leave any of it until morning. If any is left until morning, you must burn it.
This is how you must eat it: with your belt tied, your sandals on your feet, and your walking stick in your hand. Eat it quickly. It is the LORD's Passover.
On that same night I will pass through Egypt and strike down every firstborn, both people and animals. I will bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD.
The blood on your houses will be a sign for you. When I see the blood, I will pass over you. No deadly plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.
This day is to be a day for you to remember. For all time to come, you must celebrate it as a feast to the LORD. This is a law that will last forever.

For seven days you must eat bread made without yeast. On the first day remove the yeast from your houses. Anyone who eats bread made with yeast from the first day to the seventh day must be cut off from Israel.
On the first day hold a holy meeting, and another one on the seventh day. Do no work at all on those days, except to prepare food for everyone to eat. That is all you may do.
Celebrate the Feast of Bread Without Yeast, because on this very day I brought your people out of Egypt, group by group. Celebrate this day for all time to come. It is a law that will last forever.
In the first month, eat bread made without yeast from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day.
For seven days no yeast may be found in your houses. Anyone who eats anything with yeast in it must be cut off from the community of Israel, whether he is a foreigner or born in the land.
Eat nothing made with yeast. Wherever you live, you must eat bread made without yeast."
Then Moses called all the leaders of Israel and said to them, "Go at once and choose lambs for your families, and kill the Passover lamb.
Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the bowl, and put some of the blood on the top and on both sides of the door frame. Not one of you may go out of the door of his house until morning.

When the LORD passes through to strike down the Egyptians, he will see the blood on the top and sides of the door frame. Then he will pass over that door, and he will not let the destroyer come into your houses to strike you down.
You and your children must obey these instructions as a law that lasts forever.
When you come into the land the LORD will give you, as he promised, keep this ceremony.
And when your children ask you, 'What does this ceremony mean?'

then tell them, 'It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD. He passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt when he struck down the Egyptians, and he spared our homes.'" Then the people bowed down and worshipped.
The people of Israel did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.

At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn son in Egypt, from the firstborn son of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn son of the prisoner in the dungeon. He also killed the firstborn of all the animals.
Pharaoh, all his officials, and all the Egyptians got up during the night. There was loud crying in Egypt, because there was not a house without someone dead.
During the night Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Get up! Leave my people, you and the people of Israel! Go, worship the LORD, as you have asked.
Take your flocks and herds, as you said, and go. And bless me too!"
The Egyptians kept urging the people to hurry and leave the country. "If you do not," they said, "we will all die!"
So the people took their dough before the yeast was added. They wrapped their bread bowls in clothes and carried them on their shoulders.
The people of Israel did as Moses said. They asked the Egyptians for things made of silver and gold, and for clothes.
The LORD had made the Egyptians kind to the people, and they gave them what they asked for. So the Israelites took away the riches of the Egyptians.
The people of Israel travelled from Rameses to Succoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the children.
Many other people went with them, as well as large flocks and herds of animals.
They baked flat loaves from the dough they had brought out of Egypt. The dough had no yeast, because they had been driven out of Egypt and had no time to make food ready for themselves.
The people of Israel had lived in Egypt for four hundred and thirty years.
At the end of the four hundred and thirty years, to the very day, all the LORD's people left Egypt like an army.
The LORD kept watch that night to bring them out of Egypt. So on this night all the people of Israel must keep watch to honour the LORD, for all time to come.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "These are the rules for the Passover: No foreigner may eat it.
But any slave you have bought may eat it after you have circumcised him.
A foreigner living with you for a while, or a hired worker, may not eat it.
It must be eaten inside one house. Do not take any of the meat outside the house. Do not break any of its bones.
The whole community of Israel must celebrate it.

If a foreigner living among you wants to celebrate the LORD's Passover, all the males in his household must be circumcised. Then he may take part like someone born in the land. But no man who is not circumcised may eat it.
The same law applies to the person born in the land and to the foreigner living among you."
All the people of Israel did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.
And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of Egypt, group by group, like an army.
The LORD said to Moses,
"Set apart for me every firstborn male. The first male born to every mother among the people of Israel belongs to me, whether it is a person or an animal."
Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, where you were slaves. The LORD brought you out of there with his mighty hand. Do not eat anything made with yeast.
Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving.

The LORD promised your ancestors that he would give you the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey. When he brings you there, you must keep this ceremony in this month.
For seven days eat bread made without yeast, and on the seventh day hold a feast to honour the LORD.
Eat bread made without yeast for those seven days. Nothing with yeast in it is to be seen among you. No yeast is to be seen anywhere in your land.
On that day tell your son, 'I do this because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
This ceremony will be like a sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead, so that the law of the LORD will always be on your lips. For the LORD brought you out of Egypt with his mighty hand.
So you must keep this law at the right time every year.
The LORD will bring you into the land of the Canaanites and give it to you, as he promised you and your ancestors.
Then you must give to the LORD the first male born to every mother. Every firstborn male of your animals belongs to the LORD.
You may buy back every firstborn donkey by giving a lamb in its place. If you do not buy it back, you must break its neck. And you must buy back every firstborn son among your children.
In the days to come, when your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' tell him, 'With his mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, where we were slaves.

When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in Egypt, both people and animals. That is why I sacrifice to the LORD every firstborn male animal, but I buy back each of my firstborn sons.'
It will be like a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead, because the LORD brought us out of Egypt with his mighty hand."

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, even though it was shorter. God said, "If they face war, they might change their minds and go back to Egypt."
So God led the people the long way round, through the desert towards the Red Sea. The people of Israel left Egypt ready for battle.

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because Joseph had made the people of Israel promise him. He had said, "God will surely come to help you. When he does, you must carry my bones up from this place with you."
They left Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the desert.
During the day the LORD went ahead of them in a pillar of cloud to show them the way. At night he went ahead of them in a pillar of fire to give them light. So they could travel by day or by night.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never left its place in front of the people.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
"Tell the people of Israel to turn back and camp near Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. Camp by the sea, right across from Baal Zephon.
Pharaoh will think, 'The people of Israel are wandering around the land in confusion. The desert has closed them in.'

And I will make Pharaoh stubborn, and he will chase after them. But I will win glory for myself through Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD." So the people of Israel did this.

When the king of Egypt was told that the people had run away, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them. They said, "What have we done? We have let the people of Israel go, and now they will not work for us!"
So Pharaoh got his chariot ready and took his army with him.
He took six hundred of his best chariots, along with all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers in charge of all of them.
The LORD made Pharaoh king of Egypt stubborn, and he chased after the people of Israel, who were marching out boldly.
The Egyptians chased after them. All of Pharaoh's horses and chariots, his horsemen and his army, caught up with them as they were camped by the sea near Pi Hahiroth, across from Baal Zephon.
As Pharaoh came near, the people of Israel looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them. They were terrified and cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, "Were there no graves in Egypt, so you brought us out here to die in the desert? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt?
Did we not tell you in Egypt, 'Leave us alone, and let us work for the Egyptians'? It would have been better for us to work for the Egyptians than to die in the desert!"
Moses answered the people, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and you will see how the LORD will save you today. The Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.
The LORD will fight for you. You only need to be still."
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Why are you crying out to me? Tell the people of Israel to move on.
Raise your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea to divide the water, so that the people of Israel can go through the sea on dry ground.
I will make the Egyptians stubborn, and they will go in after them. And I will win glory for myself through Pharaoh and all his army, through his chariots and his horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I win glory through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."
Then the angel of God, who had been travelling in front of Israel's army, moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them and stood behind them.
It came between the army of Egypt and the army of Israel. All night the cloud brought darkness to one side and light to the other side. So neither went near the other all night long.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. All that night the LORD pushed the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The water was divided.
The people of Israel went through the middle of the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians chased them and followed them into the middle of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen.
Just before dawn, the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion.
He made the wheels of their chariots come off, so that they could hardly drive. And the Egyptians said, "Let us get away from the Israelites! The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!"
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the water will flow back over the Egyptians, their chariots, and their horsemen."
So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea went back to its normal place. The Egyptians tried to run away from it, but the LORD swept them into the middle of the sea.
The water flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen, the whole army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them was left alive.
