The Gershonite clans of the Levites received from the half-tribe of Manasseh Golan in Bashan, a city of safety for anyone who had killed someone, and Be Eshterah, each with its fields. That was two towns.
From the tribe of Issachar they received Kishion, Daberath,
Jarmuth and En Gannim, each with its fields. That was four towns.
From the tribe of Asher they received Mishal, Abdon,
Helkath and Rehob, each with its fields. That was four towns.
From the tribe of Naphtali they received Kedesh in Galilee, a city of safety for anyone who had killed someone, Hammoth Dor and Kartan, each with its fields. That was three towns.
In all, the Gershonite clans received thirteen towns with their fields.
The Merarite clans, the rest of the Levites, received from the tribe of Zebulun Jokneam, Kartah,
Dimnah and Nahalal, each with its fields. That was four towns.
From the tribe of Reuben they received Bezer, Jahaz,
Kedemoth and Mephaath, each with its fields. That was four towns.
From the tribe of Gad they received Ramoth in Gilead, a city of safety for anyone who had killed someone, Mahanaim,
Heshbon and Jazer, each with its fields. That was four towns in all.
In all, the Merarite clans, the last of the Levite clans, received twelve towns by lot.
Altogether the Levites received forty-eight towns with their fields inside the land of the Israelites.
Each of these towns had fields around it. This was true for all of them.
So the LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to give their ancestors. They took it and settled there.
The LORD gave them rest on every side, just as he had sworn to their ancestors. Not one of their enemies could stand against them. The LORD gave all their enemies into their hands.
Not one of all the good promises the LORD had made to the people of Israel failed. Every one came true.
Then Joshua called together the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
He said to them, "You have done everything Moses, the servant of the LORD, commanded you, and you have obeyed me in everything I told you.
For a long time now, right up to today, you have not abandoned your fellow Israelites. You have carefully done the work the LORD your God gave you.
Now the LORD your God has given your brothers rest, as he promised. So go back home to your own land, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you east of the Jordan.

But be very careful to obey the commands and the law Moses gave you: love the LORD your God, live the way he wants, obey his commands, hold on to him tightly, and serve him with all your heart and all your soul."
Then Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went home.
Moses had given land in Bashan to one half of the tribe of Manasseh, and Joshua had given the other half land west of the Jordan with their relatives. When Joshua sent them home, he blessed them
and said, "Go back home with your great wealth: large herds of animals, silver, gold, bronze, iron and lots of clothing. Share with your relatives what you took from your enemies."

So the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh left the rest of Israel at Shiloh in Canaan to go back to Gilead, their own land, which they had received as the LORD commanded through Moses.
When they came to Geliloth near the Jordan, still in the land of Canaan, they built a large, impressive altar there by the river.
The other Israelites heard people say, "Look, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar at the border of Canaan, near the Jordan, on the Israelite side."
When the Israelites heard this, the whole community gathered at Shiloh to go to war against them.
So the Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead.
With him they sent ten leaders, one for each tribe of Israel. Each one was head of a family group among the clans of Israel.
They went to the people of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead and said to them,
"The whole community of the LORD says: How could you be so unfaithful to the God of Israel? How could you turn away from the LORD today and build yourselves an altar, rebelling against him?
Was the sin at Peor not enough for us? To this day we have not been cleansed from it, even though a plague struck the LORD's people.
And now you are turning away from the LORD! If you rebel against the LORD today, tomorrow he will be angry with the whole community of Israel.

If the land you own is unclean, come over to the LORD's land, where the LORD's tent stands, and share our land with us. But do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building another altar besides the altar of the LORD our God.
Remember Achan son of Zerah. He was unfaithful about the things set apart for destruction, and God's anger fell on the whole community of Israel. He was not the only one who died for his sin."
Then the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered the heads of the clans of Israel,
"The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows, and let Israel know too! If we did this in rebellion or unfaithfulness to the LORD, do not spare us today.
If we built this altar to turn away from the LORD, or to offer burnt offerings, grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself punish us.
No! We did it because we were worried. We feared that one day your children might say to our children, 'What do you have to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?
The LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you people of Reuben and Gad. You have no share in the LORD.' Then your children might cause our children to stop worshipping the LORD.
So we said, 'Let us build an altar, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices,

but as a witness between us and you and the generations after us. It will show that we too worship the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings, sacrifices and peace offerings.' Then in the future your children will not be able to say to ours, 'You have no share in the LORD.'

We said, 'If they ever say this to us or to our children, we will answer: Look at this copy of the LORD's altar, which our ancestors built. It is not for burnt offerings or sacrifices. It is a witness between us and you.'

We would never rebel against the LORD or turn away from him today by building another altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings or sacrifices, besides the altar of the LORD our God that stands in front of his tent."
When Phinehas the priest and the leaders of the community, the heads of the clans of Israel, heard what the people of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh said, they were pleased.

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest said to them, "Today we know that the LORD is with us, because you have not been unfaithful to him in this. Now you have saved the Israelites from the LORD's punishment."
Then Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the leaders left the people of Reuben and Gad in Gilead and went back to the Israelites in Canaan and told them what had happened.
The Israelites were glad to hear it, and they praised God. They spoke no more about going to war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and Gad lived.
And the people of Reuben and Gad named the altar Witness, saying, "It is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
A long time passed, and the LORD gave Israel rest from all their enemies around them. Joshua was by then very old.
He called all Israel together, with their elders, leaders, judges and officers, and said to them, "I am very old now.
You have seen everything the LORD your God did to all these nations for your sake. It was the LORD your God who fought for you.
Look, I have given you the land of the nations that are still left, as well as the nations I have already defeated, to be shared among your tribes, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west.
The LORD your God himself will push them out ahead of you and drive them away. You will take their land, as the LORD your God promised you.
So be very strong. Be careful to obey everything written in the book of the law of Moses. Do not turn away from it to the right or to the left.
Do not mix with the nations still left among you. Do not speak the names of their gods or make promises by them. Do not serve them or bow down to them.
Instead, hold on tightly to the LORD your God, as you have done until now.
The LORD has driven out great and strong nations ahead of you. To this day no one has been able to stand against you.
One of you can chase away a thousand, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as he promised.
So be very careful to love the LORD your God.
But if you turn away and join yourselves to the people of these nations still left among you, and marry them and mix with them,

then you can be sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive these nations out ahead of you. Instead, they will become a trap and a snare for you, a whip on your backs and thorns in your eyes, until you disappear from this good land the LORD your God has given you.

Now I am about to go the way of everyone on earth. You know with all your heart and soul that not one of all the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed. Every one has come true. Not one has failed.
But just as every good thing the LORD your God promised has come true, so he will also bring on you every bad thing he warned about, until he has destroyed you from this good land he has given you.

If you break the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you to keep, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them, the LORD's anger will burn against you. You will quickly disappear from the good land he has given you."
Then Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He called the elders, leaders, judges and officers of Israel, and they came and stood before God.

Joshua said to all the people, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Long ago your ancestors lived on the other side of the Euphrates River, including Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor. They worshipped other gods.
But I took your father Abraham from the land beyond the river and led him all through Canaan. I gave him many descendants. I gave him Isaac,
and to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau the hill country of Seir as his own, but Jacob and his family went down to Egypt.
Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with the plagues I did there. After that I brought you out.
When I brought your ancestors out of Egypt, you came to the sea. The Egyptians chased them with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea.

But they cried out to the LORD, and he put darkness between you and the Egyptians. He brought the sea over them and covered them. You saw with your own eyes what I did to Egypt. Then you lived in the desert for a long time.
I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan. They fought against you, but I gave them into your hands. I destroyed them ahead of you, and you took their land.
Then Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, got ready to fight against Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you.
But I would not listen to Balaam, so he blessed you again and again, and I saved you from Balak.

Then you crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The people of Jericho fought against you, as did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites and Jebusites. But I gave them into your hands.
I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove them out, including the two Amorite kings. You did not do it with your own sword or bow.
I gave you land you had not worked for and cities you had not built, and now you live in them. You eat from vineyards and olive trees you did not plant.'
So now, honour the LORD and serve him with all your heart and truly. Throw away the gods your ancestors worshipped beyond the Euphrates River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.

But if serving the LORD seems wrong to you, then choose today whom you will serve: the gods your ancestors served beyond the river, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living. But as for me and my family, we will serve the LORD."
The people answered, "We would never leave the LORD to serve other gods!

It was the LORD our God who brought us and our parents up out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. He did those great miracles in front of our eyes. He protected us on our whole journey and among all the nations we passed through.
The LORD drove out all the nations ahead of us, including the Amorites who lived in this land. We too will serve the LORD, because he is our God."
Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD. He is a holy God. He is a jealous God, and he will not ignore your rebellion and your sins.
If you leave the LORD and serve foreign gods, he will turn against you and bring trouble on you and destroy you, even after he has been good to you."
But the people said to Joshua, "No! We will serve the LORD."
Then Joshua said, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD." "Yes, we are witnesses," they answered.
"Then throw away the foreign gods that are among you," said Joshua, "and give your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel."
The people said to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey him."
That day at Shechem, Joshua made a covenant for the people, and he gave them rules and laws.
Joshua wrote these things in the book of the law of God. Then he took a large stone and set it up under the big oak tree near the holy place of the LORD.
He said to all the people, "Look, this stone will be a witness against us. It has heard everything the LORD said to us. It will be a witness against you if you are unfaithful to your God."
Then Joshua sent the people away, each to their own land.
After this, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of a hundred and ten.
They buried him on his own land at Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
Israel served the LORD all the time Joshua was alive, and all the time of the elders who lived after him and had seen everything the LORD had done for Israel.

The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem, in the piece of land Jacob had bought for a hundred silver coins from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem. This land belonged to Joseph's descendants.
And Eleazar son of Aaron died. He was buried at Gibeah, the hill that had been given to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim.
Judg: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the LORD, "Which tribe should go first to fight the Canaanites for us?"
The LORD answered, "Judah will go. Look, I have given the land into their hands."

The people of Judah said to their relatives, the people of Simeon, "Come with us into the land given to us, and let us fight the Canaanites together. Then we will go with you into your land." So Simeon went with them.
When Judah attacked, the LORD gave the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands, and they killed ten thousand men at Bezek.
There they found Adoni-Bezek and fought against him, and they defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites.
Adoni-Bezek ran away, but they chased him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes.

Adoni-Bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off have picked up scraps under my table. Now God has paid me back for what I did to them." They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah attacked Jerusalem and captured it. They killed its people with the sword and set the city on fire.
After that, the people of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites living in the hill country, the Negev in the south, and the western foothills.
They attacked the Canaanites living in Hebron, which used to be called Kiriath Arba, and defeated Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.
From there they went to attack the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath Sepher.
Caleb said, "I will give my daughter Aksah in marriage to the man who attacks and captures Kiriath Sepher."
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it, so Caleb gave him his daughter Aksah as his wife.
When she came to Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got down from her donkey, Caleb asked her, "What would you like?"
She answered, "Do me a special favour. Since you have given me land in the dry south, give me springs of water too." So Caleb gave her the upper and lower springs.

The descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the people of Judah from the City of Palm Trees into the Desert of Judah, in the Negev near Arad. They went and lived among the people there.
Then Judah went with their relatives from Simeon and attacked the Canaanites living in Zephath. They completely destroyed the city, so it was called Hormah, which means Destruction.
Judah also captured Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, each with its land around it.
The LORD was with the people of Judah. They took the hill country, but they could not drive out the people living on the plains, because they had iron chariots.
As Moses had promised, Hebron was given to Caleb, and he drove out the three sons of Anak from there.
But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So the Jebusites still live there with the people of Benjamin today.
The descendants of Joseph attacked Bethel, and the LORD was with them.
They sent men to spy out Bethel, which used to be called Luz.
The spies saw a man coming out of the city and said to him, "Show us how to get into the city, and we will be kind to you."
So he showed them, and they killed the people of the city with the sword. But they let the man and his whole family go.
He went to the land of the Hittites, where he built a city and called it Luz. That is still its name today.
But the people of Manasseh did not drive out the people of Beth Shan, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam or Megiddo and their villages, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in that land.
When Israel became strong, they made the Canaanites do forced labour, but they never drove them out completely.
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, so the Canaanites kept living there among them.
Zebulun did not drive out the people living in Kitron or Nahalol. The Canaanites lived among them, but they were made to do forced labour.
Asher did not drive out the people living in Akko, Sidon, Ahlab, Akzib, Helbah, Aphek or Rehob.
So the people of Asher lived among the Canaanites of the land, because they did not drive them out.

Naphtali did not drive out the people living in Beth Shemesh or Beth Anath. They lived among the Canaanites of the land, but the people of Beth Shemesh and Beth Anath were made to do forced labour for them.
The Amorites pushed the people of Dan back into the hill country and would not let them come down to the plains.
The Amorites were determined to stay in Mount Heres, Aijalon and Shaalbim. But when the descendants of Joseph grew stronger, the Amorites were made to do forced labour.
The border of the Amorites ran from Scorpion Pass to Sela and beyond.
The angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bokim and said, "I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land I promised your ancestors. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you,
and you must not make any treaty with the people of this land. You must tear down their altars.' But you have not obeyed me. Why have you done this?
So now I tell you: I will not drive them out ahead of you. They will be like thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a trap for you."
When the angel of the LORD said these things to all the Israelites, the people cried loudly.
They called that place Bokim, which means Crying, and they offered sacrifices there to the LORD.
After Joshua had sent the people away, each of the Israelites went to take the land given to them.
The people served the LORD all the time Joshua was alive, and all the time of the elders who lived after him and had seen all the great things the LORD had done for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of a hundred and ten.
They buried him on his own land at Timnath Heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
After that whole generation had died, another generation grew up who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel.
Then the Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's eyes and served the Baals.
They left the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of Egypt. They followed and worshipped the gods of the peoples around them, and they made the LORD angry.
They left the LORD and served Baal and the Ashtoreths.
In his anger against Israel, the LORD handed them over to raiders who robbed them. He sold them to their enemies all around, and they could no longer stand against them.
Whenever Israel went out to fight, the LORD's hand was against them to defeat them, just as he had warned and sworn to them. They were in great trouble.
Then the LORD raised up judges, leaders who saved them from the raiders.

Yet they did not listen to their judges. They were unfaithful to the LORD and worshipped other gods and bowed down to them. They quickly turned away from the path their ancestors had walked, the path of obeying the LORD's commands. They did not do as their ancestors had done.

Whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, he was with that judge and saved them from their enemies as long as the judge lived. The LORD felt sorry for them as they groaned under those who treated them cruelly and crushed them.

But when the judge died, the people went back to even worse ways than their ancestors. They followed other gods, serving and worshipping them. They refused to give up their evil practices and stubborn ways.
So the LORD was very angry with Israel. He said, "This nation has broken the covenant I gave their ancestors and has not listened to me.
So I will no longer drive out ahead of them any of the nations Joshua left when he died.
I will use them to test Israel and see whether they will keep the way of the LORD and walk in it as their ancestors did."
So the LORD let those nations stay. He did not drive them out quickly or give them into Joshua's hands.
These are the nations the LORD left in the land to test the Israelites who had not been through any of the wars in Canaan.
He did this only to teach war to the new generations of Israelites who had never fought in battle before.
These nations were the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites living in the Lebanon mountains from Mount Baal Hermon to Lebo Hamath.
They were left to test the Israelites, to see whether they would obey the commands the LORD had given their ancestors through Moses.
The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites.
They married their daughters and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they served their gods.
The Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherah poles.
So the LORD was angry with Israel and sold them to Cushan-Rishathaim, king of Aram Naharaim in Mesopotamia. The Israelites served him for eight years.
But when they cried out to the LORD, he raised up someone to save them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
The Spirit of the LORD came on him, and he became Israel's judge and went to war. The LORD gave Cushan-Rishathaim king of Aram into his hands, and Othniel defeated him.
So the land had peace for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died.
Again the Israelites did evil in the LORD's eyes. Because they did this evil, the LORD made Eglon king of Moab strong against Israel.
Eglon got the Ammonites and Amalekites to join him. He came and attacked Israel, and they captured the City of Palm Trees.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

Again the Israelites cried out to the LORD, and he gave them a saviour: Ehud son of Gera from the tribe of Benjamin, a left-handed man. The Israelites sent him to take their tribute payment to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud had made a double-edged sword about half a metre long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his clothes.
He gave the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, who was a very fat man.
After Ehud had handed over the tribute, he sent away the men who had carried it.
But near the stone idols at Gilgal he turned back and said, "Your Majesty, I have a secret message for you." The king said, "Quiet!" and all his servants left the room.
Ehud went up to him while he was sitting alone in the cool upstairs room of his palace. Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." As the king got up from his seat,
Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh and pushed it into the king's belly.
Even the handle went in after the blade, and the fat closed over it. Ehud did not pull the sword out, and it came out at his back.
Then Ehud went out to the porch. He shut the doors of the upstairs room behind him and locked them.
After he had gone, the servants came and found the doors of the upstairs room locked. They said, "He must be relieving himself in the inner room."
They waited until they were embarrassed, but he still did not open the doors. So they took a key and unlocked them. There lay their master on the floor, dead.
While they were waiting, Ehud escaped. He passed by the stone idols and escaped to Seirah.
When he arrived, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came down with him from the hills, with Ehud leading them.

He told them, "Follow me, because the LORD has given your enemy Moab into your hands." So they followed him down and took control of the river crossings of the Jordan leading to Moab. They did not let anyone cross over.
At that time they killed about ten thousand Moabites, all of them strong and brave fighters. Not one escaped.
That day Moab was put under Israel's control, and the land had peace for eighty years.
After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath, who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox stick. He too saved Israel.
After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the LORD's eyes.
So the LORD sold them to Jabin, a king of Canaan who ruled in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth Haggoyim.
Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots, and he cruelly crushed the Israelites for twenty years. So they cried out to the LORD for help.
At that time Deborah, a prophet and the wife of Lappidoth, was leading Israel as judge.
She used to sit under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came to her to settle their disputes.

She sent for Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, "The LORD, the God of Israel, commands you: 'Go and gather ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun, and lead them up to Mount Tabor.
I will lure Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his soldiers, to the Kishon River, and I will give him into your hands.'"
Barak said to her, "If you go with me, I will go. But if you do not go with me, I will not go."
Deborah said, "Very well, I will go with you. But you will not get the honour for this journey, because the LORD will hand Sisera over to a woman." So Deborah went with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali together at Kedesh. Ten thousand men followed him, and Deborah also went with him.
Now Heber the Kenite had left the other Kenites, the descendants of Hobab, Moses' brother-in-law. He had set up his tent near the big tree at Zaanannim, near Kedesh.
Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor.
So Sisera called out all his nine hundred iron chariots and all his soldiers, from Harosheth Haggoyim to the Kishon River.
Then Deborah said to Barak, "Go! This is the day the LORD has given Sisera into your hands. The LORD has gone ahead of you!" So Barak went down Mount Tabor with ten thousand men behind him.
As Barak advanced, the LORD threw Sisera and all his chariots and army into panic before Barak's swords. Sisera jumped down from his chariot and ran away on foot.
Barak chased the chariots and the army as far as Harosheth Haggoyim. All of Sisera's soldiers were killed with the sword. Not one was left.
But Sisera ran away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and Heber's family.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Come in, my lord, come right in. Do not be afraid." So he went into her tent, and she covered him with a blanket.
He said, "Please give me some water. I am thirsty." She opened a skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him up again.
He told her, "Stand at the entrance of the tent. If anyone comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say 'No.'"
But Jael, Heber's wife, picked up a tent peg and a hammer and quietly went to him while he lay fast asleep, worn out. She drove the peg through his head into the ground, and he died.

Just then Barak came by, chasing Sisera, and Jael went out to meet him. "Come," she said, "I will show you the man you are looking for." So he went in with her, and there lay Sisera, dead, with the tent peg through his head.
On that day God defeated Jabin, the Canaanite king, in front of the Israelites.
And the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him.
On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song:
"When the leaders in Israel lead the way, and the people gladly offer themselves, praise the LORD!
Listen, you kings! Pay attention, you rulers! I will sing to the LORD. I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.
LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the land of Edom, the earth shook, the skies poured, and the clouds poured down water.
The mountains shook before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the main roads were empty. Travellers went along winding side paths.
Village life stopped in Israel. It stopped until I, Deborah, came, until I came as a mother in Israel.
When they chose new gods, war came to the city gates. Not a shield or spear was seen among forty thousand in Israel.
My heart is with Israel's leaders, who gladly offered themselves among the people. Praise the LORD!
You who ride on white donkeys, sitting on fine blankets, and you who walk along the road, think about this!
Away from the noise of the archers, at the watering places, they tell of the LORD's victories, the victories of his villagers in Israel. Then the LORD's people went down to the city gates.
Wake up, wake up, Deborah! Wake up, wake up, and sing a song! Get up, Barak! Lead away your prisoners, son of Abinoam!
Then the few who were left came down to the nobles. The LORD's people came down to me against the mighty.
Some came from Ephraim, whose roots were in Amalek. Benjamin came with your people after you. From Makir came leaders, and from Zebulun those who carry a commander's staff.
The princes of Issachar were with Deborah. Issachar was with Barak, rushing after him into the valley. Among the clans of Reuben there was much thinking and searching of heart.
Why did you stay among the sheep pens, listening to the shepherds whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there was much searching of heart.
Gilead stayed east of the Jordan. And Dan, why did you stay by the ships? Asher stayed on the coast and remained in its harbours.
But the people of Zebulun risked their lives, and so did Naphtali on the high fields.
Kings came and fought. The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. But they took away no silver.
From the heavens the stars fought. From their paths in the sky they fought against Sisera.
The Kishon River swept them away, the ancient river, the Kishon River. March on, my soul, be strong!
Then the horses' hooves thundered as his mighty horses galloped and galloped.
'Curse Meroz,' said the angel of the LORD. 'Bitterly curse its people, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.'
Most blessed of women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. She is most blessed of women who live in tents.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a fine bowl she brought him cream.
She reached for the tent peg with her hand, and for the worker's hammer with her right hand. She struck Sisera and crushed his head. She smashed and pierced the side of his head.
At her feet he sank down. He fell and lay there. At her feet he sank and fell. Where he sank, there he fell, dead.
Sisera's mother looked out through the window. Behind the lattice she cried out, 'Why is his chariot taking so long to come? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots so slow?'
The wisest of her ladies answered her, and she kept telling herself,

'They must be finding and sharing out the goods they took: a girl or two for each man, colourful clothes as plunder for Sisera, colourful embroidered clothes, two pieces of embroidered cloth for my neck, all taken as plunder.'
So may all your enemies die, LORD! But may all who love you be like the sun when it rises in its strength." Then the land had peace for forty years.
The Israelites did evil in the LORD's eyes, so for seven years he gave them into the hands of the Midianites.
The Midianites were so powerful and cruel that the Israelites made hiding places for themselves in the mountains, in caves and in strongholds.
Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites, the Amalekites and other peoples from the east came and attacked them.
They camped on the land and destroyed the crops all the way to Gaza. They left nothing alive in Israel to eat, not a sheep, a cow or a donkey.
They came up with their animals and their tents like swarms of locusts. It was impossible to count them or their camels. They came into the land to ruin it.
Midian made Israel so poor that the Israelites cried out to the LORD for help.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian,
he sent them a prophet, who said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I brought you up out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery.
I saved you from the power of Egypt and from all who crushed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land.
I told you, I am the LORD your God. Do not worship the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you live. But you have not listened to me.'"

The angel of the LORD came and sat under the big oak tree at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash, from the family of Abiezer. His son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
The angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, "The LORD is with you, mighty warrior!"

Gideon answered, "Pardon me, my lord, but if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are all the wonderful things our ancestors told us about when they said, 'Did not the LORD bring us up out of Egypt?' But now the LORD has left us and handed us over to Midian."
The LORD turned to him and said, "Go in the strength you have and save Israel from Midian. I am the one sending you."
Gideon said, "Pardon me, my Lord, but how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least important in my family."
The LORD answered, "I will be with you, and you will strike down all the Midianites as if they were only one man."
Gideon replied, "If you are pleased with me, give me a sign that it is really you talking to me.
Please do not leave until I come back and bring my offering and set it before you." And the LORD said, "I will wait until you come back."

Gideon went inside and cooked a young goat, and from about ten kilograms of flour he made bread without yeast. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought them out to the angel under the oak tree and offered them.
The angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the bread, put them on this rock, and pour out the broth." Gideon did so.
Then the angel of the LORD touched the meat and the bread with the tip of the staff in his hand. Fire came out of the rock and burned up the meat and the bread. And the angel of the LORD disappeared.
When Gideon realised it was the angel of the LORD, he cried out, "Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!"
But the LORD said to him, "Peace! Do not be afraid. You are not going to die."
So Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and called it The LORD Is Peace. It still stands today in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
That same night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, the second bull, the one seven years old. Tear down your father's altar to Baal, and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.
Then build a proper altar to the LORD your God on top of this high place. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering, using the wood of the Asherah pole you cut down."
So Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the LORD told him. But because he was afraid of his family and the men of the town, he did it at night instead of in the daytime.
In the morning, when the men of the town got up, they saw that Baal's altar had been torn down and the Asherah pole beside it cut down, and the second bull had been offered on the new altar.
They asked each other, "Who did this?" After they had searched and asked around, they were told, "Gideon son of Joash did it."
The men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son. He must die, because he has torn down Baal's altar and cut down the Asherah pole beside it."

But Joash said to the crowd standing around him, "Are you going to fight for Baal? Are you trying to save him? Whoever fights for him will be put to death by morning! If Baal really is a god, he can defend himself when someone tears down his altar."
So that day they called Gideon Jerub-Baal, which means, "Let Baal fight with him," because he tore down Baal's altar.
Then all the Midianites, Amalekites and other eastern peoples joined forces. They crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came on Gideon, and he blew a trumpet, calling the Abiezrites to follow him.
He sent messengers all through Manasseh, calling them to follow him, and also to Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali. They too came up to meet him.
Gideon said to God, "If you are going to save Israel through me, as you promised,
look, I will put a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground around it is dry, then I will know that you will save Israel through me, as you said."
And that is what happened. Gideon got up early the next day, squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew, a whole bowl of water.
Then Gideon said to God, "Do not be angry with me. Let me ask just one more thing. Let me test with the fleece one more time. This time make the fleece dry and the ground covered with dew."
That night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and all the ground was covered with dew.
Early in the morning Jerub-Baal, that is Gideon, and all his men camped at the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian was north of them in the valley near the hill of Moreh.
The LORD said to Gideon, "You have too many men for me to give Midian into their hands. Israel might boast against me and say, 'We saved ourselves by our own strength.'
So announce to the army, 'Anyone who is afraid and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead.'" So twenty-two thousand men went home, and ten thousand stayed.

But the LORD said to Gideon, "There are still too many men. Take them down to the water, and I will sort them out for you there. If I say, 'This one will go with you,' he will go. But if I say, 'This one will not go with you,' he will not go."
So Gideon took the men down to the water. There the LORD told him, "Separate those who lap the water with their tongues like a dog from those who kneel down to drink."
Three hundred men lapped the water, bringing it to their mouths with their hands. All the rest knelt down to drink.
The LORD said to Gideon, "With the three hundred men who lapped, I will save you and give the Midianites into your hands. Let all the others go home."
So Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites home but kept the three hundred, who took over the food and trumpets of the others. The camp of Midian lay below him in the valley.
That night the LORD said to Gideon, "Get up and go down against the camp, because I have given it into your hands.
If you are afraid to attack, go down to the camp with your servant Purah.
Listen to what they are saying. After that you will feel brave enough to attack the camp." So he and Purah his servant went down to the edge of the camp, where the armed guards were.

The Midianites, the Amalekites and all the other eastern peoples were spread out in the valley, as thick as locusts. Their camels were as many as the grains of sand on the seashore. No one could count them.

Gideon arrived just as a man was telling a friend about his dream. He said, "I had a dream. A round loaf of barley bread came rolling into the Midianite camp. It hit a tent so hard that the tent turned over and fell flat."
His friend answered, "This can only be the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has given the Midianites and the whole camp into his hands."

When Gideon heard the dream and what it meant, he bowed down and worshipped God. Then he went back to the camp of Israel and called out, "Get up! The LORD has given the Midianite army into your hands!"
He divided the three hundred men into three groups. He gave each man a trumpet and an empty clay jar with a burning torch inside.
He told them, "Watch me and do what I do. When I get to the edge of the camp, do exactly as I do.
When I and all who are with me blow our trumpets, then you also blow your trumpets all around the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon!'"

Gideon and the hundred men with him reached the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle part of the night, just after the guards had been changed. They blew their trumpets and smashed the jars in their hands.
All three groups blew their trumpets and smashed their jars. Holding the torches in their left hands and the trumpets in their right hands, they shouted, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"
Each man stood in his place around the camp. The whole Midianite army ran away, crying out as they fled.

When the three hundred trumpets sounded, the LORD made the men in the camp turn on each other with their swords. The army ran away as far as Beth Shittah toward Zererah, and as far as the border of Abel Meholah near Tabbath.
Israelites from Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh were called out, and they chased the Midianites.

Gideon sent messengers all through the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and take control of the waters of the Jordan ahead of them, as far as Beth Barah." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they took control of the Jordan as far as Beth Barah.

They also captured two of the Midianite leaders, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. They kept chasing the Midianites and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon, who was by the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim said to Gideon, "Why have you treated us like this? Why did you not call us when you went to fight Midian?" And they argued with him angrily.
But he answered them, "What have I done compared to you? Are not the leftover grapes of Ephraim better than the whole grape harvest of my clan, Abiezer?
God gave Oreb and Zeeb, the Midianite leaders, into your hands. What could I do compared to you?" When he said this, they stopped being angry with him.
Gideon and his three hundred men came to the Jordan and crossed it. They were exhausted, but they kept chasing the enemy.
He said to the men of Sukkoth, "Please give my soldiers some bread. They are worn out, and I am still chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."
But the officials of Sukkoth said, "Have you already captured Zebah and Zalmunna? Why should we give bread to your army?"
Gideon replied, "Just for that, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hands, I will tear your flesh with desert thorns and briers."
From there he went up to Penuel and asked the same of them, but they answered him as the men of Sukkoth had.
So he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come back safely, I will tear down this tower."

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with an army of about fifteen thousand men. These were all that were left of the armies of the eastern peoples, because a hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had been killed.
Gideon went up along the road of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army by surprise, while they felt safe.
Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian, ran away, but he chased them and captured them, and he threw their whole army into panic.
Then Gideon son of Joash came back from the battle by the Pass of Heres.
He caught a young man from Sukkoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for him the names of the seventy-seven officials and elders of Sukkoth.

Then Gideon came to the men of Sukkoth and said, "Here are Zebah and Zalmunna. You made fun of me about them, saying, 'Have you already captured Zebah and Zalmunna? Why should we give bread to your worn-out men?'"
He took the elders of the town and taught the men of Sukkoth a lesson by punishing them with desert thorns and briers.
He also tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the town.
Then he asked Zebah and Zalmunna, "What were the men you killed at Tabor like?" They answered, "They were like you. Each one looked like a king's son."
Gideon said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my own mother. As surely as the LORD lives, if you had spared their lives, I would not kill you."
He turned to Jether, his oldest son, and said, "Kill them!" But Jether did not draw his sword, because he was only a boy and was afraid.
Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Come, do it yourself. A man is judged by his strength." So Gideon stepped forward and killed them, and took the moon-shaped ornaments off their camels' necks.
The Israelites said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you, your son and your grandson, because you have saved us from Midian."
But Gideon told them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you."
But he said, "I do have one request. Each of you give me an earring from the things you took in battle." It was the custom of the Ishmaelites to wear gold earrings.
They answered, "We will gladly give them." So they spread out a cloak, and each man threw an earring onto it from what he had taken.
The gold earrings he asked for weighed about twenty kilograms. This did not count the ornaments, the necklaces, the purple clothes worn by the kings of Midian, or the chains on their camels' necks.
Gideon made the gold into an ephod, a priestly vest, and put it in his town, Ophrah. All Israel was unfaithful to God by worshipping it there, and it became a trap for Gideon and his family.
So Midian was defeated by the Israelites and did not rise up again. In Gideon's lifetime the land had peace for forty years.
Jerub-Baal son of Joash went back home to live.
Gideon had seventy sons of his own, because he had many wives.
His concubine, who lived in Shechem, also gave birth to a son, whom he named Abimelek.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites were again unfaithful to God and worshipped the Baals. They made Baal-Berith their god.
They forgot the LORD their God, who had saved them from all their enemies around them.
They also were not loyal to the family of Jerub-Baal, that is Gideon, for all the good things he had done for Israel.
Abimelek son of Jerub-Baal went to his mother's brothers in Shechem. He said to them and to all his mother's family,
"Ask all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you: to have all seventy sons of Jerub-Baal rule over you, or just one man?' Remember, I am your own flesh and blood."
His mother's brothers told all this to the leaders of Shechem, and they decided to follow Abimelek, because they said, "He is our relative."
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-Berith. With it Abimelek hired worthless, reckless men, and they followed him.
He went to his father's home in Ophrah, and on one stone he murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerub-Baal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerub-Baal, escaped by hiding.
Then all the leaders of Shechem and Beth Millo gathered beside the big tree at the stone pillar in Shechem and made Abimelek king.
When Jotham was told about this, he climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim and shouted to them, "Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God may listen to you!
One day the trees went out to choose a king for themselves. They said to the olive tree, 'Be our king.'
But the olive tree answered, 'Should I give up my oil, which is used to honour gods and people, just to sway over the trees?'
Next the trees said to the fig tree, 'Come and be our king.'
But the fig tree replied, 'Should I give up my sweet, good fruit, just to sway over the trees?'
Then the trees said to the vine, 'Come and be our king.'
But the vine answered, 'Should I give up my new wine, which cheers gods and people, just to sway over the trees?'
Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, 'Come and be our king.'
The thornbush said to the trees, 'If you really want to make me your king, come and rest in my shade. But if not, let fire come out of the thornbush and burn up the cedars of Lebanon!'
Now, have you acted honestly and in good faith by making Abimelek king? Have you been fair to Jerub-Baal and his family? Have you treated him as he deserved?
Remember, my father fought for you. He risked his life to save you from Midian.

But today you have turned against my father's family. You have murdered his seventy sons on one stone, and made Abimelek, the son of his slave woman, king over the leaders of Shechem, just because he is your relative.
So if you have acted honestly and in good faith toward Jerub-Baal and his family today, then may you be happy with Abimelek, and may he be happy with you!
But if not, let fire come out from Abimelek and burn up you leaders of Shechem and Beth Millo. And let fire come out from you leaders of Shechem and Beth Millo and burn up Abimelek!"
Then Jotham ran away. He escaped to Beer and lived there, because he was afraid of his brother Abimelek.
Abimelek ruled over Israel for three years.
Then God sent an evil spirit to cause trouble between Abimelek and the leaders of Shechem, and they turned against Abimelek.

God did this so that the crime against Jerub-Baal's seventy sons, the spilling of their blood, would be paid back on their brother Abimelek, who murdered them, and on the leaders of Shechem, who helped him do it.
To work against him, the leaders of Shechem put men on the hilltops to wait in hiding, and they robbed everyone who passed by. This was reported to Abimelek.
Then Gaal son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his brothers, and the leaders of Shechem trusted him.
They went out into the fields, picked the grapes, crushed them, and held a festival. They went into the temple of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelek.

Gaal son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelek, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not Jerub-Baal's son, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the family of Hamor, Shechem's father! Why should we serve Abimelek?
If only these people were under my command! Then I would get rid of him." And he challenged Abimelek, "Gather your whole army and come out!"
When Zebul, the governor of the city, heard what Gaal son of Ebed said, he was very angry.
He secretly sent messengers to Abimelek, saying, "Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against you.
So tonight, you and your men should come and hide in the fields.
In the morning, at sunrise, attack the city. When Gaal and his men come out against you, do whatever you can to them."
So Abimelek and all his troops set out by night and hid near Shechem in four groups.
Gaal son of Ebed had gone out and was standing at the entrance of the city gate just as Abimelek and his troops came out of their hiding place.
When Gaal saw them, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the tops of the mountains!" Zebul replied, "You are seeing the shadows of the mountains and thinking they are men."
But Gaal spoke up again: "Look, people are coming down from the centre of the land, and one group is coming from the direction of the fortune-tellers' tree."
Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your big talk now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelek that we should serve him?' Are these not the men you made fun of? Go out and fight them!"
So Gaal led the leaders of Shechem out and fought Abimelek.
Abimelek chased him, and Gaal ran away. Many were wounded and fell all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Then Abimelek stayed in Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem so they could no longer live there.
The next day the people of Shechem went out to the fields, and this was reported to Abimelek.
So he took his men, divided them into three groups and hid in the fields. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose up and attacked them.
Abimelek and the groups with him rushed forward and took their position at the entrance of the city gate. Then two groups attacked those in the fields and struck them down.
Abimelek attacked the city all that day until he captured it and killed its people. Then he destroyed the city and scattered salt over it.
When the leaders in the tower of Shechem heard this, they went into the stronghold of the temple of El-Berith.
Abimelek heard that they had gathered there.
So he and all his men went up Mount Zalmon. He took an axe, cut off some branches and put them on his shoulders. He told the men with him, "Quick! Do what you have seen me do!"

So all the men cut branches and followed Abimelek. They piled them against the stronghold and set it on fire with the people inside. So all the people in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women, also died.
Next Abimelek went to Thebez. He surrounded it and captured it.
But inside the city there was a strong tower, and all the men and women of the city ran into it. They locked themselves in and climbed up onto the roof of the tower.
Abimelek went to the tower and attacked it. As he came near the entrance of the tower to set it on fire,
a woman dropped a large grinding stone on his head and cracked his skull.
He quickly called to the young man who carried his weapons, "Draw your sword and kill me, so that people will not say, 'A woman killed him.'" So the young man stabbed him, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelek was dead, they all went home.
In this way God paid Abimelek back for the evil he had done to his father by murdering his seventy brothers.
God also made the men of Shechem pay for all their evil. The curse of Jotham son of Jerub-Baal came upon them.
After Abimelek's time, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He was from the tribe of Issachar and lived in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.
He led Israel as judge for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.
After him came Jair from Gilead, who led Israel as judge for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons, who rode thirty donkeys. They ruled thirty towns in Gilead, which are still called the Settlements of Jair today.
When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon.

Again the Israelites did evil in the LORD's eyes. They served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, and the gods of Aram, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites and the Philistines. They left the LORD and no longer served him.
So the LORD became angry with Israel and sold them to the Philistines and the Ammonites.
That year these nations crushed and broke the Israelites. For eighteen years they crushed all the Israelites living east of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim. Israel was in great trouble.
Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, "We have sinned against you. We have left our God and served the Baals."
The LORD answered, "When the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites and the Philistines,
the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites crushed you, and you cried to me for help, did I not save you from them?
But you have left me and served other gods, so I will not save you any more.
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you when you are in trouble!"
But the Israelites said to the LORD, "We have sinned. Do with us whatever you think best, but please save us now."
Then they got rid of the foreign gods among them and served the LORD. And he could no longer bear to see Israel suffer.
The Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead. The Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The leaders of the people of Gilead said to each other, "Whoever will begin the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of everyone living in Gilead."
Jephthah from Gilead was a mighty warrior. His father was Gilead, and his mother was a prostitute.
Gilead's wife also gave him sons. When they grew up, they drove Jephthah away. "You will not get any share of our family's property," they said, "because you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah ran away from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. A group of worthless men gathered around him and went out raiding with him.
Some time later, the Ammonites went to war against Israel.
When this happened, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.
They said to him, "Come and be our commander, so we can fight the Ammonites."
Jephthah said to them, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why do you come to me now, when you are in trouble?"
The elders of Gilead answered, "That is why we are turning to you now. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will be head over everyone living in Gilead."
Jephthah answered, "Suppose you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me. Will I really be your head?"
The elders of Gilead replied, "The LORD is our witness. We will certainly do as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their head and commander. And he repeated all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, asking, "What do you have against me, that you have come to attack my country?"

The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "When Israel came up out of Egypt, they took away my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, all the way to the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully."
Jephthah sent messengers back to the king of the Ammonites,
saying, "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
When Israel came up out of Egypt, they went through the desert to the Red Sea and on to Kadesh.

Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us go through your country,' but the king of Edom would not listen. They sent the same message to the king of Moab, and he refused too. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Next they travelled through the desert, going around the lands of Edom and Moab. They passed along the eastern side of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. They did not go into Moab's land, because the Arnon was its border.
Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, 'Please let us pass through your country to our own place.'
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his land. He gathered all his army, camped at Jahaz and fought against Israel.
Then the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his army into Israel's hands, and they defeated them. Israel took over all the land of the Amorites who lived in that country.
They took all of it, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the desert to the Jordan.
Now since the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven the Amorites out ahead of his people Israel, what right do you have to take it over?
Will you not take what your god Chemosh gives you? In the same way, we will take whatever the LORD our God has given us.
Are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever argue with Israel or fight against them?
For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, the villages around them, and all the towns along the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during all that time?
I have not wronged you, but you are doing wrong by attacking me. Let the LORD, the Judge, decide the dispute today between the Israelites and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites paid no attention to the message Jephthah sent him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah. He went across Gilead and Manasseh, passed through Mizpah in Gilead, and from there went on against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a promise to the LORD: "If you give the Ammonites into my hands,
whatever comes out of the door of my house to meet me when I come home safely from fighting the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it as a burnt offering."
Then Jephthah went to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into his hands.
He destroyed twenty towns from Aroer to the area of Minnith, as far as Abel Keramim, in a great defeat. So the Ammonites were brought under Israel's control.
When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, who should come out to meet him but his daughter, dancing to the sound of tambourines! She was his only child. He had no other son or daughter.
When he saw her, he tore his clothes and cried, "Oh no, my daughter! You have brought me great sorrow and trouble, because I have made a promise to the LORD that I cannot break."
She said, "My father, you have made a promise to the LORD. Do to me what you promised, now that the LORD has paid back your enemies, the Ammonites."
Then she said, "Grant me just one request. Give me two months to wander in the hills with my friends and cry because I will never marry."
"You may go," he said. He let her go for two months. She and her friends went into the hills and cried because she would never marry.
After two months she came back to her father, and he did to her as he had promised. She had never slept with a man. From this came a custom in Israel
that each year the young women of Israel go out for four days to remember the daughter of Jephthah from Gilead.

The men of Ephraim called out their troops, crossed over to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you go to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We are going to burn down your house with you inside!"
Jephthah answered, "My people and I were in a great struggle with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not save me from them.
When I saw that you would not help, I took my life in my hands and crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD gave me the victory. So why have you come up today to fight me?"

Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck them down, because the Ephraimites had said, "You people of Gilead are just runaways from Ephraim and Manasseh."

The men of Gilead captured the river crossings of the Jordan leading to Ephraim. Whenever a runaway from Ephraim said, "Let me cross over," the men of Gilead asked, "Are you from Ephraim?" If he said, "No,"

they said, "All right, say 'Shibboleth.'" If he said "Sibboleth," because he could not say the word correctly, they grabbed him and killed him at the river crossings of the Jordan. Forty-two thousand Ephraimites were killed at that time.
Jephthah led Israel as judge for six years. Then Jephthah from Gilead died and was buried in a town in Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem led Israel.

He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage to men outside his clan, and he brought in thirty young women from outside his clan as wives for his sons. Ibzan led Israel for seven years.
Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon from the tribe of Zebulun led Israel for ten years.
Then Elon died and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, led Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He led Israel for eight years.
Then Abdon son of Hillel died and was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
Again the Israelites did evil in the LORD's eyes, so the LORD gave them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man named Manoah from Zorah, from the tribe of Dan. His wife was unable to have children and had none.
The angel of the LORD appeared to her and said, "You have not been able to have children, but you are going to become pregnant and give birth to a son.
So be careful not to drink wine or any other strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.
You will become pregnant and have a son. No razor may ever be used on his head, because the boy will be set apart to God as a Nazirite from birth. He will begin to save Israel from the Philistines."
Then the woman went to her husband and told him, "A man of God came to me. He looked like an angel of God, very frightening. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

But he said to me, 'You will become pregnant and have a son. So do not drink wine or other strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from birth until the day he dies.'"
Then Manoah prayed to the LORD: "Please, Lord, let the man of God you sent come to us again to teach us how to bring up the boy who is to be born."
God heard Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she was out in the field. But her husband Manoah was not with her.
She ran quickly and told her husband, "He is here! The man who came to me the other day has appeared again!"
Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he asked, "Are you the one who talked to my wife?" "I am," he said.
So Manoah asked him, "When your words come true, what rules should we follow for the boy's life and work?"
The angel of the LORD answered, "Your wife must do everything I told her.
She must not eat anything that comes from the grapevine, nor drink wine or any other strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. She must obey everything I have commanded her."
Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please stay until we prepare a young goat for you."
The angel of the LORD replied, "Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." Manoah did not realise that it was the angel of the LORD.
Then Manoah asked the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that we may honour you when your words come true?"
He replied, "Why do you ask my name? It is too wonderful to understand."
Then Manoah took a young goat, together with a grain offering, and sacrificed it on a rock to the LORD. And while Manoah and his wife watched, the LORD did an amazing thing.
As the flame rose up from the altar toward the sky, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell with their faces to the ground.
The angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah realised that it was the angel of the LORD.
"We are sure to die," he said to his wife. "We have seen God!"
But his wife answered, "If the LORD meant to kill us, he would not have accepted our burnt offering and grain offering. He would not have shown us all these things or told us all this now."
The woman gave birth to a boy and named him Samson. He grew, and the LORD blessed him.
The Spirit of the LORD began to stir him while he was in Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah, and there he saw a young Philistine woman.
When he came back, he told his father and mother, "I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."

His father and mother answered, "Is there not a suitable woman among your relatives or among all our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?" But Samson told his father, "Get her for me. She is the right one for me."
His parents did not know that this was from the LORD, who was looking for a chance to act against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. As they came to the vineyards of Timnah, suddenly a young lion came roaring toward him.
The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on Samson, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as easily as he might tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then he went down and talked with the woman, and he liked her very much.
Some time later, when he went back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the lion's body. In it was a swarm of bees and some honey.

He scooped out the honey with his hands and ate it as he walked along. When he came back to his parents, he gave them some, and they ate it too. But he did not tell them he had taken the honey from the lion's body.
Then his father went down to see the woman. And Samson held a feast there, as was the custom for young men.
When the people saw him, they chose thirty young men to be his companions.
Samson said to them, "Let me tell you a riddle. If you can give me the answer within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen shirts and thirty sets of clothes.
If you cannot tell me the answer, you must give me thirty linen shirts and thirty sets of clothes." "Tell us your riddle," they said. "Let us hear it."
He replied, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." For three days they could not give the answer.
On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Trick your husband into telling us the answer to the riddle, or we will burn you and your father's family to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?"

Then Samson's wife cried in front of him and said, "You hate me! You do not really love me. You have given my people a riddle, but you have not told me the answer." "I have not even told my father or mother," he replied, "so why should I tell you?"
She cried the rest of the seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he finally told her, because she kept pushing him. She in turn told the answer to her people.

Before sunset on the seventh day the men of the town said to him, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" Samson said to them, "If you had not ploughed with my young cow, you would not have solved my riddle."

Then the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on him. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty of their men, took their belongings and gave their clothes to those who had answered the riddle. Burning with anger, he went back up to his father's home.
And Samson's wife was given to one of his companions who had been his best man.
Later, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat and went to visit his wife. He said, "I am going to my wife's room." But her father would not let him go in.
"I was sure you hated her," he said, "so I gave her to your friend. Is not her younger sister more beautiful? Please take her instead."
Samson said to them, "This time I will not be to blame when I do harm to the Philistines."
So he went out and caught three hundred foxes. He tied them tail to tail in pairs and fastened a torch to every pair of tails.
He lit the torches and let the foxes loose in the Philistines' standing grain. He burned up the stacks of cut grain and the standing grain, and the olive groves too.

When the Philistines asked, "Who did this?" they were told, "Samson, the son-in-law of the man from Timnah, because his wife was given to his friend." So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson said to them, "Since you acted like this, I will not stop until I get my revenge on you."
He attacked them without mercy and killed many of them. Then he went down and stayed in a cave in the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah, spreading out near Lehi.
The people of Judah asked, "Why have you come to fight us?" They answered, "We have come to tie up Samson and do to him what he did to us."

Then three thousand men from Judah went down to the cave in the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?" He answered, "I only did to them what they did to me."
They said to him, "We have come to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said, "Promise me that you will not kill me yourselves."
"We agree," they answered. "We will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We will not kill you." So they tied him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock.
As he came near Lehi, the Philistines came toward him shouting. Then the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and they fell off his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, grabbed it, and killed a thousand men with it.
Then Samson said, "With a donkey's jawbone I have made donkeys of them, piles on piles. With a donkey's jawbone I have killed a thousand men."
When he finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone. And the place was called Ramath Lehi, which means Jawbone Hill.
Because he was very thirsty, he cried out to the LORD, "You have given your servant this great victory. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"

Then God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength came back and he felt alive again. So the spring was called En Hakkore, which means Caller's Spring. It is still there in Lehi.
Samson led Israel as judge for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
One day Samson went to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her.
The people of Gaza were told, "Samson is here!" So they surrounded the place and waited for him all night at the city gate. They kept quiet all night, saying, "At dawn we will kill him."

But Samson lay there only until the middle of the night. Then he got up and took hold of the doors of the city gate, together with the two posts, and tore them loose, bar and all. He lifted them onto his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
Some time later, he fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines went to her and said, "See if you can trick him into telling you the secret of his great strength and how we can overpower him, so we can tie him up and make him helpless. Each one of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver."
So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me the secret of your great strength, and how you can be tied up and made helpless."
Samson answered her, "If anyone ties me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become as weak as any other man."
Then the rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him with them.

Men were hiding in the room, and she called to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" But he snapped the bowstrings as easily as a piece of string snaps when it comes near a flame. So the secret of his strength was not discovered.
Then Delilah said to Samson, "You have made a fool of me. You lied to me. Now please tell me how you can be tied up."
He said, "If anyone ties me tightly with new ropes that have never been used, I will become as weak as any other man."

So Delilah took new ropes and tied him with them. Then, with men hiding in the room, she called to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" But he snapped the ropes off his arms as if they were threads.

Delilah then said to Samson, "All this time you have been making a fool of me and lying to me. Tell me how you can be tied up." He replied, "If you weave the seven braids of my hair into the cloth on your loom and tighten it with the pin, I will become as weak as any other man."

So while he was sleeping, she wove his hair into the cloth and tightened it with the pin. Again she called to him, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" He woke up from his sleep and pulled out the pin and the loom with the cloth.
Then she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when you will not trust me? This is the third time you have made a fool of me and have not told me the secret of your great strength."
She kept nagging him day after day until he was sick to death of it.

So he told her everything. "No razor has ever been used on my head," he said, "because I have been a Nazirite set apart to God since I was born. If my head were shaved, my strength would leave me, and I would become as weak as any other man."

When Delilah saw that he had told her everything, she sent this message to the rulers of the Philistines: "Come back once more. He has told me everything." So the rulers of the Philistines came, bringing the silver with them.
She got him to fall asleep with his head on her lap. Then she called for a man to shave off the seven braids of his hair. So she began to overpower him, and his strength left him.
Then she called, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" He woke up from his sleep and thought, "I will go out as before and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.
Then the Philistines grabbed him and gouged out his eyes. They took him down to Gaza and tied him up with bronze chains, and they made him grind grain in the prison.
But the hair on his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
The rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate. They said, "Our god has given Samson, our enemy, into our hands."
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, "Our god has given our enemy into our hands, the one who destroyed our land and killed so many of us."
While they were in high spirits, they shouted, "Bring out Samson to entertain us!" So they called Samson out of the prison, and he performed for them. They made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy who was leading him by the hand, "Put me where I can feel the pillars that hold up the temple, so I can lean against them."
The temple was crowded with men and women. All the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about three thousand men and women watching Samson perform.
Then Samson prayed to the LORD, "Lord GOD, remember me. Please, God, give me strength just once more, so that with one blow I can pay back the Philistines for my two eyes."
Then Samson reached toward the two middle pillars that held up the temple. Putting his right hand on one and his left hand on the other, he pushed against them.

Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines!" Then he pushed with all his strength, and the temple fell on the rulers and all the people in it. So he killed many more people when he died than he had killed while he lived.

Then his brothers and his father's whole family went down to get him. They brought him back and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. Samson had led Israel as judge for twenty years.
There was a man named Micah who lived in the hill country of Ephraim.
