He said to his mother, "Someone took eleven hundred pieces of silver from you, and I heard you curse the thief. Well, I have the silver. I took it." Then his mother said, "May the LORD bless you, my son!"

When he gave the eleven hundred pieces of silver back to his mother, she said, "I am giving this silver to the LORD for my son, to make a carved idol covered with silver. So now I give it back to you."
After he gave the silver back to his mother, she took two hundred pieces of it to a silversmith, who used it to make the idol. It was put in Micah's house.
Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and some household gods. He set apart one of his sons to be his priest.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did whatever they thought was right.
A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, from the clan of Judah, had been living there.
He left Bethlehem in Judah to look for another place to live. On his way he came to Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim.
Micah asked him, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am looking for a place to stay."
Then Micah said to him, "Live with me and be my father and priest. I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food." So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to live with him, and the young man became like one of his sons.
Then Micah set apart the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house.
And Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because this Levite has become my priest."
In those days Israel had no king. And in those days the tribe of Dan was looking for a place of their own to settle, because they had not yet received their share of land among the tribes of Israel.

So the people of Dan sent five brave men from their clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. They told them, "Go and explore the land." The men came to the hill country of Ephraim and stayed overnight at Micah's house.
When they were near Micah's house, they recognised the voice of the young Levite. So they went over and asked him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?"
He told them what Micah had done for him, and said, "He has hired me, and I am his priest."
Then they said to him, "Please ask God for us whether our journey will be successful."
The priest answered them, "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey."

So the five men left and came to Laish. They saw that the people there were living in safety, like the Sidonians, peaceful and unsuspecting. They had everything they needed, and no one there was harming them. They lived far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone else.
When the men went back to Zorah and Eshtaol, their relatives asked them, "What did you find?"
They answered, "Come on, let us attack them! We have seen the land, and it is very good. Why are you sitting still? Do not wait. Go and take the land.
When you get there, you will find people who suspect nothing, and the land is large. God has given it into your hands, a land that has everything you could want."
So six hundred men of the tribe of Dan, armed for battle, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol.
On the way they camped near Kiriath Jearim in Judah. That is why the place west of Kiriath Jearim is still called Mahaneh Dan, which means Camp of Dan.
From there they went on to the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah's house.

Then the five men who had spied out the land of Laish said to their relatives, "Did you know that one of these houses has an ephod, household gods and a carved idol covered with silver? Now you know what to do."
So they turned in there and went to the house of the young Levite at Micah's place and greeted him.
The six hundred men of Dan, armed for battle, stood at the entrance of the gate.
The five men who had spied out the land went inside and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods, while the priest and the six hundred armed men stood at the entrance of the gate.
When the men went into Micah's house and took the idol, the ephod, the household gods and the silver image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"

They answered him, "Be quiet! Do not say a word. Come with us and be our father and priest. Is it not better for you to be priest for a whole tribe and clan in Israel than for just one man's household?"
The priest was very pleased. He took the ephod, the household gods and the idol and went along with the people.
They turned and set out again, putting their children, their animals and their belongings in front of them.
When they had gone some distance from Micah's house, the men who lived near Micah were called together and caught up with the people of Dan.
As they shouted after them, the people of Dan turned and said to Micah, "What is wrong with you, that you have called out your men to fight?"
He answered, "You took the gods I made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have? How can you ask, 'What is wrong with you?'"
The people of Dan answered, "Do not argue with us, or some angry men may attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives."
So the people of Dan went on their way. Micah saw that they were too strong for him, so he turned around and went home.
Then they took what Micah had made, and his priest, and went on to Laish, against a peaceful people who suspected nothing. They attacked them with swords and burned down their city.

There was no one to rescue them, because they lived far from Sidon and had no dealings with anyone else. The city was in a valley near Beth Rehob. The people of Dan rebuilt the city and settled there.
They named it Dan after their ancestor Dan, who was a son of Israel, though the city used to be called Laish.
There the people of Dan set up the idol for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the time the land was taken into captivity.
They kept using the idol Micah had made the whole time the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days Israel had no king. A Levite who lived in a remote area of the hill country of Ephraim took a concubine, a second wife, from Bethlehem in Judah.
But she was unfaithful to him. She left him and went back to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah. After she had been there four months,

her husband went to her to speak kindly to her and persuade her to come back. He took his servant and two donkeys with him. She took him into her father's house, and when her father saw him, he gladly welcomed him.
His father-in-law, the young woman's father, persuaded him to stay, so he stayed with him three days, eating and drinking and sleeping there.
On the fourth day they got up early, and he got ready to leave. But the young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Have something to eat first to give you strength. Then you can go."
So the two of them sat down to eat and drink together. Afterward the woman's father said, "Please stay tonight and enjoy yourself."
When the man got up to go, his father-in-law urged him to stay, so he stayed there that night too.
On the morning of the fifth day he got up early to leave, but the woman's father said, "Have something to eat to give you strength. Wait until afternoon!" So the two of them ate together.

Then the man, with his concubine and his servant, got up to leave. But his father-in-law, the young woman's father, said, "Look, it is almost evening. Please spend the night here. The day is nearly over. Stay and enjoy yourself. Early tomorrow morning you can get up and go home."
But the man did not want to stay another night. He got up and left, and went toward Jebus, which is Jerusalem, with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine.
When they were near Jebus and the day was almost gone, the servant said to his master, "Come, let us stop at this city of the Jebusites and spend the night."
His master replied, "No. We will not go into a city of foreigners, where the people are not Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah."
He added, "Come, let us try to reach Gibeah or Ramah and spend the night in one of those places."
So they went on, and the sun set as they came near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They stopped there to spend the night in Gibeah. They went and sat in the city square, but no one took them into their home for the night.
That evening an old man came in from his work in the fields. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah. The people of the place were from the tribe of Benjamin.
When he looked and saw the traveller in the city square, the old man asked, "Where are you going? Where did you come from?"

He answered, "We are on our way from Bethlehem in Judah to a remote area in the hill country of Ephraim, where I live. I have been to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD. No one has taken me into their house.
We have straw and food for our donkeys, and bread and wine for ourselves, for me, your servant woman, and the young man with us. We do not need anything."
"You are welcome at my house," the old man said. "Let me take care of whatever you need. Only do not spend the night in the square."
So he took him into his house and fed his donkeys. After they had washed their feet, they had something to eat and drink.

While they were enjoying themselves, some wicked men of the city surrounded the house. They pounded on the door and shouted to the old man who owned the house, "Bring out the man who came to your house so we can have sex with him."
The owner of the house went outside and said to them, "No, my friends, do not be so evil. This man is my guest. Do not do this terrible thing.
Look, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out to you now. You can abuse them and do whatever you want to them. But do not do such a terrible thing to this man."
But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them. They raped her and abused her all night, and at dawn they let her go.
At daybreak the woman went back to the house where her master was staying. She fell down at the door and lay there until it was light.
When her master got up in the morning and opened the door of the house to go on his way, there lay his concubine, fallen in the doorway, with her hands on the doorstep.
He said to her, "Get up. Let us go." But there was no answer. Then he put her on his donkey and set out for home.
When he reached home, he took a knife and cut her body into twelve parts, limb by limb, and sent them into all the areas of Israel.
Everyone who saw it was saying to one another, "Such a thing has never been seen or done, not since the day the Israelites came up out of Egypt. Just imagine! We must do something! So speak up!"
Then all the Israelites from Dan to Beersheba, and from the land of Gilead, came out together as one and gathered before the LORD at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people of the tribes of Israel took their places in the gathering of God's people. There were four hundred thousand soldiers on foot, armed with swords.
The people of Benjamin heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. Then the Israelites said, "Tell us how this terrible thing happened."
So the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, said, "My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
During the night the men of Gibeah came after me and surrounded the house, planning to kill me. They raped my concubine, and she died.
I took her body, cut it into pieces and sent one piece to each region of Israel's land, because they had done this evil and shameful thing in Israel.
Now, all you Israelites, speak up and tell me what you have decided."
All the people stood up together as one and said, "None of us will go home. Not one of us will return to his house.
This is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it as the lot decides.

We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, a hundred from every thousand, and a thousand from every ten thousand, to get supplies for the army. Then, when the army arrives at Gibeah in Benjamin, it can punish them for all the shameful things done in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered together against the city, united as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men all through the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this terrible crime that was done among you?
Now hand over those wicked men of Gibeah so that we can put them to death and remove this evil from Israel." But the people of Benjamin would not listen to their fellow Israelites.
Instead, they came from their towns and gathered at Gibeah to fight against the Israelites.
That day the people of Benjamin gathered twenty-six thousand swordsmen from their towns, besides seven hundred chosen men from those living in Gibeah.
Among all these soldiers there were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed. Each of them could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
Not counting Benjamin, Israel gathered four hundred thousand swordsmen, all of them trained fighters.
The Israelites went up to Bethel and asked God, "Which of us should go first to fight against the people of Benjamin?" The LORD replied, "Judah will go first."
The next morning the Israelites got up and camped near Gibeah.
The Israelites went out to fight the people of Benjamin and took up battle positions against them at Gibeah.
The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand Israelites on the battlefield that day.
But the men of Israel encouraged one another and again took up their positions where they had stood on the first day.

The Israelites went up and cried before the LORD until evening. They asked the LORD, "Shall we go up again to fight against our relatives, the people of Benjamin?" The LORD answered, "Go up against them."
So on the second day the Israelites went near to attack Benjamin.
This time, when the people of Benjamin came out from Gibeah to meet them, they killed another eighteen thousand Israelites, all of them armed with swords.

Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up to Bethel. There they sat crying before the LORD. They went without food that day until evening and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD.
And the Israelites asked the LORD what to do. In those days the covenant box of God was there,

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, served before it. They asked, "Shall we go up again to fight against our relatives, the people of Benjamin, or should we stop?" The LORD answered, "Go, because tomorrow I will give them into your hands."
Then Israel set men in hiding all around Gibeah.
On the third day they went up against the people of Benjamin and took up positions against Gibeah as they had done before.

The people of Benjamin came out to meet them and were drawn away from the city. They began to kill some of the Israelites as before, about thirty men, in the open field and on the roads, one leading to Bethel and the other to Gibeah.
The people of Benjamin said, "We are beating them as before." But the Israelites said, "Let us run away and draw them away from the city onto the roads."
All the men of Israel moved from their places and took up positions at Baal Tamar, and the Israelites in hiding rushed out of their places west of Gibeah.
Then ten thousand of Israel's best men attacked Gibeah. The fighting was very hard, and the people of Benjamin did not realise that disaster was close.
The LORD defeated Benjamin in front of Israel. That day the Israelites killed twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin, all armed with swords.
Then the people of Benjamin saw that they were beaten. The men of Israel had given way before Benjamin, because they were counting on the men they had hidden near Gibeah.
Those who had been hiding rushed suddenly into Gibeah, spread out and killed everyone in the city with the sword.
The men of Israel had agreed with those in hiding that they would send up a great cloud of smoke from the city as a signal.

Then the men of Israel would turn around in the battle. The people of Benjamin had begun to strike down the Israelites, about thirty of them, and they said, "We are beating them as in the first battle."
But when the column of smoke began to rise from the city, the people of Benjamin turned and saw the smoke of the whole city going up into the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned on them, and the men of Benjamin were terrified, because they saw that disaster had come on them.
So they ran from the Israelites toward the desert, but they could not escape the battle. And the men of Israel who came out of the towns cut them down there.
They surrounded the people of Benjamin, chased them and easily trampled them down in the area east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them brave fighters.

The rest turned and ran toward the desert to the rock of Rimmon. But the Israelites cut down five thousand men along the roads. They kept chasing them as far as Gidom and struck down two thousand more.
In all, twenty-five thousand men of Benjamin who carried swords fell that day, all of them brave fighters.
But six hundred men turned and ran into the desert to the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed four months.
The men of Israel went back to Benjamin's land and put all the towns to the sword, including the people, the animals and everything else they found. They set fire to every town they came to.
The men of Israel had made a promise at Mizpah: "None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a man from Benjamin."
The people went to Bethel, where they sat before God until evening, crying loudly and bitterly.
"LORD, God of Israel," they cried, "why has this happened to Israel? Why is one tribe missing from Israel today?"
Early the next day the people built an altar there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

Then the Israelites asked, "Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come to the gathering before the LORD?" They had made a solemn promise that anyone who did not come to the LORD at Mizpah must be put to death.
The Israelites felt sorry for their relatives, the people of Benjamin. "Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel," they said.
"How can we find wives for those who are left, since we have promised by the LORD not to give them any of our daughters in marriage?"
Then they asked, "Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come to the LORD at Mizpah?" They found that no one from Jabesh Gilead had come to the camp for the gathering.
When they counted the people, they found that none of the people of Jabesh Gilead were there.
So the community sent twelve thousand of their best fighting men with orders to go to Jabesh Gilead and kill everyone living there with the sword, including the women and children.
"This is what you must do," they said. "Kill every male and every woman who has slept with a man."
Among the people living in Jabesh Gilead they found four hundred young women who had never slept with a man, and they took them to the camp at Shiloh in Canaan.
Then the whole community sent a message of peace to the people of Benjamin at the rock of Rimmon.
So the men of Benjamin came back at that time and were given the women of Jabesh Gilead who had been spared. But there were not enough for all of them.
The people felt sorry for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a gap in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the community said, "The women of Benjamin have been killed. How can we find wives for the men who are left?
The survivors of Benjamin must have heirs," they said, "so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out.
But we cannot give them our daughters as wives, since we Israelites have promised, 'Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to a man from Benjamin.'
But look, there is the yearly festival of the LORD at Shiloh, north of Bethel, east of the road that goes from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
So they told the men of Benjamin, "Go and hide in the vineyards
and watch. When the young women of Shiloh come out to dance, rush out of the vineyards. Each of you catch a wife from the women of Shiloh and go home to the land of Benjamin.

When their fathers or brothers come to complain to us, we will say, 'Please be kind to them for our sake. We did not get wives for them in the war, and you did not give your daughters to them, so you are not guilty of breaking your promise.'"

So that is what the men of Benjamin did. Each man caught one of the young women as they were dancing and carried her off to be his wife. Then they went back to their own land, rebuilt their towns and settled in them.
At that time the Israelites left that place and went home to their own tribes and clans, each to their own land.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did whatever they thought was right.
Ruth: In the days when the judges led Israel, there was a famine in the land. So a man from Bethlehem in Judah went with his wife and two sons to live for a while in the country of Moab.
The man's name was Elimelek, his wife's name was Naomi, and his two sons were named Mahlon and Kilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went to Moab and lived there.
Then Elimelek, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
They married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other Ruth. After they had lived there about ten years,
both Mahlon and Kilion also died. Naomi was left alone, without her two sons and her husband.
While she was in Moab, Naomi heard that the LORD had come to help his people by giving them food again. So she and her daughters-in-law got ready to go back home from Moab.
With her two daughters-in-law she left the place where she had been living and set out on the road that would take them back to the land of Judah.
Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's home. May the LORD be kind to you, as you have been kind to your dead husbands and to me.
May the LORD give each of you rest in the home of a new husband." Then she kissed them goodbye, and they cried loudly
and said to her, "No! We will go back with you to your people."
But Naomi said, "Go home, my daughters. Why would you come with me? Am I going to have any more sons who could become your husbands?
Go home, my daughters. I am too old to have another husband. Even if I thought there was still hope for me, even if I had a husband tonight and then gave birth to sons,
would you wait until they grew up? Would you stay unmarried for them? No, my daughters. My life is much more bitter than yours, because the LORD's hand has turned against me!"
At this they cried loudly again. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth held on to her.
"Look," said Naomi, "your sister-in-law is going back to her people and her gods. Go back with her."
But Ruth replied, "Do not ask me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me severely if anything but death separates you and me."
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.
So the two women went on until they came to Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was stirred up because of them. The women said, "Can this be Naomi?"
"Do not call me Naomi, which means Pleasant," she told them. "Call me Mara, which means Bitter, because the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? The LORD has spoken against me. The Almighty has brought trouble on me."
So Naomi came back from Moab with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law. They arrived in Bethlehem as the barley harvest was beginning.
Naomi had a relative on her husband's side named Boaz. He was a rich and important man from the clan of Elimelek.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go out to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone who is kind to me." Naomi said to her, "Go ahead, my daughter."
So she went out and began picking up grain in the fields behind the harvest workers. As it happened, she ended up working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek.
Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted the harvest workers, "The LORD be with you!" "The LORD bless you!" they answered.
Boaz asked the man in charge of his workers, "Who does that young woman belong to?"
The man answered, "She is the Moabite woman who came back from Moab with Naomi.

She said, 'Please let me pick up the leftover grain from among the bundles behind the workers.' She came into the field and has kept working from morning till now, except for a short rest in the shelter."
So Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen to me, my daughter. Do not go and pick up grain in another field. Do not go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me.
Watch where the men are harvesting, and follow along behind the women. I have told the men not to touch you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled."
At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground. She asked him, "Why have you been so kind to notice me, a foreigner?"

Boaz replied, "I have been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband died. I know how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to find shelter."
"May I keep finding favour with you, my lord," she said. "You have comforted me and spoken kindly to me, your servant, even though I am not even one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here. Have some bread and dip it in the sauce." When she sat down with the harvest workers, he gave her some roasted grain. She ate all she wanted and had some left over.
When she got up to pick up grain again, Boaz told his men, "Let her pick up grain even among the bundles, and do not embarrass her.
Even pull out some stalks for her from the bundles and leave them for her to pick up. Do not tell her off."
So Ruth picked up grain in the field until evening. Then she beat out the barley she had gathered, and it came to about fifteen kilograms.
She carried it back to town, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gathered. Ruth also brought out and gave her what she had left over after she had eaten enough.

Her mother-in-law asked her, "Where did you pick up grain today? Where did you work? Blessed be the man who noticed you!" Then Ruth told her mother-in-law about the one at whose place she had been working. "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz," she said.

"The LORD bless him!" Naomi said to her daughter-in-law. "He has not stopped showing his kindness to the living and the dead." She added, "That man is our close relative. He is one of our family protectors, who can redeem us."
Then Ruth the Moabite said, "He even said to me, 'Stay with my workers until they finish harvesting all my grain.'"
Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, "It is good for you, my daughter, to go with the women who work for him. In someone else's field you might be harmed."
So Ruth stayed close to the women of Boaz to pick up grain until the barley and wheat harvests were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
One day Ruth's mother-in-law Naomi said to her, "My daughter, I must find a home for you, where you will be well cared for.
Boaz, whose women you have been working with, is our relative. Tonight he will be separating the barley from the chaff on the threshing floor.
So wash, put on perfume, and get dressed in your best clothes. Then go down to the threshing floor, but do not let him know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, notice the place where he is lying. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down. He will tell you what to do."
"I will do whatever you say," Ruth answered.
So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law told her to do.
When Boaz had finished eating and drinking and was in a good mood, he went to lie down at the far end of the pile of grain. Ruth went over quietly, uncovered his feet and lay down.
In the middle of the night something startled the man. He turned over, and there was a woman lying at his feet!
"Who are you?" he asked. "I am your servant Ruth," she said. "Spread the corner of your garment over me, because you are a family protector who can redeem me."
"The LORD bless you, my daughter," he replied. "This kindness is even greater than what you showed earlier. You have not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor.
And now, my daughter, do not be afraid. I will do for you all you ask. All the people of my town know that you are a woman of fine character.
It is true that I am a family protector who can redeem you, but there is another man who is a closer relative than I.

Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he wants to do his duty as your family protector, good. Let him redeem you. But if he is not willing, as surely as the LORD lives, I will do it. Lie here until morning."
So she lay at his feet until morning, but she got up before anyone could be recognised. He said, "No one must know that a woman came to the threshing floor."
He also said, "Bring me the shawl you are wearing and hold it out." When she did so, he poured six measures of barley into it and put it on her. Then he went back to town.
When Ruth came to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked, "How did it go, my daughter?" Then she told her everything Boaz had done for her
and added, "He gave me these six measures of barley, saying, 'Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'"
Then Naomi said, "Wait, my daughter, until you find out what happens. The man will not rest until the matter is settled today."

Meanwhile Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down there. Just then the family protector he had mentioned came along. Boaz said, "Come over here, my friend, and sit down." So he went over and sat down.
Boaz took ten of the elders of the town and said, "Sit here," and they did so.
Then he said to the family protector, "Naomi, who has come back from Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our relative Elimelek.

I thought I should tell you about it and suggest that you buy it in front of these people sitting here and in front of the elders of my people. If you will redeem it, do so. But if you will not, tell me, so I will know. No one has the right to do it except you, and I am next in line." "I will redeem it," he said.
Then Boaz said, "On the day you buy the land from Naomi, you also take Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's widow, so that the dead man's name stays with his property."
At this, the family protector said, "Then I cannot redeem it, because I might put my own property in danger. You redeem it yourself. I cannot do it."

In earlier times in Israel, this was the custom for redeeming and trading property: to make it final, one person took off a sandal and gave it to the other. This was how agreements were made official in Israel.
So the family protector said to Boaz, "Buy it yourself." And he took off his sandal.
Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "Today you are witnesses that I have bought from Naomi all the property of Elimelek, Kilion and Mahlon.

I have also taken Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's widow, as my wife, so that the dead man's name will stay with his property. Then his name will not disappear from among his family or from his hometown. Today you are witnesses!"

Then the elders and all the people at the gate said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman who is coming into your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the family of Israel. May you do well in Ephrathah and be famous in Bethlehem.
Through the children the LORD gives you by this young woman, may your family be like that of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah."
So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. When he made love to her, the LORD enabled her to become pregnant, and she gave birth to a son.
The women said to Naomi, "Praise the LORD, who today has not left you without a family protector. May he become famous in Israel!
He will give you new life and take care of you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."
Then Naomi took the child in her arms and cared for him.
The women living there said, "Naomi has a son!" And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
This is the family line of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron,
Hezron the father of Ram, Ram the father of Amminadab,
Amminadab the father of Nahshon, Nahshon the father of Salmon,
Salmon the father of Boaz, Boaz the father of Obed,
Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David.
1Sam: There was a man named Elkanah from Ramathaim Zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. He was the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, from the tribe of Ephraim.
He had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Every year Elkanah went up from his town to worship and offer sacrifices to the LORD of Heaven's Armies at Shiloh. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served there as priests of the LORD.
Whenever Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he gave shares of the meat to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But he gave Hannah a double share, because he loved her, even though the LORD had kept her from having children.
Because the LORD had kept her from having children, her rival Peninnah kept teasing her cruelly to upset her.
This went on year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, Peninnah teased her until she cried and would not eat.
Her husband Elkanah would say to her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why do you not eat? Why are you so sad? Do I not mean more to you than ten sons?"
Once, when they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh, Hannah stood up. Eli the priest was sitting on his chair by the doorpost of the LORD's house.
Deeply hurt, Hannah prayed to the LORD, crying bitterly.

She made a promise, saying, "LORD of Heaven's Armies, if you will only look at your servant's misery and remember me, and not forget your servant but give her a son, then I will give him to the LORD for his whole life. No razor will ever be used on his head."
As she kept on praying to the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was praying in her heart. Her lips were moving, but her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk.
He said to her, "How long are you going to stay drunk? Put away your wine!"
"That is not so, my lord," Hannah replied. "I am a woman who is deeply troubled. I have not been drinking wine or beer. I was pouring out my soul to the LORD.
Do not think your servant is a wicked woman. I have been praying here out of my great pain and sorrow."
Eli answered, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel give you what you have asked of him."
She said, "May your servant find favour in your eyes." Then she went on her way and ate something, and her face was no longer sad.
Early the next morning they got up and worshipped before the LORD, and then went back home to Ramah. Elkanah made love to his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In time Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, "Because I asked the LORD for him."
When her husband Elkanah went up with all his family to offer the yearly sacrifice to the LORD and to keep his promise,
Hannah did not go. She said to her husband, "After the boy stops nursing, I will take him and present him before the LORD, and he will live there always."

"Do what seems best to you," her husband Elkanah told her. "Stay here until you have stopped nursing him. Only may the LORD keep his word." So she stayed at home and nursed her son until she had stopped nursing him.

After he stopped nursing, she took the boy with her, young as he was, along with a three-year-old bull, about ten kilograms of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh.
When the bull had been sacrificed, they brought the boy to Eli.
Hannah said to him, "Please, my lord, as surely as you live, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this child, and the LORD has given me what I asked of him.
So now I give him to the LORD. For his whole life he will be given to the LORD." And they worshipped the LORD there.
Then Hannah prayed: "My heart is full of joy in the LORD. The LORD has made me strong. I can laugh at my enemies, because I am glad that you have saved me.
No one is holy like the LORD. There is no one besides you. There is no rock like our God.
Stop your proud talk. Do not let arrogant words come from your mouth. The LORD is a God who knows everything, and he weighs what people do.
The bows of the mighty warriors are broken, but those who stumbled are given strength.
Those who had plenty now work for food, but those who were hungry are hungry no more. The woman who could not have children has given birth to seven, but the woman with many sons pines away.
The LORD brings death and gives life. He brings people down to the grave and raises them up.
The LORD makes some poor and some rich. He brings some down and lifts others up.

He lifts the poor from the dust and raises the needy from the rubbish heap. He seats them with princes and gives them a place of honour. The foundations of the earth belong to the LORD, and on them he has set the world.
He will guard the steps of his faithful people, but the wicked will be silenced in darkness. No one wins by their own strength.
Those who oppose the LORD will be broken to pieces. He will thunder against them from heaven. The LORD will judge the whole earth. He will give strength to his king and make his chosen one strong."
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy stayed and served the LORD under Eli the priest.
Eli's sons were wicked men. They had no respect for the LORD.
This was how the priests treated the people: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come while the meat was boiling, holding a three-pronged fork.
He would stab it into the pan or kettle or pot, and the priest would take for himself whatever the fork brought up. They did this to all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the person offering the sacrifice, "Give the priest some meat to roast. He will not take boiled meat from you, only raw."
If the person said to him, "Let the fat be burned first, and then take whatever you want," the servant would answer, "No, give it to me now. If you do not, I will take it by force."
The sin of these young men was very great in the LORD's eyes, because they treated the LORD's offering with contempt.
But Samuel served before the LORD. He was a boy wearing a linen ephod, a priest's vest.
Each year his mother made him a little robe and took it to him when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, "May the LORD give you children by this woman to take the place of the one she prayed for and gave to the LORD." Then they would go home.
And the LORD was kind to Hannah. She became pregnant and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.
Now Eli was very old. He heard about everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they slept with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
So he said to them, "Why do you do such things? I hear from all the people about the evil things you are doing.
No, my sons. The report I hear spreading among the LORD's people is not good. You are leading them into sin.

If one person sins against another, God may help settle it. But if someone sins against the LORD, who will speak for them?" But his sons did not listen to their father, because the LORD had decided to put them to death.
And the boy Samuel kept growing, and he was liked more and more by the LORD and by the people.
Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him, "This is what the LORD says: 'Did I not clearly show myself to your ancestor's family when they were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt?

I chose your ancestor out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before me. I also gave your ancestor's family all the food offerings the Israelites burn.

So why do you treat with contempt the sacrifices and offerings I commanded for my house? Why do you honour your sons more than me by making yourselves fat on the best parts of every offering made by my people Israel?'

So the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I did promise that your family would serve me as priests forever.' But now the LORD says: 'Never again! I will honour those who honour me, but those who despise me will be treated with contempt.
The time is coming when I will cut short your strength and the strength of your family, so that no one in your family will live to old age.
You will see trouble in my house. Even though good things will be done for Israel, no one in your family will ever live to old age.
Every one of you that I do not cut off from serving at my altar will only bring tears to your eyes and sadness to your heart. All your descendants will die in the prime of life.
What happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will be a sign to you: they will both die on the same day.
I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and mind. I will give him a family that lasts, and they will serve my chosen king forever.
Then everyone left in your family will come and bow down before him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread. They will beg, "Please give me some priestly work so I can have food to eat."'"
The boy Samuel served the LORD under Eli. In those days messages from the LORD were rare, and there were not many visions.
One night Eli, whose eyes had become so weak that he could hardly see, was lying down in his usual place.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the house of the LORD, where the covenant box of God was.
Then the LORD called Samuel. Samuel answered, "Here I am."
He ran to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." But Eli said, "I did not call you. Go back and lie down." So he went and lay down.
Again the LORD called, "Samuel!" And Samuel got up and went to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." "My son," Eli said, "I did not call. Go back and lie down."
Samuel did not yet know the LORD. The word of the LORD had not yet been shown to him.
The LORD called Samuel a third time, and Samuel got up and went to Eli and said, "Here I am. You called me." Then Eli realised that the LORD was calling the boy.
So Eli told Samuel, "Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The LORD came and stood there, calling as before, "Samuel! Samuel!" Then Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant is listening."
And the LORD said to Samuel, "Look, I am about to do something in Israel that will make the ears of everyone who hears about it tingle.
At that time I will carry out against Eli everything I said about his family, from beginning to end.
I told him that I would punish his family forever because of the sin he knew about. His sons made themselves cursed, and he did not stop them.
So I swore to the family of Eli, 'The sin of Eli's family will never be paid for by sacrifice or offering.'"
Samuel lay down until morning, and then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He was afraid to tell Eli about the vision,
but Eli called him and said, "Samuel, my son." Samuel answered, "Here I am."
"What was it he said to you?" Eli asked. "Do not hide it from me. May God punish you severely if you hide from me anything he told you."
So Samuel told him everything, hiding nothing from him. Then Eli said, "He is the LORD. Let him do what he thinks is best."
The LORD was with Samuel as he grew up, and he made all of Samuel's words come true.
And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was truly a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD kept appearing at Shiloh, and there he showed himself to Samuel through his word.
And Samuel's word came to all Israel. Now the Israelites went out to fight against the Philistines. The Israelites camped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines at Aphek.
The Philistines lined up for battle to face Israel. As the battle spread, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who killed about four thousand of them on the battlefield.

When the soldiers came back to camp, the elders of Israel asked, "Why did the LORD let the Philistines defeat us today? Let us bring the covenant box of the LORD here from Shiloh, so that it may go with us and save us from our enemies."

So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought back the covenant box of the LORD of Heaven's Armies, who sits on his throne between the cherubim. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the covenant box of God.
When the covenant box of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave such a loud shout that the ground shook.
Hearing the noise, the Philistines asked, "What is all this shouting in the Hebrew camp?" When they learned that the box of the LORD had come into the camp,
the Philistines were afraid. "A god has come into their camp," they said. "Oh no! Nothing like this has happened before.
We are in trouble! Who will save us from the power of these mighty gods? They are the gods who struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the desert.
Be strong, Philistines! Be men, or you will become slaves of the Hebrews, as they have been your slaves. Be men, and fight!"
So the Philistines fought, and the Israelites were defeated, and every man ran back to his tent. It was a terrible defeat. Israel lost thirty thousand foot soldiers.
The box of God was captured, and Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
That same day a man from the tribe of Benjamin ran from the battle line and went to Shiloh. His clothes were torn, and there was dust on his head.

When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his chair by the side of the road, watching, because his heart was worried about the box of God. When the man came into the town and told what had happened, the whole town cried out.
Eli heard the crying and asked, "What is all this noise?" The man hurried over to Eli
who was ninety-eight years old and whose eyes had stopped working so that he could not see.
He told Eli, "I have just come from the battle line. I ran from it this very day." Eli asked, "What happened, my son?"

The man who brought the news replied, "Israel ran away from the Philistines, and the army has suffered heavy losses. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the box of God has been captured."
When he mentioned the box of God, Eli fell backward off his chair by the side of the gate. His neck was broken, and he died, because he was old and heavy. He had led Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near the time of birth. When she heard the news that the box of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she went into labour and gave birth, overcome by her pains.
As she was dying, the women helping her said, "Do not be afraid. You have given birth to a son." But she did not answer or pay any attention.
She named the boy Ichabod, which means No Glory, saying, "The glory has left Israel." She said this because the box of God had been captured and because her father-in-law and her husband had died.
She said, "The glory has left Israel, because the box of God has been captured."
After the Philistines captured the box of God, they took it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
They carried the box of God into the temple of their god Dagon and set it beside Dagon's statue.
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next day, there was Dagon, fallen on his face on the ground in front of the box of the LORD. They lifted Dagon up and put him back in his place.

But the next morning when they got up, there was Dagon, fallen on his face on the ground again in front of the box of the LORD. His head and hands had been broken off and were lying in the doorway. Only his body was left.
That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and everyone who enters Dagon's temple in Ashdod do not step on the doorway.
The LORD's hand was heavy on the people of Ashdod and the villages around it. He brought disaster on them and struck them with painful swellings.
When the people of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, "The box of the God of Israel must not stay here with us, because his hand is heavy on us and on our god Dagon."

So they called together all the rulers of the Philistines and asked them, "What shall we do with the box of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Move the box of the God of Israel to Gath." So they moved the box of the God of Israel there.
But after they had moved it, the LORD's hand was against that city, throwing it into a great panic. He struck the people of the city, young and old, with an outbreak of swellings.
So they sent the box of God to Ekron. As it was coming into Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought the box of the God of Israel to us to kill us and our people!"

So they called together all the rulers of the Philistines and said, "Send the box of the God of Israel away. Let it go back to its own place, or it will kill us and our people." Deadly panic had filled the city. God's hand was very heavy on it.
Those who did not die were struck with swellings, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
The box of the LORD had been in Philistine land for seven months.
Then the Philistines called for their priests and fortune-tellers and asked, "What shall we do with the box of the LORD? Tell us how we should send it back to its place."

They answered, "If you send back the box of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty. Be sure to send a guilt offering to him. Then you will be healed, and you will understand why his hand has not turned away from you."

The Philistines asked, "What guilt offering should we send to him?" They replied, "Five gold swellings and five gold rats, one for each of the five Philistine rulers, because the same plague has struck both you and your rulers.
Make models of the swellings and of the rats that are ruining the country, and give honour to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lift his hand from you and your gods and your land.
Why make your hearts stubborn as the Egyptians and Pharaoh did? When God had dealt harshly with them, did they not let the Israelites go on their way?
Now then, get a new cart ready, with two cows that have had calves and have never been yoked. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves away and pen them up.
Take the box of the LORD and put it on the cart. Beside it, put a chest with the gold objects you are sending him as a guilt offering. Then send it on its way,

and watch. If it goes up toward its own land, toward Beth Shemesh, then the LORD has brought this great disaster on us. But if it does not, then we will know that it was not his hand that struck us. It just happened by chance."
So they did this. They took two cows that had calves, hitched them to the cart and penned up their calves.
They put the box of the LORD on the cart, together with the chest holding the gold rats and the models of the swellings.

Then the cows went straight up toward Beth Shemesh. They kept on the road, mooing all the way, and did not turn to the right or to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the border of Beth Shemesh.
The people of Beth Shemesh were harvesting their wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the box, they were overjoyed.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stopped there beside a large rock. The people chopped up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the box of the LORD, together with the chest holding the gold objects, and placed them on the large rock. That day the people of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices to the LORD.
The five rulers of the Philistines saw all this and then went back to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold swellings the Philistines sent as a guilt offering to the LORD: one each for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron.

And the number of the gold rats matched the number of Philistine towns belonging to the five rulers, both the walled cities and the country villages. The large rock where they set the box of the LORD is still a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.

But God struck down some of the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the box of the LORD. He struck down fifty thousand and seventy of them. The people mourned because of the terrible blow the LORD had dealt them.
The people of Beth Shemesh asked, "Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God? Where can the box go from here?"
Then they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath Jearim, saying, "The Philistines have sent back the box of the LORD. Come down and take it up to your town."
So the men of Kiriath Jearim came and took the box of the LORD up to Abinadab's house on the hill. They set apart his son Eleazar to guard the box of the LORD.
The box stayed at Kiriath Jearim a long time, twenty years in all. And all the people of Israel turned back to the LORD with sorrow.

Samuel said to all the people of Israel, "If you are really coming back to the LORD with all your hearts, get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths among you. Give yourselves completely to the LORD and serve him only, and he will save you from the Philistines."
So the Israelites got rid of their Baals and Ashtoreths and served the LORD only.
Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you."

When they had gathered at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out before the LORD. That day they went without food and confessed, "We have sinned against the LORD." Samuel was leading Israel as judge at Mizpah.
When the Philistines heard that Israel had gathered at Mizpah, their rulers came up to attack them. When the Israelites heard about it, they were afraid of the Philistines.
They said to Samuel, "Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, so that he will save us from the Philistines."
Then Samuel took a young lamb and offered it whole as a burnt offering to the LORD. He cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to attack Israel. But that day the LORD thundered with loud thunder against the Philistines and threw them into such panic that they were defeated by Israel.
The men of Israel rushed out of Mizpah and chased the Philistines, striking them down all the way to a place below Beth Kar.
Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, which means Stone of Help, saying, "Until now the LORD has helped us."
So the Philistines were defeated, and they stopped coming into Israel's land. As long as Samuel lived, the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines.

The towns the Philistines had taken from Israel, from Ekron to Gath, were given back to Israel, and Israel took back the land around them from the Philistines. There was also peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel continued as Israel's judge all the days of his life.
Every year he travelled around from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, judging Israel in all those places.
Then he would go back to Ramah, where his home was, and he led Israel from there too. And he built an altar there to the LORD.
When Samuel grew old, he made his sons judges over Israel.
His oldest son was named Joel and his second son Abijah. They served as judges at Beersheba.
But his sons did not live the way he did. They were greedy for money. They took bribes and twisted justice.
So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, "You are old, and your sons do not live the way you do. Now give us a king to lead us, like all the other nations have."
But when they said, "Give us a king to lead us," Samuel was unhappy. So he prayed to the LORD.
The LORD told him, "Listen to everything the people are saying to you. It is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected me as their king.
They are doing to you what they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until now. They have left me and served other gods.
So listen to them. But warn them seriously, and let them know what the king who rules over them will do."
Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said, "This is what the king who rules over you will do: He will take your sons and make them serve with his chariots and horses, and they will run in front of his chariots.
He will make some of them commanders of thousands and of fifties. Others will plough his fields and harvest his crops, and others will make weapons of war and parts for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to make perfume and to cook and bake.
He will take the best of your fields, vineyards and olive groves and give them to his officials.
He will take a tenth of your grain and of your grapes and give it to his officers and officials.
He will take your male and female servants, your best young men and your donkeys, and use them for his own work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
When that day comes, you will cry out because of the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you in that day."
But the people refused to listen to Samuel. "No!" they said. "We want a king over us.
Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to lead us and to go out in front of us and fight our battles."
When Samuel heard everything the people said, he repeated it to the LORD.
The LORD answered, "Listen to them and give them a king." Then Samuel said to the Israelites, "Everyone go back to your own town."
There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bekorath, son of Aphiah. He was an important and wealthy man.
Kish had a son named Saul, a fine young man. No one in Israel was more handsome than he was, and he was a head taller than anyone else.
One day the donkeys belonging to Saul's father Kish got lost. So Kish said to his son Saul, "Take one of the servants with you and go and look for the donkeys."

So Saul went through the hill country of Ephraim and the area around Shalisha, but they did not find them. They went on into the area of Shaalim, but the donkeys were not there. Then he went through the land of Benjamin, but they still did not find them.
When they reached the area of Zuph, Saul said to the servant with him, "Come, let us go back home, or my father will stop thinking about the donkeys and start worrying about us."
But the servant replied, "Look, in this town there is a man of God. He is highly respected, and everything he says comes true. Let us go there now. Maybe he will tell us which way to go."
Saul said to his servant, "If we go, what can we give the man? The food in our bags is gone. We have no gift to take to the man of God. What do we have?"
The servant answered him again. "Look," he said, "I have a quarter of a shekel of silver. I will give it to the man of God so that he will tell us which way to go."
In the past in Israel, if someone went to ask God something, they would say, "Come, let us go to the seer," because the prophet of today used to be called a seer.
"Good," Saul said to his servant. "Come, let us go." So they set out for the town where the man of God lived.
As they were going up the hill to the town, they met some young women coming out to get water, and they asked them, "Is the seer here?"
"He is," they answered. "He is just ahead of you. Hurry, he has just come to our town today, because the people have a sacrifice at the place of worship on the hill.

As soon as you enter the town, you will find him before he goes up to the hill to eat. The people will not start eating until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice. After that, those who are invited will eat. Go up now. You should find him about this time."
So they went up to the town, and as they were entering it, there was Samuel, coming toward them on his way up to the place of worship.
The day before Saul came, the LORD had told Samuel,

"About this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him as ruler over my people Israel. He will save my people from the Philistines. I have looked on my people, because their cry has reached me."
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD said to him, "This is the man I told you about. He will rule my people."
Saul came up to Samuel in the gateway and asked, "Please tell me where the seer's house is."
"I am the seer," Samuel replied. "Go up ahead of me to the place of worship, because today you are to eat with me. In the morning I will let you go and will tell you everything that is on your mind.
As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them. They have been found. And who is all Israel longing for? Is it not you and your father's whole family?"
Saul answered, "But I am from Benjamin, the smallest tribe of Israel, and my clan is the least important of all the clans of Benjamin. Why do you say such a thing to me?"
Then Samuel brought Saul and his servant into the hall and seated them at the head of the guests, about thirty people in all.
Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the piece of meat I gave you, the one I told you to set aside."

So the cook took up the thigh with what was on it and set it in front of Saul. Samuel said, "Here is what was kept for you. Eat, because it was set aside for you for this occasion, from the time I said, 'I have invited guests.'" And Saul ate with Samuel that day.
After they came down from the place of worship to the town, Samuel talked with Saul on the flat roof of his house.
They got up about daybreak, and Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Get ready, and I will send you on your way." When Saul got ready, he and Samuel went outside together.

As they were going down to the edge of the town, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us." The servant did so, and Samuel said, "But you stay here for a while, so that I may give you a message from God."
Then Samuel took a small jar of olive oil and poured it on Saul's head and kissed him, saying, "The LORD has anointed you as ruler over his people.

When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel's tomb at Zelzah, on the border of Benjamin. They will say to you, 'The donkeys you went to look for have been found. Now your father has stopped thinking about them and is worried about you. He is asking, What shall I do about my son?'

Then you will go on from there until you reach the big oak tree at Tabor. Three men going up to worship God at Bethel will meet you there. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.
They will greet you and offer you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from them.

After that you will go to Gibeah of God, where there is a Philistine army camp. As you come near the town, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the place of worship on the hill. They will be playing harps, tambourines, flutes and lyres, and they will be prophesying.
The Spirit of the LORD will come powerfully on you, and you will prophesy with them. You will be changed into a different person.
Once these signs have happened, do whatever needs to be done, because God is with you.
Go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will surely come down to you to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. But you must wait seven days until I come to you and tell you what to do."
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul's heart, and all these signs came true that day.
When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him. The Spirit of God came powerfully on him, and he joined in their prophesying.
When all those who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked each other, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
A man who lived there answered, "And who is their father?" So it became a saying: "Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
After Saul stopped prophesying, he went to the place of worship.
Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, "Where have you been?" "Looking for the donkeys," he said. "But when we saw they could not be found, we went to Samuel."
Saul's uncle said, "Tell me what Samuel said to you."
Saul replied, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But he did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about becoming king.
Samuel called the people of Israel together before the LORD at Mizpah.
He said to them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I saved you from the power of Egypt and of all the kingdoms that crushed you.'

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your disasters and troubles. You have said, 'No, set a king over us.' So now, present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and clans."
When Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, the tribe of Benjamin was chosen by lot.
Then he brought the tribe of Benjamin forward clan by clan, and Matri's clan was chosen. Finally Saul son of Kish was chosen. But when they looked for him, he was nowhere to be found.
So they asked the LORD, "Has the man come here yet?" And the LORD said, "Yes, he has hidden himself among the supplies."
They ran and brought him out, and as he stood among the people he was a head taller than any of the others.
Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the man the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." Then the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
Samuel explained to the people the rights and duties of a king. He wrote them down in a book and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to their own home.
Saul also went home to Gibeah, together with a group of brave men whose hearts God had touched.
But some worthless people said, "How can this man save us?" They looked down on him and brought him no gifts. But Saul kept quiet.
Nahash the Ammonite came up and surrounded Jabesh Gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."
But Nahash the Ammonite replied, "I will make a treaty with you only on one condition: that I gouge out the right eye of every one of you, and so bring shame on all Israel."
The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days so we can send messengers all through Israel. If no one comes to save us, we will surrender to you."
When the messengers came to Gibeah, where Saul lived, and told the people these terms, they all cried loudly.
Just then Saul was coming in from the fields behind his oxen, and he asked, "What is wrong with everyone? Why are they crying?" Then they told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God came powerfully on him, and he burned with anger.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent the pieces by messengers all through Israel, saying, "This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not follow Saul and Samuel." Then the fear of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out together as one.
When Saul counted them at Bezek, there were three hundred thousand men from Israel and thirty thousand from Judah.

They told the messengers who had come, "Say to the men of Jabesh Gilead, 'By the time the sun is hot tomorrow, you will be saved.'" When the messengers went and told this to the men of Jabesh, they were overjoyed.
They said to the Ammonites, "Tomorrow we will surrender to you, and you can do to us whatever you like."

The next day Saul divided his men into three groups. Before dawn they broke into the camp of the Ammonites and slaughtered them until the hottest part of the day. Those who survived were scattered so that no two of them were left together.
Then the people said to Samuel, "Who was it that asked, 'Shall Saul rule over us?' Bring them here, and we will put them to death."
But Saul said, "No one will be put to death today, because this day the LORD has saved Israel."
Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there confirm Saul as king again."
So all the people went to Gilgal and made Saul king in the presence of the LORD. There they offered peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites celebrated with great joy.
Samuel said to all Israel, "I have listened to everything you asked of me, and I have given you a king.
Now you have a king to lead you. As for me, I am old and grey, and my sons are here with you. I have been your leader from my youth until now.

Here I stand. Speak against me in the presence of the LORD and his chosen king. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated? Whom have I crushed? From whom have I taken a bribe to look the other way? If I have done any of these things, I will pay it back."
They answered, "You have not cheated us or crushed us. You have not taken anything from anyone."
Samuel said to them, "The LORD is a witness against you, and his chosen king is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand." "He is a witness," they said.
Then Samuel said to the people, "It was the LORD who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors up out of Egypt.
Now stand here, because I am going to bring a case against you before the LORD, reminding you of all the good things the LORD has done for you and your ancestors.
After Jacob went to Egypt, your ancestors cried out to the LORD for help. The LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your ancestors out of Egypt and settled them in this place.
But they forgot the LORD their God. So he sold them to Sisera, the commander of the army of Hazor, and to the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them.
They cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned. We have left the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. But now save us from our enemies, and we will serve you.'
Then the LORD sent Jerub-Baal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel. He saved you from your enemies all around you, so that you lived in safety.
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was coming against you, you said to me, 'No, we want a king to rule over us,' even though the LORD your God was your king.
Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you asked for. Look, the LORD has set a king over you.
If you honour the LORD and serve and obey him, and do not rebel against his commands, and if both you and the king who rules over you follow the LORD your God, all will be well.
But if you do not obey the LORD, and if you rebel against his commands, his hand will be against you, as it was against your ancestors.
Now then, stand still and see this great thing the LORD is about to do before your eyes!
Is it not wheat harvest now? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain. Then you will realise what an evil thing you did in the eyes of the LORD when you asked for a king."
Then Samuel called on the LORD, and that same day the LORD sent thunder and rain. So all the people were filled with fear of the LORD and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, "Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die. We have added to all our other sins the evil of asking for a king."
"Do not be afraid," Samuel replied. "You have done all this evil, yet do not turn away from the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not turn away after useless idols. They cannot help you or save you, because they are useless.
For the sake of his great name the LORD will not reject his people, because the LORD was pleased to make you his own.
As for me, I will never sin against the LORD by stopping my prayers for you. And I will teach you the way that is good and right.
But be sure to honour the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. Think of the great things he has done for you.
But if you keep on doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away."
Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he ruled over Israel for forty-two years.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with him at Mikmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with his son Jonathan at Gibeah in Benjamin. He sent the rest of the men back home.
Jonathan attacked the Philistine camp at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Then Saul had the trumpet blown all through the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear!"
All Israel heard the news: "Saul has attacked the Philistine camp, and now Israel has become hateful to the Philistines." So the people were called to join Saul at Gilgal.
The Philistines gathered to fight Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and soldiers as many as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Mikmash, east of Beth Aven.
When the Israelites saw that they were in danger and their army was hard pressed, they hid in caves and bushes, among the rocks, and in pits and holes in the ground.
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed at Gilgal, and all the soldiers with him were trembling with fear.
He waited seven days, the time set by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and Saul's men began to leave him.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.
Just as he finished offering it, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him.
"What have you done?" asked Samuel. Saul replied, "When I saw that the men were leaving me, and that you did not come at the set time, and that the Philistines were gathering at Mikmash,
I thought, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not asked the LORD for his help.' So I felt I had to offer the burnt offering."
"You have acted foolishly," Samuel said. "You have not kept the command the LORD your God gave you. If you had, he would have made your kingdom over Israel last forever.
But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart and has chosen him to lead his people, because you have not kept the LORD's command."
Then Samuel left Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the men who were with him. There were about six hundred.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the men with them were staying at Geba in Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Mikmash.
Raiding groups went out from the Philistine camp in three groups. One turned toward Ophrah in the area of Shual,
another toward Beth Horon, and the third toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboyim, facing the desert.
Not a single blacksmith could be found in the whole land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, "Otherwise the Hebrews will make swords or spears!"
So all the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to have their ploughs, hoes, axes and sickles sharpened.
The price was two-thirds of a shekel for sharpening ploughs and hoes, and a third of a shekel for sharpening forks and axes and for fixing ox sticks.
So on the day of the battle, not one of the soldiers with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear in his hand. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
Now a group of Philistine soldiers had gone out to the pass at Mikmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his weapons, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine camp on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the edge of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree in Migron. About six hundred men were with him.
Among them was Ahijah, who was wearing an ephod. He was a son of Ichabod's brother Ahitub, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the LORD's priest at Shiloh. No one knew that Jonathan had left.
On each side of the pass that Jonathan planned to cross to reach the Philistine camp there was a steep cliff. One was called Bozez and the other Seneh.
One cliff stood to the north toward Mikmash, the other to the south toward Geba.

Jonathan said to his young weapon carrier, "Come, let us go over to the camp of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act for us. Nothing can stop the LORD from saving, whether by many people or by few."
"Do all that you have in mind," his weapon carrier said. "Go ahead. I am with you heart and soul."
Jonathan said, "Come on, then. We will cross over toward the men and let them see us.
If they say to us, 'Wait there until we come to you,' we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' we will climb up, because that will be our sign that the LORD has given them into our hands."
So both of them showed themselves to the Philistine camp. "Look!" said the Philistines. "The Hebrews are crawling out of the holes they were hiding in."

The men of the camp shouted to Jonathan and his weapon carrier, "Come up to us and we will teach you a lesson." So Jonathan said to his weapon carrier, "Climb up after me. The LORD has given them into the hands of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up, using his hands and feet, with his weapon carrier right behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his weapon carrier killed them behind him.
In that first attack Jonathan and his weapon carrier killed about twenty men in an area about half the size of a small field.
Then panic struck the whole Philistine army, in the camp and in the field. Even the soldiers in the camp and the raiding groups trembled. The ground shook. It was a panic sent by God.
Saul's lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the army running in every direction.
Then Saul said to the men with him, "Count the troops and see who has left us." When they counted, they found that Jonathan and his weapon carrier were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the box of God here." At that time it was with the Israelites.
While Saul was talking to the priest, the noise in the Philistine camp grew louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, "Stop what you are doing."
Then Saul and all his men gathered and went into battle. They found the Philistines in total confusion, striking each other with their swords.
Some Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, and had gone up with them to their camp, now changed sides and joined the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
All the Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were running away, and they joined the battle and chased after them.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved on past Beth Aven.

Now the Israelites were exhausted that day, because Saul had made the army take an oath, saying, "Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening comes, before I have taken revenge on my enemies!" So none of the troops tasted food.
The whole army entered the woods, and there was honey on the ground.
When they went into the woods, they saw the honey dripping, but no one dared to put any in their mouth, because they were afraid of the oath.
