But Jonathan had not heard that his father had made the army take the oath. So he reached out the end of the stick in his hand and dipped it into the honeycomb. He raised his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the soldiers told him, "Your father made the army take a strict oath, saying, 'Cursed be anyone who eats food today!' That is why the men are so weak."
Jonathan said, "My father has made trouble for the country. See how my eyes brightened when I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better it would have been if the men had eaten today some of the food they took from their enemies. Then we would have killed many more Philistines!"
That day, after the Israelites had struck down the Philistines from Mikmash to Aijalon, they were exhausted.
They rushed at the things they had taken and grabbed sheep, cattle and calves. They killed them on the ground and ate the meat with the blood still in it.
Then someone said to Saul, "Look, the men are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with blood still in it." "You have broken faith," Saul said. "Roll a large stone over here at once."

Then he said, "Go out among the men and tell them, 'Each of you bring me your cattle and sheep, and kill them here and eat them. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with blood still in it.'" So that night everyone brought his ox and killed it there.
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and rob them until dawn. Let us not leave one of them alive." "Do whatever seems best to you," they replied. But the priest said, "Let us ask God here first."
So Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into Israel's hands?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul then said, "Come here, all you leaders of the army. Let us find out what sin has been done today.
As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it was my son Jonathan, he must die." But not one of the men said a word.
Saul then said to all the Israelites, "You stand over there. I and my son Jonathan will stand over here." "Do what seems best to you," the men replied.
Then Saul prayed to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Show us the right answer." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the men were cleared.
Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and Jonathan my son." And Jonathan was taken.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." So Jonathan told him, "I only tasted a little honey with the end of my stick. And now I must die!"
Saul said, "May God punish me severely if you do not die, Jonathan."

But the men said to Saul, "Should Jonathan die, the one who has won this great victory for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, because he did this today with God's help." So the men rescued Jonathan, and he was not put to death.
Then Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and they went back to their own land.
After Saul became king over Israel, he fought against his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he punished them.
He fought bravely and defeated the Amalekites, saving Israel from those who had robbed them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi and Malki-Shua. His older daughter was named Merab, and the younger one Michal.
His wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of Saul's army was Abner son of Ner, who was Saul's uncle.
Saul's father Kish and Abner's father Ner were sons of Abiel.
All Saul's life there was bitter war with the Philistines. Whenever Saul saw a strong or brave man, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, "I am the one the LORD sent to anoint you king over his people Israel. So listen now to the message from the LORD.
This is what the LORD of Heaven's Armies says: 'I will punish the Amalekites for what they did to Israel when they attacked them on the way up from Egypt.
Now go and attack the Amalekites and completely destroy everything that belongs to them. Do not spare them. Put to death men and women, children and babies, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.'"
So Saul called the army together at Telaim and counted them: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, plus ten thousand from Judah.
Saul went to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley.

Then he said to the Kenites, "Go away. Leave the Amalekites so that I do not destroy you along with them, because you were kind to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.
Then Saul attacked the Amalekites all the way from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt.
He captured Agag king of the Amalekites alive, and he completely destroyed all his people with the sword.

But Saul and the army spared Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, everything that was good. They were not willing to destroy them completely. But everything that was worthless and weak they destroyed.
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel:
"I am sorry that I made Saul king, because he has turned away from me and has not carried out my commands." Samuel was upset, and he cried out to the LORD all that night.
Early in the morning Samuel got up and went to meet Saul. But he was told, "Saul has gone to Carmel. There he has set up a monument in his own honour, and then he went on down to Gilgal."
When Samuel reached him, Saul said, "The LORD bless you! I have carried out the LORD's commands."
But Samuel said, "Then what is this bleating of sheep in my ears? What is this mooing of cattle that I hear?"
Saul answered, "The soldiers brought them from the Amalekites. They spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God, but we completely destroyed the rest."
"Enough!" Samuel said to Saul. "Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." "Tell me," Saul replied.
Samuel said, "Although you once thought of yourself as unimportant, did you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
And he sent you on a mission, saying, 'Go and completely destroy those sinners, the Amalekites. Fight against them until you have wiped them out.'
Why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush at the plunder and do evil in the LORD's eyes?"
"But I did obey the LORD," Saul said. "I went on the mission the LORD gave me. I completely destroyed the Amalekites and brought back Agag their king.
The soldiers took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what was set apart for destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal."
But Samuel replied, "Does the LORD take as much pleasure in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the LORD? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen is better than the fat of rams.
Rebellion is as sinful as witchcraft, and stubbornness is as bad as worshipping idols. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you as king."
Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned. I broke the LORD's command and your instructions. I was afraid of the people, so I gave in to them.
Now please forgive my sin and come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD."
But Samuel said to him, "I will not go back with you. You have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel!"
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to one of your neighbours, someone better than you.
He who is the Glory of Israel does not lie or change his mind, because he is not a human being who changes his mind."
Saul replied, "I have sinned. But please honour me in front of the elders of my people and in front of Israel. Come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God."
So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshipped the LORD.
Then Samuel said, "Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites." Agag came to him confidently, thinking, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."
But Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women." And Samuel put Agag to death before the LORD at Gilgal.
Then Samuel left for Ramah, and Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel never went to see Saul again until the day he died, but he was sad about Saul. And the LORD was sorry that he had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you be sad about Saul, now that I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I have chosen one of his sons to be king."
But Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears about it, he will kill me." The LORD said, "Take a young cow with you and say, 'I have come to offer a sacrifice to the LORD.'
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. You are to anoint for me the one I point out to you."
Samuel did what the LORD said. When he arrived at Bethlehem, the elders of the town came out trembling to meet him. They asked, "Have you come in peace?"

Samuel replied, "Yes, in peace. I have come to offer a sacrifice to the LORD. Make yourselves holy and come to the sacrifice with me." Then he made Jesse and his sons holy and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and thought, "Surely this is the one the LORD has chosen, standing here before the LORD."

But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look at how handsome or tall he is, because I have rejected him. The LORD does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart."
Then Jesse called Abinadab and had him walk in front of Samuel. But Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Then Jesse had Shammah walk by, but Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Jesse had seven of his sons walk in front of Samuel, but Samuel said to him, "The LORD has not chosen any of these."

So he asked Jesse, "Are these all the sons you have?" "There is still the youngest," Jesse answered. "He is looking after the sheep." Samuel said, "Send for him. We will not sit down to eat until he arrives."
So Jesse sent for him and brought him in. He had a healthy, glowing look, with fine eyes and a handsome face. Then the LORD said, "Get up and anoint him. This is the one."
So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in front of his brothers. From that day on, the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on David. Then Samuel went back to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of the LORD had left Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD tormented him.
Saul's servants said to him, "Look, an evil spirit from God is tormenting you.
Let our lord command his servants here to look for someone who plays the harp well. When the evil spirit from God comes on you, he will play, and you will feel better."
So Saul said to his servants, "Find someone who plays well and bring him to me."

One of the servants answered, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp. He is a brave man and a warrior. He speaks well and is a fine-looking man. And the LORD is with him."
Then Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me your son David, who is with the sheep."
So Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine and a young goat, and sent them with his son David to Saul.
David came to Saul and started serving him. Saul liked him very much, and David became one of his weapon carriers.
Then Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, "Let David stay in my service, because I am pleased with him."
Whenever the spirit from God came on Saul, David would take his harp and play. Then relief would come to Saul. He would feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for war. They came together at Sokoh in Judah and camped between Sokoh and Azekah, at Ephes Dammim.
Saul and the Israelites gathered and camped in the Valley of Elah, and they lined up for battle to face the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites on another, with the valley between them.
A champion named Goliath, from Gath, came out of the Philistine camp. He was about three metres tall.
He wore a bronze helmet and a coat of armour made of bronze scales, weighing about fifty-seven kilograms.
He had bronze armour on his legs, and a bronze spear was slung on his back.
The handle of his spear was as thick as a weaver's rod, and its iron point weighed about seven kilograms. The man carrying his shield walked ahead of him.
Goliath stood and shouted to the soldiers of Israel, "Why are you lining up for battle? I am a Philistine, and you are Saul's servants. Choose one of your men and have him come down to me.
If he can fight and kill me, we will become your slaves. But if I beat him and kill him, you will become our slaves and serve us."
Then the Philistine said, "Today I challenge the armies of Israel! Give me a man so we can fight each other."
When Saul and all the Israelites heard what the Philistine said, they were terrified and lost their courage.
Now David was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons, and in Saul's time he was very old.
Jesse's three oldest sons had followed Saul to the war. The oldest was Eliab, the second was Abinadab, and the third was Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul,
but David went back and forth from Saul to look after his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening and stood there.
One day Jesse said to his son David, "Take this basket of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread, and hurry to your brothers in the camp.
Take these ten cheeses to the commander of their unit. See how your brothers are, and bring back some news from them.
They are with Saul and all the men of Israel in the Valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines."

Early in the morning David left the sheep with someone to look after them, loaded up and set out, as Jesse had told him. He reached the camp just as the army was going out to its battle positions, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines were lining up facing each other.
David left his things with the man in charge of supplies, ran to the battle line and asked his brothers how they were.
As he was talking with them, Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, stepped out from his lines and shouted his usual challenge, and David heard it.
Whenever the Israelites saw the man, they all ran from him in great fear.

The Israelites had been saying, "Do you see this man who keeps coming out? He comes out to challenge Israel. The king will give great riches to the man who kills him. He will also give him his daughter in marriage, and his family will not have to pay taxes in Israel."

David asked the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away this shame from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should challenge the armies of the living God?"
They told him what would be done for the man who killed him.

When Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him speaking with the men, he became angry with him and asked, "Why have you come down here? And who did you leave those few sheep with in the desert? I know how proud you are and how wicked your heart is. You only came down to watch the battle."
"Now what have I done?" said David. "Can I not even speak?"
He then turned away to someone else and asked the same question, and the men answered him as before.
What David said was overheard and reported to Saul, and Saul sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Let no one lose heart because of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him."
Saul replied, "You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him. You are only a young man, and he has been a warrior since he was young."
But David said to Saul, "Your servant has been looking after his father's sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep from the flock,
I went after it, struck it and rescued the sheep from its mouth. When it turned on me, I grabbed it by its hair, struck it and killed it.
Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has challenged the armies of the living God.
The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you."
Then Saul dressed David in his own clothes. He put a coat of armour on him and a bronze helmet on his head.
David put on Saul's sword over the clothes and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. "I cannot go in these," he said to Saul, "because I am not used to them." So he took them off.
Then he took his shepherd's stick in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and put them in the pocket of his shepherd's bag. With his sling in his hand, he went toward the Philistine.
Meanwhile, the Philistine, with his shield carrier in front of him, kept coming closer to David.
He looked David over and saw that he was only a young man, healthy and handsome, and he looked down on him.
He said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
"Come here," he said, "and I will give your flesh to the birds and the wild animals!"

David said to the Philistine, "You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Heaven's Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have challenged.

This day the LORD will give you into my hands. I will strike you down and cut off your head. This very day I will give the dead bodies of the Philistine army to the birds and the wild animals, and the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel.
All those gathered here will know that the LORD does not save by sword or spear. The battle belongs to the LORD, and he will give all of you into our hands."
As the Philistine moved closer to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him.
Reaching into his bag, he took out a stone, slung it and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell face down on the ground.
So David won the fight against the Philistine with a sling and a stone. Without a sword in his hand, he struck down the Philistine and killed him.

David ran and stood over him. He took hold of the Philistine's sword and pulled it out of its holder. After he killed him, he cut off his head with the sword. When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran.

Then the men of Israel and Judah rose up with a shout and chased the Philistines to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron. The bodies of the Philistines were scattered along the Shaaraim road to Gath and Ekron.
When the Israelites came back from chasing the Philistines, they robbed their camp.
David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem. He put the Philistine's weapons in his own tent.

As Saul watched David going out to meet the Philistine, he said to Abner, commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is that young man?" Abner replied, "As surely as you live, Your Majesty, I do not know."
The king said, "Find out whose son this young man is."
As soon as David came back from killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul. David was still holding the Philistine's head.
"Whose son are you, young man?" Saul asked him. David said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem."
After David had finished talking with Saul, Jonathan became one in spirit with David, and he loved him as he loved himself.
From that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him go back home to his father's house.
And Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his other clothes, and even his sword, his bow and his belt.
Whatever mission Saul sent him on, David was so successful that Saul put him in charge of the soldiers. This pleased all the people, and Saul's officers as well.

When the men were coming home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out from all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul. They sang and danced with joy, playing tambourines and other instruments.
As they danced, they sang: "Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."
Saul was very angry. This song upset him. "They have given David tens of thousands," he thought, "but me only thousands. What more can he get but the kingdom?"
From that time on, Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God came powerfully on Saul. He was raving like a madman in his house while David was playing the harp, as he usually did. Saul had a spear in his hand,
and he threw it, saying to himself, "I will pin David to the wall." But David escaped from him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had left Saul.
So Saul sent David away from him and made him commander over a thousand men. David led the troops in their battles.
In everything he did he had great success, because the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw how successful he was, he was even more afraid of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he led them in their battles.

Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only serve me bravely and fight the LORD's battles." Saul thought, "I will not raise a hand against him. Let the Philistines do that!"
But David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came for Merab, Saul's daughter, to be given to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah.
Now Saul's daughter Michal was in love with David. When Saul was told about it, he was pleased.
"I will give her to him," he thought, "so that she may be a trap for him and the Philistines may kill him." So Saul said to David, "Now you have a second chance to become my son-in-law."
Then Saul ordered his servants: "Speak to David privately and say, 'Look, the king likes you, and all his servants love you. Now become his son-in-law.'"
They repeated these words to David. But David said, "Do you think it is a small thing to become the king's son-in-law? I am only a poor man and not well known."
When Saul's servants told him what David had said,
Saul replied, "Say to David, 'The king wants no other bride price than a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on his enemies.'" Saul's plan was to have David killed by the Philistines.
When the servants told David this, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. So before the time was up,

David took his men with him and went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought back their foreskins and counted them all out to the king so that he could become the king's son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage.
When Saul realised that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved him,
he became even more afraid of David, and he remained David's enemy for the rest of his life.
The Philistine commanders kept going out to battle, and every time they did, David had more success than the rest of Saul's officers, and his name became very famous.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, liked David very much.
So he warned David, "My father Saul is looking for a chance to kill you. Be careful tomorrow morning. Go into hiding and stay there.
I will go out and stand with my father in the field where you are. I will speak to him about you and tell you what I find out."
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, "Let not the king do wrong to his servant David. He has not wronged you, and what he has done has helped you greatly.

He took his life in his hands when he killed the Philistine. The LORD won a great victory for all Israel, and you saw it and were glad. Why then would you do wrong to an innocent man like David by killing him for no reason?"
Saul listened to Jonathan and made this promise: "As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death."
So Jonathan called David and told him everything. He brought him to Saul, and David served Saul as before.
Once more war broke out. David went out and fought the Philistines. He defeated them so badly that they ran away from him.
But an evil spirit from the LORD came on Saul as he was sitting in his house with his spear in his hand. While David was playing the harp,
Saul tried to pin him to the wall with his spear. But David dodged it, and the spear stuck in the wall. That night David ran away and escaped.
Saul sent men to David's house to watch it and to kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, warned him, "If you do not run for your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."
So Michal let David down through a window, and he ran away and escaped.
Then Michal took a household idol and laid it on the bed. She covered it with clothes and put some goats' hair at the head.
When Saul sent the men to capture David, Michal said, "He is sick."
Then Saul sent the men back to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in his bed so that I can kill him."
But when the men went in, there was the idol in the bed, with goats' hair at the head.
Saul said to Michal, "Why did you trick me like this and send my enemy away so that he escaped?" Michal told him, "He said to me, 'Let me get away. Why should I kill you?'"
When David had run away and escaped, he went to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went to Naioth and stayed there.
Saul was told, "David is in Naioth at Ramah."
So he sent men to capture him. But when they saw a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing there as their leader, the Spirit of God came on Saul's men, and they also prophesied.
Saul was told about it, and he sent more men, and they prophesied too. Saul sent men a third time, and they also prophesied.
Finally, he himself left for Ramah and went to the great well at Seku. He asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" "Over in Naioth at Ramah," they said.
So Saul went to Naioth at Ramah. But the Spirit of God came even on him, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth.
He took off his robes and also prophesied in Samuel's presence. He lay naked all that day and all that night. That is why people say, "Is Saul also one of the prophets?"
Then David ran away from Naioth at Ramah and went to Jonathan. He asked, "What have I done? What crime have I committed? How have I wronged your father, that he is trying to kill me?"
"Never!" Jonathan replied. "You are not going to die! Look, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would he hide this from me? It is not true!"

But David took an oath and said, "Your father knows very well that you like me, and he has said to himself, 'Jonathan must not know this, or he will be upset.' Yet as surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I am only one step away from death."
Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you want me to do, I will do for you."
So David said, "Look, tomorrow is the New Moon festival, and I am supposed to eat with the king. But let me go and hide in the field until the evening of the day after tomorrow.
If your father misses me, tell him, 'David begged me to let him hurry to Bethlehem, his hometown, because a yearly sacrifice is being made there for his whole clan.'
If he says, 'Very well,' then I am safe. But if he loses his temper, you can be sure that he has decided to harm me.
As for you, be kind to me, because you have made a covenant with me before the LORD. If I am guilty, kill me yourself. Why hand me over to your father?"
"Never!" Jonathan said. "If I had the smallest idea that my father had decided to harm you, would I not tell you?"
David asked, "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"
"Come," Jonathan said, "let us go out into the field." So they went there together.

Then Jonathan said to David, "I promise by the LORD, the God of Israel, that by this time tomorrow or the day after, I will find out what my father is thinking. If he feels good toward you, will I not send you word and let you know?
But if my father plans to harm you, may the LORD punish me severely if I do not let you know and send you away safely. May the LORD be with you as he has been with my father.
And as long as I live, show me the faithful love of the LORD, so that I may not be killed.
And do not ever stop being kind to my family, not even when the LORD has wiped out every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the family of David, saying, "May the LORD call David's enemies to account."
And Jonathan made David repeat his promise, because he loved David as he loved himself.
Then Jonathan said to David, "Tomorrow is the New Moon festival. You will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
The day after tomorrow, toward evening, go to the place where you hid when this trouble began, and wait by the stone called Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I were shooting at a target.

Then I will send a boy and say, 'Go and find the arrows.' If I say to him, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you. Bring them here,' then come, because, as surely as the LORD lives, you are safe. There is no danger.
But if I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then you must go, because the LORD has sent you away.
And about what we have promised each other, remember, the LORD is a witness between you and me forever."
So David hid in the field. When the New Moon festival came, the king sat down to eat.
He sat in his usual place by the wall, opposite Jonathan, and Abner sat next to Saul. But David's place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, because he thought, "Something must have happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean. Surely he is unclean."
But the next day, the second day of the month, David's place was empty again. Then Saul said to his son Jonathan, "Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered, "David begged me to let him go to Bethlehem.

He said, 'Let me go, because our family is having a sacrifice in the town, and my brother has told me to be there. If you are my friend, let me go and see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to the king's table."

Saul's anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a wicked, rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have taken the side of the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of the mother who gave birth to you?
As long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be safe. Now send for him and bring him to me, because he must die!"
"Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" Jonathan asked his father.
But Saul threw his spear at him to kill him. Then Jonathan knew that his father had decided to kill David.
Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger. On that second day of the festival he did not eat, because he was upset about how his father had shamefully treated David.
In the morning Jonathan went out to the field to meet David at the time they had agreed. He had a small boy with him.
He said to the boy, "Run and find the arrows I shoot." As the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy came to the place where Jonathan's arrow had fallen, Jonathan called out after him, "Is the arrow not beyond you?"
Then he shouted, "Hurry! Go quickly! Do not stop!" The boy picked up the arrow and came back to his master.
The boy knew nothing about all this. Only Jonathan and David knew.
Then Jonathan gave his weapons to the boy and said, "Go, carry them back to town."

After the boy had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone and bowed down before Jonathan three times, with his face to the ground. Then they kissed each other and cried together, but David cried the most.

Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace. We have sworn friendship with each other in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD is a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and my descendants forever.'" Then David left, and Jonathan went back to the town.
David went to Nob, to Ahimelek the priest. Ahimelek was trembling when he met him, and asked, "Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?"

David answered Ahimelek the priest, "The king sent me on a mission and told me, 'No one must know anything about the mission I am sending you on, or about my orders.' As for my men, I have told them to meet me at a certain place.
Now then, what do you have here? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you can find."
But the priest answered David, "I do not have any ordinary bread here. But there is some holy bread, if the men have kept themselves away from women."
David replied, "Yes, women have been kept away from us, as always when I set out. The men's bodies are holy even on ordinary missions. How much more today!"

So the priest gave him the holy bread, since there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence. It had been taken away from before the LORD and replaced with fresh bread on the day it was removed.
Now one of Saul's servants was there that day, kept there before the LORD. He was Doeg the Edomite, the head of Saul's shepherds.
David asked Ahimelek, "Do you have a spear or a sword here? I have not brought my sword or any other weapon, because the king's mission was urgent."

The priest replied, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here. It is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want it, take it. There is no other sword here." David said, "There is none like it. Give it to me."
That day David ran away from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath.
But the servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Is he not the one they sing about in their dances: 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"
David took these words to heart and was very afraid of Achish king of Gath.
So he pretended to be mad in front of them. While he was with them, he acted like a madman, scribbling on the doors of the gate and letting spit run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "Look at the man! He is mad! Why bring him to me?
Do I not have enough madmen already, that you have to bring this fellow here to act like a madman in front of me? Must this man come into my house?"
David left Gath and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and his father's family heard about it, they went down to him there.
All those who were in trouble or in debt or unhappy gathered around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.
From there David went to Mizpah in Moab and said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother come and stay with you until I learn what God will do for me."
So he left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him as long as David was in the stronghold.
But the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah." So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.
Saul heard that David and his men had been found. Saul was sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, with his spear in his hand, and all his officials were standing around him.
Saul said to them, "Listen, men of Benjamin! Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?

Is that why you have all plotted against me? No one tells me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you cares about me or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant to wait in hiding to attack me, as he is doing today."
But Doeg the Edomite, who was standing with Saul's officials, said, "I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelek son of Ahitub at Nob.
Ahimelek asked the LORD what David should do. He also gave him food and the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
Then the king sent for the priest Ahimelek son of Ahitub and all his family, who were the priests at Nob, and they all came to the king.
Saul said, "Listen now, son of Ahitub." "Yes, my lord," he answered.

Saul said to him, "Why have you plotted against me, you and the son of Jesse? You gave him bread and a sword and asked God for help for him, so that he has turned against me and lies in wait for me, as he does today."
Ahimelek answered the king, "Who among all your servants is as faithful as David? He is the king's son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard, and highly respected in your house.
Was that the first time I asked God for help for him? Of course not! Please do not blame your servant or any of my family, because your servant knows nothing at all about this whole affair."
But the king said, "You will surely die, Ahimelek, you and your father's whole family."

Then the king ordered the guards beside him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too have sided with David. They knew he was running away, yet they did not tell me." But the king's officials would not raise a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.
The king then ordered Doeg, "You turn and strike down the priests." So Doeg the Edomite turned and struck them down. That day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
He also attacked Nob, the town of the priests, with the sword. He killed its men and women, its children and babies, and its cattle, donkeys and sheep.
But Abiathar, a son of Ahimelek son of Ahitub, escaped and ran away to join David.
He told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.
Then David said to Abiathar, "That day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, I knew he would be sure to tell Saul. I am to blame for the death of your father's whole family.
Stay with me and do not be afraid. The man who wants to kill you also wants to kill me. You will be safe with me."
David was told, "Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are stealing the grain from the threshing floors."
So David asked the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" The LORD answered him, "Go, attack the Philistines and save Keilah."
But David's men said to him, "Even here in Judah we are afraid. How much more if we go to Keilah against the Philistine army!"
Once again David asked the LORD, and the LORD answered him, "Go down to Keilah, because I am going to give the Philistines into your hands."
So David and his men went to Keilah and fought the Philistines. He carried off their animals and struck them down badly. So David saved the people of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelek had run to David at Keilah, he had brought the ephod down with him.
Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, and he said, "God has handed him over to me, because David has trapped himself by going into a town with gates and bars."
So Saul called up all his forces for battle, to go down to Keilah and surround David and his men.
When David learned that Saul was planning evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod."
David said, "LORD, God of Israel, your servant has heard for certain that Saul plans to come to Keilah and destroy the town because of me.
Will the leaders of Keilah hand me over to him? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? LORD, God of Israel, please tell your servant." And the LORD said, "He will come down."
Again David asked, "Will the leaders of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will."
So David and his men, about six hundred in number, left Keilah and kept moving from place to place. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he did not go there.
David stayed in the desert strongholds and in the hills of the Desert of Ziph. Day after day Saul searched for him, but God did not give David into his hands.
While David was at Horesh in the Desert of Ziph, he learned that Saul had come out to kill him.
And Saul's son Jonathan went to David at Horesh and helped him find strength in God.
"Do not be afraid," he said. "My father Saul will not lay a hand on you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you. Even my father Saul knows this."
The two of them made a covenant before the LORD. Then Jonathan went home, but David stayed at Horesh.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hakilah, south of Jeshimon?
Now, Your Majesty, come down whenever it pleases you, and we will be responsible for handing him over to the king."
Saul replied, "The LORD bless you for your kindness to me.
Go and get more information. Find out where David usually goes and who has seen him there. I am told he is very cunning.
Find out about all the hiding places he uses, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. If he is in the area, I will track him down among all the clans of Judah."
So they set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. But David and his men were in the Desert of Maon, in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men began the search. When David was told about it, he went down to the rock and stayed in the Desert of Maon. When Saul heard this, he went into the Desert of Maon chasing David.

Saul was going along one side of the mountain, and David and his men were on the other side, hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his forces were closing in on David and his men to capture them,
a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Come quickly! The Philistines are raiding the land."
Then Saul stopped chasing David and went to fight the Philistines. That is why they call this place Sela Hammahlekoth, which means Rock of Parting.
And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En Gedi.
After Saul came back from chasing the Philistines, he was told, "David is in the Desert of En Gedi."
So Saul took three thousand of the best men from all Israel and set out to look for David and his men near the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
He came to the sheep pens along the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. David and his men were far back in the cave.

David's men said, "This is the day the LORD spoke of when he said to you, 'I will give your enemy into your hands for you to deal with as you wish.'" Then David crept up quietly and cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
Afterward, David felt guilty because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD's chosen king, or lay my hand on him. He is the LORD's anointed."
With these words David held his men back and did not let them attack Saul. And Saul left the cave and went on his way.
Then David went out of the cave and called out to Saul, "My lord the king!" When Saul looked behind him, David bowed down with his face to the ground.
He said to Saul, "Why do you listen when people say, 'David is trying to harm you'?

This day you have seen with your own eyes how the LORD gave you into my hands in the cave. Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not lay my hand on my lord, because he is the LORD's anointed.'

See, my father, look at this piece of your robe in my hand! I cut off the corner of your robe but did not kill you. Now understand and see that I am not guilty of doing wrong or rebelling. I have not wronged you, but you are hunting me down to take my life.
May the LORD judge between you and me. And may the LORD pay you back for the wrongs you have done to me, but my hand will not touch you.
As the old saying goes, 'From evildoers come evil deeds,' so my hand will not touch you.
Who has the king of Israel come out against? Who are you chasing? A dead dog? A flea?
May the LORD be our judge and decide between us. May he look into my case and defend me. May he save me from your hand."
When David finished saying this, Saul asked, "Is that your voice, David my son?" And he cried loudly.
"You are more righteous than I," he said. "You have treated me well, but I have treated you badly.
You have just now told me about the good you did to me. The LORD gave me into your hands, but you did not kill me.
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him get away unharmed? May the LORD reward you well for the way you treated me today.
I know that you will surely be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be firmly established in your hands.
Now promise me by the LORD that you will not kill off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father's family."
So David gave his promise to Saul. Then Saul went back home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Samuel died, and all Israel gathered and mourned for him. They buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David went down into the Desert of Paran.
A certain man in Maon, who had property at Carmel, was very rich. He had a thousand goats and three thousand sheep, and he was cutting the wool from his sheep at Carmel.
His name was Nabal and his wife's name was Abigail. She was a wise and beautiful woman, but her husband was harsh and mean in his dealings. He was from the family of Caleb.
While David was in the desert, he heard that Nabal was cutting the wool from his sheep.
So he sent ten young men and said to them, "Go up to Nabal at Carmel and greet him in my name.
Say to him: 'Long life to you! Peace and good health to you and your family, and to all that is yours!
I hear that it is sheep-shearing time. When your shepherds were with us, we did not harm them, and the whole time they were at Carmel nothing of theirs went missing.
Ask your own servants and they will tell you. So please be kind to my young men, since we have come at a happy time of feasting. Please give your servants and your son David whatever you can spare.'"
When David's men arrived, they gave Nabal this message in David's name. Then they waited.
Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is this David? Who is this son of Jesse? Many servants are running away from their masters these days.
Why should I take my bread and water, and the meat I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men coming from who knows where?"
David's men turned around and went back. When they arrived, they told him every word.
David said to his men, "Each of you, put on your sword!" So they did, and David put on his sword too. About four hundred men went up with David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies.
One of the servants told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the desert to greet our master, but he shouted insults at them.
Yet these men were very good to us. They did not harm us, and the whole time we were out in the fields near them nothing went missing.
Night and day they were like a wall around us the whole time we were looking after our sheep near them.
Now think it over and see what you can do, because disaster is coming on our master and his whole household. He is such a wicked man that no one can talk to him."

Abigail acted quickly. She took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five sheep ready for cooking, a large basket of roasted grain, a hundred cakes of raisins and two hundred cakes of pressed figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
Then she told her servants, "Go on ahead. I will follow you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
As she came riding her donkey down into a mountain valley, there were David and his men coming down toward her, and she met them.
David had just said, "It has been useless, all my watching over this fellow's property in the desert so that nothing of his went missing. He has paid me back evil for good.
May God punish me severely if by morning I leave alive even one male of all who belong to him!"
When Abigail saw David, she quickly got off her donkey and bowed down before him with her face to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, "Pardon your servant, my lord, and let me speak to you. Hear what your servant has to say. Let the blame be on me alone.
Please, my lord, pay no attention to that wicked man Nabal. He is just like his name. His name means Fool, and foolishness goes with him. As for me, your servant, I did not see the men my lord sent.

And now, my lord, as surely as the LORD your God lives and as you live, since the LORD has kept you from killing and from taking revenge with your own hands, may your enemies and all who want to harm my lord be like Nabal.
And let this gift, which your servant has brought to my lord, be given to the men who follow you.

Please forgive your servant's wrong. The LORD will certainly give my lord a family line of kings that will last, because you fight the LORD's battles. Let no wrongdoing be found in you as long as you live.

Even if someone is chasing you to take your life, your life will be bound safely in the bundle of the living by the LORD your God. But the lives of your enemies he will hurl away as a stone is thrown from a sling.
When the LORD has done for my lord every good thing he promised and has made you ruler over Israel,
you will not have on your conscience the heavy burden of having killed for no reason or of having taken revenge yourself. And when the LORD has given my lord success, remember your servant."
David said to Abigail, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel, who has sent you today to meet me.
May you be blessed for your good sense, and for keeping me today from killing and from taking revenge with my own hands.

Truly, as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me from harming you, if you had not come quickly to meet me, not one male belonging to Nabal would have been left alive by morning."
Then David accepted from her hand what she had brought him and said, "Go home in peace. I have heard your words and granted your request."
When Abigail went to Nabal, he was in the house holding a feast like that of a king. He was in high spirits and very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until morning.
In the morning, when Nabal was sober, his wife told him all these things. His heart failed him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Praise the LORD, who has taken my side against Nabal for insulting me. He has kept his servant from doing wrong and has brought Nabal's wrongdoing down on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife.
His servants went to Carmel and said to Abigail, "David has sent us to you to take you to become his wife."
She bowed down with her face to the ground and said, "Here is your servant, ready to serve you and wash the feet of my lord's servants."
Abigail quickly got on a donkey and, with her five female servants, went with David's messengers and became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they both became his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Paltiel son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites went to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding on the hill of Hakilah, which faces Jeshimon?"
So Saul went down to the Desert of Ziph with three thousand of Israel's best soldiers to look for David there.
Saul camped beside the road on the hill of Hakilah facing Jeshimon, but David stayed in the desert. When he saw that Saul had followed him there,
he sent out spies and learned that Saul had definitely arrived.

Then David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the commander of the army, had lain down. Saul was lying inside the camp, with the army camped around him.
David then asked Ahimelek the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, "Who will go down into the camp with me to Saul?" "I will go with you," said Abishai.
So David and Abishai went to the army by night, and there was Saul, lying asleep inside the camp with his spear stuck in the ground near his head. Abner and the soldiers were lying around him.
Abishai said to David, "Today God has given your enemy into your hands. Now let me pin him to the ground with one thrust of the spear. I will not need to strike him twice."
But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him! Who can lay a hand on the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?
As surely as the LORD lives," he said, "the LORD himself will strike him. Either his time will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and be killed.
But the LORD forbid that I should lay a hand on the LORD's anointed. Now take the spear and the water jug that are near his head, and let us go."
So David took the spear and the water jug near Saul's head, and they left. No one saw it or knew about it, and no one woke up. They were all sleeping, because the LORD had put them into a deep sleep.
Then David crossed over to the other side and stood on top of the hill some distance away. There was a wide space between them.
He called out to the army and to Abner son of Ner, "Abner, are you not going to answer me?" Abner replied, "Who are you who calls to the king?"
David said, "You are a man, are you not? And who is like you in Israel? Why did you not guard your lord the king? Someone came to destroy your lord the king.

What you have done is not good. As surely as the LORD lives, you and your men deserve to die, because you did not guard your master, the LORD's anointed. Look around you. Where are the king's spear and water jug that were near his head?"
Saul recognised David's voice and said, "Is that your voice, David my son?" David replied, "Yes it is, my lord the king."
And he added, "Why is my lord chasing his servant? What have I done, and what wrong am I guilty of?

Now let my lord the king listen to his servant's words. If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may he accept an offering. But if people have done it, may they be cursed before the LORD! They have now driven me from my share in the LORD's land and have said, 'Go and serve other gods.'
Now do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. The king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains."

Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Come back, David my son. Because you treated my life as precious today, I will not try to harm you again. Surely I have acted like a fool and have made a terrible mistake."
David answered, "Here is the king's spear. Let one of your young men come over and get it.
The LORD rewards everyone for their right actions and faithfulness. The LORD gave you into my hands today, but I would not lay a hand on the LORD's anointed.
As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and save me from all trouble."
Then Saul said to David, "May you be blessed, David my son. You will do great things and surely succeed." So David went on his way, and Saul went back home.

But David thought to himself, "One of these days I will be killed by Saul. The best thing I can do is escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will give up searching for me anywhere in Israel, and I will slip out of his hand."
So David and the six hundred men with him left and went over to Achish son of Maok, king of Gath.
David and his men settled in Gath with Achish. Each man had his family with him, and David had his two wives: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.
When Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, he stopped searching for him.

Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favour in your eyes, let me be given a place in one of the country towns, so that I can live there. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?"
So on that day Achish gave him Ziklag, and it has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since.
David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months.
Now David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites and the Amalekites. These peoples had lived in the land from long ago, in the area stretching to Shur and as far as Egypt.
Whenever David attacked an area, he did not leave a man or woman alive, but took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels and clothes. Then he returned to Achish.
When Achish asked, "Where did you go raiding today?" David would say, "Against the Negev of Judah," or "Against the Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "Against the Negev of the Kenites."

He did not leave a man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, for he thought, "They might tell about us and say, 'This is what David did.'" And this was his practice the whole time he lived in Philistine territory.
Achish trusted David and said to himself, "He has made himself so hated by his people, the Israelites, that he will be my servant for life."
In those days the Philistines gathered their forces to fight against Israel. Achish said to David, "You must understand that you and your men will go out with me in the army."
David said, "Then you will see for yourself what your servant can do." Achish replied, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life."
Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in his own town of Ramah. Saul had driven the mediums and spiritists out of the land.
The Philistines assembled and came and set up camp at Shunem, while Saul gathered all Israel and set up camp at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid, and terror filled his heart.
He asked the LORD for guidance, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams, by the Urim, or by prophets.
Saul then said to his servants, "Find me a woman who is a medium, so that I may go and ask her." "There is one in Endor," they said.
So Saul disguised himself, putting on other clothes, and at night he and two men went to the woman. "Consult a spirit for me," he said, "and bring up for me the one I name."
But the woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done. He has cut off the mediums and spiritists from the land. Why have you set a trap for my life to get me killed?"
Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As surely as the LORD lives, you will not be punished for this."
Then the woman asked, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" "Bring up Samuel," he said.
When the woman saw Samuel, she screamed at the top of her voice and said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!"
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman said, "I see a spirit coming up out of the earth."
"What does he look like?" he asked. "An old man wearing a robe is coming up," she said. Then Saul knew it was Samuel, and he bowed down with his face to the ground.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" "I am in great distress," Saul said. "The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do."
Samuel said, "Why do you ask me, now that the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy?
The LORD has done what he said through me. The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hands and given it to one of your neighbours, to David.
Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out his fierce anger against the Amalekites, the LORD has done this to you today.

The LORD will give both Israel and you into the hands of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will also give the army of Israel into the hands of the Philistines."
Immediately Saul fell full length on the ground, filled with fear because of Samuel's words. His strength was gone, for he had eaten nothing all that day and all that night.
When the woman came to Saul and saw that he was badly shaken, she said, "Look, your servant has obeyed you. I took my life in my hands and did what you told me to do.
Now please listen to your servant and let me give you some food so you can eat and have the strength to go on your way."
He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his men joined the woman in urging him, and he listened to them. He got up from the ground and sat on the couch.
The woman had a fattened calf at the house, which she killed at once. She took some flour, kneaded it and baked bread without yeast.
Then she set it before Saul and his men, and they ate. That same night they got up and left.
The Philistines gathered all their forces at Aphek, and Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel.
As the Philistine rulers marched with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men were marching at the rear with Achish.

The commanders of the Philistines asked, "What about these Hebrews?" Achish replied, "Is this not David, who was an officer of Saul king of Israel? He has already been with me for over a year, and from the day he left Saul until now, I have found no fault in him."

But the Philistine commanders were angry with him and said, "Send the man back, so that he may return to the place you gave him. He must not go with us into battle, or he will turn against us during the fighting. How better could he win back his master's favour than by taking the heads of our own men?
Is this not the David they sang about in their dances: 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

So Achish called David and said to him, "As surely as the LORD lives, you have been reliable, and I would be pleased to have you serve with me in the army. From the day you came to me until today, I have found no fault in you, but the rulers do not approve of you.
So turn back and go in peace. Do nothing to displease the Philistine rulers."
"But what have I done?" asked David. "What have you found against your servant from the day I came to you until now? Why can I not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"
Achish answered, "I know that you have been as pleasing in my eyes as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go up with us into battle.'
So get up early, along with your master's servants who have come with you, and leave in the morning as soon as it is light."
So David and his men got up early in the morning to go back to the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
David and his men reached Ziklag on the third day. Now the Amalekites had raided the Negev and Ziklag. They had attacked Ziklag and burned it,
and had taken captive the women and everyone else in it, both young and old. They killed none of them, but carried them off as they went on their way.
When David and his men reached Ziklag, they found it burned, and their wives, sons and daughters taken captive.
So David and his men wept aloud until they had no strength left to weep.
David's two wives had been captured: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David was in great distress because the men were talking of stoning him. Each one was bitter in spirit because of his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
Then David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelek, "Bring me the ephod." Abiathar brought it to him.
And David asked the LORD, "Should I chase this raiding party? Will I catch them?" "Chase them," he answered. "You will certainly catch them and succeed in rescuing everyone."
David and the six hundred men with him came to the Besor Valley, where some stayed behind.
Two hundred of them were too exhausted to cross the valley, but David and the other four hundred continued the chase.
They found an Egyptian in a field and brought him to David. They gave him water to drink and food to eat:
part of a cake of pressed figs and two cakes of raisins. He ate and was revived, for he had not eaten any food or drunk any water for three days and three nights.
David asked him, "Who do you belong to? Where do you come from?" He said, "I am an Egyptian, the slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me when I became ill three days ago.
We raided the Negev of the Kerethites, some territory belonging to Judah, and the Negev of Caleb. And we burned Ziklag."
David asked him, "Can you lead me down to this raiding party?" He answered, "Swear to me before God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will take you down to them."

He led David down, and there they were, scattered over the countryside, eating, drinking and celebrating because of the huge amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from Judah.
David fought them from dusk until the evening of the next day. None of them got away, except four hundred young men who rode off on camels and fled.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing was missing: young or old, boy or girl, plunder or anything else they had taken. David brought everything back.
He took all the flocks and herds, and his men drove them ahead of the other livestock, saying, "This is David's plunder."

Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and who had been left behind at the Besor Valley. They came out to meet David and the men with him. As David and his men approached, he greeted them.

But all the evil men and troublemakers among David's followers said, "Because they did not go out with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered. However, each man may take his wife and children and go."
David replied, "No, my brothers, you must not do that with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and handed over to us the raiding party that came against us.
Who will listen to what you say? The share of the man who stayed with the supplies is to be the same as that of the man who went down to the battle. All will share alike."
David made this a rule and law for Israel from that day to this.
When David reached Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, who were his friends, saying, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD's enemies."
He sent it to those who were in Bethel, Ramoth in the Negev and Jattir;
to those in Aroer, Siphmoth, Eshtemoa
and Rakal; to those in the towns of the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites;
to those in Hormah, Bor Ashan, Athak
and Hebron; and to those in all the other places where David and his men had roamed.
Now the Philistines fought against Israel. The Israelites fled before them, and many fell dead on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines chased Saul and his sons hard, and they killed his sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malki-Shua.
The fighting grew fierce around Saul, and when the archers caught up with him, they wounded him badly.

Saul said to his armour-bearer, "Draw your sword and run me through, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and abuse me." But his armour-bearer was terrified and would not do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
When the armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his sword and died with him.
So Saul and his three sons and his armour-bearer and all his men died together that same day.

When the Israelites along the valley and those across the Jordan saw that the Israelite army had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their towns and fled. And the Philistines came and occupied them.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and they sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to spread the news in the temple of their idols and among their people.
They put his armour in the temple of the Ashtoreths and fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan.
When the people of Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all their brave men marched through the night to Beth Shan. They took down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall and went to Jabesh, where they burned them.
Then they took their bones and buried them under a tamarisk tree at Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.
2Sam: After Saul died, David came back from defeating the Amalekites and stayed two days in Ziklag.
On the third day a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dust on his head. When he came to David, he bowed down to the ground to show respect.
David asked him, "Where have you come from?" He said, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."
David said, "What happened? Please tell me." He answered, "The army ran away from the battle, and many of the people fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."
David asked the young man who brought the news, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and I saw Saul leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen were closing in on him.
He looked behind him, saw me, and called to me. I answered, 'Here I am.'
He asked me, 'Who are you?' I told him, 'I am an Amalekite.'
Then he said to me, 'Please stand over me and kill me. I am in terrible pain, but I am still alive.'
So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew he could not live after he had fallen. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to you, my lord."
Then David grabbed his own clothes and tore them, and all the men with him did the same.
They mourned and cried and went without food until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the LORD's people, and for the nation of Israel, because they had been killed by the sword.
David asked the young man who brought the news, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite."
David said to him, "Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to kill the LORD's chosen king?"
Then David called one of his young men and said, "Go and strike him down!" So he struck him, and he died.
David said to him, "Your blood is on your own head. Your own mouth spoke against you when you said, 'I killed the LORD's chosen king.'"
Then David sang this sad song about Saul and his son Jonathan.
He ordered that the people of Judah be taught this song, called the Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:
"Israel, your glory lies dead on your hills! How the mighty heroes have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath. Do not announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, or the daughters of the Philistines will be glad, and the daughters of those outsiders will celebrate.

Mountains of Gilboa, let no dew or rain fall on you, and let no fields grow crops for offerings. For there the shield of the mighty was made dirty and thrown away. The shield of Saul was no longer rubbed with oil.
Jonathan's bow never turned back from the blood of the dead and the bodies of the strong. Saul's sword never came back empty.
Saul and Jonathan were loved and kind in their lives, and in their death they were not separated. They were faster than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, cry for Saul. He dressed you in fine red clothes and put gold jewellery on your clothes.
How the mighty heroes have fallen in the middle of the battle! Jonathan lies dead on your hills.
I am heartbroken for you, my brother Jonathan. You were so dear to me. Your love for me was wonderful, greater than the love of women.
How the mighty heroes have fallen, and their weapons of war are destroyed!"
After this, David asked the LORD, "Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?" The LORD said, "Go up." David asked, "Where should I go?" The LORD said, "To Hebron."
So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal from Carmel.
David also brought the men who were with him, each with his family, and they lived in the towns around Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came and anointed David as king over the people of Judah. They told David, "The men of Jabesh Gilead are the ones who buried Saul."
So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead to say to them, "May the LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to your master Saul by burying him.
Now may the LORD show you his faithful love and truth. I will also be good to you because you have done this.
So now be strong and brave. Your master Saul is dead, and the people of Judah have anointed me as their king."
But Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, had taken Ishbosheth, Saul's son, across to Mahanaim.
There he made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ishbosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he ruled for two years. But the people of Judah followed David.
David was king in Hebron over the people of Judah for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner, with the servants of Ishbosheth son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David's servants also went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. One group sat down on one side of the pool, and the other group on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and fight in front of us!" Joab said, "Let them get up."
So they got up and were counted off: twelve for Benjamin and Ishbosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants.
Each man grabbed his opponent by the head and pushed his sword into the other man's side, and they all fell down together. So that place in Gibeon was called Helkath Hazzurim.
The battle that day was very fierce, and Abner and the men of Israel were beaten by David's servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel could run as fast as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased Abner, and he did not turn to the right or to the left as he followed him.
Abner looked back and said, "Is that you, Asahel?" He answered, "Yes, it is."
Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right or your left. Catch one of the young men and take his armour for yourself." But Asahel would not stop chasing him.
Abner said again to Asahel, "Stop following me. Why should I have to strike you down? How could I then face your brother Joab?"

But Asahel would not turn away. So Abner struck him in the stomach with the back end of his spear, and the spear came out of his back. He fell down and died right there. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped and stood still.
But Joab and Abishai chased Abner. As the sun went down, they came to the hill of Ammah, near Giah, on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The men of Benjamin gathered behind Abner and formed one group, and they stood on the top of a hill.
Then Abner called out to Joab, "Must the sword keep on killing forever? Don't you know this will end in bitterness? How long before you tell your men to stop chasing their own brothers?"
Joab said, "As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken, my men would have kept chasing their brothers until morning."
So Joab blew the trumpet, and all his men stopped. They did not chase Israel any more, and they stopped fighting.
Abner and his men marched all that night through the Arabah valley. They crossed the Jordan, went through the whole region of Bithron, and came to Mahanaim.
Joab came back from chasing Abner and gathered all his men. Nineteen of David's men were missing, as well as Asahel.
But David's servants had killed three hundred and sixty of Abner's men from Benjamin.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron as day was breaking.
The war between Saul's family and David's family went on for a long time. David grew stronger and stronger, while Saul's family grew weaker and weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, whose mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel.
His second son was Chileab, whose mother was Abigail, the widow of Nabal from Carmel. The third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
The fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith. The fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital.
The sixth was Ithream, whose mother was Eglah, David's wife. These sons were born to David in Hebron.
While the war went on between Saul's family and David's family, Abner was making himself more and more powerful in Saul's family.
Saul had a slave wife named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. Ishbosheth said to Abner, "Why did you sleep with my father's slave wife?"

Abner was very angry at what Ishbosheth said. He answered, "Do you think I am a dog working for Judah? Until today I have been loyal to the family of your father Saul, to his brothers, and to his friends. I have not handed you over to David. Yet today you accuse me of doing wrong with this woman!
May God punish me, and even more, if I do not do for David what the LORD promised him with an oath:
to take the kingdom away from Saul's family and to set up David's throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan all the way to Beersheba."
Ishbosheth could not say another word to Abner, because he was afraid of him.
Then Abner sent messengers to David to speak for him. They said, "Who does this land belong to? Make an agreement with me, and I will help you bring all Israel over to your side."
David said, "Good. I will make an agreement with you. But I ask one thing of you: Do not come to see me unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come."
Then David sent messengers to Ishbosheth, Saul's son, to say, "Give me my wife Michal. I paid for her with one hundred foreskins of the Philistines."
So Ishbosheth sent men to take her away from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband went with her, crying all the way, and followed her as far as Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go back home!" So he went back.
Abner spoke with the leaders of Israel. He said, "For some time now you have wanted David to be your king.
Now do it! For the LORD has said about David, 'Through my servant David I will save my people Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies.'"
Abner also spoke to the people of Benjamin. Then he went to Hebron to tell David everything that Israel and the whole tribe of Benjamin had agreed to.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, and David made a feast for Abner and the men with him.

Abner said to David, "Let me go now and gather all Israel to you, my lord the king. They will make an agreement with you, and you will rule over everything you want." So David sent Abner away, and he left in peace.

Just then David's servants and Joab came back from a raid, bringing a large amount of goods they had taken. But Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away, and he had left in peace.
When Joab and all his army arrived, Joab was told, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king let him go, and he has left in peace."
So Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Abner came to you. Why did you let him go? Now he is gone!
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to trick you, to learn all your movements, coming and going, and to find out everything you are doing."
Then Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Sirah, but David did not know about it.

When Abner came back to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gateway as if to talk with him privately. There he stabbed him in the stomach, and Abner died. Joab did this to pay him back for the death of his brother Asahel.
Later, when David heard about it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the LORD of the death of Abner son of Ner.

Let the blame fall on Joab and on all his father's family. May Joab's family always have someone with a running sore, or a skin disease, or someone who needs a walking stick, or who dies by the sword, or who does not have enough food."
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
