Then David said to Joab and all the people with him, "Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn as you walk in front of Abner's body." King David himself walked behind the stretcher carrying the body.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king cried loudly at Abner's grave, and all the people cried too.
The king sang this sad song for Abner: "Should Abner have died like a fool dies?
Your hands were not tied, and your feet were not put in chains. You fell like someone who falls before wicked men." And all the people cried over him again.

Then all the people came to urge David to eat something while it was still day. But David made a promise: "May God punish me, and even more, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down."
All the people noticed this, and it pleased them. In fact, everything the king did pleased all the people.
So that day all the people and all Israel understood that the king had no part in the killing of Abner son of Ner.
Then the king said to his servants, "Don't you know that a great leader has fallen in Israel today?
Even though I am the chosen king, I am weak today. These sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me. May the LORD pay back the evildoer for the evil he has done."
When Saul's son Ishbosheth heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost all courage, and all the Israelites were afraid.

Saul's son had two men who were leaders of raiding groups. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, from the tribe of Benjamin. Beeroth was counted as part of Benjamin,
because the people of Beeroth had run away to Gittaim, and they have lived there as foreigners to this day.

Saul's son Jonathan had a son who was crippled in both feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and ran, but as she hurried away, he fell and became crippled. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, set out and came to Ishbosheth's house in the heat of the day, while he was resting at noon.
They went into the house as if to get some wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah escaped.

They had come into the house while he was lying on his bed in his bedroom. They stabbed him and killed him, and cut off his head. They took his head and travelled all night along the road through the Arabah valley.

They brought Ishbosheth's head to David at Hebron and said to the king, "Here is the head of Ishbosheth, son of Saul, your enemy who tried to kill you! Today the LORD has paid back Saul and his family for you, my lord the king."
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon from Beeroth: "As surely as the LORD lives, who has rescued me from every trouble,
when a man told me, 'Saul is dead,' he thought he was bringing good news. But I grabbed him and killed him in Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news.
How much more must I now punish wicked men who have killed an innocent man on his own bed in his own house! Shouldn't I make you pay for his blood and wipe you off the earth?"

So David gave orders to his young men, and they killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies beside the pool in Hebron. But they took Ishbosheth's head and buried it in Abner's grave in Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Look, we are your own flesh and blood.

In the past, when Saul was our king, you were the one who led Israel out to battle and brought them back. And the LORD said to you, 'You will be the shepherd of my people Israel. You will be their ruler.'"
So all the leaders of Israel came to the king at Hebron. King David made an agreement with them there in front of the LORD, and they anointed David as king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he ruled for forty years.
He ruled over Judah in Hebron for seven years and six months, and he ruled over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem for thirty-three years.

The king and his men marched to Jerusalem to fight the Jebusites, who lived there. The Jebusites said to David, "You will never get in here. Even the blind and the lame can keep you out." They thought, "David cannot get in here."
But David captured the strong fortress of Zion, which became the City of David.

That day David said, "Whoever attacks the Jebusites must go up through the water tunnel to reach those 'lame and blind' enemies whom David hates." That is why people say, "The blind and the lame cannot come into the house."
David lived in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built up the area around it, from the Millo inward.
David became more and more powerful, because the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, with cedar logs, carpenters, and stone workers, and they built a palace for David.
Then David knew that the LORD had made him king over Israel and had made his kingdom great for the sake of his people Israel.
After David moved from Hebron to Jerusalem, he took more slave wives and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went up to search for him. But David heard about it and went down to the fortress.
The Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD, "Should I go and attack the Philistines? Will you give them into my power?" The LORD answered David, "Go, for I will surely give the Philistines into your power."

So David went to Baal Perazim and defeated them there. He said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies in front of me, like a flood of water bursting through." That is why the place was called Baal Perazim.
The Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.
Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
When David asked the LORD, he answered, "Do not attack them from the front. Go around behind them and attack them in front of the mulberry trees.
When you hear a sound like marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, move quickly. That will mean the LORD has gone out ahead of you to strike down the Philistine army."
David did as the LORD commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines all the way from Geba to Gezer.
Once again David gathered all the best soldiers of Israel, thirty thousand men.
David and all his men set out from Baale Judah to bring up God's ark from there. The ark is called by the Name, the name of the LORD of Armies, who sits on his throne above the winged creatures.
They put God's ark on a new cart and brought it out of Abinadab's house on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, Abinadab's sons, were guiding the new cart.
They brought it out of Abinadab's house on the hill with God's ark on it, and Ahio walked in front of the ark.
David and all the people of Israel were celebrating in front of the LORD with all kinds of instruments made of cypress wood: harps, lyres, tambourines, rattles, and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and took hold of God's ark.
The LORD's anger burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of what he had done wrong. He died there beside God's ark.
David was upset because the LORD had burst out in anger against Uzzah. He named that place Perez Uzzah, and it is still called that today.
David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the LORD's ark ever come to me?"
So David would not take the LORD's ark into the City of David to be with him. Instead he took it aside to the house of Obed-Edom from Gath.
The LORD's ark stayed in the house of Obed-Edom from Gath for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom and his whole family.

King David was told, "The LORD has blessed Obed-Edom's family and everything he has, because of God's ark." So David went and brought God's ark up from Obed-Edom's house to the City of David with great joy.
When the men carrying the LORD's ark had taken six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fat calf.
David danced in front of the LORD with all his strength. He was wearing a linen ephod, a priest's apron.
So David and all the people of Israel brought up the LORD's ark with shouts of joy and the sound of trumpets.
As the LORD's ark came into the City of David, Michal, Saul's daughter, looked out of a window. She saw King David leaping and dancing in front of the LORD, and she hated him in her heart.
They brought in the LORD's ark and put it in its place inside the tent David had set up for it. Then David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings in front of the LORD.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Armies.
Then he gave food to everyone in the whole crowd of Israel, both men and women. Each person got a loaf of bread, a cake of dates, and a cake of raisins. Then all the people went home.

When David went home to bless his family, Michal, Saul's daughter, came out to meet him. She said, "How great the king of Israel looked today! He uncovered himself in front of his servants' slave girls, like a foolish man with no shame!"

David said to Michal, "I did it in front of the LORD. He chose me instead of your father or anyone from his family, and he made me ruler over the LORD's people Israel. So I will celebrate in front of the LORD.
I will make myself look even more foolish than this, and I will be humble in my own eyes. But those slave girls you spoke about will honour me."
And Michal, Saul's daughter, had no children for the rest of her life.
The king was living in his palace, and the LORD had given him peace from all his enemies around him.
Then the king said to Nathan the prophet, "Look, I am living in a palace made of cedar, but God's ark is kept in a tent."
Nathan said to the king, "Go and do whatever you have in mind, for the LORD is with you."
But that same night the LORD's message came to Nathan:
"Go and tell my servant David, 'This is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the people of Israel up out of Egypt until today. I have moved from place to place in a tent, a holy tent.
Wherever I have gone with all the people of Israel, did I ever say to any of the leaders I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
So now tell my servant David, 'This is what the LORD of Armies says: I took you from the fields where you followed the sheep, and made you ruler over my people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went, and I have destroyed all your enemies in front of you. I will make your name great, like the names of the greatest people on earth.

I will give my people Israel a place of their own and plant them there, so they can live in their own home and not be disturbed any more. Wicked people will not crush them any more, as they did at the start,
ever since the time I appointed judges to lead my people Israel. I will give you peace from all your enemies. And the LORD tells you that he himself will build a house for you, a family of kings.
When your life is over and you die and are buried with your ancestors, I will raise up one of your own sons to be king after you, and I will make his kingdom strong.
He is the one who will build a house for my name, and I will make the throne of his kingdom last forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. When he does wrong, I will correct him with the rod, the way people correct their children, with blows from human hands.
But my faithful love will never be taken away from him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed to make way for you.
Your family and your kingdom will last forever before me. Your throne will stand firm forever.'"
Nathan told David everything the LORD had said and showed him in this vision.
Then King David went in and sat in front of the LORD. He said, "Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?
And as if this was not enough for you, Lord GOD, you have also spoken about the future of your servant's family for a long time to come. Is this the way you usually deal with people, Lord GOD?
What more can I, David, say to you? You know your servant, Lord GOD.
Because of your promise, and because you wanted to, you have done all these great things and made them known to your servant.
That is why you are great, LORD God! There is no one like you, and there is no God except you. We have heard this with our own ears.

And what other nation on earth is like your people Israel? You, God, went out to rescue them to be your own people and to make your name known. You did great and wonderful things for your land in front of your people, whom you rescued from Egypt, from the nations and their gods.
You made your people Israel your very own people forever, and you, LORD, became their God.
Now, LORD God, keep forever the promise you made about your servant and his family. Do what you have said.
Then your name will be honoured forever, and people will say, 'The LORD of Armies is God over Israel!' And the family of your servant David will stand firm before you.
LORD of Armies, God of Israel, you have shown this to your servant and said, 'I will build a house for you.' That is why your servant has found the courage to pray this prayer to you.
Now, Lord GOD, you are God! Your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.
So now please bless your servant's family, so that it will continue forever before you. For you, Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing the family of your servant will be blessed forever."
After this, David defeated the Philistines and brought them under his control. He took Metheg Ammah, their main city, out of the Philistines' hands.

He also defeated Moab. He made the prisoners lie down on the ground and measured them off with a cord. Two lengths of the cord were put to death, and one full length were allowed to live. So the Moabites became David's servants and paid him taxes.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to take back control along the Euphrates River.
David captured one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers from him. He crippled all the chariot horses, but kept enough of them for one hundred chariots.
When the Syrians from Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David killed twenty-two thousand of them.
Then David put groups of soldiers in the Syrian kingdom of Damascus, and the Syrians became his servants and paid him taxes. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields that Hadadezer's officers carried and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, towns that belonged to Hadadezer, King David took a large amount of bronze.
Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated Hadadezer's whole army.

So Toi sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and congratulate him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer, because Hadadezer had been at war with Toi. Joram brought gifts made of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David gave these gifts to the LORD, together with the silver and gold he had taken from all the nations he had conquered:
from Syria, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek. He also gave the goods he had taken from Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David became famous after he came back from killing eighteen thousand Syrians in the Valley of Salt.
He put groups of soldiers all through Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David ruled over all Israel, and he did what was fair and right for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah was in charge of the army. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests. Seraiah was the royal secretary.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the Kerethites and Pelethites, the king's guards. And David's sons were his chief officials.
David asked, "Is anyone still left from Saul's family? I want to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake."
There was a servant from Saul's family named Ziba, and they called him to come to David. The king asked him, "Are you Ziba?" He answered, "I am your servant."
The king asked, "Is there anyone still alive from Saul's family? I want to show him God's kindness." Ziba answered the king, "Jonathan still has a son who is crippled in both feet."
The king asked, "Where is he?" Ziba said, "He is at the house of Makir son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar."
So King David sent for him and had him brought from the house of Makir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, came to David and bowed down low with his face to the ground. David said, "Mephibosheth?" He answered, "I am your servant."

David said to him, "Don't be afraid. I will certainly be kind to you for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will give back to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table."
Mephibosheth bowed down and said, "Who am I, your servant, that you should care about a dead dog like me?"
Then the king called Saul's servant Ziba and said to him, "I have given your master's grandson everything that belonged to Saul and his family.

You, your sons, and your servants must farm the land for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master's grandson will have food to eat. But Mephibosheth himself will always eat at my table." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "I, your servant, will do everything my lord the king commands." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's own sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. Everyone who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table. He was crippled in both feet.
Some time later, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his place.

David said, "I will be kind to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father was kind to me." So David sent some of his officials to comfort Hanun about his father's death. When David's officials arrived in the land of the Ammonites,

the Ammonite leaders said to Hanun their master, "Do you really think David is honouring your father by sending men to comfort you? No! David has sent them to look around the city, to spy on it, and then destroy it."
So Hanun took David's officials, shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their clothes off in the middle at their buttocks, and sent them away.
When David was told about this, he sent messengers to meet them, because the men were deeply ashamed. The king said, "Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then come home."

The Ammonites realised that they had made David their enemy. So they sent and hired twenty thousand Syrian foot soldiers from Beth Rehob and Zobah, the king of Maacah with one thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
When David heard about it, he sent Joab with the whole army of his best fighting men.
The Ammonites came out and got ready for battle at the entrance to their city gate. The Syrians from Zobah and Rehob and the men from Tob and Maacah stayed by themselves in the open field.
Joab saw that there were enemy troops in front of him and behind him. So he chose some of the best soldiers in Israel and lined them up to face the Syrians.
He put the rest of the men under the command of his brother Abishai, who lined them up to face the Ammonites.
Joab said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, you must come and help me. But if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and help you.
Be brave! Let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. And may the LORD do what he thinks is best."
So Joab and his men moved forward to fight the Syrians, and the Syrians ran away from him.
When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians were running away, they also ran from Abishai and went back into their city. Then Joab returned from fighting the Ammonites and came back to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians saw that Israel had defeated them, they gathered together again.
Hadadezer sent for the Syrians who lived on the other side of the Euphrates River, and they came to Helam. Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, led them.
When David was told about this, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, and came to Helam. The Syrians lined up to face David and fought against him.
But the Syrians ran away from Israel. David killed seven hundred Syrian chariot drivers and forty thousand horsemen. He also struck down Shobach, the commander of their army, and he died there.
All the kings who served Hadadezer saw that Israel had defeated them, so they made peace with Israel and became their servants. After that, the Syrians were afraid to help the Ammonites any more.

In the spring, the time when kings go off to war, David sent out Joab with his officers and the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and surrounded the city of Rabbah. But David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening David got up from his bed and walked around on the roof of the palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing. She was very beautiful.
David sent someone to find out who she was. The man said, "Isn't this Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite?"
Then David sent messengers to bring her. She came to him, and he slept with her. She had just finished the washing that made her clean after her monthly period. Then she went back home.
The woman became pregnant, and she sent a message to David: "I am pregnant."
So David sent a message to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came, David asked him how Joab was, how the soldiers were, and how the war was going.
Then David said to Uriah, "Go home and wash your feet and rest." Uriah left the palace, and the king sent a gift after him.
But Uriah did not go home. He slept at the door of the palace with all his master's servants.
David was told, "Uriah did not go home." So David said to Uriah, "You have just come back from a journey. Why didn't you go home?"

Uriah said to David, "The ark and the armies of Israel and Judah are staying in tents. My master Joab and your officers are camping in the open fields. How could I go home to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, I will not do such a thing!"
Then David said to Uriah, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink with him, and David got him drunk. But in the evening Uriah went out to sleep on his mat among his master's servants. He still did not go home.
The next morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Put Uriah at the front, where the fighting is worst. Then pull back from him so that he will be struck down and die."
So while Joab was surrounding the city, he put Uriah at a place where he knew the enemy's strongest fighters were.
The men of the city came out and fought against Joab. Some of David's soldiers were killed, and Uriah the Hittite also died.
Then Joab sent David a full report about the battle.
He told the messenger, "When you finish telling the king everything about the battle,
the king may become angry and ask you, 'Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Didn't you know they would shoot arrows from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Wasn't it a woman who threw a large millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' If he asks this, then tell him, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.'"
So the messenger went and told David everything Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The enemy was stronger than us. They came out to fight us in the open field, but we pushed them back to the entrance of the city gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's men were killed, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too."

David said to the messenger, "Tell Joab this: 'Don't let this upset you. The sword kills one person as easily as another. Attack the city more strongly and destroy it.' Encourage Joab with these words."
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband Uriah was dead, she mourned for him.
When the time of mourning was over, David sent for her and brought her to his palace. She became his wife and had a son by him. But the LORD was not pleased with what David had done.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. Nathan came to him and said, "There were two men in a certain town. One was rich, and the other was poor.
The rich man had a great many sheep and cattle.

But the poor man had nothing except one little female lamb that he had bought and raised. It grew up with him and his children. It ate from his plate, drank from his cup, and slept in his arms. It was like a daughter to him.

One day a traveller came to visit the rich man. The rich man did not want to take one of his own sheep or cattle to cook for his visitor. Instead, he took the poor man's lamb and cooked it for the man who had come to him."
David became very angry with the rich man. He said to Nathan, "As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He must pay back four lambs for that one, because he did such a thing and had no pity!"
Then Nathan said to David, "You are that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul.
I gave you your master's palace and put your master's wives into your arms. I gave you the people of Israel and Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have given you much more.

So why have you treated the LORD's word with contempt by doing what is evil in his eyes? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You had him killed by the sword of the Ammonites.
So now the sword will never leave your family, because you treated me with contempt and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own wife.'

This is what the LORD says: 'I am going to bring trouble on you from your own family. Right in front of your eyes I will take your wives and give them to someone close to you, and he will sleep with your wives in broad daylight.
You did your sin in secret, but I will do this openly in front of all Israel, in the light of day.'"
Then David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan answered David, "The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die.
But because what you did has given the LORD's enemies a reason to speak against him, the son born to you will die."
Then Nathan went home. The LORD struck the child that Uriah's widow had borne to David, and the child became very sick.
David begged God for the child. He went without food, and he went in and spent the nights lying on the ground.
The older leaders of his household stood beside him and tried to get him up from the ground, but he refused, and he would not eat any food with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead. They said, "While the child was still alive, we spoke to David, but he would not listen to us. How can we tell him the child is dead? He may do something to hurt himself."
But David noticed that his servants were whispering to each other, and he understood that the child was dead. He asked his servants, "Is the child dead?" They answered, "Yes, he is dead."

Then David got up from the ground. He washed, put on lotion, and changed his clothes. He went into the house of the LORD and worshipped. Then he went home and asked for food, and they served him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, "Why are you acting like this? While the child was alive, you fasted and cried for him. But now that the child is dead, you get up and eat!"
David answered, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and cried. I thought, 'Who knows? Maybe the LORD will be kind to me and let the child live.'
But now he is dead. Why should I go without food? Can I bring him back again? One day I will go to him, but he will not come back to me."
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He slept with her, and she had a son, and David named him Solomon. The LORD loved the child,
and he sent word through Nathan the prophet that the baby should be named Jedidiah, which means loved by the LORD, because the LORD loved him.
Meanwhile, Joab was fighting against Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and he captured the royal fortress.
Joab sent messengers to David to say, "I have fought against Rabbah and captured its water supply.
Now bring the rest of the army together, surround the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture it, and it will be named after me."
So David gathered the whole army, went to Rabbah, attacked it, and captured it.

He took the crown off their king's head and put it on his own head. It was made of gold, about thirty-four kilograms, and it had precious stones in it. David also carried away a great amount of goods from the city.

He brought out the people who lived there and made them work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them work at making bricks. He did this to all the Ammonite towns. Then David and his whole army went back to Jerusalem.
Some time later, Amnon son of David fell in love with Tamar. She was the beautiful sister of Absalom, another son of David.
Amnon wanted her so much that he made himself sick over his sister Tamar. She was a virgin, and it seemed impossible for Amnon to do anything to her.
But Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very clever and cunning man.
He asked Amnon, "You are the king's son. Why do you look so miserable every morning? Won't you tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her make the food in front of me, so I can watch her and eat it from her hand.'"

So Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to him, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of special cakes in front of me, so I can eat them from her hand."
So David sent a message to Tamar at the palace: "Please go to your brother Amnon's house and make some food for him."
So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. She took some dough, kneaded it, made cakes while he watched, and baked them.
Then she took the pan and served him the cakes, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, "Send everyone out of here." So everyone went out.
Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into my bedroom so I can eat from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.
But when she held them out for him to eat, he grabbed her and said, "Come to bed with me, my sister!"
She said to him, "No, my brother! Don't force me! Such a thing should never be done in Israel. Don't do this shameful thing!
Where could I go with my shame? And you would be like one of the worst fools in Israel. Please, just speak to the king. He will not stop you from marrying me."
But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, so he forced her and raped her.
Then Amnon hated her very much. He hated her even more than he had loved her before. Amnon said to her, "Get up and get out!"
She said to him, "No! Sending me away now is an even greater wrong than what you have already done to me!" But he would not listen to her.
He called his personal servant and said, "Get this woman out of my sight, and lock the door behind her."
She was wearing a long robe with sleeves, because that is what the king's unmarried daughters wore. So his servant put her out and locked the door behind her.
Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe she was wearing. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying loudly as she went.

Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? For now, my sister, keep quiet about it. He is your brother. Don't let this break your heart." So Tamar lived in her brother Absalom's house, lonely and sad.
When King David heard about all this, he was very angry.
Absalom did not say a word to Amnon, good or bad. He hated Amnon because Amnon had raped his sister Tamar.
Two full years later, Absalom's sheep were being sheared at Baal Hazor, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons to come.
Absalom went to the king and said, "My sheep are being sheared. Will the king and his officials please come and join me?"
The king answered Absalom, "No, my son. We should not all go. We would only be a burden to you." Absalom kept urging him, but the king still would not go. Instead, he gave Absalom his blessing.
Then Absalom said, "If you won't come, then please let my brother Amnon come with us." The king asked him, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom kept urging him, so the king let Amnon and all his other sons go with Absalom.

Absalom ordered his servants, "Watch Amnon. When he is happy from drinking wine and I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Don't be afraid. I am the one giving you this order. Be strong and brave!"
So Absalom's servants did to Amnon what Absalom had ordered. Then all the king's other sons got up, jumped on their mules, and ran away.
While they were still on the way, a report came to David: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons. Not one of them is left!"
The king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground. All his servants stood beside him with their clothes torn too.

But Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah, said, "My lord, don't think they have killed all the young princes, the king's sons. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been planning this ever since the day Amnon raped his sister Tamar.
So, my lord the king, don't believe that all your sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."
Meanwhile, Absalom ran away. Then the young man who was keeping watch looked up and saw many people coming down the road along the hillside behind him.
Jonadab said to the king, "Look, the king's sons are coming! It is just as your servant said."
As soon as he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived, crying loudly. The king and all his servants also cried very hard.
But Absalom ran away and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day.
After Absalom ran away to Geshur, he stayed there for three years.
King David's heart longed to go out to Absalom, because he had got over the death of Amnon.
Joab son of Zeruiah could see that the king's heart longed for Absalom.

So Joab sent someone to Tekoa to bring a wise woman from there. He said to her, "Please pretend to be in mourning. Put on mourning clothes and don't use any lotion. Act like a woman who has been mourning for someone who died a long time ago.
Then go to the king and say these words to him." And Joab told her exactly what to say.
The woman from Tekoa went to the king. She bowed down with her face to the ground to show respect and said, "Help me, my king!"
The king asked her, "What is the matter?" She answered, "I am a widow. My husband is dead.
I, your servant, had two sons. They got into a fight out in the field, and there was no one to separate them. One of them struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole family has turned against me, your servant. They say, 'Hand over the brother who killed his brother, so we can kill him for taking his brother's life. That way we will also get rid of the heir.' They want to put out the last spark of hope I have left. They would leave my husband with no name and no one to carry on his family on the earth."
The king said to the woman, "Go home, and I will give an order to protect you."
The woman from Tekoa said to the king, "My lord the king, let the blame fall on me and my father's family. Let the king and his throne be free of any blame."
The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will never trouble you again."

Then she said, "Please, let the king call on the LORD your God, so that the relative who wants revenge will not kill any more and destroy my son." The king said, "As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."
Then the woman said, "Please let your servant say one more thing to my lord the king." He said, "Go on."
The woman said, "Then why have you planned something like this against God's people? When you say this, you are judging yourself, because you have not brought home your own son whom you sent away.

All of us must die. We are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not just take away life. Instead, he makes ways for the person who was sent away not to stay cut off from him.
I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid. I thought, 'I will speak to the king. Maybe he will do what I ask.'
Maybe the king will listen and rescue me from the man who wants to cut off both me and my son from the land God gave us.
And I thought, 'May the word of my lord the king give me peace.' For my lord the king is like an angel of God, able to tell good from bad. May the LORD your God be with you."
Then the king said to the woman, "Do not hide anything from me that I ask you." The woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king asked, "Did Joab put you up to all this?" The woman answered, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything you say. Yes, it was your servant Joab who told me to do this. He put all these words in my mouth.
Your servant Joab did this to change the way things are. But my lord is as wise as an angel of God. You know everything that happens on earth."
Then the king said to Joab, "All right. I will do it. Go and bring back the young man Absalom."
Joab bowed down with his face to the ground to show respect, and he blessed the king. Joab said, "Today I know that you are pleased with me, my lord the king, because you have done what I asked."
Then Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king said, "He must go to his own house. He must not come to see me." So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king.
In all Israel there was no man praised as much as Absalom for his good looks. From the bottom of his feet to the top of his head there was nothing wrong with him.

He cut his hair once a year, at the end of each year, because it became too heavy for him. When he weighed the hair he had cut, it weighed two hundred shekels by the royal standard, about two and a half kilograms.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter. His daughter's name was Tamar, and she was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. Absalom sent for him a second time, but he still would not come.
So Absalom said to his servants, "Look, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley growing there. Go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab went to Absalom's house and asked him, "Why did your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom answered Joab, "I sent a message telling you to come here. I wanted to send you to the king to ask him, 'Why did I come back from Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there.' Now let me see the king. If I am guilty of anything, let him put me to death."
So Joab went to the king and told him. Then the king called for Absalom, and he came and bowed down with his face to the ground before the king. And the king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him.

He would get up early and stand beside the road that led to the city gate. Whenever someone came with a case for the king to judge, Absalom would call out to him, "Which town are you from?" The man would answer, "I am from one of the tribes of Israel."
Then Absalom would say, "Look, your case is good and right, but the king has no one to listen to you."
Absalom would also say, "I wish I were made judge in this land! Then anyone with a case or complaint could come to me, and I would make sure he was treated fairly."
And whenever someone came near to bow down to him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.
Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came to the king for judgment. In this way he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
After forty years, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron to keep a promise I made to the LORD.
While I, your servant, was living in Geshur in Syria, I made this promise: 'If the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD.'"
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he got up and went to Hebron.
But Absalom sent secret messengers through all the tribes of Israel to say, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, shout, 'Absalom is king in Hebron!'"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited as guests, and they went innocently, knowing nothing about the plan.
While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel from Giloh, who was David's adviser, to come from his town of Giloh. So the plot grew stronger, and more and more people joined Absalom.
A messenger came to David and said, "The hearts of the people of Israel have gone over to Absalom."

Then David said to all his officials who were with him in Jerusalem, "Get up! We must run away, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Hurry, or he will quickly catch up with us, bring disaster on us, and kill the people of the city with the sword."
The king's officials answered him, "Your servants are ready to do whatever our lord the king decides."
So the king left, with his whole household following him. But he left ten of his slave wives behind to take care of the palace.
The king went out with all the people following him, and they stopped at the last house.
All his officials marched past him, along with all the Kerethites and Pelethites, the king's guards. All six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath also marched past the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you coming with us? Go back and stay with the new king. You are a foreigner, an exile from your own land. Go back to your own place.

You only came yesterday. Should I make you wander around with us today, when I don't even know where I am going? Go back, and take your brothers with you. May the LORD show you his faithful love and truth."
But Ittai answered the king, "As surely as the LORD lives, and as surely as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king is, whether it means life or death, there your servant will be."
David said to Ittai, "Go ahead and march on." So Ittai the Gittite marched on with all his men and all the children who were with him.
All the people of the land cried loudly as all the people passed by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people went on toward the wilderness.
Zadok was there too, and all the Levites with him were carrying the ark of God's covenant. They set down God's ark, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had finished leaving the city.
Then the king said to Zadok, "Take God's ark back into the city. If the LORD is pleased with me, he will bring me back and let me see the ark and the place where it stays again.
But if he says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then here I am. Let him do to me whatever he thinks is best."
The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Aren't you a seer, someone who sees what God is doing? Go back to the city in peace, with your son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan.
I will wait at the river crossings in the wilderness until I get a message from you telling me what is happening."
So Zadok and Abiathar took God's ark back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David went up the Mount of Olives, crying as he went. His head was covered and he walked barefoot. All the people with him also covered their heads and cried as they went up.
Someone told David, "Ahithophel is one of those plotting with Absalom." So David prayed, "LORD, please make Ahithophel's advice foolish."
When David reached the top of the hill, where people worshipped God, Hushai the Arkite came to meet him. His coat was torn and he had dust on his head.
David said to him, "If you come with me, you will only be a burden to me.
But if you go back to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, my king. I used to serve your father, but now I will serve you,' then you can help me by spoiling Ahithophel's advice.
The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there with you. Tell them everything you hear in the king's palace.
Their two sons are there with them: Ahimaaz son of Zadok, and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send them to me with everything you hear."
So David's friend Hushai arrived in the city just as Absalom was coming into Jerusalem.

When David had gone a little past the top of the hill, Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, came to meet him. He had a pair of donkeys with saddles on them, carrying two hundred loaves of bread, one hundred bunches of raisins, one hundred pieces of summer fruit, and a skin bag full of wine.

The king asked Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's family to ride. The bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for anyone who becomes weak in the wilderness to drink."
The king asked, "Where is your master's grandson?" Ziba answered the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem. He said, 'Today the people of Israel will give me back my grandfather's kingdom.'"
Then the king said to Ziba, "Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba said, "I bow down to you. May I always please you, my lord the king."
When King David came to Bahurim, a man from Saul's family came out of the town. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he cursed David as he came out.
He threw stones at David and at all of King David's officials, even though all the people and the strong fighting men were on David's right and left.
As Shimei cursed, he said, "Get out, get out, you murderer, you wicked man!

The LORD is paying you back for all the blood of Saul's family. You took his place as king, and now the LORD has given the kingdom to your son Absalom. Look, you are ruined by your own evil, because you are a murderer!"
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over there and cut off his head."
But the king said, "What has this got to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing me because the LORD told him, 'Curse David,' then who can ask him, 'Why are you doing this?'"

Then David said to Abishai and all his officials, "My own son, my own flesh and blood, is trying to kill me. So this man from Benjamin has even more reason to do this! Leave him alone and let him curse, because the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps the LORD will see the wrong being done to me and will give me good things in return for the cursing I receive today."
So David and his men kept going along the road. Shimei walked along the hillside across from him, cursing as he went, throwing stones at him and throwing dust in the air.
The king and all the people with him were very tired when they arrived, and he rested there.
Meanwhile, Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
Then David's friend Hushai the Arkite came to Absalom and said to him, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this how you show loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with your friend?"
Hushai said to Absalom, "No, I will belong to the one chosen by the LORD, by these people, and by all the men of Israel. I will stay with him.
Besides, who should I serve? Shouldn't I serve the son? Just as I served your father, so I will serve you."
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give us your advice. What should we do?"

Ahithophel answered Absalom, "Sleep with your father's slave wives, the ones he left to take care of the palace. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself hateful to your father, and everyone who supports you will become even stronger."
So they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof of the palace, and Absalom slept with his father's slave wives where all Israel could see.
In those days, the advice Ahithophel gave was treated like a word from God himself. That is how both David and Absalom thought of all of Ahithophel's advice.
Ahithophel also said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight to chase David.
I will attack him while he is tired and weak. I will make him panic, and all the people with him will run away. I will kill only the king,
and I will bring all the people back to you. When the man you are after is dead, everyone will come back, and all the people will be at peace."
This plan seemed good to Absalom and to all the leaders of Israel.
But Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Arkite too. Let's hear what he has to say."
When Hushai came, Absalom said to him, "Ahithophel has given this advice. Should we do what he says? If not, tell us your idea."
Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the advice Ahithophel has given is not good."

Hushai went on, "You know your father and his men. They are strong fighters, and they are as fierce as a mother bear whose cubs have been stolen. Besides, your father is an experienced soldier. He will not spend the night with the people.

Even now he is probably hiding in a cave or some other place. If some of your men are killed at the start of the fighting, whoever hears about it will say, 'Absalom's followers are being slaughtered!'
Then even the bravest soldier, with a heart like a lion, will lose all courage. For all Israel knows that your father is a strong fighter and that the men with him are brave.
So this is my advice: Gather all Israel to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the grains of sand by the sea. Then lead them into battle yourself.
We will attack David wherever he is found. We will come down on him like dew falling on the ground. Not one of them will be left alive, neither David nor any of his men.
If he goes into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down into the valley until not even a small stone is left there."

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The advice of Hushai the Arkite is better than the advice of Ahithophel." The LORD had decided to spoil Ahithophel's good advice, so that the LORD could bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai told the priests Zadok and Abiathar, "Ahithophel advised Absalom and the leaders of Israel to do this, but I advised them to do that.

Now send a message to David quickly. Tell him, 'Do not spend the night at the river crossings in the wilderness. Cross over the river at once, or the king and all the people with him will be wiped out.'"
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En Rogel. A servant girl would go and give them messages, and they would go and tell King David. They could not risk being seen going into the city.
But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So the two of them left quickly and went to the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his yard, and they climbed down into it.
The man's wife took a cover and spread it over the opening of the well, and spread grain on top of it, so no one knew they were there.

When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they asked, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman answered, "They have crossed over the stream." The men searched but could not find them, so they went back to Jerusalem.

After the men had gone, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed out of the well and went to tell King David. They said to him, "Get up and cross the river quickly, because Ahithophel has given advice against you."
So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan River. By sunrise, every one of them had crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he put a saddle on his donkey and went home to his own town. He put his affairs in order and then hanged himself. He died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David came to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan River with all the men of Israel.

Absalom had made Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra, an Israelite, who had married Abigail. She was the daughter of Nahash and the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom set up camp in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Makir son of Ammiel from Lo Debar, and Barzillai from Rogelim in Gilead
brought beds, bowls, and clay pots. They also brought wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, and roasted seeds,
honey, butter, sheep, and cheese from cows' milk for David and the people with him to eat. They said, "The people must be hungry, tired, and thirsty in the wilderness."
David counted the men who were with him and put commanders over groups of a thousand and groups of a hundred.

He sent the army out in three groups. Joab led one third, Joab's brother Abishai son of Zeruiah led another third, and Ittai the Gittite led the last third. The king told the soldiers, "I will certainly go out with you myself."

But the men said, "You must not go out. If we have to run away, they won't care about us. Even if half of us die, they won't care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. So it is better for you to stay in the city and be ready to send us help."
The king said to them, "I will do whatever you think is best." So the king stood beside the city gate while all the army marched out in groups of hundreds and thousands.
The king gave an order to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai: "For my sake, be gentle with the young man Absalom." All the soldiers heard the king give this order to the commanders about Absalom.
So David's army went out into the countryside to fight against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
There the army of Israel was defeated by David's men. A great many were killed that day, twenty thousand men.
The battle spread out over the whole countryside, and the forest killed more people that day than the sword did.

Then Absalom happened to meet some of David's men. Absalom was riding his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a large oak tree. Absalom's head got caught in the tree, and he was left hanging in mid-air while the mule kept going.
One of the men saw this and told Joab, "I just saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree."
Joab said to the man who told him, "You saw him? Then why didn't you strike him down to the ground right there? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a soldier's belt."

But the man said to Joab, "Even if I were given a thousand pieces of silver, I would not lift my hand against the king's son. We all heard the king order you, Abishai, and Ittai, 'For my sake, make sure no one harms the young man Absalom.'
If I had betrayed the king and killed his son, the king would have found out, because nothing is hidden from the king. And you would not have stood up for me."
Joab said, "I'm not going to waste time with you." So he took three spears in his hand and plunged them into Absalom's heart while he was still alive, hanging in the oak tree.
Then ten young men who carried Joab's armour surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Then Joab blew the trumpet, and his men stopped chasing Israel, because Joab held them back.
They took Absalom's body, threw it into a large pit in the forest, and piled a huge heap of stones over it. Meanwhile, all the Israelites ran away to their own homes.

While Absalom was still alive, he had set up a stone pillar for himself in the King's Valley. He said, "I have no son to keep my name alive." So he named the pillar after himself, and it is still called Absalom's Monument today.
Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and take the good news to the king that the LORD has rescued him from his enemies."
Joab told him, "You are not the one to take the news today. You can do it another day, but not today, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to a man from Cush, "Go and tell the king what you have seen." The man from Cush bowed down to Joab and ran off.
But Ahimaaz son of Zadok said to Joab again, "No matter what happens, please let me run after the man from Cush." Joab said, "My son, why do you want to go? You will get no reward for this news."
He answered, "No matter what happens, I want to run." So Joab said, "Run!" Then Ahimaaz ran by the road through the plain and passed the man from Cush.
David was sitting between the inner and outer gates of the city. The watchman went up to the roof over the gate by the wall. As he looked out, he saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he must be bringing news." The runner came closer and closer.
Then the watchman saw another man running. He called down to the gatekeeper, "Look, another man is running alone!" The king said, "He must be bringing news too."
The watchman said, "I think the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man. He must be bringing good news."

Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground and said, "Praise the LORD your God! He has handed over the men who rebelled against my lord the king."
The king asked, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent me, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I don't know what it was about."
The king said, "Step aside and stand here." So he stepped aside and stood there.
Then the man from Cush arrived and said, "Good news for my lord the king! Today the LORD has rescued you from all who rose up against you."
The king asked the man from Cush, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The man from Cush answered, "May all the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up to harm you, end up like that young man!"
The king was deeply shaken. He went up to the room over the gate and cried. As he went, he said, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was told, "The king is crying and mourning for Absalom."
So for the whole army, the victory that day turned into mourning, because the soldiers heard people say, "The king is grieving for his son."
That day the soldiers crept quietly into the city, like soldiers who are ashamed because they ran away from battle.
The king covered his face and cried loudly, "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Then Joab went into the house to the king and said, "Today you have shamed all your men. They saved your life today, and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives and your slave wives.

You love those who hate you, and you hate those who love you. Today you have made it clear that your commanders and soldiers mean nothing to you. I can see that you would be happy if Absalom were alive today and all of us were dead.

Now get up, go out, and encourage your men. I promise by the LORD that if you don't go out, not one man will be left with you by tonight. That would be worse for you than all the trouble you have had from your youth until now."
So the king got up and sat at the city gate. When the people were told, "The king is sitting at the gate," they all came to him. Meanwhile, the Israelites had all run away to their homes.

All through the tribes of Israel, the people were arguing with each other. They said, "The king rescued us from our enemies. He saved us from the Philistines. But now he has run away from the land because of Absalom.
And Absalom, whom we anointed to rule over us, has died in battle. So why is no one talking about bringing the king back?"

King David sent a message to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: "Ask the leaders of Judah, 'Why are you the last to bring the king back to his palace? I have heard what all Israel is saying about bringing the king back to his home.
You are my relatives, my own flesh and blood. So why should you be the last to bring the king back?'
And tell Amasa, 'You are my own flesh and blood. May God punish me, and even more, if I do not make you commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"
So David won the hearts of all the men of Judah, and they were united as one. They sent word to the king: "Come back, you and all your officials."
So the king started back and came to the Jordan River. The men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin, who lived in Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin were with him. Ziba, the servant of Saul's family, was there too, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed into the Jordan to meet the king.
They crossed back and forth to bring the king's family over and to do whatever the king wanted. As the king was about to cross the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera fell down in front of him.
He said to the king, "My lord, please don't hold me guilty. Don't remember the wrong your servant did on the day you left Jerusalem. Please put it out of your mind.
I, your servant, know that I have sinned. That is why I have come today, the first from all the tribes of Joseph to come down and meet my lord the king."
But Abishai son of Zeruiah said, "Shouldn't Shimei be put to death for this? He cursed the LORD's chosen king!"

David said, "What has this got to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why are you acting like my enemies today? Should anyone in Israel be put to death today? Don't I know that today I am king over Israel again?"
So the king said to Shimei, "You will not die." And the king made him a promise with an oath.
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, also came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came back safely.
When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king asked him, "Mephibosheth, why didn't you go with me?"
He answered, "My lord the king, my servant tricked me. I said, 'Saddle a donkey for me so I can ride with the king,' because I, your servant, am crippled.
But Ziba has told lies about me to you, my lord the king. But my lord the king is like an angel of God, so do whatever you think is right.

All my grandfather's family deserved nothing but death from my lord the king. Yet you gave me a place among those who eat at your own table. So what right do I have to ask anything more from the king?"
The king said to him, "Why say any more? I have decided that you and Ziba will divide the land between you."
Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all! It is enough for me that my lord the king has come home safely."
Barzillai from Gilead also came down from Rogelim. He went with the king to the Jordan to see him safely across.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided food for the king while he stayed at Mahanaim, because he was a very rich man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Come with me to Jerusalem, and I will take care of you there."
But Barzillai answered the king, "How many more years do I have to live, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king?

Today I am eighty years old. Can I still tell what is good and what is bad? Can your servant taste what he eats and drinks? Can I still hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be an extra burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will just go a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king give me such a reward?

Please let your servant go back, so I can die in my own town near the grave of my father and mother. But here is your servant Kimham. Let him go with my lord the king, and do for him whatever you think is good."
The king answered, "Kimham will go with me, and I will do for him whatever you think is good. And whatever you ask of me, I will do for you."
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Kimham went with him. All the soldiers of Judah and half the soldiers of Israel went with the king.

Soon all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, "Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, steal the king away? Why did they bring the king and his family across the Jordan, together with all David's men?"
All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten any of the king's food? Has he given us any gifts?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, so we have more right to David than you do. Why did you treat us with contempt? Weren't we the first to speak about bringing back our king?" But the men of Judah spoke even more harshly than the men of Israel.

Now a troublemaker named Sheba son of Bikri, from the tribe of Benjamin, happened to be there. He blew a trumpet and shouted, "We have no share in David! We have no part in Jesse's son! Everyone go home, Israel!"
So all the men of Israel left David and followed Sheba son of Bikri. But the men of Judah stayed with their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

When David came back to his palace in Jerusalem, he took the ten slave wives he had left to take care of the palace and put them in a house under guard. He gave them food, but he did not sleep with them again. They were kept shut away until the day they died, living like widows.
Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together within three days, and be here yourself."
So Amasa went to call the men of Judah together, but he took longer than the time the king had given him.
David said to Abishai, "Sheba son of Bikri will do us more harm than Absalom did. Take my men and go after him, before he gets into strong walled cities and escapes from us."
So Joab's men, the Kerethites, the Pelethites, and all the strongest fighters, left Jerusalem with Abishai to chase Sheba son of Bikri.

When they reached the large rock at Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his soldier's uniform, with a belt around his waist and a sword in its sheath. As he stepped forward, the sword fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, "How are you, my brother?" Then Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's other hand. Joab stabbed him in the stomach, and his insides spilled out on the ground. Joab did not need to strike him again, and Amasa died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went on chasing Sheba son of Bikri.
One of Joab's young men stood beside Amasa's body and shouted, "Whoever supports Joab and whoever is for David, follow Joab!"

Amasa lay in the middle of the road, rolling in his own blood. The man saw that all the soldiers were stopping to look. So he dragged Amasa's body off the road into a field and threw a cloth over it, because everyone who came by was stopping.
Once the body was moved off the road, all the men went on with Joab to chase Sheba son of Bikri.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth Maacah, and through the whole area of the Berites, who gathered together and followed him.
Joab's men came and surrounded Sheba in Abel of Beth Maacah. They built a ramp of earth up against the city wall, and all the soldiers with Joab began battering the wall to knock it down.
Then a wise woman called out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab to come here so I can speak to him."
Joab came near, and the woman asked, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." She said to him, "Listen to what your servant has to say." He answered, "I am listening."
She said, "In the old days people used to say, 'Go and get advice from Abel,' and that is how they settled their problems.
We are peaceful and faithful people in Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is like a mother in Israel. Why do you want to swallow up what belongs to the LORD?"
Joab answered, "Never! I would never swallow up or destroy anything!

That is not what this is about. A man named Sheba son of Bikri, from the hill country of Ephraim, has rebelled against King David. Just hand him over, and I will leave the city." The woman said to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

Then the woman went to all the people with her wise advice. They cut off the head of Sheba son of Bikri and threw it out to Joab. So Joab blew the trumpet, and his men left the city and went home. And Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was in charge of the whole army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the Kerethites and Pelethites.
Adoniram was in charge of the forced labour. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Sheva was the royal secretary. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
And Ira from Jair was David's priest and chief official.

While David was king, there was a famine for three years in a row. So David asked the LORD about it. The LORD said, "It is because of Saul and his family. They are guilty of murder, because Saul killed the Gibeonites."

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites. They were what was left of the Amorites. The Israelites had promised with an oath to spare them, but Saul had tried to wipe them out because he was so eager to help the people of Israel and Judah.
David asked the Gibeonites, "What can I do for you? How can I make up for the wrong that was done, so that you will bless the LORD's people?"
The Gibeonites answered him, "We do not want silver or gold from Saul or his family. And we do not have the right to put anyone in Israel to death." David said, "I will do whatever you ask."
They answered the king, "Saul tried to destroy us. He planned to wipe us out so that we would have no place anywhere in Israel.
So hand over seven of his male descendants to us. We will hang them in front of the LORD at Gibeah, Saul's town, the town of the man the LORD chose." The king said, "I will hand them over."
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, because of the promise David and Jonathan had made to each other in front of the LORD.

Instead, the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul. He also took the five sons Saul's daughter Merab had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai from Meholah.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who hanged them on a hill in front of the LORD. All seven of them died together. They were put to death in the first days of the harvest, just as the barley harvest was beginning.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on a rock. She stayed there from the beginning of the harvest until the rain fell on the bodies. She did not let the birds land on them during the day or the wild animals come near them at night.
When David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's slave wife, had done,

he went and got the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the people of Jabesh Gilead. They had secretly taken the bodies from the public square in Beth Shan, where the Philistines had hung them up after they killed Saul on Mount Gilboa.
David brought the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from there, and they also gathered up the bones of the seven men who had been hanged.

They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the tomb of Saul's father Kish, at Zela in the land of Benjamin. They did everything the king commanded. After that, God answered their prayers for the land.
Once again there was war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his men to fight the Philistines, and he became very tired.

Ishbi-Benob, one of the descendants of the giants, had a bronze spear tip that weighed three hundred shekels, about three and a half kilograms. He was wearing new armour, and he planned to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's rescue. He struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men made him promise, "You must never go out with us to battle again. You are the lamp of Israel, and we must not let that light go out."
Some time later there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbekai from Hushah killed Saph, another descendant of the giants.
In another battle with the Philistines at Gob, Elhanan son of Jaare-Oregim from Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath from Gath, whose spear had a shaft as thick as the bar on a weaver's loom.
There was another battle at Gath. A huge man was there who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He too was a descendant of the giants.
When he made fun of Israel, Jonathan son of Shimei, David's brother, killed him.
These four were descendants of the giants in Gath, and they were killed by David and his men.
David sang the words of this song to the LORD on the day the LORD rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul.
He said: "The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and the one who rescues me.
God is my rock, and I run to him for safety. He is my shield and my strong saviour, my high tower and my safe place. My Saviour, you save me from violent people.
I call to the LORD, who deserves all praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
The waves of death surrounded me. Floods of evil swept over me and made me afraid.
The ropes of the grave were wrapped around me. The traps of death were set in front of me.
In my trouble I called to the LORD. Yes, I cried to my God. From his temple he heard my voice. My cry reached his ears.
Then the earth shook and trembled. The foundations of the heavens rocked and shook, because he was angry.
Smoke came out of his nose, and burning fire came out of his mouth. Burning coals blazed out from him.
He opened the heavens and came down. Dark clouds were under his feet.
He rode on a winged creature and flew. He soared on the wings of the wind.
He wrapped himself in darkness like a tent, with dark rain clouds and thick clouds of the sky.
From the brightness around him, burning coals of fire blazed out.
The LORD thundered from heaven. The voice of the Most High was heard.
He shot his arrows and scattered his enemies. He sent lightning and threw them into confusion.
Then the bottom of the sea could be seen, and the foundations of the world were uncovered, when the LORD spoke sharply, at the blast of breath from his nose.
He reached down from above and took hold of me. He pulled me out of deep waters.
He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from those who hated me, because they were too strong for me.
They attacked me on the day I was in trouble, but the LORD held me up.
He brought me out into a wide, open place. He rescued me because he was pleased with me.
The LORD rewarded me because I did what was right. He gave back to me because my hands were clean.
For I have followed the ways of the LORD. I have not done evil by turning away from my God.
I have kept all his laws in front of me. I have not turned away from his rules.
I was without fault before him, and I kept myself from sin.
So the LORD has rewarded me for doing what is right, because he has seen that my hands are clean.
To people who are faithful, you show that you are faithful. To people who are without fault, you show that you are without fault.
To people who are pure, you show that you are pure. But to people who are crooked, you show that you are clever.
You save humble people, but your eyes watch proud people so that you can bring them down.
LORD, you are my lamp. The LORD lights up my darkness.
With your help I can charge against an army. With my God I can climb over a wall.
God's way is perfect. The LORD's word has been tested and is true. He is a shield for everyone who runs to him for safety.
For who is God except the LORD? And who is a rock except our God?
God is my strong fortress, and he makes my way perfect.
He makes my feet as sure as the feet of a deer, and he helps me stand safely on the high places.
He trains my hands for battle, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.
You have given me your shield that saves me. Your gentle help has made me great.
You made a wide path for my feet, so that my ankles did not slip.
I chased my enemies and destroyed them. I did not turn back until they were wiped out.
I wiped them out and struck them down, so that they could not get up. They fell under my feet.
You gave me strength for the battle. You made my attackers bow down under me.
You made my enemies turn their backs and run, and I destroyed those who hated me.
They looked for help, but no one saved them. They even called to the LORD, but he did not answer them.
I crushed them as fine as the dust of the earth. I stamped on them and trampled them like mud in the streets.
You rescued me when my own people fought against me. You kept me as the leader of nations. People I did not know now serve me.
Foreigners bow down to me. As soon as they hear about me, they obey me.
Foreigners lose their courage, and they come trembling out of their hiding places.
The LORD lives! Praise be to my rock! May God, the rock who saves me, be honoured!
He is the God who pays back my enemies for me, and he puts nations under my control.
He sets me free from my enemies. You lift me up above those who attack me. You rescue me from violent people.
So I will thank you, LORD, among the nations. I will sing praises to your name.
He gives great victories to his king. He shows his faithful love to his chosen king, to David and his descendants forever."
These are the last words of David. This is what David son of Jesse says, the man God lifted up high, the king chosen by the God of Jacob, the sweet song writer of Israel:
"The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me. His word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel spoke. The Rock of Israel said to me, 'A king who rules people fairly, who rules with respect for God,
is like the light of morning when the sun comes up, a morning without clouds. He is like the sunshine after rain that makes fresh grass grow from the ground.'

Isn't that how God has treated my family? He has made a covenant with me that lasts forever, arranged in every detail and sure. He will make my salvation complete and give me everything I long for. Won't he make it grow?
But wicked people are like thorns that are thrown away. No one can pick them up with bare hands.
Whoever touches them must use an iron tool or the shaft of a spear. They will be completely burned up in the fire where they lie."
These are the names of David's mighty warriors: Josheb-Basshebeth the Tahkemonite was chief of the officers. He was also called Adino the Eznite. He killed eight hundred men at one time.

Next to him was Eleazar son of Dodai the Ahohite. He was one of the three mighty warriors with David when they stood up to the Philistines who had gathered for battle. The other Israelite soldiers had pulled back,
