but Eleazar stood his ground and struck down Philistines until his hand was so tired that it stuck to his sword. The LORD gave a great victory that day. The other soldiers came back to him only to take things from the dead.
Next to him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines had gathered at a place where there was a field full of lentils, and the Israelite soldiers ran away from them.
But Shammah stood in the middle of the field and defended it. He struck down the Philistines, and the LORD gave a great victory.
At harvest time, three of the thirty chief warriors went down to meet David at the cave of Adullam. A group of Philistines was camping in the Valley of Rephaim.
At that time David was in the fortress, and some Philistine soldiers were guarding Bethlehem.
David had a strong longing and said, "Oh, if only someone would bring me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!"

So the three mighty warriors broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it. Instead, he poured it out as an offering to the LORD.

He said, "LORD, I could never drink this! It is like drinking the blood of these men who risked their lives to get it." So he would not drink it. These were some of the brave things the three mighty warriors did.
Abishai, the brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was the leader of the Three. He once fought three hundred men with his spear and killed them, and he became as famous as the Three.
He was the most honoured of the Three and became their commander, but he was not one of the Three.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a brave man from Kabzeel who did great things. He killed two of Moab's greatest warriors. He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion.
And he killed a huge Egyptian who had a spear in his hand. Benaiah went against him with only a club. He grabbed the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.
These were the brave things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did, and he became as famous as the Three mighty warriors.
He was more honoured than the Thirty, but he was not one of the Three. David put him in charge of his bodyguard.
These were among the Thirty: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem,
Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,
Helez the Paltite, Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa,
Abiezer from Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai from Netophah,
Heleb son of Baanah from Netophah, Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah in Benjamin,
Benaiah from Pirathon, Hiddai from the ravines of Gaash,
Abi-Albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,
Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,
Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite,
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite, Eliam son of Ahithophel from Giloh,
Hezro from Carmel, Paarai the Arbite,
Igal son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai from Beeroth, who carried the armour of Joab son of Zeruiah,
Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
and Uriah the Hittite. There were thirty-seven in all.
Once again the LORD was angry with Israel, and he stirred up David against them. He said to David, "Go and count the people of Israel and Judah."
So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I will know how many there are."
But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God make the people a hundred times more than there are now, and may my lord the king live to see it. But why does my lord the king want to do this?"
But the king's order was stronger than the objections of Joab and the army commanders. So Joab and the commanders left the king and went out to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan River and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley of Gad. Then they went on to Jazer.
Then they went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim Hodshi, and on to Dan Jaan and around toward Sidon.
They went to the fortress of Tyre and to all the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites. Finally they went to Beersheba in the south of Judah.
After they had gone through the whole land, they came back to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab reported the number of people to the king. In Israel there were eight hundred thousand strong men who could fight with a sword, and in Judah there were five hundred thousand.

After David had counted the people, his heart troubled him. David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly by what I have done. Now, LORD, I beg you, take away the guilt of your servant. I have done a very foolish thing."
Before David got up the next morning, the LORD's message came to the prophet Gad, David's seer:
"Go and tell David, 'This is what the LORD says: I am giving you three choices. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

So Gad went to David and said to him, "Should there be seven years of famine in your land? Or should you run away from your enemies for three months while they chase you? Or should there be three days of deadly disease in your land? Think about it now and decide what answer I should give to the one who sent me."
David said to Gad, "I am in a terrible situation. Let us fall into the hands of the LORD, because his mercy is great. But do not let me fall into human hands."
So the LORD sent a deadly disease on Israel from that morning until the time he had set. Seventy thousand people died, from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel reached out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD felt sorry about the disaster. He said to the angel who was killing the people, "That is enough! Put your hand down." The LORD's angel was then at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel who was striking down the people, he said to the LORD, "I am the one who has sinned and done wrong. These people are like sheep. What have they done? Please punish me and my family instead."
That day Gad came to David and said to him, "Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
So David went up, as Gad told him and as the LORD commanded.
Araunah looked out and saw the king and his officials coming toward him. So he went out and bowed down in front of the king with his face to the ground.

Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to see his servant?" David answered, "To buy your threshing floor, so that I can build an altar to the LORD and stop the disease that is killing the people."
Araunah said to David, "My lord the king, take whatever you want and offer it. Here are oxen for the burnt offering, and here are the threshing boards and the oxen's yokes to use for wood.
My king, I, Araunah, give all this to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept your offering."

But the king said to Araunah, "No, I will pay you for it. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, about six hundred grams.
David built an altar to the LORD there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered his prayer for the land, and the disease stopped killing the people of Israel.
1Kgs: King David was now very old. His servants covered him with blankets, but he could not keep warm.

So his servants said to him, "Let us look for a young unmarried woman for our lord the king. She can wait on the king and take care of him. She can lie beside you, so that our lord the king will keep warm."
So they searched all over Israel for a beautiful young woman. They found Abishag from Shunem and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful. She took care of the king and served him, but the king did not have sex with her.
Now Adonijah, the son of David's wife Haggith, began to make himself important. He said, "I will be king." So he got chariots and horsemen for himself, and fifty men to run ahead of him.
His father had never once corrected him by asking, "Why are you doing that?" He was also very handsome, and he was born next after Absalom.
Adonijah talked with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they followed him and helped him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's mighty warriors did not join Adonijah.
Adonijah sacrificed sheep, cattle, and fat calves at the Stone of Zoheleth near En Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials from Judah.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty warriors, or his brother Solomon.
Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, "Haven't you heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has made himself king, and our lord David doesn't even know about it?
Now let me give you some advice, so that you can save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.

Go in to King David and say to him, 'My lord the king, didn't you promise me with an oath, "Your son Solomon will surely be king after me, and he will sit on my throne"? Then why has Adonijah become king?'
While you are still there talking with the king, I will come in after you and tell him that what you said is true."
So Bathsheba went to see the king in his room. He was very old, and Abishag from Shunem was taking care of him.
Bathsheba bowed down low to show respect to the king. The king asked, "What do you want?"
She said to him, "My lord, you yourself promised me with an oath by the LORD your God, 'Your son Solomon will surely be king after me, and he will sit on my throne.'
But now Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, don't even know about it.
He has sacrificed a great many cattle, fat calves, and sheep. He has invited all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army. But he did not invite your servant Solomon.
My lord the king, all Israel is watching you. They are waiting for you to tell them who will sit on your throne after you.
If you don't, then as soon as my lord the king dies and is buried with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals."
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.
The king was told, "Nathan the prophet is here." He came in and bowed down in front of the king with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, "My lord the king, did you say, 'Adonijah will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne'?

Today he went down and sacrificed a great many cattle, fat calves, and sheep. He invited all the king's sons, the army commanders, and Abiathar the priest. Right now they are eating and drinking with him and shouting, 'Long live King Adonijah!'
But he did not invite me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, or Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Has my lord the king done this without telling your servants who should sit on the throne after you?"
Then King David said, "Call Bathsheba in here." So she came in and stood in front of the king.
The king made this promise: "As surely as the LORD lives, who has rescued me from every trouble,

I will do today what I promised you with an oath by the LORD, the God of Israel. I said, 'Your son Solomon will surely be king after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place.' I will certainly do it today."
Then Bathsheba bowed down with her face to the ground to show respect to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"
King David said, "Call in Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada." When they came before the king,
he said to them, "Take my officials with you. Put my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to the Gihon spring.
There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet must anoint him king over Israel. Blow the trumpet and shout, 'Long live King Solomon!'
Then come back up with him, and he will come and sit on my throne and be king in my place. I have chosen him to be ruler over Israel and Judah."
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so too.
Just as the LORD has been with my lord the king, may he be with Solomon. May he make Solomon's throne even greater than the throne of my lord King David!"
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Kerethites and Pelethites went down. They put Solomon on King David's mule and took him to the Gihon spring.
Zadok the priest took the horn of olive oil from the holy tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people shouted, "Long live King Solomon!"
All the people followed him back up, playing flutes and celebrating with great joy. They were so loud that the ground shook with the noise.
Adonijah and all his guests heard the noise just as they were finishing their meal. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he asked, "Why is the city in such an uproar?"
While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, "Come in. You are a good man, and you must be bringing good news."
Jonathan answered Adonijah, "Not at all! Our lord King David has made Solomon king.
The king sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Kerethites and Pelethites with him, and they put him on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king at the Gihon spring. They have come up from there celebrating, and the whole city is ringing with the noise. That is the sound you hear.
What's more, Solomon is now sitting on the royal throne.

The king's officials have also come to congratulate our lord King David. They said, 'May your God make Solomon's name even more famous than yours, and his throne greater than yours!' And the king bowed down in worship on his bed.
The king also said, 'Praise the LORD, the God of Israel! Today he has let my own eyes see one of my sons sitting on my throne.'"
Then all of Adonijah's guests were terrified. They got up and each one went his own way.
Adonijah was afraid of Solomon, so he got up and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.

Then Solomon was told, "Adonijah is afraid of King Solomon. He is holding on to the horns of the altar and saying, 'Let King Solomon first promise me with an oath that he will not kill his servant with the sword.'"
Solomon said, "If he shows himself to be a good man, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if any evil is found in him, he will die."
Then King Solomon sent men, and they brought Adonijah down from the altar. He came and bowed down to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go home."
When the time came near for David to die, he gave these instructions to his son Solomon:
"I am about to go the way everyone on earth must go. So be strong and act like a man.

Do what the LORD your God tells you. Walk in his ways, and keep his laws, commands, rules, and teachings, as they are written in the Law of Moses. Then you will do well in everything you do and wherever you go.

And the LORD will keep the promise he made to me. He said, 'If your descendants are careful to live faithfully before me with all their heart and soul, you will always have a man on the throne of Israel.'

You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me. He killed the two commanders of Israel's armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them in a time of peace as if it were war, and their blood splashed on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet.
Deal with him in your wisdom. Do not let him grow old and go down to the grave in peace.
But be kind to the sons of Barzillai from Gilead. Let them eat at your table, because they helped me when I ran away from your brother Absalom.

And remember Shimei son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim, who is with you. He put a terrible curse on me on the day I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan River, I promised him by the LORD, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.'
But now do not let him go unpunished. You are wise, and you will know what to do to him. Make sure he dies a bloody death in his old age."
Then David died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David.
David had ruled over Israel for forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was made very secure.
Then Adonijah son of Haggith went to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. She asked him, "Have you come in peace?" He answered, "Yes, in peace."
Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Go ahead."
He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine. All Israel expected me to be king. But things changed, and the kingdom went to my brother, because the LORD gave it to him.
Now I have one thing to ask of you. Please don't refuse me." She said, "Go ahead."
He said, "Please ask King Solomon to give me Abishag from Shunem to be my wife. He won't say no to you."
Bathsheba said, "All right. I will speak to the king for you."

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him for Adonijah. The king stood up to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat down on his throne and had a throne brought for the king's mother, and she sat at his right side.
She said, "I have one small thing to ask of you. Please don't refuse me." The king said to her, "Ask, my mother. I will not refuse you."
She said, "Let Abishag from Shunem be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife."

King Solomon answered his mother, "Why are you asking for Abishag from Shunem for Adonijah? You might as well ask for the kingdom for him too! After all, he is my older brother, and Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah are on his side!"
Then King Solomon made a promise by the LORD: "May God punish me, and even more, if Adonijah does not pay with his life for asking this!
The LORD has made me secure on the throne of my father David and has given me a royal family, as he promised. So as surely as the LORD lives, Adonijah will be put to death today!"
So King Solomon gave orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck Adonijah down, and he died.

Then the king said to Abiathar the priest, "Go back to your own fields in Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I will not put you to death now, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD for my father David, and you shared in all the hardships my father went through."
So Solomon removed Abiathar from being the LORD's priest. This made the LORD's word come true, which he had spoken at Shiloh about the family of Eli.
When the news reached Joab, he ran to the LORD's holy tent and took hold of the horns of the altar. Joab had supported Adonijah, although he had not supported Absalom.
King Solomon was told, "Joab has run to the LORD's tent and is standing beside the altar." Then Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go and strike him down."

Benaiah went into the LORD's tent and said to Joab, "The king says, 'Come out!'" But Joab answered, "No, I will die here." Benaiah went back to the king and told him, "This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me."
Then the king said to Benaiah, "Do as he says. Strike him down and bury him. Then my father's family and I will no longer be blamed for the innocent blood Joab spilled.

The LORD will pay him back for the blood he spilled. Without my father David knowing it, he attacked and killed two men who were better and more honest than he was: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army.
May the guilt for their blood be on Joab and his descendants forever. But may the LORD give peace forever to David, his descendants, his family, and his throne."
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up and struck Joab down and killed him. He was buried at his own home in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada in charge of the army in Joab's place, and he put Zadok the priest in Abiathar's place.
Then the king sent for Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there. Do not go anywhere else.
On the day you leave and cross the Kidron Valley, you can be sure that you will die. Your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei answered the king, "That is fair. Your servant will do what my lord the king has said." And Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
But three years later, two of Shimei's slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei was told, "Your slaves are in Gath."
So Shimei got up, put a saddle on his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to look for his slaves. He went and brought his slaves back from Gath.
Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had come back.

So the king sent for Shimei and said to him, "Didn't I make you promise by the LORD? Didn't I warn you, 'On the day you leave to go anywhere else, you can be sure that you will die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is fair. I will obey.'
So why did you not keep your promise to the LORD and obey the command I gave you?"
The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your heart all the evil you did to my father David. Now the LORD will pay you back for your evil.
But King Solomon will be blessed, and David's throne will be secure before the LORD forever."
Then the king gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck Shimei down, and he died. So the kingdom was made secure in Solomon's hands.

Solomon made a marriage agreement with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, by marrying Pharaoh's daughter. He brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his own palace, the LORD's temple, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people were still offering sacrifices at the high places, the local places of worship, because a temple for the LORD's name had not yet been built.
Solomon loved the LORD and followed the laws of his father David. But he also offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, because that was the most important high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream at night. God said, "Ask for whatever you want me to give you."

Solomon answered, "You showed great and faithful love to your servant, my father David, because he lived before you faithfully, rightly, and with an honest heart. And you have continued to show him this great love by giving him a son to sit on his throne today.
Now, LORD my God, you have made me, your servant, king in place of my father David. But I am like a little child. I don't know how to lead.
Your servant is here among the people you have chosen, a great nation with too many people to count.
So give your servant a heart that understands, so that I can judge your people and know the difference between right and wrong. For who is able to rule this great people of yours?"
The Lord was pleased that Solomon had asked for this.

So God said to him, "You have asked for this. You did not ask for a long life for yourself, or for riches, or for the death of your enemies. Instead you asked for understanding, so that you can judge fairly.
So I will do what you asked. I will give you a wise and understanding heart. There has never been anyone like you before, and there will never be anyone like you again.
I will also give you what you did not ask for: both riches and honour. As long as you live, no other king will be as great as you.
And if you follow my ways and keep my laws and commands, as your father David did, I will give you a long life."

Then Solomon woke up and realised it had been a dream. He went back to Jerusalem and stood in front of the ark of the LORD's covenant. He offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and gave a feast for all his officials.
One day two women who were prostitutes came to the king and stood in front of him.
One of them said, "Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house. I had a baby while she was there with me.
Three days after my baby was born, this woman also had a baby. We were alone. There was no one else in the house except the two of us.
During the night this woman's son died, because she rolled over on top of him.
She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while I, your servant, was asleep. She put him in her arms and put her dead son in my arms.
When I got up in the morning to feed my son, I saw that he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning light, I saw that he was not the son I had given birth to."

The other woman said, "No! The living one is my son, and the dead one is yours." But the first woman said, "No! The dead one is yours, and the living one is mine." And so they argued in front of the king.
Then the king said, "One of you says, 'My son is alive and your son is dead.' The other says, 'No! Your son is dead and mine is alive.'"
Then the king said, "Bring me a sword." So they brought a sword to the king.
The king said, "Cut the living child in two, and give half to one woman and half to the other."

Then the real mother of the living child was filled with love for her son. She said to the king, "Please, my lord, give her the living baby! Don't kill him!" But the other woman said, "He won't be mine or yours. Cut him in two!"
Then the king gave his decision: "Give the living baby to the first woman. Do not kill him. She is his mother."
When all Israel heard about the king's decision, they respected him deeply, because they saw that God had given him wisdom to judge fairly.
King Solomon ruled over all Israel.
These were his chief officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, were royal secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the district governors. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king's close adviser.
Ahishar was in charge of the palace. Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labour.
Solomon had twelve district governors over all Israel. They provided food for the king and his household. Each one had to provide food for one month of the year.
These are their names: Ben-Hur, in the hill country of Ephraim.
Ben-Deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan.
Ben-Hesed, in Arubboth. Sokoh and all the land of Hepher also belonged to him.
Ben-Abinadab, in all the hills of Dor. He was married to Taphath, Solomon's daughter.
Baana son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, and all of Beth Shean next to Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah, and on past Jokmeam.

Ben-Geber, in Ramoth Gilead. The towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead belonged to him, and so did the region of Argob in Bashan, with its sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars on the gates.
Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz, in Naphtali. He was married to Basemath, Solomon's daughter.
Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and in Bealoth.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri, in Gilead, the land that had belonged to Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. He was the only governor over that whole region.
The people of Judah and Israel were as many as the grains of sand on the seashore. They ate and drank and were happy.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. These countries paid him taxes and served him for his whole life.
Every day Solomon's household needed thirty measures of fine flour and sixty measures of ordinary flour,
ten fat cattle, twenty cattle from the pastures, and one hundred sheep, as well as deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fat poultry.
He ruled over all the kingdoms west of the Euphrates River, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all the kings west of the river. And he had peace on every side.
As long as Solomon lived, the people of Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan to Beersheba. Each family sat under its own grapevine and its own fig tree.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen.
The district governors provided food for King Solomon and for everyone who ate at his table. Each one did this in his own month, and they made sure nothing was missing.
They also brought barley and straw for the chariot horses and the fast horses to the right places, each one doing his share.
God gave Solomon very great wisdom and understanding, and a mind as wide as the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the east, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone else, even wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and wiser than Heman, Kalkol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He became famous in all the nations around.
He spoke three thousand proverbs, and he wrote one thousand and five songs.
He talked about plants, from the great cedar tree of Lebanon to the small hyssop plant that grows out of walls. He also taught about animals, birds, creatures that crawl on the ground, and fish.
People from every nation came to listen to Solomon's wisdom. They were sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard about his wisdom.
Hiram king of Tyre had always been a friend of David. When he heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father's place, he sent his officials to Solomon.
Solomon sent this message back to Hiram:
"You know that my father David could not build a temple for the name of the LORD his God. He was always fighting wars with the enemies all around him, until the LORD put them under his feet.
But now the LORD my God has given me peace on every side. There are no enemies and no disasters.
So I plan to build a temple for the name of the LORD my God, just as the LORD told my father David: 'Your son, whom I will put on your throne in your place, will build the temple for my name.'

So now give orders for cedar trees from Lebanon to be cut down for me. My workers will work with your workers, and I will pay your workers whatever wages you decide. You know that none of us can cut timber as well as the people of Sidon."
When Hiram heard Solomon's message, he was very happy. He said, "Praise the LORD today! He has given David a wise son to rule over this great nation."
Hiram sent this answer to Solomon: "I have received the message you sent me. I will do everything you want about the cedar logs and the cypress logs.

My workers will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will tie them together into rafts and float them by sea to the place you choose. There I will have them taken apart, and you can collect them. In return, you will do what I want by providing food for my household."
So Hiram gave Solomon all the cedar and cypress logs he wanted.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat as food for his household, and twenty measures of pure olive oil. Solomon did this for Hiram year after year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, just as he had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
King Solomon forced men from all over Israel to work for him. There were thirty thousand workers.
He sent them to Lebanon in groups of ten thousand men each month. They spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labour.
Solomon also had seventy thousand men who carried loads and eighty thousand men who cut stone in the hills.
Besides these, there were three thousand three hundred foremen in charge of the work, who directed the workers.
At the king's command, they cut large, expensive blocks of stone to make a foundation of shaped stones for the temple.
Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and men from Gebal cut and prepared the timber and the stone for building the temple.

Solomon began to build the LORD's temple four hundred and eighty years after the people of Israel came out of Egypt. It was in the fourth year of his rule over Israel, in the month of Ziv, the second month.

The temple King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. That is about twenty-seven metres long, nine metres wide, and thirteen and a half metres high.
The porch at the front of the main hall was twenty cubits wide, the same as the width of the temple. It stuck out ten cubits from the front of the temple.
He made windows for the temple with frames that could not be opened.
Against the outside walls of the main hall and the inner room, he built a structure with floors of side rooms all around.

The lowest floor was five cubits wide, the middle floor six cubits wide, and the third floor seven cubits wide. He made ledges around the outside of the temple wall, so that the beams would not have to be pushed into the walls of the temple.
The stones used to build the temple were cut and shaped at the quarry. So no hammer, axe, or any other iron tool was heard at the temple while it was being built.
The entrance to the lowest floor of side rooms was on the south side of the temple. Stairs went up to the middle floor, and from there to the third floor.
So Solomon built the temple and finished it. He made the roof with beams and boards of cedar.
He built the side rooms all along the temple. Each floor was five cubits high, and they were joined to the temple with cedar beams.
Then the LORD's message came to Solomon:
"About this temple you are building: if you follow my laws, obey my rules, and keep all my commands, I will do for you what I promised your father David.
I will live among the people of Israel, and I will never leave my people Israel."
So Solomon built the temple and finished it.
He covered the inside walls with cedar boards from the floor to the ceiling. He covered the floor with cypress boards.
He built a room twenty cubits long at the back of the temple, using cedar boards from the floor to the ceiling. This was the inner room, the Most Holy Place.
The main hall in front of the inner room was forty cubits long.
The inside of the temple was cedar, carved with gourds and open flowers. Everything was covered with cedar, so no stone could be seen.
He prepared the inner room inside the temple to hold the ark of the LORD's covenant.
The inner room was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He covered it with pure gold. He also covered the cedar altar.
Solomon covered the inside of the temple with pure gold. He hung gold chains across the front of the inner room, and covered it with gold.
He covered the whole inside of the temple with gold until it was all finished. He also covered with gold the whole altar that belonged to the inner room.
In the inner room he made two winged creatures out of olive wood. Each was ten cubits high.
Each wing of the first winged creature was five cubits long. From the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits.
The second winged creature also measured ten cubits. Both were the same size and the same shape.
Each winged creature was ten cubits high.

He put the winged creatures in the inner room of the temple, with their wings spread out. One wing of the first touched one wall, and one wing of the second touched the other wall. Their other wings touched each other in the middle of the room.
He covered the winged creatures with gold.
On all the walls around the temple, in both the inner and outer rooms, he carved pictures of winged creatures, palm trees, and open flowers.
He also covered the floors of both the inner and outer rooms with gold.
For the entrance to the inner room he made doors of olive wood. The top beam and the side posts were five-sided.
On the two olive wood doors he carved winged creatures, palm trees, and open flowers. He covered them with gold, spreading gold over the winged creatures and palm trees.
For the entrance to the main hall he also made door posts of olive wood. They were four-sided.
He made two doors of cypress wood. Each door had two parts that could fold.
He carved winged creatures, palm trees, and open flowers on them, and he covered the carvings evenly with gold.
He built the inner courtyard with three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams.
The foundation of the LORD's temple was laid in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv.
The temple was finished in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, the eighth month. Every part of it was finished exactly as planned. It took Solomon seven years to build it.
Solomon also built his own palace. It took him thirteen years to finish it all.

He built the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon. It was one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. It stood on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams resting on the pillars.
The roof was made of cedar laid over the forty-five beams that rested on the pillars, fifteen beams in each row.
There were window frames in three rows, with windows facing each other in sets of three.
All the doorways and door posts had square frames, and the windows faced each other in sets of three.
He also made the Hall of Pillars. It was fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. In front of it was a porch with pillars and a roof over it.
He built the Hall of the Throne, also called the Hall of Justice, where he would judge the people. It was covered with cedar from floor to ceiling.

The palace where Solomon himself would live was built in another courtyard behind the hall, and it was made in the same way. He also built a palace like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married.

All these buildings were made from expensive stones, cut to size and smoothed with saws on the inside and outside. This was done from the foundation all the way to the top, and from the outside all the way to the great courtyard.
The foundations were laid with large, expensive stones, some ten cubits long and some eight cubits long.
Above them were more expensive stones, cut to size, and cedar beams.
The great courtyard was surrounded by a wall made of three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams, just like the inner courtyard of the LORD's temple and its porch.
King Solomon sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre.

Hiram's mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man from Tyre who worked with bronze. Hiram was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill to do every kind of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and did all the work he was given.
He made two bronze pillars. Each was eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits around.
He also made two tops of melted bronze to put on top of the pillars. Each top was five cubits high.
Each top had a net of criss-cross patterns and chains twisted together. There were seven on each top.
He made two rows of bronze pomegranates around each net to decorate the tops of the pillars. He did the same for both tops.
The tops of the pillars in the porch were shaped like lilies, four cubits high.
On the tops of both pillars, above the rounded part next to the net, there were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around.
He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple. The pillar on the south side he named Jakin, and the pillar on the north side he named Boaz.
The tops of the pillars were shaped like lilies. And so the work on the pillars was finished.
He made a large round bowl of melted bronze, called the Sea. It was ten cubits across from rim to rim and five cubits high. It was thirty cubits around.
Below its rim, all the way around, were two rows of gourds, ten to every cubit. They were cast in one piece with the Sea.
The Sea stood on twelve bronze bulls. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. The Sea rested on top of them, and their back ends faced the centre.
It was as thick as the width of a hand. Its rim was like the rim of a cup, shaped like a lily flower. It held two thousand baths of water, about forty-four thousand litres.
He also made ten bronze stands. Each was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
This is how the stands were made: they had side panels attached to frames.
On the panels between the frames were lions, bulls, and winged creatures. On the frames above and below the lions and bulls were hanging decorations shaped like wreaths.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles. At the four corners were supports for a basin, cast with wreaths on each side.
Inside the stand was a round opening one cubit deep, with a frame around it one and a half cubits across. Around the opening there were carvings. The side panels of the stands were square, not round.
The four wheels were under the panels, and the axles of the wheels were joined to the stand. Each wheel was one and a half cubits high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. Their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all made of cast metal.
Each stand had four handles, one at each corner, made in one piece with the stand.
At the top of each stand was a round band half a cubit high. The supports and panels at the top were made in one piece with the stand.
He carved winged creatures, lions, and palm trees on the surfaces of the supports and panels, wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.
This is how he made the ten stands. They were all cast in the same mould and were the same size and shape.
Then he made ten bronze basins. Each basin held forty baths of water and measured four cubits across. There was one basin for each of the ten stands.
He put five stands on the south side of the temple and five on the north side. He put the Sea on the south side, at the south-east corner of the temple.
Hiram also made pots, shovels, and bowls. So Hiram finished all the work King Solomon had given him to do for the LORD's temple:
the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped tops on the pillars, and the two nets that covered the two bowl-shaped tops on the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two nets, two rows of pomegranates for each net, covering the bowl-shaped tops on the pillars;
the ten stands and the ten basins on the stands;
the Sea and the twelve bulls under it;
and the pots, shovels, and bowls. All these things that Hiram made for King Solomon for the LORD's temple were made of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay moulds in the plain of the Jordan, between Sukkoth and Zarethan.
Solomon did not weigh any of these things, because there were so many. The weight of the bronze was never known.
Solomon also made all the things that were in the LORD's temple: the gold altar, and the gold table where the special bread was placed before God;
the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, in front of the inner room; and the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs;
the pure gold cups, wick trimmers, bowls, dishes, and fire pans; and the gold hinges for the doors of the inner room, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the main hall of the temple.

So all the work King Solomon did for the LORD's temple was finished. Then he brought in the things his father David had set apart for God, the silver, the gold, and the other objects, and put them in the treasure rooms of the LORD's temple.

Then King Solomon called together in Jerusalem the leaders of Israel, all the heads of the tribes and the chiefs of the families of Israel. He wanted them to bring up the ark of the LORD's covenant from Zion, the City of David.
All the men of Israel gathered before King Solomon at the festival in the month of Ethanim, the seventh month.
When all the leaders of Israel had arrived, the priests lifted up the ark.
They brought up the LORD's ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy things that were in the tent. The priests and Levites carried them up.
King Solomon and all the people of Israel who had gathered with him stood in front of the ark. They sacrificed so many sheep and cattle that no one could count them.
Then the priests carried the ark of the LORD's covenant to its place in the inner room of the temple, the Most Holy Place, and put it under the wings of the winged creatures.
The winged creatures spread their wings over the place where the ark was, and covered the ark and its carrying poles from above.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place in front of the inner room, but not from outside. They are still there today.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets Moses had put there at Mount Horeb. That is where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel after they came out of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the LORD's temple.
The priests could not stay to do their work because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled his temple.
Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would live in thick darkness.
But I have built a wonderful temple for you, a place where you can live forever."
Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel while they stood there.
He said, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel! With his own mouth he made a promise to my father David, and with his own hand he has kept it. He said,
'Since the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel to build a temple for my name. But I have chosen David to rule my people Israel.'
My father David wanted with all his heart to build a temple for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to my father David, 'You wanted with all your heart to build a temple for my name, and it was good that you wanted to.
But you are not the one to build the temple. Your own son will build the temple for my name.'

Now the LORD has kept the promise he made. I have taken my father David's place, and I sit on the throne of Israel, just as the LORD promised. And I have built the temple for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
I have made a place there for the ark, which holds the LORD's covenant. That is the covenant he made with our ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt."
Then Solomon stood in front of the LORD's altar, facing all the people of Israel. He spread out his hands toward heaven
and said: "LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven above or on earth below. You keep your covenant and show your faithful love to your servants who follow you with all their heart.
You have kept your promise to your servant, my father David. With your own mouth you promised, and with your own hand you have done it, as we see today.

So now, LORD, God of Israel, keep the other promise you made to your servant, my father David. You said, 'You will always have a descendant sitting before me on the throne of Israel, if your sons are careful to live before me as you have done.'
So now, God of Israel, please let the promise you made to your servant, my father David, come true.
But will God really live on earth? Even the highest heavens cannot hold you. How much less this temple I have built!
But please listen to your servant's prayer and his request, LORD my God. Hear the cry and the prayer your servant is praying to you today.
May your eyes watch over this temple night and day, this place where you said, 'My name will be there.' May you hear the prayer your servant prays toward this place.
Listen to the requests of your servant and your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, where you live, and when you hear, forgive.
If someone wrongs his neighbour and is made to take an oath, and he comes and takes the oath in front of your altar in this temple,
then hear from heaven and act. Judge between your servants. Punish the guilty person as he deserves, and show that the innocent person is not guilty, as he deserves.
When your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they have sinned against you, and then they turn back to you, praise your name, and pray and beg you in this temple,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel. Bring them back to the land you gave to their ancestors.
When the sky is shut and there is no rain because your people have sinned against you, and then they pray toward this place, praise your name, and turn from their sin because you have punished them,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Teach them the right way to live, and send rain on the land you gave your people as their own.

When there is famine or deadly disease in the land, or when the crops are ruined by disease or mould, locusts or grasshoppers, or when enemies surround one of their cities, whatever disaster or sickness comes,
and when any of your people Israel pray or ask for help, each one knowing the pain in his own heart, and spreading out his hands toward this temple,
then hear from heaven, where you live. Forgive and act. Deal with each person according to everything he does, since you know his heart. For you alone know the hearts of all people.
Then they will respect you all the time they live in the land you gave to our ancestors.
And foreigners who are not from your people Israel may come from far away because of your name.
They will hear about your great name, your mighty hand, and your powerful arm. When they come and pray toward this temple,

then hear from heaven, where you live, and do whatever the foreigner asks of you. Then all the peoples of the earth will know your name and respect you, as your people Israel do. They will know that this temple I have built is called by your name.
When your people go out to fight against their enemies, wherever you send them, and when they pray to the LORD toward the city you have chosen and the temple I have built for your name,
then hear their prayer and their requests from heaven, and help them win their cause.

When they sin against you, for there is no one who does not sin, and you become angry with them and hand them over to their enemies, who take them away as prisoners to the enemy's land, far away or near,
then if they change their hearts in the land where they are prisoners, and turn back and beg you there, saying, 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly,'

and if they come back to you with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them away, and pray to you toward the land you gave their ancestors, toward the city you have chosen and the temple I have built for your name,
then hear their prayer and their requests from heaven, where you live, and help them win their cause.
Forgive your people who have sinned against you. Forgive all the wrongs they have done against you. Make those who captured them show them mercy.
For they are your people and your own special possession. You brought them out of Egypt, out of that furnace for melting iron.
May your eyes be open to the requests of your servant and of your people Israel. May you listen to them whenever they cry out to you.
For you chose them out of all the peoples of the earth to be your own special possession, as you said through your servant Moses when you brought our ancestors out of Egypt, Lord GOD."
When Solomon finished praying all this prayer and these requests to the LORD, he stood up in front of the LORD's altar, where he had been kneeling with his hands spread out toward heaven.
He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, saying in a loud voice:
"Praise the LORD! He has given rest to his people Israel, just as he promised. Not one word has failed of all the good promises he gave through his servant Moses.
May the LORD our God be with us, as he was with our ancestors. May he never leave us or give up on us.
May he turn our hearts toward him, so that we will follow all his ways and keep the commands, laws, and rules he gave our ancestors.
And may these words I have prayed to the LORD stay near the LORD our God day and night. May he help his servant and his people Israel with whatever each day needs.
Then all the peoples of the earth will know that the LORD is God, and there is no other.
So you must be completely faithful to the LORD our God. Follow his laws and keep his commands, as you are doing today."
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices to the LORD.
Solomon offered peace offerings to the LORD: twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the LORD's temple.

On that same day the king made holy the middle part of the courtyard in front of the LORD's temple. There he offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar in front of the LORD was too small to hold them all.

So Solomon and all Israel with him celebrated the festival at that time. It was a great crowd of people who came from as far as Lebo Hamath in the north and the stream of Egypt in the south. They celebrated before the LORD our God for seven days and then seven more days, fourteen days in all.
On the next day he sent the people home. They blessed the king and went home happy and glad in their hearts for all the good things the LORD had done for his servant David and for his people Israel.
Solomon finished building the LORD's temple and the royal palace, and he had done everything he wanted to do.
Then the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.

The LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and the request you made to me. I have made this temple you built holy, and I have put my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will always be there.
As for you, if you live before me as your father David did, with an honest heart and doing what is right, and if you do everything I command and keep my laws and rules,
then I will make your royal throne over Israel last forever. I promised this to your father David when I said, 'You will always have a descendant on the throne of Israel.'
But if you or your children turn away from me and do not keep the commands and laws I have given you, and if you go and serve other gods and worship them,
then I will remove Israel from the land I have given them. I will reject this temple I have made holy for my name. Israel will become a joke and an insult among all the nations.
This temple is so great now, but everyone who passes by will be shocked and will whistle in surprise. They will ask, 'Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?'

And people will answer, 'Because they left the LORD their God, who brought their ancestors out of Egypt. They held on to other gods and worshipped and served them. That is why the LORD brought all this disaster on them.'"
It took Solomon twenty years to build the two buildings, the LORD's temple and the royal palace.
Hiram king of Tyre had given Solomon all the cedar, cypress, and gold he wanted. So King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee.
But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the towns Solomon had given him, he was not pleased with them.
He said, "My brother, what kind of towns are these you have given me?" So he called that area the Land of Kabul, meaning good for nothing, and it is still called that today.
Hiram had sent the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, about four thousand kilograms.
This is the story of the forced labour King Solomon used to build the LORD's temple, his own palace, the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, and the cities of Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had attacked and captured Gezer. He burned it down and killed the Canaanites who lived there. Then he gave the city as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
So Solomon rebuilt Gezer. He also built Lower Beth Horon,
Baalath, and Tamar in the wilderness of his land.
He also built all his cities for storing supplies, and cities for his chariots and his horses. He built whatever he wanted to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land he ruled.
There were still people left from the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. These people were not Israelites.
They were the descendants of the nations the Israelites had not been able to destroy completely. Solomon forced them to work as slaves, and they still do today.
But Solomon did not make slaves of any Israelites. They were his soldiers, his officials, his commanders, his captains, and the commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
There were also five hundred and fifty chief officers in charge of Solomon's projects. They directed the people who did the work.
After Pharaoh's daughter moved from the City of David to the palace Solomon had built for her, he built the Millo.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built for the LORD. He also burned incense with them in front of the LORD. So he finished the temple.
King Solomon also built a fleet of ships at Ezion Geber, near Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom.
Hiram sent his own men, sailors who knew the sea, to serve on the ships with Solomon's men.
They sailed to Ophir and brought back four hundred and twenty talents of gold, about fourteen thousand kilograms, to King Solomon.
The queen of Sheba heard about how famous Solomon was because of the name of the LORD. So she came to test him with hard questions.

She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large group of servants and camels carrying spices, a great amount of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about everything she had on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. Nothing was too hard for the king to explain to her.
The queen of Sheba saw how wise Solomon was. She saw the palace he had built,
the food on his table, the seating of his officials, his servants in their uniforms, his cup-bearers, and the burnt offerings he made at the LORD's temple. It took her breath away.
She said to the king, "Everything I heard in my own country about your achievements and your wisdom is true.
But I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes. And I was not told even half of it! Your wisdom and wealth are much greater than what I heard.
How happy your people must be! How happy are these officials who always stand before you and listen to your wisdom!

Praise the LORD your God! He was pleased with you and put you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD's love for Israel lasts forever, he has made you king, so that you can do what is fair and right."

Then she gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, about four thousand kilograms, a very large amount of spices, and precious stones. Never again did anyone bring as many spices as the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
Hiram's ships, which brought gold from Ophir, also brought large amounts of almug wood and precious stones from Ophir.

The king used the almug wood to make railings for the LORD's temple and for the royal palace, and to make harps and lyres for the musicians. No such almug wood has ever been brought in or seen since that day.

King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she wanted and asked for, besides all the gifts he had already given her out of his royal riches. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
Every year Solomon received six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, about twenty-three thousand kilograms.
This did not include the money from traders and merchants, and from all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold. Each shield used six hundred shekels of gold, about seven kilograms.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold. Each used three minas of gold, almost two kilograms. The king put them in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon.
Then the king made a large throne of ivory and covered it with the finest gold.
The throne had six steps, and its back had a rounded top. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. Nothing like it had ever been made in any other kingdom.

All of King Solomon's drinking cups were made of gold, and all the dishes in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon were made of pure gold. Nothing was made of silver, because silver was thought to be of little value in Solomon's time.
The king had a fleet of trading ships at sea, together with Hiram's ships. Once every three years the ships came back carrying gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon was greater in riches and wisdom than all the other kings of the earth.
People from all over the world wanted to visit Solomon to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Year after year, everyone who came brought a gift: things made of silver and gold, clothes, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon gathered chariots and horses. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He kept some in the chariot cities and some with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as common as the fig trees in the western hills.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt. The king's traders bought them in herds, each herd at a set price.
A chariot from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse cost one hundred and fifty shekels. The traders also sold them to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with Pharaoh's daughter. There were women from the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites.

They came from the nations the LORD had warned Israel about. He had said, "Do not marry them, and do not let them marry you, because they will surely turn your hearts to follow their gods." But Solomon held on to these women in love.
He had seven hundred wives who were princesses, and three hundred concubines. His wives turned his heart away.
When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart to follow other gods. His heart was not fully true to the LORD his God, as the heart of his father David had been.
Solomon followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom, the hateful idol of the Ammonites.
Solomon did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He did not follow the LORD completely, as his father David had.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the hateful idol of Moab, on the hill east of Jerusalem. He built one for Molech, the hateful idol of the Ammonites, too.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods.
The LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
The LORD had commanded him about this very thing, that he must not follow other gods. But Solomon did not obey what the LORD commanded.
So the LORD said to Solomon, "Because you have done this, and have not kept my covenant and my laws that I commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.
But for the sake of your father David, I will not do it while you are alive. I will tear it out of your son's hand.
Even then, I will not tear away the whole kingdom. I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of my servant David, and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen."
The LORD raised up an enemy against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite. He came from the royal family of Edom.
Long before, when David was at war with Edom, Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the dead, and he killed every male in Edom.
Joab and all Israel stayed there six months, until he had killed every male in Edom.
But Hadad ran away to Egypt with some Edomite officials who had served his father. Hadad was only a little boy then.
They set out from Midian and came to Paran. They took men from Paran with them and went to Egypt, to Pharaoh the king of Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, food, and land.
Pharaoh liked Hadad so much that he gave him a wife: the sister of his own wife, Queen Tahpenes.
Tahpenes' sister gave birth to Hadad's son Genubath. Tahpenes raised him in Pharaoh's palace, and Genubath lived there among Pharaoh's own sons.
While Hadad was in Egypt, he heard that David had died and that Joab the army commander was dead too. So Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me go, so I can return to my own country."
Pharaoh asked him, "What do you lack here with me, that you want to go back to your own country?" Hadad answered, "Nothing. But please let me go."
God raised up another enemy against Solomon: Rezon the son of Eliada. He had run away from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.
After David defeated Zobah, Rezon gathered men around him and became the leader of a gang of raiders. They went to Damascus, settled there, and ruled in Damascus.
Rezon was Israel's enemy as long as Solomon lived, adding to the trouble Hadad caused. He hated Israel, and he ruled over Syria.
Jeroboam the son of Nebat also rebelled against the king. He was an Ephraimite from Zeredah and one of Solomon's officials. His mother was a widow named Zeruah.
This is how he came to rebel against the king. Solomon was building the Millo and filling in the gap in the wall of the city of his father David.
Jeroboam was a strong and able man. When Solomon saw how hard the young man worked, he put him in charge of all the forced workers from the tribes of Joseph.
At that time, Jeroboam was going out of Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the open country.
Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces.
He said to Jeroboam, "Take ten pieces for yourself. This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Look, I am going to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand, and I will give you ten tribes.
But Solomon will keep one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.

I will do this because they have left me and worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites. They have not walked in my ways. They have not done what is right in my eyes or kept my laws and rules, as Solomon's father David did.
But I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon's hand. I will let him rule as long as he lives, for the sake of my servant David, whom I chose and who kept my commands and laws.
I will take the kingdom from his son's hand and give ten tribes of it to you.
I will give one tribe to his son, so that my servant David will always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I chose to put my name.
I will take you, and you will rule over everything your heart desires. You will be king over Israel.

If you listen to everything I command you, walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my laws and commands, as my servant David did, then I will be with you. I will build you a family line that lasts, as I did for David, and I will give Israel to you.
Because of this, I will humble David's descendants, but not forever.'"
So Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam got up and ran away to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt. He stayed in Egypt until Solomon died.
The rest of what Solomon did, all his deeds and his wisdom, are written in the book of the acts of Solomon.
Solomon ruled in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.
Then Solomon died and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam became king after him.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had gone there to make him king.
Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard about it. He was still in Egypt, where he had run away from King Solomon, and he was living there.
The people sent for him, and Jeroboam and the whole assembly of Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam. They said,
"Your father put a heavy load on us. Now make the hard work and the heavy load your father put on us lighter, and we will serve you."
Rehoboam answered, "Go away for three days, then come back to me." So the people left.
King Rehoboam asked advice from the older men who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. He asked, "What do you advise me to answer these people?"
They said, "If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them, and give them a kind answer, they will be your servants forever."
But Rehoboam rejected the advice the older men gave him. He asked advice from the young men who had grown up with him and now served him.
He asked them, "What do you advise? How should we answer these people who told me, 'Make the load your father put on us lighter'?"

The young men who had grown up with him said, "These people told you, 'Your father made our load heavy, but make it lighter for us.' Tell them this: 'My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.
My father put a heavy load on you, but I will make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.'"
On the third day, Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam, just as the king had told them: "Come back to me on the third day."
The king answered the people harshly. He rejected the advice the older men had given him.
He followed the advice of the young men and said, "My father made your load heavy, but I will make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions."
So the king did not listen to the people. This was from the LORD, so that what the LORD had said through Ahijah from Shiloh to Jeroboam the son of Nebat would come true.

When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, they answered him, "What share do we have in David? We have no part in the son of Jesse! Go home to your tents, Israel! David, look after your own house now!" So the Israelites went home.
But Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah.
Then King Rehoboam sent out Adoram, who was in charge of the forced workers, but all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam quickly climbed into his chariot and escaped to Jerusalem.
So Israel has rebelled against David's family to this day.
When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had come back, they called him to a meeting and made him king over all Israel. No one stayed loyal to David's family except the tribe of Judah.

When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he gathered all the people of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, one hundred and eighty thousand chosen soldiers. They were going to fight against Israel and win the kingdom back for Rehoboam the son of Solomon.
But God's word came to Shemaiah the man of God. God said,
"Speak to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the people of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people. Tell them,

'The LORD says: Do not go up and fight against your relatives, the people of Israel. Every one of you, go home, because I have made this happen.'" So they obeyed the LORD's word and went home, just as the LORD had said.
Then Jeroboam built up Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. From there he went out and built up Penuel.
Jeroboam thought to himself, "Now the kingdom might go back to David's family.

If these people go up to offer sacrifices at the LORD's temple in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to their master, Rehoboam king of Judah. Then they will kill me and go back to Rehoboam king of Judah."
So after getting advice, the king made two gold calves. He told the people, "It is too much trouble for you to go up to Jerusalem. Look, Israel, here are your gods who brought you up out of Egypt!"
He put one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan.
This became a sin, because the people went as far as Dan to worship the calf there.
Jeroboam built shrines on high places and chose priests from all kinds of people, even though they were not from the tribe of Levi.

Jeroboam started a festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the festival in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. He did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made. He also placed in Bethel the priests of the high places he had made.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a month he had chosen on his own, he went up to the altar he had made in Bethel. He started a festival for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense.
By the LORD's command, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar, ready to burn incense.

By the LORD's command, the man of God shouted against the altar, "Altar! Altar! This is what the LORD says: 'A son named Josiah will be born into David's family. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense on you, and human bones will be burned on you.'"
That same day he gave a sign. He said, "This is the sign the LORD has given: The altar will split apart, and the ashes on it will spill out."

When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God shouted against the altar in Bethel, he pointed at him from the altar and said, "Grab him!" But the hand he stretched out against the man dried up, so that he could not pull it back.
The altar also split apart, and the ashes spilled out of it, just as the man of God had said in the sign the LORD gave him.

Then the king said to the man of God, "Please ask the LORD your God to be kind to me, and pray for me, so my hand will be healed." So the man of God prayed to the LORD, and the king's hand was healed. It became just as it was before.
The king said to the man of God, "Come home with me and have something to eat, and I will give you a gift."
But the man of God answered the king, "Even if you gave me half of everything you own, I would not go with you. I will not eat bread or drink water in this place.
The LORD commanded me, 'Do not eat bread or drink water, and do not go back the same way you came.'"
So he left by a different road, and did not go back the way he had come to Bethel.
Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. His sons came and told him everything the man of God had done there that day. They also told their father what he had said to the king.
Their father asked them, "Which way did he go?" His sons had seen which road the man of God from Judah had taken.
He told his sons, "Put a saddle on my donkey." So they saddled the donkey for him, and he rode off on it.
He went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak tree. He asked him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" He answered, "I am."
Then the prophet said to him, "Come home with me and eat some bread."
The man of God said, "I cannot go back with you or go into your home. I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
The LORD told me, 'Do not eat bread or drink water there, and do not go back the same way you came.'"

The old prophet said to him, "I am a prophet too, just like you. An angel gave me a message from the LORD. He said, 'Bring him back to your house so he can eat bread and drink water.'" But he was lying to him.
So the man of God went back with him and ate bread and drank water in his house.
While they were sitting at the table, the LORD's word came to the old prophet who had brought him back.
He shouted to the man of God who had come from Judah, "This is what the LORD says: 'You have disobeyed the LORD's word. You have not kept the command the LORD your God gave you.
You came back and ate bread and drank water in the place where he told you, "Do not eat bread or drink water." So your body will not be buried in the tomb of your ancestors.'"
When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the old prophet saddled a donkey for him.
As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him. His body lay on the road, with the donkey standing beside it. The lion stood beside the body too.
Some men passed by and saw the body lying on the road, with the lion standing next to it. They went and told about it in the town where the old prophet lived.

When the old prophet who had brought him back heard about it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the LORD's word. So the LORD gave him to the lion, and it has torn him and killed him, just as the LORD warned him."
He told his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled it.
He went and found the body lying on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. The lion had not eaten the body or attacked the donkey.
The prophet picked up the body of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back to his own town to mourn for him and bury him.
He laid the body in his own tomb, and they mourned over him, crying, "Oh, my brother!"
After he buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones.
What he shouted by the LORD's command against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the towns of Samaria will surely come true."
Even after this, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil ways. Again he chose priests for the high places from all kinds of people. Anyone who wanted to be a priest, he set apart for the high places.
This sin brought down Jeroboam's family. It led to them being cut off and wiped off the face of the earth.
At that time Jeroboam's son Abijah became sick.
Jeroboam said to his wife, "Please get up and dress up so no one will know you are my wife. Then go to Shiloh. The prophet Ahijah is there, the one who told me I would be king over this people.
Take ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey with you, and go to him. He will tell you what will happen to the boy."
Jeroboam's wife did what he said. She got up, went to Shiloh, and came to Ahijah's house. Ahijah could not see, because he had become blind in his old age.
But the LORD had told Ahijah, "Jeroboam's wife is coming to ask you about her son, because he is sick. Tell her what I tell you. When she comes, she will pretend to be someone else."
So when Ahijah heard her footsteps at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you pretending to be someone else? I have been sent to you with bad news.
Go and tell Jeroboam, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: "I lifted you up from among the people and made you ruler over my people Israel.

I tore the kingdom away from David's family and gave it to you. But you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commands and followed me with all his heart, doing only what was right in my eyes.
You have done more evil than all who came before you. You have made yourself other gods, idols of metal, to make me angry, and you have turned your back on me.

So I am going to bring disaster on Jeroboam's family. I will cut off every male in Jeroboam's family in Israel, slave or free. I will burn up Jeroboam's family completely, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone.
Dogs will eat anyone in Jeroboam's family who dies in the city, and birds will eat those who die in the open country. The LORD has said it!"'
As for you, get up and go home. When you step into the city, the boy will die.

All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. He is the only one from Jeroboam's family who will be buried in a grave, because he is the only one in that family in whom the LORD, the God of Israel, has found something good.
The LORD will raise up a king over Israel who will cut off Jeroboam's family. This is the day! Yes, even now.

The LORD will strike Israel, so that it shakes like a reed in the water. He will pull Israel up out of this good land he gave their ancestors and scatter them beyond the Euphrates River, because they made Asherah poles and made the LORD angry.
He will give Israel up because of the sins Jeroboam committed and made Israel commit."
Then Jeroboam's wife got up, left, and went to Tirzah. As soon as she stepped through the doorway of her house, the boy died.
