All Israel buried him and mourned for him, just as the LORD had said through his servant the prophet Ahijah.
The rest of what Jeroboam did, how he fought and how he ruled, is written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jeroboam ruled for twenty-two years. Then he died, and his son Nadab became king after him.

Meanwhile, Solomon's son Rehoboam ruled in Judah. He was forty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother was Naamah, an Ammonite.
The people of Judah did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. By their sins they made him more jealous than their ancestors had ever done.
They also built high places, sacred stone pillars, and Asherah poles for themselves on every high hill and under every green tree.
There were even male shrine prostitutes in the land. The people did all the disgusting things of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's rule, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem.
He carried off the treasures of the LORD's temple and the treasures of the king's palace. He took everything, including all the gold shields Solomon had made.
So King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them. He gave them to the commanders of the guards who guarded the entrance to the king's palace.
Whenever the king went into the LORD's temple, the guards carried the shields, and afterward they brought them back to the guardroom.
The rest of what Rehoboam did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam the whole time.
Rehoboam died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His mother was Naamah, an Ammonite. His son Abijam became king after him.
In the eighteenth year that Jeroboam son of Nebat was king, Abijam became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for three years. His mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
He did all the same sins his father had done before him. His heart was not fully true to the LORD his God, as the heart of his ancestor David had been.
But for David's sake, the LORD his God gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem. He gave him a son to rule after him, and he kept Jerusalem strong.
He did this because David had done what was right in the LORD's eyes. All his life David never turned away from anything the LORD commanded him, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam as long as Abijam lived.
The rest of what Abijam did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah. There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
Abijam died and was buried in the city of David. His son Asa became king after him.
In the twentieth year that Jeroboam was king of Israel, Asa became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for forty-one years. His grandmother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did what was right in the LORD's eyes, as his ancestor David had done.
He drove the male shrine prostitutes out of the land and got rid of all the idols his ancestors had made.
He even removed his grandmother Maacah from being queen mother, because she had made a disgusting image for the goddess Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
The high places were not removed, but Asa's heart was fully true to the LORD all his life.
He brought into the LORD's temple the silver, the gold, and the objects that he and his father had set apart for God.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel as long as they both lived.
Baasha king of Israel attacked Judah. He built up the town of Ramah so that no one could go in or out to Asa king of Judah.

Then Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasuries of the LORD's temple and of the king's palace. He gave it to his officials and sent them to Ben-Hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus. Ben-Hadad was the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion. Asa said,

"Let us make a treaty, as there was between my father and your father. Look, I am sending you a gift of silver and gold. Go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so he will leave me alone."
Ben-Hadad agreed with King Asa. He sent his army commanders to attack the towns of Israel. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, all of Chinneroth, and all the land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard about it, he stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah.
Then King Asa gave an order to all Judah, and no one was excused. They carried away the stones and wood Baasha had been using to build Ramah. With them King Asa built up Geba in Benjamin, and Mizpah.
The rest of what Asa did, all his power, all his deeds, and the towns he built, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah. But when he was old, he got a disease in his feet.
Asa died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his ancestor David. His son Jehoshaphat became king after him.
Jeroboam's son Nadab became king of Israel in the second year that Asa was king of Judah. Nadab ruled Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He followed the ways of his father and the sin his father had made Israel commit.
Baasha son of Ahijah, from the tribe of Issachar, made a plot against Nadab. Baasha killed him at Gibbethon, a Philistine town that Nadab and all Israel were attacking.
Baasha killed Nadab in the third year that Asa was king of Judah, and became king in his place.
As soon as Baasha became king, he killed Jeroboam's whole family. He did not leave Jeroboam anyone alive. He destroyed them all, just as the LORD had said through his servant Ahijah from Shiloh.
This happened because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had made Israel commit, and because he had made the LORD, the God of Israel, angry.
The rest of what Nadab did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel as long as they both lived.
In the third year that Asa was king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king of all Israel in Tirzah. He ruled for twenty-four years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He followed the ways of Jeroboam and the sin Jeroboam had made Israel commit.
The LORD's word came to Jehu son of Hanani with a message against Baasha. The LORD said,
"I lifted you up out of the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel. But you followed the ways of Jeroboam and made my people Israel sin, and their sins have made me angry.
So I am going to wipe out Baasha and his family completely. I will make your family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Dogs will eat Baasha's family members who die in the city, and birds will eat those who die in the open country."
The rest of what Baasha did, his deeds and his power, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah. His son Elah became king after him.

The LORD's word had come through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his family. It was because of all the evil Baasha did in the LORD's eyes, making him angry by what he did, becoming like Jeroboam's family, and also because he killed Jeroboam's family.
In the twenty-sixth year that Asa was king of Judah, Baasha's son Elah became king of Israel in Tirzah. He ruled for two years.

Zimri, one of his officials, who commanded half of his chariots, made a plot against him. Elah was in Tirzah at the time, getting drunk in the house of Arza, the man in charge of the palace in Tirzah.
Zimri came in, struck Elah down, and killed him. This was in the twenty-seventh year that Asa was king of Judah. Then Zimri became king in his place.
As soon as Zimri became king and sat on the throne, he killed Baasha's whole family. He did not leave a single male alive, not among his relatives or his friends.
So Zimri destroyed Baasha's whole family, just as the LORD had said against Baasha through the prophet Jehu.
This happened because of all the sins of Baasha and his son Elah. They sinned and made Israel sin, and they made the LORD, the God of Israel, angry with their worthless idols.
The rest of what Elah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
In the twenty-seventh year that Asa was king of Judah, Zimri ruled in Tirzah for seven days. The army was camped near Gibbethon, a Philistine town.
The soldiers in the camp heard that Zimri had made a plot and killed the king. So that same day, there in the camp, all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel.
Then Omri and all Israel with him went up from Gibbethon and surrounded Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city had been captured, he went into the strongest part of the king's palace. He set the palace on fire around himself and died.
He died because of the sins he committed. He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, following the ways of Jeroboam and the sin Jeroboam had made Israel commit.
The rest of what Zimri did, and his plot against the king, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel split into two groups. Half of them wanted to make Tibni son of Ginath king, and the other half followed Omri.
But Omri's followers were stronger than the followers of Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.
In the thirty-first year that Asa was king of Judah, Omri became king of Israel. He ruled for twelve years, six of them in Tirzah.
He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for about seventy kilograms of silver. He built a city on the hill and named it Samaria, after Shemer, who had owned the hill.
Omri did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He was more wicked than all the kings before him.
He followed all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins Jeroboam had made Israel commit. They made the LORD, the God of Israel, angry with their worthless idols.
The rest of what Omri did, and the power he showed, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Omri died and was buried in Samaria. His son Ahab became king after him.
In the thirty-eighth year that Asa was king of Judah, Omri's son Ahab became king of Israel. Ahab son of Omri ruled over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the LORD's eyes than all the kings before him.
As if it were not enough to commit the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, he also married Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians. Then he began to serve Baal and worship him.
He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he built in Samaria.
Ahab also made an Asherah pole. He did more to make the LORD, the God of Israel, angry than all the kings of Israel before him.

While Ahab was king, Hiel from Bethel rebuilt Jericho. Laying its foundations cost him the life of his oldest son Abiram, and setting up its gates cost him the life of his youngest son Segub. This happened just as the LORD had said through Joshua son of Nun.
Elijah from Tishbe, who lived in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, the God I serve, there will be no dew or rain in the next few years unless I say so."
Then the LORD's word came to Elijah. He said,
"Leave here, go east, and hide by the Cherith Brook, east of the Jordan River.
You will drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to bring you food there."
So Elijah did what the LORD said. He went and lived by the Cherith Brook, east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.
After a while the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.
Then the LORD's word came to him. He said,
"Get up and go to Zarephath, a town that belongs to Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to feed you."
So Elijah got up and went to Zarephath. When he came to the town gate, he saw a widow there gathering sticks. He called to her, "Please bring me a little water in a cup so I can drink."
As she was going to get it, he called to her, "Please bring me a piece of bread too."

She said, "As surely as the LORD your God lives, I have no bread baked. I only have a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. I am gathering a couple of sticks so I can go home and make a last meal for me and my son. We will eat it, and then we will die."
Elijah said to her, "Do not be afraid. Go home and do what you said. But first make a small loaf of bread for me and bring it to me. Then make something for yourself and your son.
This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'The jar of flour will not run out, and the jug of oil will not run dry, until the day the LORD sends rain on the land.'"
She went and did what Elijah told her. And there was food every day for Elijah, for her, and for her family.
The jar of flour did not run out, and the jug of oil did not run dry, just as the LORD had said through Elijah.
Some time later, the son of the woman who owned the house became sick. He grew worse and worse, until he stopped breathing.
She said to Elijah, "Man of God, what do you have against me? Did you come here to remind me of my sin and kill my son?"
Elijah said to her, "Give me your son." He took the boy from her arms, carried him up to the upstairs room where he was staying, and laid him on his own bed.
Then he cried out to the LORD, "LORD my God, have you brought trouble even on this widow I am staying with, by letting her son die?"
He stretched himself out over the boy three times and cried out to the LORD, "LORD my God, please let this boy's life come back into him!"
The LORD heard Elijah's cry. The boy's life came back into him, and he lived again.
Elijah picked up the boy and carried him down from the room into the house. He gave him to his mother and said, "Look, your son is alive!"
Then the woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the LORD's word you speak is true."
A long time later, in the third year of the drought, the LORD's word came to Elijah: "Go and show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain on the land."
So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was very bad in Samaria.
Ahab called for Obadiah, the man in charge of his palace. Obadiah had great respect for the LORD.
When Jezebel was killing the LORD's prophets, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them in two caves, fifty in each, and gave them bread and water.
Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs and all the streams. Maybe we can find some grass to keep the horses and mules alive, so we will not lose all our animals."
So they divided the land between them to search it. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went another way by himself.
As Obadiah was walking along, Elijah met him. Obadiah recognized him, bowed down with his face to the ground, and said, "Is it really you, my master Elijah?"
Elijah answered, "Yes, it is me. Go and tell your master, 'Elijah is here.'"
Obadiah said, "What have I done wrong, that you are handing me, your servant, over to Ahab to be killed?

As surely as the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my master has not sent people to look for you. When they said, 'He is not here,' he made that kingdom or nation swear that they could not find you.
And now you tell me, 'Go and tell your master, "Elijah is here."'

As soon as I leave you, the LORD's Spirit will carry you away to who knows where. Then when I tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have respected the LORD since I was young.
Has no one told you, my master, what I did when Jezebel was killing the LORD's prophets? I hid a hundred of the LORD's prophets in two caves, fifty in each, and gave them bread and water.
And now you tell me, 'Go and tell your master, "Elijah is here."' He will kill me!"
Elijah said, "As surely as the LORD of Armies lives, the God I serve, I will show myself to Ahab today."
So Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, "Is that you, the one who brings trouble on Israel?"
Elijah answered, "I have not brought trouble on Israel. You and your father's family have. You have turned away from the LORD's commands and followed the Baals.
Now send out word and gather all Israel to meet me on Mount Carmel. Bring the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah, who eat at Jezebel's table."
So Ahab sent word to all the Israelites and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.

Elijah went up to all the people and said, "How long will you keep going back and forth between two choices? If the LORD is God, follow him. But if Baal is God, follow him." The people did not say a word.
Then Elijah said to them, "I am the only one of the LORD's prophets left, but Baal has four hundred and fifty prophets.

Bring us two bulls. Let Baal's prophets choose one bull for themselves. Let them cut it into pieces and put it on the wood, but not light a fire. I will get the other bull ready, put it on the wood, and not light a fire either.
Then you call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the LORD. The God who answers with fire is the true God." All the people answered, "That is a good idea."
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose one bull for yourselves and get it ready first, since there are so many of you. Call on the name of your god, but do not light a fire."

So they took the bull that was given to them and got it ready. Then they called on the name of Baal from morning until noon. They shouted, "Baal, answer us!" But there was no sound, and no one answered. They danced around the altar they had made.

At noon Elijah began to make fun of them. "Shout louder!" he said. "He is a god, isn't he? Maybe he is busy thinking, or he has gone off somewhere, or he is on a trip. Or maybe he is asleep and needs to be woken up!"
So they shouted louder, and they cut themselves with swords and spears, as they usually did, until blood flowed all over them.
Noon passed, and they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice. But there was no sound, no answer, and no one paid any attention.
Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come here to me." All the people came close to him. He repaired the LORD's altar, which had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, one for each of the tribes descended from Jacob, the man the LORD had spoken to, saying, "Your name will be Israel."
With the stones he built an altar in the LORD's name. Around the altar he dug a ditch big enough to hold about fifteen litres of seed.
He arranged the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and laid it on the wood. Then he said, "Fill four large jars with water and pour it on the offering and on the wood."
He said, "Do it again," and they did it again. He said, "Do it a third time," and they did it a third time.
The water ran down all around the altar, and he even filled the ditch with water.

At the time of the evening sacrifice, the prophet Elijah stepped forward and prayed, "LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things because you told me to.
Answer me, LORD, answer me, so these people will know that you, LORD, are God, and that you are turning their hearts back to you."
Then fire from the LORD fell and burned up the offering, the wood, the stones, and the dirt. It even dried up the water in the ditch.
When all the people saw this, they fell face down on the ground and cried, "The LORD is God! The LORD is God!"
Then Elijah said to them, "Grab the prophets of Baal! Do not let any of them get away!" They grabbed them, and Elijah took them down to the Kishon Brook and killed them there.
Elijah said to Ahab, "Go, eat and drink, because I hear the sound of heavy rain coming."
So Ahab went off to eat and drink. But Elijah climbed to the top of Mount Carmel. He bowed down to the ground and put his face between his knees.
He said to his servant, "Go up and look toward the sea." The servant went up and looked, and said, "There is nothing there." Seven times Elijah told him, "Go back and look."

The seventh time, the servant said, "I see a small cloud, as small as a man's hand, rising from the sea." Elijah said, "Go and tell Ahab, 'Get your chariot ready and go down before the rain stops you.'"
Very soon the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall. Ahab rode off to Jezreel.
The LORD's power came on Elijah. He tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to the entrance of Jezreel.
Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, "May the gods punish me, and even more, if by this time tomorrow I do not make your life like the life of one of those prophets!"
Elijah was afraid. He got up and ran for his life. He came to Beersheba in Judah and left his servant there.

Then he went on alone a whole day's walk into the desert. He came to a broom bush, sat down under it, and asked God to let him die. "I have had enough, LORD," he said. "Take my life. I am no better than my ancestors."
He lay down under the bush and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, "Get up and eat."
He looked around, and there by his head was a loaf of bread baked on hot coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and then lay down again.
The LORD's angel came back a second time, touched him, and said, "Get up and eat, because the journey ahead is too long for you."
So he got up, ate, and drank. That food gave him strength to walk forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.
There he went into a cave and spent the night. Then the LORD's word came to him. The LORD said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He answered, "I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Armies. The Israelites have turned away from your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and now they are trying to kill me too."

The LORD said, "Go out and stand on the mountain in front of the LORD." Then the LORD passed by. A great and powerful wind tore the mountains apart and broke the rocks into pieces in front of the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire there was a quiet, gentle whisper.
When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak, went out, and stood at the entrance of the cave. Then a voice said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He answered, "I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Armies. The Israelites have turned away from your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and now they are trying to kill me too."
The LORD said to him, "Go back the way you came, and go to the desert of Damascus. When you get there, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.
Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi to be king over Israel. And anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel Meholah, to be prophet in your place.
Jehu will kill anyone who escapes the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will kill anyone who escapes the sword of Jehu.
But I have kept seven thousand people in Israel for myself. They have not bowed down to Baal, and they have not kissed his idol."
So Elijah left there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve pairs of oxen ahead of him, and he was driving the twelfth pair. Elijah went over to him and threw his cloak over him.
Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, "Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you." Elijah said, "Go on back. What have I done to stop you?"

So Elisha went back. He took his pair of oxen and killed them. He used the wooden plowing gear to cook the meat, and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah, and became his helper.
Ben-Hadad king of Syria gathered his whole army. Thirty-two kings were with him, with their horses and chariots. He went up, surrounded Samaria, and attacked it.
He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel to say, "This is what Ben-Hadad says:
'Your silver and gold are mine, and your wives and your best children are mine too.'"
The king of Israel answered, "Just as you say, my master the king. I am yours, and everything I have is yours."
The messengers came back and said, "This is what Ben-Hadad says: 'I sent you a message saying, "Give me your silver, your gold, your wives, and your children."
But about this time tomorrow I will send my officials to you. They will search your palace and the houses of your officials. They will take away everything you value.'"

Then the king of Israel called together all the leaders of the land and said, "See how this man is looking for trouble! When he sent for my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, I did not refuse him."
All the leaders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen to him, and do not agree to it."

So Ahab told Ben-Hadad's messengers, "Tell my master the king, 'I will do everything you asked your servant the first time, but I cannot do this.'" The messengers left and took the answer back to Ben-Hadad.
Then Ben-Hadad sent another message to Ahab: "May the gods punish me, and even more, if there is enough dust left in Samaria for each of my soldiers to get a handful!"
The king of Israel answered, "Tell him, 'A man putting on his armour should not boast like a man taking it off after the battle.'"
Ben-Hadad heard this message while he and the kings were drinking in their tents. He said to his officials, "Get ready to attack!" So they got ready to attack the city.
Then a prophet came to Ahab king of Israel and said, "This is what the LORD says: 'Do you see this huge army? I am going to hand it over to you today. Then you will know that I am the LORD.'"

Ahab asked, "Who will do it?" The prophet said, "This is what the LORD says: 'The young officers of the district governors will do it.'" Ahab asked, "Who will start the battle?" The prophet answered, "You will."
So Ahab called up the young officers of the district governors, two hundred and thirty-two men. Then he called up the rest of the Israelites, seven thousand in all.
They marched out at noon. Ben-Hadad and the thirty-two kings helping him were in their tents, getting drunk.
The young officers of the district governors went out first. Ben-Hadad's scouts reported to him, "Men are coming out of Samaria."
He said, "Whether they have come out to make peace or to fight, take them alive."
The young officers of the district governors marched out of the city, with the army behind them.
Each one killed the enemy soldier he fought. The Syrians ran away, and Israel chased them. But Ben-Hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with some of his horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and attacked the horses and chariots, and he defeated the Syrians with heavy losses.
Afterward, the prophet came to the king of Israel and said, "Go and make your army stronger, and think about what you must do, because next spring the king of Syria will attack you again."

Meanwhile, the officials of the king of Syria told him, "Their gods are gods of the hills. That is why they were too strong for us. But if we fight them on the flat land, we will surely be stronger than they are.
Do this: remove all the kings from their commands and put army officers in their places.

Build an army like the one you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. Then we will fight Israel on the flat land, and we will surely be stronger than they are." He agreed with them and did it.
The next spring Ben-Hadad gathered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel.
The Israelites were also gathered and given supplies, and they marched out to meet them. The Israelites camped facing them like two little flocks of goats, while the Syrians covered the countryside.

A man of God came to the king of Israel and said, "This is what the LORD says: 'The Syrians think the LORD is a god of the hills and not a god of the valleys. So I will hand this whole huge army over to you, and you will know that I am the LORD.'"
For seven days the two armies camped facing each other. On the seventh day the battle began. The Israelites killed one hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in one day.
The rest ran away into the city of Aphek, and the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of them. Ben-Hadad also ran into the city and hid in an inner room.

His officials said to him, "Look, we have heard that the kings of Israel are merciful. Let us put on sackcloth, tie ropes around our heads, and go out to the king of Israel. Maybe he will spare your life."

So they put on sackcloth and tied ropes around their heads. They went to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-Hadad says, 'Please let me live.'" Ahab answered, "Is he still alive? He is my brother."

The men were watching for a good sign, and they quickly caught his word. "Yes, your brother Ben-Hadad!" they said. Ahab said, "Go and bring him." When Ben-Hadad came out, Ahab had him climb up into his chariot.

Ben-Hadad said to him, "I will give back the towns my father took from your father. You may set up your own market streets in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." Ahab said, "With this agreement I will set you free." So he made a treaty with him and let him go.
By the LORD's command, one of the prophets' group said to another, "Please hit me!" But the man refused to hit him.
So the prophet said, "Because you did not obey the LORD, as soon as you leave me a lion will kill you." And as soon as the man left, a lion found him and killed him.
Then the prophet found another man and said, "Please hit me." So the man hit him and wounded him.
Then the prophet went and waited by the road for the king. He disguised himself by pulling his headband down over his eyes.

As the king passed by, the prophet called out to him, "Your servant went into the middle of the battle, and a man came over to me with a prisoner. He said, 'Guard this man. If he goes missing, you will pay for his life with your life, or else pay about thirty-four kilograms of silver.'
But while your servant was busy here and there, the man disappeared." The king of Israel said to him, "That is your sentence. You have said it yourself."
Then the prophet quickly pulled the headband away from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.

The prophet said to the king, "This is what the LORD says: 'You have set free the man I had marked for destruction. So your life will take the place of his life, and your people the place of his people.'"
The king of Israel went home to Samaria, sulking and angry.
Some time later, there was a man named Naboth from Jezreel who owned a vineyard in Jezreel. It was right next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.

Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard so I can use it for a vegetable garden, since it is close to my palace. In exchange I will give you a better vineyard. Or if you prefer, I will pay you what it is worth."
But Naboth said to Ahab, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the land I inherited from my ancestors!"

So Ahab went home sulking and angry because of what Naboth from Jezreel had said: "I will not give you the land I inherited from my ancestors." He lay on his bed, turned his face to the wall, and would not eat.
His wife Jezebel came in and asked him, "Why are you so upset that you will not eat?"
He told her, "I spoke to Naboth from Jezreel and said, 'Sell me your vineyard. Or if you like, I will give you another vineyard for it.' But he said, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'"
His wife Jezebel said, "Is this how you rule as king of Israel? Get up, eat something, and cheer up. I will get you the vineyard of Naboth from Jezreel."
So she wrote letters in Ahab's name, stamped them with his seal, and sent them to the leaders and important men who lived in Naboth's town.
In the letters she wrote: "Announce a day of fasting, and give Naboth a seat of honour among the people.
Then seat two worthless men across from him, and have them accuse him, saying, 'You cursed God and the king!' Then take him out and stone him to death."
The leaders and important men of Naboth's town did just what Jezebel told them in the letters she had sent them.
They announced a fast and gave Naboth a seat of honour among the people.

Then the two worthless men came in and sat across from him. They accused Naboth in front of the people, saying, "Naboth cursed God and the king!" So they took him outside the town and stoned him to death.
Then they sent word to Jezebel: "Naboth has been stoned, and he is dead."

As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned to death, she said to Ahab, "Get up and take the vineyard of Naboth from Jezreel, the one he refused to sell you. Naboth is not alive anymore. He is dead."
When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take the vineyard of Naboth from Jezreel for himself.
Then the LORD's word came to Elijah from Tishbe. He said,
"Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who rules in Samaria. He is in Naboth's vineyard right now. He has gone there to take it for himself.

Tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Have you murdered a man and also taken his land?' Then tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: In the same place where dogs licked up Naboth's blood, dogs will lick up your blood, yes, yours!'"
Ahab said to Elijah, "So you have found me, my enemy!" Elijah answered, "Yes, I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the LORD's eyes.
The LORD says, 'I am going to bring disaster on you. I will wipe you out and cut off every male in Ahab's family in Israel, slave or free.
I will make your family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the family of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have made me angry and have made Israel sin.'
And about Jezebel the LORD says, 'Dogs will eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.'
Dogs will eat anyone in Ahab's family who dies in the city, and birds will eat those who die in the open country."
There was never anyone like Ahab, who sold himself to do what was evil in the LORD's eyes, urged on by his wife Jezebel.
He did disgusting things by worshipping idols, just as the Amorites had done, the people the LORD drove out ahead of the Israelites.
When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went without food. He even slept in sackcloth and walked around quietly in sorrow.
Then the LORD's word came to Elijah from Tishbe. He said,
"Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself, I will not bring the disaster while he is alive. I will bring it on his family in his son's time."
For three years there was no war between Syria and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to visit the king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his officials, "You know that Ramoth Gilead belongs to us. So why are we doing nothing to take it back from the king of Syria?"
He asked Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat answered the king of Israel, "I am with you all the way. My people are your people, and my horses are your horses."
But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, "First, please ask what the LORD says."

So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and asked them, "Should I go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" They answered, "Go, because the Lord will hand it over to the king."
But Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there not a prophet of the LORD here whom we can ask?"

The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man through whom we can ask the LORD. He is Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, because he never says anything good about me, only bad." Jehoshaphat said, "The king should not say that."
So the king of Israel called one of his officials and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once."

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were dressed in their royal robes, sitting on their thrones at the threshing floor by the entrance to the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying in front of them.
Zedekiah son of Kenaanah had made iron horns. He said, "This is what the LORD says: 'With these you will gore the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"
All the other prophets said the same thing: "Attack Ramoth Gilead and win, because the LORD will hand it over to the king."
The messenger who had gone to get Micaiah said to him, "Look, all the other prophets agree and are saying good things to the king. Please let your message agree with theirs, and say something good."
But Micaiah said, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will say only what the LORD tells me."

When he came to the king, the king asked him, "Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should we hold back?" Micaiah answered, "Go and win, because the LORD will hand it over to the king."
The king said to him, "How many times must I make you promise to tell me nothing but the truth in the LORD's name?"
Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These people have no master. Let each one go home in peace.'"
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you that he never says anything good about me, only bad?"
Micaiah went on, "So listen to the LORD's word. I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, with all the armies of heaven standing around him, on his right and on his left.
The LORD said, 'Who will trick Ahab into attacking Ramoth Gilead, so he will die there?' One said one thing, and another said something else.
Then a spirit came forward, stood before the LORD, and said, 'I will trick him.'
The LORD asked, 'How?' The spirit said, 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' The LORD said, 'You will trick him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.'
So now, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours. The LORD has decided to bring disaster on you."
Then Zedekiah son of Kenaanah walked up and slapped Micaiah in the face. He said, "Which way did the LORD's Spirit go when he left me to speak to you?"
Micaiah answered, "You will find out on the day you go and hide in an inner room."
The king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son.
Tell them, 'This is what the king says: Put this man in prison and give him nothing but a little bread and water until I come back safely.'"
Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, then the LORD has not spoken through me." Then he added, "Listen to this, all you people!"
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle.
The king of Syria had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, "Do not fight anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel."
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought, "That must be the king of Israel!" So they turned to attack him. But Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.

But someone shot an arrow without aiming, and it hit the king of Israel between the pieces of his armour. The king told his chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle. I am badly wounded."
The battle raged all day long. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and he died that evening. The blood from his wound ran down onto the floor of the chariot.
As the sun was setting, a shout went through the army: "Every man back to his own town! Every man back to his own land!"
So the king died, and he was brought to Samaria and buried there.
They washed his chariot at the pool of Samaria, where the prostitutes bathed, and dogs licked up his blood, just as the LORD had said.
The rest of what Ahab did, all his deeds, the ivory palace he built, and all the towns he built, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Ahab died, and his son Ahaziah became king after him.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah in the fourth year that Ahab was king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother was Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi.

He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn away from them. He did what was right in the LORD's eyes. But the high places were not removed, and the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there.
Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.
The rest of what Jehoshaphat did, the power he showed, and the wars he fought, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
He drove out of the land the rest of the male shrine prostitutes who were still there from the time of his father Asa.
At that time there was no king in Edom. A governor ruled there.
Jehoshaphat built large trading ships to sail to Ophir for gold. But they never sailed, because they were wrecked at Ezion Geber.
Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my sailors go with your sailors on the ships." But Jehoshaphat refused.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his ancestor David. His son Jehoram became king after him.
Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year that Jehoshaphat was king of Judah. He ruled Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He followed the ways of his father and mother, and the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin.
He served Baal and worshipped him. He made the LORD, the God of Israel, angry, just as his father had done.
2Kgs: After Ahab died, the land of Moab rebelled against Israel.

Ahaziah fell through the lattice window of his upstairs room in Samaria and was badly hurt. So he sent messengers and told them, "Go and ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will get better from this injury."

But the LORD's angel said to Elijah from Tishbe, "Get up and go meet the messengers of the king of Samaria. Ask them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron?
So this is what the LORD says: You will never get up from the bed you are lying on. You will surely die.'" So Elijah went.
When the messengers came back to the king, he asked them, "Why have you come back?"

They said, "A man came to meet us. He told us, 'Go back to the king who sent you and tell him, "This is what the LORD says: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending men to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron? So you will never get up from the bed you are lying on. You will surely die."'"
The king asked them, "What did the man look like who came to meet you and told you this?"
They answered, "He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist." The king said, "That was Elijah from Tishbe."
Then the king sent an army captain with his fifty men to Elijah. The captain went up to Elijah, who was sitting on top of a hill, and said, "Man of God, the king says, 'Come down!'"
Elijah answered the captain, "If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and burn up you and your fifty men!" Then fire came down from heaven and burned up the captain and his fifty men.
The king sent another captain with his fifty men. This captain said to Elijah, "Man of God, the king says, 'Come down at once!'"
Elijah answered, "If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and burn up you and your fifty men!" Then God's fire came down from heaven and burned up the captain and his fifty men.

The king sent a third captain with his fifty men. This third captain went up and fell on his knees in front of Elijah. He begged him, "Man of God, please value my life and the lives of these fifty men, your servants.
Fire came down from heaven and burned up the first two captains and their men. But now, please value my life."
The LORD's angel said to Elijah, "Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him." So Elijah got up and went down with him to the king.

Elijah told the king, "This is what the LORD says: 'You sent messengers to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron. Is it because there is no God in Israel to ask? Because you did this, you will never get up from the bed you are lying on. You will surely die.'"
So Ahaziah died, just as the LORD had said through Elijah. Because Ahaziah had no son, Joram became king after him. This was in the second year that Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat was king of Judah.
The rest of what Ahaziah did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
When the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were leaving Gilgal.

Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, because the LORD has sent me to Bethel." But Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel together.
The group of prophets at Bethel came out to Elisha and asked, "Do you know that the LORD is going to take your master from you today?" Elisha said, "Yes, I know. Do not talk about it."

Then Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, because the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." So they went to Jericho.
The group of prophets at Jericho came to Elisha and asked, "Do you know that the LORD is going to take your master from you today?" He answered, "Yes, I know. Do not talk about it."

Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, because the LORD has sent me to the Jordan River." But Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." So the two of them walked on.
Fifty men from the group of prophets went and stood at a distance, facing them, while Elijah and Elisha stood by the Jordan.
Elijah took off his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the water with it. The water split to the right and to the left, and the two of them crossed over on dry ground.
When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken away from you?" Elisha answered, "Please let me receive a double share of your spirit."
Elijah said, "You have asked for something hard. But if you see me when I am taken from you, you will have it. If you do not see me, you will not."
As they were walking along and talking, suddenly a chariot of fire and horses of fire came between them. And Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Elisha saw it and cried out, "My father! My father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!" Then he could not see him anymore. Elisha took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two.
He picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah, went back, and stood on the bank of the Jordan.

He took the cloak that had fallen from Elijah and struck the water with it. He said, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" When he struck the water, it split to the right and to the left, and Elisha crossed over.
The group of prophets from Jericho, who were watching, saw him and said, "The spirit of Elijah is now on Elisha." They came to meet him and bowed down to the ground in front of him.

They said, "Look, we your servants have fifty strong men with us. Please let them go and look for your master. Maybe the LORD's Spirit has picked him up and set him down on some mountain or in some valley." Elisha said, "No, do not send them."
But they kept pressing him until he was too embarrassed to refuse. So he said, "Send them." They sent fifty men, who searched for three days but did not find Elijah.
When they came back to Elisha, who was staying in Jericho, he said to them, "Didn't I tell you not to go?"
The men of Jericho said to Elisha, "Look, master, this town is in a good place, as you can see. But the water is bad, and the land does not produce crops."
Elisha said, "Bring me a new bowl and put salt in it." So they brought it to him.
He went out to the spring and threw the salt into it. He said, "This is what the LORD says: 'I have healed this water. It will never again cause death or make the land unable to produce.'"
And the water has stayed healed to this day, just as Elisha said.
From there Elisha went up to Bethel. As he was walking along the road, some young men came out of the town and made fun of him. They said, "Go on up, baldy! Go on up, baldy!"
He turned around, looked at them, and cursed them in the LORD's name. Then two female bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the young men to pieces.
Elisha went on from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he went back to Samaria.
Joram son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year that Jehoshaphat was king of Judah. He ruled for twelve years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, but not as much as his father and mother had done. He got rid of the sacred stone pillar of Baal that his father had made.
But he kept on doing the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin. He did not turn away from them.
Mesha king of Moab raised sheep. Every year he had to pay the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams.
But after Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
So at that time King Joram went out from Samaria and called up all Israel for war.

He also sent a message to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to fight against Moab?" Jehoshaphat answered, "I will go. I am with you all the way. My people are your people, and my horses are your horses."
Then he asked, "Which way should we attack?" Joram answered, "Through the desert of Edom."
So the king of Israel set out with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. After they had marched around for seven days, there was no water left for the army or for the animals with them.
The king of Israel cried, "Oh no! The LORD has brought us three kings together only to hand us over to Moab!"

But Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there not a prophet of the LORD here, so we can ask the LORD through him?" One of the king of Israel's officials answered, "Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He used to pour water on Elijah's hands."
Jehoshaphat said, "The LORD's word is with him." So the king of Israel, Jehoshaphat, and the king of Edom went down to see him.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What do you want with me? Go to the prophets of your father and mother." The king of Israel answered, "No, because it is the LORD who has brought us three kings together to hand us over to Moab."
Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD of Armies lives, the God I serve, if I did not respect Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even look at you or notice you.
But now bring me someone who plays the harp." While the harpist was playing, the LORD's power came on Elisha.
He said, "This is what the LORD says: 'Dig ditches all over this valley.'
The LORD says, 'You will not see wind or rain, but this valley will be filled with water. Then you, your cattle, and your other animals will drink.'
This is an easy thing for the LORD. He will also hand Moab over to you.
You will conquer every walled city and every important town. You will cut down every good tree, block up all the springs, and ruin every good field by covering it with stones."
The next morning, about the time of the morning sacrifice, water came flowing from the direction of Edom, and the land was filled with water.
Meanwhile, all the people of Moab had heard that the kings had come to fight against them. So everyone old enough to put on armour, young and old, was called up and stationed at the border.
When they got up early the next morning, the sun was shining on the water. To the Moabites across the valley, the water looked as red as blood.
They said, "That is blood! The kings must have fought and killed each other. Now, Moab, let's go and take what they left behind!"
But when the Moabites came to Israel's camp, the Israelites rose up and attacked them, and they ran away. The Israelites pushed on into the land, killing the Moabites.

They destroyed the towns. Each man threw a stone onto every good field until it was covered. They blocked up all the springs and cut down all the good trees. Only Kir Hareseth was left with its stone walls standing, but men with slings surrounded it and attacked it.
When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took seven hundred swordsmen with him to try to break through to the king of Edom, but they failed.
Then he took his oldest son, who was to be king after him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the city wall. Great anger came against Israel, so they left him and went back to their own land.

One day the wife of a man from the group of prophets cried out to Elisha, "My husband, your servant, is dead. You know he respected the LORD. But now the man he owed money to is coming to take my two sons as his slaves."
Elisha asked her, "How can I help you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?" She said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a small jar of oil."
Elisha said, "Go around and borrow empty jars from all your neighbours. Get as many as you can.
Then go inside and shut the door behind you and your sons. Pour oil into all the jars, and as each one is filled, set it aside."
So she left him and shut the door behind her and her sons. They kept bringing jars to her, and she kept pouring.
When all the jars were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another jar." He answered, "There are no more jars." Then the oil stopped flowing.
She went and told the man of God. He said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debts. You and your sons can live on what is left."
One day Elisha went to Shunem. An important woman lived there, and she begged him to stay and eat a meal. After that, whenever he passed by, he stopped there to eat.
She said to her husband, "I can tell that this man who often comes our way is a holy man of God.
Let's build a small room on the roof and put a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp in it for him. Then he can stay there whenever he comes to us."
One day Elisha came, went up to the room, and lay down there.
He said to his servant Gehazi, "Call the Shunammite woman." So Gehazi called her, and she came and stood in front of him.

Elisha told Gehazi, "Tell her, 'You have gone to all this trouble for us. What can we do for you? Can we speak to the king or the army commander for you?'" She answered, "I live safely among my own people."
Elisha asked, "Then what can be done for her?" Gehazi answered, "Well, she has no son, and her husband is old."
Elisha said, "Call her." So Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway.
Elisha said, "About this time next year, you will be holding a son in your arms." She said, "No, my master, man of God! Do not lie to your servant."
But the woman became pregnant, and about that same time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her.
The child grew. One day he went out to his father, who was with the workers harvesting the grain.
He said to his father, "My head! My head hurts!" His father told a servant, "Carry him to his mother."
The servant picked him up and took him to his mother. The boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died.
She carried him up and laid him on the bed of the man of God. Then she shut the door and went out.
She called to her husband and said, "Please send me one of the servants and a donkey, so I can hurry to the man of God and come right back."
He asked, "Why go to him today? It is not a New Moon or a Sabbath." She said, "It will be all right."
She saddled the donkey and told her servant, "Lead on, and go fast. Do not slow down for me unless I tell you."
So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her in the distance, he said to his servant Gehazi, "Look, there is the Shunammite woman!
Run to meet her and ask her, 'Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is your child all right?'" She answered, "Everything is all right."

But when she reached the man of God on the hill, she took hold of his feet. Gehazi came over to push her away, but the man of God said, "Leave her alone! She is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me. He has not told me why."
Then she said, "Did I ask you for a son, my master? Didn't I tell you, 'Do not raise my hopes'?"

Elisha said to Gehazi, "Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my walking stick, and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet them. If anyone greets you, do not answer. Lay my walking stick on the boy's face."
But the boy's mother said, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." So Elisha got up and followed her.
Gehazi went on ahead and laid the walking stick on the boy's face, but there was no sound or sign of life. So he went back to meet Elisha and told him, "The boy has not woken up."
When Elisha reached the house, there was the boy, lying dead on his bed.
Elisha went in, shut the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.
Then he got on the bed and lay on the boy, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, and hands to hands. As he stretched out over him, the boy's body began to grow warm.
Elisha got up and walked back and forth in the house once. Then he went up and stretched out over the boy again. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Elisha called Gehazi and said, "Call the Shunammite woman." So he called her. When she came in, Elisha said, "Pick up your son."
She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed down to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.

Elisha went back to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land. The group of prophets was sitting in front of him, and he told his servant, "Put the big pot on the fire and cook some stew for these prophets."

One of them went out into the fields to gather plants. He found a wild vine and picked as many wild gourds as his clothes could hold. He came back and cut them up into the pot of stew, not knowing what they were.
They served the stew to the men. But as they began eating, they cried out, "Man of God, there is death in the pot!" And they could not eat it.
Elisha said, "Bring me some flour." He threw it into the pot and said, "Serve it to the people so they can eat." And there was nothing harmful in the pot anymore.

A man came from Baal Shalishah, bringing the man of God twenty loaves of barley bread made from the first grain of the harvest, along with some fresh heads of grain in his sack. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat."
His servant asked, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" But Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat, because the LORD says, 'They will eat and have some left over.'"
So he set it before them. They ate and had some left over, just as the LORD had said.

Naaman was the commander of the army of the king of Syria. His master thought very highly of him and respected him, because through Naaman the LORD had given Syria victory. He was a brave soldier, but he had a skin disease called leprosy.
Raiding parties from Syria had gone into Israel and taken a young girl captive. She became a servant to Naaman's wife.
She said to her mistress, "If only my master would go to the prophet in Samaria! He would heal him of his leprosy."
Naaman went and told his master the king what the girl from Israel had said.

The king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So Naaman left. He took with him about three hundred and forty kilograms of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten sets of clothes.
He took the letter to the king of Israel. It said, "With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you, so that you can heal him of his leprosy."

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God? Can I kill and bring back to life? Why does this man send someone to me to be healed of leprosy? You can see he is trying to pick a fight with me!"

When Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent him this message: "Why have you torn your clothes? Send the man to me, and he will know there is a prophet in Israel."
So Naaman went with his horses and chariots and stopped at the door of Elisha's house.
Elisha sent a messenger out to say to him, "Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan River. Your skin will be healed, and you will be clean."
But Naaman became angry and went away. He said, "I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of the LORD his God, wave his hand over the sore spot, and heal my leprosy.
Aren't the Abana and Pharpar rivers in Damascus better than any of the waters in Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean?" So he turned and stormed off in a rage.
But his servants came to him and said, "Father, if the prophet had told you to do something hard, wouldn't you have done it? So why not do it when he simply tells you, 'Wash and be clean'?"
So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, as the man of God had told him. His skin became healthy, like the skin of a young child, and he was clean.

Then Naaman and all his men went back to the man of God. He stood in front of Elisha and said, "Now I know that there is no God in all the world except in Israel. So please accept a gift from your servant."
But Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD lives, the God I serve, I will not accept anything." Naaman kept urging him to take it, but he refused.

Naaman said, "If you will not, then please let me, your servant, take home as much soil as two mules can carry. From now on, your servant will never again offer a burnt offering or sacrifice to any other god except the LORD.

But may the LORD forgive your servant for one thing. When my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship, he leans on my arm, and I have to bow down there too. When I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the LORD forgive your servant for this."
Elisha said to him, "Go in peace." So Naaman left and went a short distance.

Then Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, thought, "My master let this Syrian, Naaman, off too easily by not accepting what he brought. As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him."
So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. When Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from his chariot to meet him and asked, "Is everything all right?"

Gehazi answered, "Everything is all right. My master sent me to say, 'Two young men from the group of prophets have just come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them thirty-four kilograms of silver and two sets of clothes.'"

Naaman said, "Please, take sixty-eight kilograms." He kept urging Gehazi to take it. He tied up the silver in two bags, with two sets of clothes, and gave them to two of his servants, who carried them ahead of Gehazi.
When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the things from the servants and hid them in the house. Then he sent the men away, and they left.
Then Gehazi went in and stood before his master. Elisha asked him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" He answered, "Your servant did not go anywhere."

But Elisha said to him, "Was my spirit not with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to take money and clothes, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and cattle, and male and female servants?
Now Naaman's leprosy will cling to you and to your descendants forever." When Gehazi left Elisha, his skin had leprosy. It was as white as snow.
The group of prophets said to Elisha, "Look, the place where we live and meet with you is too small for us.
Let us go to the Jordan River. Each of us can get a log there, and we can build a place to live." Elisha said, "Go."
Then one of them said, "Please come with us, your servants." Elisha answered, "I will come."
So he went with them. When they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees.
As one of them was cutting down a tree, the iron axe head fell into the water. He cried out, "Oh no, master! It was borrowed!"
The man of God asked, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, Elisha cut a stick, threw it into the water there, and made the iron float.
He said, "Pick it up." So the man reached out his hand and took it.
The king of Syria was at war with Israel. After talking with his officers, he said, "I will set up my camp in such and such a place."
But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel: "Be careful not to pass that place, because the Syrians are going down there."
So the king of Israel sent word to the place the man of God had warned him about. Again and again Elisha warned him, and the king was on his guard there, not just once or twice.
This made the king of Syria very upset. He called his officers and demanded, "Tell me! Which one of us is on the side of the king of Israel?"
One of his officers said, "None of us, my master the king. It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel. He tells the king of Israel even the words you speak in your bedroom."
The king said, "Go and find out where he is, so I can send men to capture him." He was told, "He is in Dothan."
So he sent horses, chariots, and a large army there. They went at night and surrounded the city.
Early the next morning, the servant of the man of God got up and went outside. He saw an army with horses and chariots all around the city. "Oh no, master! What will we do?" he asked.
Elisha answered, "Do not be afraid. Those who are with us are more than those who are with them."
Then Elisha prayed, "LORD, please open his eyes so he can see." The LORD opened the young man's eyes, and he looked and saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
As the enemy came down toward him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, "Please strike these people with blindness." So the LORD struck them with blindness, as Elisha had asked.
Elisha told them, "This is not the right road, and this is not the right city. Follow me, and I will take you to the man you are looking for." And he led them to Samaria.
When they had entered Samaria, Elisha said, "LORD, open these men's eyes so they can see." The LORD opened their eyes, and they looked and saw that they were in the middle of Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha, "My father, should I kill them? Should I kill them?"
Elisha answered, "Do not kill them. Would you kill people you had captured with your own sword and bow? Give them food and water so they can eat and drink, and then send them back to their master."

So the king prepared a great feast for them. After they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went back to their master. After that, Syrian raiding parties stopped coming into Israel's land.
Some time later, Ben-Hadad king of Syria gathered his whole army and marched up and surrounded Samaria.
There was a terrible famine in the city. The siege lasted so long that a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a small cup of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver.
One day, as the king of Israel was walking along the city wall, a woman cried out to him, "Help me, my master the king!"
He answered, "If the LORD does not help you, how can I help you? Do I have grain from the threshing floor or wine from the winepress?"
Then the king asked her, "What is the matter?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give up your son so we can eat him today, and tomorrow we will eat my son.'
So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Give up your son so we can eat him.' But she has hidden her son."
When the king heard what the woman said, he tore his clothes. As he walked along the wall, the people looked and saw that he was wearing sackcloth under his clothes, next to his skin.
He said, "May God punish me, and even more, if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head on his shoulders by the end of today!"

Elisha was sitting in his house, and the leaders of the city were sitting with him. The king sent a messenger ahead. But before the messenger arrived, Elisha said to the leaders, "Do you see how this murderer is sending someone to cut off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold it shut against him. Isn't the sound of his master's footsteps right behind him?"
While Elisha was still talking with them, the messenger came down to him. The king said, "This disaster is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

Elisha said, "Listen to the LORD's word. This is what the LORD says: 'About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, seven litres of fine flour will sell for just one piece of silver, and fourteen litres of barley will sell for one piece of silver.'"

The officer whose arm the king leaned on said to the man of God, "Even if the LORD opened windows in the sky, could this happen?" Elisha answered, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
Four men with leprosy were sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They said to each other, "Why should we sit here until we die?

If we say, 'Let's go into the city,' we will die there, because there is a famine in the city. And if we stay here, we will die too. So let's go over to the Syrian army and give ourselves up. If they spare us, we will live. If they kill us, we were going to die anyway."
So at dusk they got up and went to the Syrian camp. When they reached the edge of the camp, there was no one there.

The Lord had made the Syrian army hear the sound of chariots and horses, the noise of a great army. They had said to each other, "Look, the king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to attack us!"
So they had got up and run away at dusk. They left their tents, their horses, and their donkeys. They left the camp just as it was and ran for their lives.

When the men with leprosy reached the edge of the camp, they went into one tent and ate and drank. They took silver, gold, and clothes from it and went and hid them. Then they came back, went into another tent, took things from it too, and hid them.

Then they said to each other, "What we are doing is not right. Today is a day of good news, and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until morning, we will be punished. Let's go right now and tell the king's palace."

So they went and called out to the gatekeepers of the city. They told them, "We went into the Syrian camp, and there was no one there, not a sound of anyone. There were only horses and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were."
The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported inside the king's palace.

The king got up in the night and said to his officers, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done. They know we are starving. So they have left the camp to hide in the countryside. They are thinking, 'When the Israelites come out of the city, we will capture them alive and get into the city.'"

One of his officers answered, "Let some men take five of the horses that are still left in the city. If they die, they will be no worse off than all the other Israelites who are left here, or all those who have already died. Let's send them to see what happened."
So they took two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Syrian army. He told them, "Go and find out."

They followed the Syrians as far as the Jordan River. The whole road was covered with clothes and equipment the Syrians had thrown away as they ran in a hurry. The messengers came back and told the king.

Then the people went out and took everything from the Syrian camp. So seven litres of fine flour sold for one piece of silver, and fourteen litres of barley sold for one piece of silver, just as the LORD had said.
The king had put the officer whose arm he leaned on in charge of the gate. But the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had said when the king came down to see him.

It happened just as the man of God had told the king: "About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, fourteen litres of barley will sell for one piece of silver, and seven litres of fine flour will sell for one piece of silver."

And the officer had answered the man of God, "Even if the LORD opened windows in the sky, could this happen?" And Elisha had said, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
That is exactly what happened to him. The people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.

Elisha had told the woman whose son he had brought back to life, "Get up and leave with your family. Go and stay wherever you can, because the LORD has called for a famine. It will come on this land for seven years."
So the woman got up and did what the man of God said. She and her family went and lived in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
At the end of the seven years, she came back from the land of the Philistines. She went to the king to ask him to give back her house and her land.
At that moment the king was talking with Gehazi, the servant of the man of God. He said, "Tell me about all the great things Elisha has done."

Just as Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had brought a dead boy back to life, the woman whose son it was came in to ask the king for her house and her land. Gehazi said, "My master the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha brought back to life."

The king asked the woman about it, and she told him. Then the king gave her an official and said, "Give back everything that belonged to her, including all the crops her land produced from the day she left until now."
Elisha went to Damascus. Ben-Hadad king of Syria was sick. When the king was told, "The man of God has come here,"
he said to Hazael, "Take a gift with you and go meet the man of God. Ask the LORD through him, 'Will I get better from this sickness?'"

So Hazael went to meet Elisha. He took a gift of all the best things from Damascus, loaded on forty camels. He came and stood in front of him and said, "Your son Ben-Hadad king of Syria has sent me to ask, 'Will I get better from this sickness?'"
Elisha said to him, "Go and tell him, 'You will surely get better.' But the LORD has shown me that he will surely die."
Elisha stared at Hazael until Hazael felt uncomfortable. Then the man of God began to cry.

Hazael asked, "Why are you crying, my master?" Elisha answered, "Because I know the harm you will do to the Israelites. You will set their forts on fire, kill their young men with the sword, smash their little children to death, and rip open their pregnant women."
Hazael said, "How could your servant, who is only a dog, do such a great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you will become king of Syria."
Then Hazael left Elisha and went back to his master. Ben-Hadad asked him, "What did Elisha tell you?" Hazael answered, "He told me you would surely get better."
But the next day, Hazael took a thick cloth, soaked it in water, and spread it over the king's face until he died. Then Hazael became king in his place.
In the fifth year that Joram son of Ahab was king of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat began to rule as king of Judah.
He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eight years.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, as Ahab's family had done, because he married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes.
But for the sake of his servant David, the LORD did not want to destroy Judah. He had promised to give David and his descendants a lamp forever.
While Jehoram was king, Edom rebelled against Judah's rule and chose its own king.
So Jehoram went to Zair with all his chariots. The Edomites surrounded him and his chariot commanders, but he got up at night and attacked them, and his army ran home to their tents.
So Edom has been free from Judah's rule to this day. The town of Libnah rebelled at the same time.
The rest of what Jehoram did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Jehoram died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Ahaziah became king after him.
In the twelfth year that Joram son of Ahab was king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram began to rule as king of Judah.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for one year. His mother was Athaliah, a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel.
He followed the ways of Ahab's family and did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, as Ahab's family had done, because he was related to Ahab's family by marriage.
Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth Gilead. The Syrians wounded Joram.

So King Joram went back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Then Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, because he had been wounded.
The prophet Elisha called a man from the group of prophets and said to him, "Tuck your cloak into your belt, take this small jar of olive oil, and go to Ramoth Gilead.
When you get there, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi. Go to him, get him away from his companions, and take him into an inner room.
Then take the jar of oil, pour it on his head, and say, 'This is what the LORD says: I have anointed you king over Israel.' Then open the door and run. Do not wait."
So the young man, the young prophet, went to Ramoth Gilead.
When he arrived, he found the army commanders sitting together. He said, "I have a message for you, commander." Jehu asked, "For which of us?" He answered, "For you, commander."

So Jehu got up and went into the house. The young prophet poured the oil on his head and said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I have anointed you king over the LORD's people Israel.
You must destroy the family of your master Ahab. In this way I will punish Jezebel for the blood of my servants the prophets and the blood of all the LORD's servants she killed.
Ahab's whole family will die. I will cut off every male in Ahab's family in Israel, slave or free.
I will make Ahab's family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the family of Baasha son of Ahijah.
Dogs will eat Jezebel on the land at Jezreel, and no one will bury her.'" Then he opened the door and ran away.

When Jehu went back out to his master's officers, one of them asked him, "Is everything all right? Why did this crazy man come to you?" Jehu answered, "You know the man and the kind of things he says."
They said, "That's not true! Tell us." So Jehu said, "He told me, 'This is what the LORD says: I have anointed you king over Israel.'"
At once each of them took off his cloak and spread it under Jehu on the bare steps. Then they blew the trumpet and shouted, "Jehu is king!"
So Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi, made a plot against Joram. At that time Joram and all Israel had been guarding Ramoth Gilead against Hazael king of Syria.

But King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Syrians had given him in the battle with Hazael king of Syria. Jehu said, "If you are with me, do not let anyone slip out of the city to go and warn Jezreel."
Then Jehu got into his chariot and rode to Jezreel, because Joram was lying there wounded. Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to visit Joram.
