The lookout standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu's troops coming. He called out, "I see a group of soldiers." Joram said, "Send a horseman to meet them and ask, 'Do you come in peace?'"

So a horseman rode out to meet Jehu and said, "The king asks, 'Do you come in peace?'" Jehu answered, "What do you care about peace? Get behind me!" The lookout reported, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."
So the king sent out a second horseman. He came to them and said, "The king asks, 'Do you come in peace?'" Jehu answered, "What do you care about peace? Get behind me!"
The lookout reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back either. The driving is like the driving of Jehu son of Nimshi. He drives like a madman."

Joram ordered, "Get my chariot ready." When it was ready, Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah rode out, each in his own chariot, to meet Jehu. They met him at the field that had belonged to Naboth from Jezreel.
When Joram saw Jehu, he asked, "Do you come in peace, Jehu?" Jehu answered, "How can there be peace while your mother Jezebel's idol worship and witchcraft are everywhere?"
Joram turned his chariot around and ran away, shouting to Ahaziah, "Treason, Ahaziah!"
Jehu pulled back his bow with all his strength and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow went through his heart, and he fell down dead in his chariot.

Jehu said to Bidkar, his chariot officer, "Pick him up and throw him into the field that belonged to Naboth from Jezreel. Remember when you and I were riding together behind his father Ahab, and the LORD spoke this message against him:

'Yesterday I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons, says the LORD, and I will surely pay you back on this very piece of land, says the LORD.' So pick him up and throw him onto that land, just as the LORD said."

When Ahaziah king of Judah saw what happened, he ran away along the road to Beth Haggan. Jehu chased him, shouting, "Kill him too!" They shot him in his chariot on the way up to Gur, near Ibleam. He escaped to Megiddo and died there.
His officials carried his body in a chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his ancestors in his tomb in the city of David.
Ahaziah had become king of Judah in the eleventh year that Joram son of Ahab was king of Israel.
Then Jehu came to Jezreel. When Jezebel heard about it, she put on eye makeup, fixed her hair, and looked out of a window.
As Jehu came through the gate, she called out, "Have you come in peace, you Zimri, you murderer of your master?"
Jehu looked up at the window and called, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three palace officials looked down at him.
Jehu said, "Throw her down!" So they threw her down. Some of her blood splashed on the wall and on the horses, and the horses trampled her.
Jehu went inside and ate and drank. Then he said, "Take care of that cursed woman and bury her, because she was a king's daughter."
But when they went to bury her, they found nothing left except her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.
They went back and told Jehu. He said, "This is what the LORD said through his servant Elijah from Tishbe: 'On the land at Jezreel, dogs will eat Jezebel's flesh.
Jezebel's body will be like dung spread on the field in the land of Jezreel, so that no one will be able to say, "This is Jezebel."'"
Ahab had seventy sons living in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the officials of Jezreel, to the leaders, and to the men who were raising Ahab's sons. He wrote,
"Your master's sons are with you, and you have chariots and horses, a walled city, and weapons. So as soon as this letter reaches you,
choose the best and most able of your master's sons. Put him on his father's throne, and fight for your master's family."
But they were terrified. They said, "Two kings could not stand against him. How can we?"

So the man in charge of the palace, the governor of the city, the leaders, and the men raising the sons sent this message to Jehu: "We are your servants, and we will do anything you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever you think is best."

Then Jehu wrote them a second letter. He said, "If you are on my side and will obey me, bring the heads of your master's sons to me in Jezreel by this time tomorrow." The seventy sons of the king were being raised by the leading men of the city.
When the letter arrived, these men took the seventy sons of the king and killed them all. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu at Jezreel.
A messenger came and told Jehu, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons." Jehu said, "Put them in two piles at the entrance of the city gate until morning."
The next morning Jehu went out, stood in front of all the people, and said, "You are not to blame. It is true that I plotted against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?
Know this: not one word the LORD spoke against Ahab's family will fail to come true. The LORD has done what he said through his servant Elijah."
So Jehu killed everyone in Jezreel who was left from Ahab's family, along with all his important officials, his close friends, and his priests. He left no one alive.
Then Jehu set out for Samaria. On the way, at Beth Eked, where the shepherds sheared their sheep,
he met some relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah. He asked, "Who are you?" They answered, "We are relatives of Ahaziah. We have come down to visit the king's sons and the queen mother's sons."
Jehu ordered, "Take them alive!" So they took them alive and then killed them at the well of Beth Eked, forty-two men. He did not leave any of them alive.

When Jehu left there, he met Jehonadab son of Rechab, who was coming to meet him. Jehu greeted him and asked, "Are you as loyal to me as I am to you?" Jehonadab answered, "I am." Jehu said, "If you are, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand, and Jehu helped him up into the chariot.
Jehu said, "Come with me and see how zealous I am for the LORD." So Jehonadab rode along with him in his chariot.
When Jehu arrived in Samaria, he killed everyone in Samaria who was left from Ahab's family. He wiped them out, just as the LORD had told Elijah.
Then Jehu gathered all the people together and said, "Ahab served Baal a little. Jehu will serve him a lot.

Now call together all the prophets of Baal, all his worshippers, and all his priests. Make sure no one is missing, because I am going to offer a great sacrifice to Baal. Anyone who does not come will be put to death." But Jehu was tricking them, so he could destroy the worshippers of Baal.
Jehu said, "Call a holy gathering to honour Baal." So they announced it.
Jehu sent word through all Israel, and all the worshippers of Baal came. Not one of them stayed away. They crowded into the temple of Baal until it was full from one end to the other.
Jehu told the man in charge of the robes, "Bring out robes for all the worshippers of Baal." So he brought robes out for them.

Then Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab went into the temple of Baal. Jehu said to the worshippers of Baal, "Look around and make sure there are no servants of the LORD here with you, only worshippers of Baal."

So they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had posted eighty men outside. He had warned them, "If anyone lets even one of the people I hand over to you escape, he will pay with his own life."

As soon as Jehu finished offering the burnt offering, he ordered the guards and officers, "Go in and kill them! Do not let anyone get away." So they killed them with their swords. The guards and officers threw the bodies out and then went into the inner room of Baal's temple.
They brought out the sacred stone pillars from the temple of Baal and burned them.
They smashed the sacred stone of Baal and tore down the temple of Baal. They turned it into a public toilet, and it is still one today.
So Jehu wiped out the worship of Baal in Israel.
But Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin. He kept the gold calves at Bethel and Dan.

The LORD said to Jehu, "You have done well by doing what is right in my eyes. You have done to Ahab's family everything I wanted done. So your descendants will sit on the throne of Israel for four generations."
But Jehu was not careful to obey the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, who had made Israel sin.
In those days the LORD began to make Israel smaller. Hazael defeated the Israelites all along their borders.

He conquered the land east of the Jordan River, all the land of Gilead, where the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh lived. He took it from Aroer by the Arnon Valley all the way through Gilead and Bashan.
The rest of what Jehu did, all his deeds and all his power, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jehu died and was buried in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz became king after him.
Jehu ruled over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years.
When Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, saw that her son was dead, she set out to kill the whole royal family.

But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah, took Ahaziah's son Joash and secretly took him away from the other princes who were about to be killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom, so Athaliah could not find him, and he was not killed.
Joash stayed hidden with his nurse in the LORD's temple for six years, while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest sent for the commanders of units of a hundred, the Carites, and the guards. He brought them to the LORD's temple, made an agreement with them there, and made them swear an oath in the LORD's temple. Then he showed them the king's son.
He gave them these orders: "This is what you must do. One third of you who come on duty on the Sabbath will guard the king's palace.
Another third will be at the Sur Gate, and the last third at the gate behind the guards. You will take turns guarding the temple.
The two groups of you who go off duty on the Sabbath will guard the LORD's temple for the king.
Stand all around the king, each of you with your weapons in your hand. Anyone who comes near your lines must be killed. Stay close to the king wherever he goes."
The commanders of hundreds did everything Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each one took his men, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty, and came to Jehoiada the priest.
The priest gave the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David, which were kept in the LORD's temple.
The guards stood all around the king, each with his weapons in his hand. They stood from the south side of the temple to the north side, near the altar and the temple.

Then Jehoiada brought out the king's son. He put the crown on him and gave him a copy of the covenant. They made him king and anointed him. The people clapped their hands and shouted, "Long live the king!"
When Athaliah heard the noise of the guards and the people, she went to the crowd at the LORD's temple.

She looked and saw the king standing by the pillar, as was the custom. The commanders and trumpeters were beside the king, and all the people of the land were celebrating and blowing trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed, "Treason! Treason!"

Jehoiada the priest ordered the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army, "Bring her out between the lines of soldiers. Kill anyone who follows her." The priest had said, "She must not be killed in the LORD's temple."
So they grabbed her as she went through the horse entrance into the palace grounds, and she was killed there.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they would be the LORD's people. He also made an agreement between the king and the people.

All the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars. Then Jehoiada the priest posted guards at the LORD's temple.

He took the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and together they led the king down from the LORD's temple. They went through the Gate of the Guards into the palace, and the king took his seat on the royal throne.
All the people of the land celebrated, and the city was calm, because Athaliah had been killed with the sword at the palace.
Joash was seven years old when he became king.
Joash became king in the seventh year that Jehu was king of Israel, and he ruled in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother was Zibiah, from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the LORD's eyes all the years that Jehoiada the priest taught him.
But the high places were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there.

Joash said to the priests, "Collect all the money brought as holy gifts to the LORD's temple: the money from the census, the money people pay for their vows, and the money people bring because they want to give it to the LORD's temple.
Let each priest receive the money from the people he serves. Then use it to repair any damage you find in the temple."
But by the twenty-third year that King Joash ruled, the priests still had not repaired the temple.

So King Joash called Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and asked them, "Why are you not repairing the damage to the temple? From now on, do not keep any more money from the people you serve. Hand it over for repairing the temple."
The priests agreed not to collect any more money from the people, and not to be in charge of repairing the temple themselves.

Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and drilled a hole in its lid. He put it beside the altar, on the right side as people enter the LORD's temple. The priests who guarded the entrance put into the chest all the money that people brought to the LORD's temple.
Whenever they saw that there was a lot of money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came. They counted the money that had been brought to the LORD's temple and put it into bags.
Then they gave the measured money to the men in charge of the work on the LORD's temple. These men paid the carpenters and builders who worked on the LORD's temple,
the stonemasons and stonecutters. They also used it to buy wood and cut stone for repairing the LORD's temple, and to pay for everything else needed to repair it.
The money brought to the LORD's temple was not used to make silver cups, wick trimmers, bowls, trumpets, or any other objects of gold or silver for the temple.
Instead, it was paid to the workers, who used it to repair the LORD's temple.
They did not ask the men in charge to account for the money given to them to pay the workers, because they were completely honest.
The money from the guilt offerings and the sin offerings was not brought into the LORD's temple. It belonged to the priests.
About that time Hazael king of Syria attacked Gath and captured it. Then he decided to attack Jerusalem.

So Joash king of Judah took all the holy things that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah, had given to God, as well as his own gifts. He took all the gold found in the treasuries of the LORD's temple and of the palace, and he sent it all to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael pulled back from Jerusalem.
The rest of what Joash did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
His officials made a plot against him and killed Joash at Beth Millo, on the road that goes down to Silla.
The officials who killed him were Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer. He died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Amaziah became king after him.
In the twenty-third year that Joash son of Ahaziah was king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for seventeen years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin, and he did not turn away from them.
So the LORD was very angry with Israel. For a long time he let Hazael king of Syria and his son Ben-Hadad defeat them.
Then Jehoahaz begged the LORD for help, and the LORD listened to him, because he saw how badly the king of Syria was treating Israel.
The LORD gave Israel someone to rescue them, and they escaped from the power of Syria. Then the Israelites lived safely in their own homes as before.
But they did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam's family, who had made Israel sin. They kept on doing them. The Asherah pole also stayed standing in Samaria.

The army of Jehoahaz had been reduced to only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Syria had destroyed the rest and trampled them like dust at threshing time.
The rest of what Jehoahaz did, all his deeds and his power, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jehoahaz died and was buried in Samaria. His son Jehoash became king after him.
In the thirty-seventh year that Joash was king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for sixteen years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin. He kept on doing them.
The rest of what Jehoash did, all his deeds and the power he showed in his war against Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jehoash died, and Jeroboam took his place on the throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
Elisha became sick with the illness that would take his life. Jehoash king of Israel went down to see him and cried over him. "My father! My father!" he said. "The chariots and horsemen of Israel!"
Elisha said to him, "Get a bow and some arrows." So the king got a bow and some arrows.
Elisha said to the king of Israel, "Take the bow in your hands." When he did, Elisha put his own hands on the king's hands.

Elisha said, "Open the window that faces east." So he opened it. Elisha said, "Shoot!" and he shot. Elisha said, "That is the LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! You will completely defeat the Syrians at Aphek."
Then Elisha said, "Pick up the arrows." When the king picked them up, Elisha told him, "Strike the ground with them." He struck the ground three times and stopped.
The man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck the ground five or six times. Then you would have defeated Syria completely. But now you will defeat Syria only three times."
Then Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of Moabite raiders used to come into the land every spring.

Once, while some Israelites were burying a man, they suddenly saw a band of raiders. So they threw the man's body into Elisha's tomb. As soon as the body touched Elisha's bones, the man came back to life and stood up on his feet.
Hazael king of Syria troubled Israel the whole time Jehoahaz was king.

But the LORD was kind to the Israelites and had mercy on them. He cared for them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He did not want to destroy them, and even then he did not send them away from his presence.
Hazael king of Syria died, and his son Ben-Hadad became king after him.

Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz won back from Ben-Hadad son of Hazael the towns that Hazael had taken in war from his father Jehoahaz. Jehoash defeated Ben-Hadad three times and won back the towns of Israel.
In the second year that Jehoash son of Jehoahaz was king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash began to rule as king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Jehoaddin, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, but not as his ancestor David had done. He did everything his father Joash had done.
But the high places were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there.
As soon as he had firm control of the kingdom, he executed the officials who had murdered his father the king.

But he did not put the murderers' children to death. He obeyed what is written in the book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded: "Parents must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their parents. Each person must die for his own sin."
Amaziah killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He captured the town of Sela in battle and renamed it Joktheel, the name it still has today.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, king of Israel, with this challenge: "Come, let's meet face to face in battle."

But Jehoash king of Israel sent this answer to Amaziah king of Judah: "A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon: 'Give your daughter to my son as his wife.' Then a wild animal in Lebanon came by and trampled the thistle.
You have truly defeated Edom, and now you are proud. Enjoy your fame, but stay at home! Why ask for trouble that will bring you down, and Judah with you?"
But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went to attack. He and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other in battle at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
Israel defeated Judah, and every man of Judah ran home to his tent.

Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash and grandson of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh. Then he went to Jerusalem and tore down its wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, a section about one hundred and eighty metres long.
He took all the gold and silver and all the objects found in the LORD's temple and in the treasuries of the palace. He also took hostages, and then he went back to Samaria.
The rest of what Jehoash did, his power, and how he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam became king after him.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of what Amaziah did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Some people in Jerusalem made a plot against him, so he ran away to Lachish. But they sent men after him to Lachish, and they killed him there.
They brought his body back on horses, and he was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem, in the city of David.
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
Azariah rebuilt the town of Elath and won it back for Judah, after his father the king had died.
In the fifteenth year that Amaziah son of Joash was king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Jehoash became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for forty-one years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin.

He won back Israel's borders from Lebo Hamath in the north to the Dead Sea in the south. This was just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had said through his servant the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, from Gath Hepher.
The LORD had seen how bitterly everyone in Israel was suffering, slave or free. There was no one to help Israel.
The LORD had not said he would wipe out the name of Israel from the earth. So he saved them through Jeroboam son of Jehoash.

The rest of what Jeroboam did, all his deeds, his power, his wars, and how he won back Damascus and Hamath for Israel, which had once belonged to Judah, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Jeroboam died and was buried with the kings of Israel. His son Zechariah became king after him.
In the twenty-seventh year that Jeroboam was king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah began to rule as king of Judah.
He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his father Amaziah had done.
But the high places were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there.
The LORD struck the king with leprosy, and he had it until the day he died. He lived in a separate house. His son Jotham was in charge of the palace and ruled the people of the land.
The rest of what Azariah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Azariah died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Jotham became king after him.
In the thirty-eighth year that Azariah was king of Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for six months.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, as his ancestors had done. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin.
Shallum son of Jabesh made a plot against Zechariah. He attacked him in front of the people, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of what Zechariah did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
So the LORD's promise to Jehu came true: "Your descendants will sit on the throne of Israel for four generations."
Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the thirty-ninth year that Uzziah was king of Judah. He ruled in Samaria for one month.
Then Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah to Samaria. He attacked Shallum son of Jabesh there, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of what Shallum did, and the plot he made, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.

At that time Menahem, starting out from Tirzah, attacked the town of Tiphsah, everyone in it, and the area around it. He attacked it because its people would not open their gates to him. He ripped open all the pregnant women there.
In the thirty-ninth year that Azariah was king of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for ten years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. As long as he lived, he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin.
Then Pul king of Assyria invaded the land. Menahem gave Pul about thirty-four thousand kilograms of silver, so Pul would support him and help him keep control of the kingdom.
Menahem got the money from Israel by forcing every rich man to pay fifty pieces of silver. He gave it to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay in the land.
The rest of what Menahem did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Menahem died, and his son Pekahiah became king after him.
In the fiftieth year that Azariah was king of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin.

Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his chief officers, made a plot against him. With fifty men from Gilead, Pekah attacked Pekahiah in the strongest part of the palace in Samaria. He killed him, along with Argob and Arieh, and became king in his place.
The rest of what Pekahiah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year that Azariah was king of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for twenty years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin.

While Pekah was king of Israel, Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali. He took the people away as prisoners to Assyria.
Then Hoshea son of Elah made a plot against Pekah son of Remaliah. He attacked him, killed him, and became king in his place. This was in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah.
The rest of what Pekah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
In the second year that Pekah son of Remaliah was king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah began to rule as king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his father Uzziah had done.
But the high places were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there. Jotham built the Upper Gate of the LORD's temple.
The rest of what Jotham did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah to attack Judah.
Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his ancestor David. His son Ahaz became king after him.
In the seventeenth year that Pekah son of Remaliah was king of Israel, Ahaz son of Jotham began to rule as king of Judah.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his ancestor David had done.
Instead, he followed the ways of the kings of Israel. He even sacrificed his own son in the fire, copying the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to attack Jerusalem. They surrounded Ahaz but could not defeat him.
At that time Rezin king of Syria won back Elath for Syria and drove the people of Judah out of it. Edomites moved into Elath, and they still live there today.
Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria to say, "I am your servant and your son. Come and rescue me from the king of Syria and the king of Israel, who are attacking me."
Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the LORD's temple and in the treasuries of the palace, and sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria agreed. He attacked Damascus and captured it. He took its people away as prisoners to Kir, and he killed Rezin.
Then King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria. There he saw an altar, and he sent Uriah the priest a drawing of the altar with detailed plans for building it.
So Uriah the priest built an altar exactly like the plans King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He finished it before King Ahaz came back from Damascus.
When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he went up to it and offered sacrifices on it.
He burned his burnt offering and his grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
He moved the bronze altar that stood before the LORD. He took it from the front of the temple, from between the new altar and the LORD's temple, and put it on the north side of the new altar.

Then King Ahaz ordered Uriah the priest, "On the large new altar, burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, the king's burnt offering and grain offering, and the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings of all the people of the land. Sprinkle on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and sacrifices. But the bronze altar will be for me to use when I ask God for guidance."
Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz ordered.

King Ahaz cut off the side panels of the bronze stands and removed the basins from them. He took the huge bronze tank called the Sea down from the bronze bulls that held it up and set it on a stone base.
To please the king of Assyria, he also took away the covered walkway for the Sabbath that had been built at the temple, and the king's outside entrance to the LORD's temple.
The rest of what Ahaz did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Hezekiah became king after him.
In the twelfth year that Ahaz was king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for nine years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, but not as much as the kings of Israel before him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked Hoshea. Hoshea became his servant and paid him taxes every year.

But the king of Assyria found out that Hoshea was plotting against him. Hoshea had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and he had stopped paying taxes to the king of Assyria as he used to do each year. So the king of Assyria arrested Hoshea and put him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land. He marched to Samaria and surrounded it for three years.

In the ninth year that Hoshea was king, the king of Assyria captured Samaria. He took the Israelites away to Assyria and settled them in Halah, at the Habor River in Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes.

All this happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of Egypt and rescued them from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They worshipped other gods.
They followed the customs of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of them, and the customs the kings of Israel had started.
The Israelites secretly did things against the LORD their God that were not right. They built high places for themselves in all their towns, from the smallest watchtower to the biggest walled city.
They set up sacred stone pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
They burned incense at all the high places, as the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of them had done. They did wicked things that made the LORD angry.
They worshipped idols, even though the LORD had told them, "You must not do this."

The LORD warned Israel and Judah through all his prophets and seers. He said, "Turn from your evil ways. Keep my commands and laws, following all the Law I commanded your ancestors and sent to you through my servants the prophets."
But they would not listen. They were as stubborn as their ancestors, who did not trust the LORD their God.

They rejected his laws and the covenant he had made with their ancestors, and the warnings he had given them. They followed worthless idols and became worthless themselves. They copied the nations around them, even though the LORD had commanded them not to do what those nations did.
They turned away from all the commands of the LORD their God. They made two metal idols shaped like calves, and an Asherah pole. They worshipped all the stars in the sky, and they served Baal.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire. They practised fortune-telling and witchcraft. They gave themselves over to doing what was evil in the LORD's eyes, and made him angry.
So the LORD was very angry with Israel, and he removed them from his presence. Only the tribe of Judah was left.
But even Judah did not keep the commands of the LORD their God. They followed the customs Israel had started.
So the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel. He punished them and handed them over to raiders, until he had thrown them out of his sight.
When the LORD tore Israel away from David's family, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD and made them commit a great sin.
The Israelites kept on doing all the sins Jeroboam had done. They did not turn away from them,

until the LORD removed Israel from his presence, just as he had warned through all his servants the prophets. So the Israelites were taken from their own land as prisoners to Assyria, and they are still there today.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took over Samaria and lived in its towns.
When they first lived there, they did not worship the LORD. So the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions killed some of them.

Someone reported to the king of Assyria, "The people you took away and settled in the towns of Samaria do not know what the god of that land requires. So he has sent lions among them, and the lions are killing them, because the people do not know what he requires."
Then the king of Assyria gave this order: "Send back one of the priests you took away from there. Let him go and live there and teach the people what the god of the land requires."
So one of the priests who had been taken away from Samaria came back and lived in Bethel. He taught them how to worship the LORD.
But each nation still made its own gods. They set them up in the shrines on the high places the people of Samaria had made, each nation in the towns where it lived.
The people from Babylon made Succoth Benoth. The people from Cuthah made Nergal. The people from Hamath made Ashima.
The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak. The Sepharvites burned their children in the fire as sacrifices to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
They worshipped the LORD, but they also chose all kinds of their own people to be priests at the high places. These priests offered sacrifices for them in the shrines.
They worshipped the LORD, but they also served their own gods, following the customs of the nations they had been taken from.

To this day they still follow their old customs. They do not truly worship the LORD. They do not obey the laws, rules, teachings, and commands the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.
The LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites and commanded them, "Do not worship other gods. Do not bow down to them, serve them, or offer sacrifices to them.
Worship only the LORD, who brought you up out of Egypt with great power and a mighty arm. Bow down to him and offer sacrifices to him.
Always be careful to obey the laws, rules, teachings, and commands he wrote for you. Do not worship other gods.
Do not forget the covenant I made with you, and do not worship other gods.
Instead, worship the LORD your God. He will rescue you from the power of all your enemies."
But they would not listen. They kept on following their old customs.
So these nations worshipped the LORD, but they also served their idols. Their children and grandchildren still do the same as their ancestors did, to this day.
In the third year that Hoshea son of Elah was king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz began to rule as king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his ancestor David had done.

He removed the high places, smashed the sacred stone pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles. He also broke into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because up to that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. It was called Nehushtan.
Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. There was no one like him among all the kings of Judah, either before him or after him.
He held tight to the LORD and never stopped following him. He kept the commands the LORD had given Moses.
The LORD was with him, and he was successful in everything he did. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.
He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from the smallest watchtower to the biggest walled city.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year that Hoshea son of Elah was king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked Samaria and surrounded it.
At the end of three years the Assyrians captured it. So Samaria was captured in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year that Hoshea was king of Israel.
The king of Assyria took the Israelites away to Assyria and settled them in Halah, at the Habor River in Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes.
This happened because they had not obeyed the LORD their God. They had broken his covenant and everything Moses the LORD's servant had commanded. They would not listen, and they would not obey.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the walled cities of Judah and captured them.

So Hezekiah king of Judah sent this message to the king of Assyria at Lachish: "I have done wrong. Leave me alone, and I will pay whatever you demand." The king of Assyria demanded that Hezekiah king of Judah pay about ten thousand kilograms of silver and about one thousand kilograms of gold.
So Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in the LORD's temple and in the treasuries of the palace.
At that time Hezekiah also stripped the gold from the doors and doorposts of the LORD's temple, gold he himself had put there, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

The king of Assyria sent his supreme commander, his chief officer, and his field commander from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem, with a large army. They came up to Jerusalem and stopped by the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the road to the Washerman's Field.
They called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the record keeper, went out to meet them.
The field commander said to them, "Tell Hezekiah, 'This is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What are you trusting in?
You say you have a plan and the strength for war, but those are just empty words. Who are you trusting in, that you have rebelled against me?
Look, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a walking stick! If a man leans on it, it will stab into his hand. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is like to everyone who trusts in him.

But perhaps you will tell me, "We are trusting in the LORD our God." Isn't he the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed? Didn't Hezekiah tell Judah and Jerusalem, "You must worship only at this altar in Jerusalem"?
Now then, make a deal with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses, if you can find enough riders to put on them!
How can you push back even the weakest officer among my master's servants? Yet you trust in Egypt for chariots and horsemen!
Besides, have I come to attack and destroy this place without the LORD? The LORD himself told me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the field commander, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, because we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear."

But the field commander answered, "Did my master send me to say these things only to your master and to you? No, he sent me to the men sitting on the wall too. Like you, they will soon have to eat their own dung and drink their own urine."
Then the field commander stood and shouted in Hebrew, "Listen to the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!
This is what the king says: 'Do not let Hezekiah fool you. He cannot rescue you from my power.
Do not let Hezekiah get you to trust in the LORD by saying, "The LORD will surely rescue us. This city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria."

Do not listen to Hezekiah.' This is what the king of Assyria says: 'Make peace with me and come out to me. Then each of you will eat from your own vine and your own fig tree, and drink water from your own well,

until I come and take you to a land like your own. It is a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey. Choose life and not death! Do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying, "The LORD will rescue us."
Has the god of any nation ever rescued his land from the power of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my power?
Which of all the gods of these countries has been able to save his land from me? So how could the LORD save Jerusalem from me?'"
But the people kept quiet and did not say a word in reply, because the king had commanded, "Do not answer him."

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the record keeper, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him what the field commander had said.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went into the LORD's temple.
He sent Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They told him, "This is what Hezekiah says: 'Today is a day of trouble, punishment, and shame. We are like a woman who is ready to give birth, but has no strength to deliver the baby.

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear all the words of the field commander, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to insult the living God. Perhaps the LORD your God will punish him for the words he has heard. So pray for the few of us who are still left.'"
When King Hezekiah's officials came to Isaiah,
Isaiah said to them, "Tell your master, 'This is what the LORD says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, the insults the king of Assyria's servants have spoken against me.
Listen! I will put a spirit in him so that when he hears a certain report, he will go back to his own country. And there in his own country I will have him killed with the sword.'"
The field commander heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish. So he went back and found the king fighting against Libnah.
Then the king of Assyria heard that Tirhakah, the king of Ethiopia, was marching out to fight against him. So he again sent messengers to Hezekiah with this message:
"Tell Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let the God you trust fool you when he says, "Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria."
Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries. They destroyed them completely. Do you think you will be rescued?
Did the gods of the nations my ancestors destroyed rescue them? Did the gods rescue Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who lived in Telassar?
Where is the king of Hamath? Where is the king of Arpad? Where are the kings of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?'"
Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to the LORD's temple and spread it out before the LORD.
Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: "LORD, God of Israel, you sit on your throne above the cherubim. You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth.
Turn your ear, LORD, and listen. Open your eyes, LORD, and see. Listen to the words Sennacherib has sent to insult the living God.
It is true, LORD, that the kings of Assyria have destroyed these nations and their lands.
They have thrown their gods into the fire, because they were not gods at all. They were only wood and stone made by human hands. That is why the Assyrians could destroy them.
So now, LORD our God, please save us from his power, so that all the kingdoms of the earth will know that you alone, LORD, are God."
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent this message to Hezekiah: "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I have heard your prayer about Sennacherib king of Assyria.
This is the word the LORD has spoken against him: The young woman, the city of Zion, hates you and laughs at you. The city of Jerusalem shakes her head at you as you run away.
Who have you insulted and mocked? Who have you shouted against and looked down on so proudly? It was the Holy One of Israel!

Through your messengers you have insulted the Lord. You have said, "With my many chariots I have climbed the highest mountains, the farthest heights of Lebanon. I have cut down its tallest cedars and its best pine trees. I have reached its farthest places and its thickest forests.
I have dug wells in foreign lands and drunk their water. With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt."
Have you not heard? Long ago I planned it. In days of old I designed it, and now I have made it happen. I let you turn walled cities into piles of rubble.
That is why their people had no strength. They were frightened and ashamed. They were like grass in the field, like tender green plants, like grass on a roof that dries up before it can grow.
But I know when you sit down, when you go out, and when you come in. I know how you rage against me.
Because you rage against me, and because I have heard your proud words, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth. I will make you go back the way you came.'

This will be the sign for you, Hezekiah: This year you will eat what grows by itself, and next year what springs up from that. But in the third year you will plant and harvest, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
The people of Judah who have escaped and are left will again put roots down deep and bear fruit above.
A group of survivors will come out of Jerusalem, and people who escaped will come from Mount Zion. The LORD's burning love will make this happen.

So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: 'He will not come into this city or shoot even one arrow here. He will not come near it with a shield or build a ramp of dirt against its walls.
He will go back the same way he came. He will not come into this city, says the LORD.
I will defend this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.'"
That night the LORD's angel went out and killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the Assyrian camp. When the people got up early the next morning, there were dead bodies everywhere.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and went home. He stayed in Nineveh.

One day, while he was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. His son Esarhaddon became king after him.

In those days Hezekiah became sick and was about to die. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz went to him and said, "This is what the LORD says: 'Put your affairs in order, because you are going to die. You will not get better.'"
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD,
"Please, LORD, remember how I have lived faithfully before you with all my heart, and have done what is good in your eyes." And Hezekiah cried bitterly.
Before Isaiah had left the middle courtyard, the LORD's word came to him:

"Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, 'This is what the LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. I will heal you. On the third day from now you will go up to the LORD's temple.
I will add fifteen years to your life. I will rescue you and this city from the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.'"
Then Isaiah said, "Get a paste made of figs." They got it and put it on the boil, and Hezekiah got better.
Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, "What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I will go up to the LORD's temple on the third day?"
Isaiah answered, "This is the sign from the LORD that he will do what he has promised: Should the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?"
Hezekiah said, "It is easy for the shadow to go forward ten steps. Instead, let it go back ten steps."
Then the prophet Isaiah called out to the LORD, and the LORD made the shadow go back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz.
At that time Merodach-Baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent Hezekiah letters and a gift, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.

Hezekiah welcomed the messengers and showed them everything in his storehouses: the silver, the gold, the spices, the fine olive oil, his armoury, and everything in his treasuries. There was nothing in his palace or in his whole kingdom that Hezekiah did not show them.
Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked him, "What did those men say? Where did they come from?" Hezekiah answered, "They came from a far country, from Babylon."
Isaiah asked, "What did they see in your palace?" Hezekiah answered, "They saw everything in my palace. There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them."
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Listen to the LORD's word:
'The time is coming when everything in your palace, and all that your ancestors have stored up until this day, will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.
Some of your own descendants, born from your family line, will be taken away. They will become officials serving in the palace of the king of Babylon.'"
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The LORD's word you have spoken is good." He was thinking, "Why not, if there will be peace and safety while I am alive?"
The rest of what Hezekiah did, all his power, and how he made the pool and the tunnel that brought water into the city, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Hezekiah died, and his son Manasseh became king after him.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. His mother was Hephzibah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.

He rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed. He set up altars to Baal and made an Asherah pole, as Ahab king of Israel had done. He bowed down to all the stars in the sky and worshipped them.
He built altars in the LORD's temple, the place where the LORD had said, "I will put my name in Jerusalem."
In both courtyards of the LORD's temple, he built altars to all the stars in the sky.

He sacrificed his own son in the fire. He practised magic and fortune-telling, and he went to people who talk with spirits of the dead and to people who claim to know the future. He did a great deal of evil in the LORD's eyes and made him angry.

He took the carved Asherah idol he had made and put it in the temple. This was the temple about which the LORD had said to David and his son Solomon, "In this temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever.

I will never again make the Israelites wander from the land I gave their ancestors, if only they will be careful to do everything I have commanded them, and obey all the Law my servant Moses gave them."
But the people did not listen. Manasseh led them into doing even more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed ahead of the Israelites.
So the LORD spoke through his servants the prophets. He said,
"Manasseh king of Judah has done these disgusting things. He has done more evil than the Amorites who lived here before him, and he has led Judah into sin with his idols.
So this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I am going to bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that the ears of everyone who hears about it will ring.

I will measure Jerusalem with the same measuring line I used against Samaria, and the same plumb line I used against Ahab's family. I will wipe Jerusalem clean as someone wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down.
I will abandon the rest of my people who are left, and I will hand them over to their enemies. All their enemies will rob them and carry off their things,
because they have done what is evil in my eyes. They have made me angry from the day their ancestors came out of Egypt until today.'"

Manasseh also killed so many innocent people that he filled Jerusalem with their blood from one end to the other. This was in addition to the sin he led Judah into, doing what was evil in the LORD's eyes.
The rest of what Manasseh did, all his deeds and the sin he committed, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his own palace, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon became king after him.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for two years. His mother was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed all the ways of his father. He worshipped the idols his father had worshipped, and bowed down to them.
He turned away from the LORD, the God of his ancestors, and did not walk in the LORD's ways.
Amon's officials made a plot against him and killed the king in his palace.
But the people of the land killed all those who had plotted against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah king in his place.
The rest of what Amon did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza. His son Josiah became king after him.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah, from Bozkath.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes. He followed all the ways of his ancestor David and did not turn aside to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year that Josiah was king, he sent the secretary Shaphan son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, to the LORD's temple. He said,
"Go to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count the money that has been brought into the LORD's temple, which the doorkeepers have collected from the people.
Have them give it to the men in charge of the work on the LORD's temple. Then let them pay the workers who are repairing the damage to the temple:
the carpenters, the builders, and the stonemasons. Let them also buy wood and cut stone to repair the temple.
They do not need to account for the money they are given, because they are honest."
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the LORD's temple." He gave the book to Shaphan, and Shaphan read it.
Then Shaphan the secretary went to the king and reported, "Your officials have paid out the money that was in the temple. They have given it to the men in charge of the work on the LORD's temple."
Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read it aloud to the king.
When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.
He gave these orders to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant:

"Go and ask the LORD for me, for the people, and for all Judah about what is written in this book that has been found. The LORD's anger burning against us must be great, because our ancestors did not obey the words of this book. They did not do everything written there for us."

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to talk to the prophet Huldah. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, who was in charge of the royal robes. She lived in the New Quarter of Jerusalem.
She said to them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Tell the man who sent you to me,
This is what the LORD says: I am going to bring disaster on this place and the people who live here, just as written in the book the king of Judah has read.
They have turned away from me and burned incense to other gods. They have made me angry by all the idols their hands have made. So my anger will burn against this place, and it will not be put out.'
But tell the king of Judah, who sent you to ask the LORD, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the words you heard:

Your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I said against this place and its people, that they would be destroyed and cursed. You tore your clothes and cried before me. So I have heard you, says the LORD.

Because of this, I will let you die and join your ancestors, and you will be buried in peace. You will not see all the disaster I am going to bring on this place.'" So they took her answer back to the king.
Then the king sent for all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, and they came together to meet him.

The king went up to the LORD's temple with all the people of Judah and everyone living in Jerusalem, along with the priests and the prophets. All the people came, from the least important to the most important. He read aloud to them all the words of the Book of the Covenant, which had been found in the LORD's temple.

The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant in the LORD's presence. He promised to follow the LORD and keep his commands, his teachings, and his laws with all his heart and all his soul. He promised to carry out the words of the covenant written in this book. And all the people promised to keep the covenant.

The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests next in rank, and the doorkeepers to take out of the LORD's temple all the objects made for Baal, for Asherah, and for all the stars in the sky. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron Valley and carried the ashes to Bethel.

He got rid of the pagan priests the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense at the high places in the towns of Judah and around Jerusalem. He also got rid of those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon, the planets, and all the stars in the sky.
He took the Asherah pole out of the LORD's temple to the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem. He burned it there, ground it to powder, and scattered the dust over the graves of the common people.
He tore down the rooms of the male shrine prostitutes, which were in the LORD's temple, where women wove coverings for Asherah.

Josiah brought all the priests from the towns of Judah to Jerusalem. He made the high places where they had burned incense unfit for worship, from Geba to Beersheba. He tore down the shrines at the gates, at the entrance of the Gate of Joshua, the city governor, which was on the left as you go through the city gate.
The priests of the high places were not allowed to serve at the LORD's altar in Jerusalem, but they ate bread made without yeast with their fellow priests.
He made Topheth, in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, unfit for worship, so no one could sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire to Molech there.

He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun. They had been kept at the entrance to the LORD's temple, near the room of an official named Nathan-Melech, in the courtyard. Then Josiah burned the chariots dedicated to the sun.

The king tore down the altars the kings of Judah had built on the roof near the upstairs room of Ahaz. He also tore down the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of the LORD's temple. He smashed them to pieces there and threw the rubble into the Kidron Valley.

The king also made unfit for worship the high places east of Jerusalem, on the south side of the Hill of Corruption. King Solomon of Israel had built them for Ashtoreth, the disgusting goddess of the Sidonians, for Chemosh, the disgusting god of Moab, and for Milcom, the disgusting god of the Ammonites.
Josiah smashed the sacred stone pillars and cut down the Asherah poles, and he covered the places where they had stood with human bones.
He also tore down the altar at Bethel and the high place made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin. He burned the high place, ground it to powder, and burned the Asherah pole.

Then Josiah looked around and saw the tombs on the hillside. He had the bones taken out of the tombs and burned them on the altar to make it unfit for worship. This happened just as the LORD had said through the man of God who announced these things long before.

Josiah asked, "What is that grave marker I see?" The people of the town told him, "It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and announced the very things you have done to the altar at Bethel."
Josiah said, "Leave it alone. Do not let anyone move his bones." So they left his bones alone, along with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Josiah also removed all the shrines on the high places in the towns of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had built and which had made the LORD angry. He did to them just what he had done at Bethel.
He killed all the priests of those high places on their own altars, and he burned human bones on the altars. Then he went back to Jerusalem.
The king gave this order to all the people: "Celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant."
No Passover like this one had been celebrated since the days when the judges led Israel, not in all the time of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was celebrated to the LORD in Jerusalem.

Josiah also got rid of the people who talked with spirits of the dead, the fortune-tellers, the household gods, the idols, and all the other disgusting things seen in Judah and Jerusalem. He did this to obey the words of the Law written in the book Hilkiah the priest had found in the LORD's temple.
There was never a king like Josiah, before him or after him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, obeying all the Law of Moses.
Even so, the LORD did not turn away from his great, burning anger against Judah, because of all the things Manasseh had done to make him angry.
The LORD said, "I will also remove Judah from my presence, as I removed Israel. I will reject Jerusalem, the city I chose, and the temple, the place where I said, 'My name will be there.'"
The rest of what Josiah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
While Josiah was king, Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt went up to the Euphrates River to help the king of Assyria. King Josiah marched out to fight him, but when Necho met him at Megiddo, he killed him.

Josiah's officials carried his body in a chariot from Megiddo to Jerusalem and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land took Josiah's son Jehoahaz, anointed him, and made him king in his father's place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as his ancestors had done.

Pharaoh Necho put him in chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath, so he could not rule in Jerusalem. He forced Judah to pay about three thousand four hundred kilograms of silver and about thirty-four kilograms of gold.
Pharaoh Necho made Josiah's son Eliakim king in place of his father Josiah, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But he took Jehoahaz to Egypt, and Jehoahaz died there.
Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh the silver and gold he demanded. To do this, he taxed the land. He made each person pay silver and gold according to what they owned, to give to Pharaoh Necho.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Zebidah, the daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as his ancestors had done.
While Jehoiakim was king, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon invaded the land. Jehoiakim became his servant for three years, but then he turned and rebelled against him.
The LORD sent raiding parties of Babylonians, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites against Jehoiakim. He sent them to destroy Judah, just as the LORD had said through his servants the prophets.
These things happened to Judah because the LORD commanded it. He was removing them from his presence because of the sins of Manasseh and all he had done,
and also because of the innocent blood he had spilled. Manasseh had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was not willing to forgive.
The rest of what Jehoiakim did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
Jehoiakim died, and his son Jehoiachin became king after him.
The king of Egypt did not march out of his country again, because the king of Babylon had taken all his land, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as his father had done.
At that time the officers of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon attacked Jerusalem and surrounded the city.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon himself came to the city while his officers were surrounding it.

Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to surrender to the king of Babylon, along with his mother, his officials, his princes, and his officers. In the eighth year of his rule, the king of Babylon took Jehoiachin prisoner.

Nebuchadnezzar carried off all the treasures from the LORD's temple and from the palace. He cut into pieces all the gold objects Solomon king of Israel had made for the LORD's temple, just as the LORD had said would happen.

He took away all the people of Jerusalem as prisoners: all the princes and all the best soldiers, ten thousand people in all, along with all the skilled workers and metalworkers. Only the poorest people of the land were left.

Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin away to Babylon. He also took the king's mother, the king's wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land. He took them all as prisoners from Jerusalem to Babylon.
The king of Babylon also took to Babylon all seven thousand of the fighting men and one thousand skilled workers and metalworkers. All of them were strong and ready for war.
The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done.
It was because of the LORD's anger that all this happened to Jerusalem and Judah, until in the end he threw them out of his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah's rule, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped around the city and built siege walls all around it.
The city was kept under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so bad that the people had no food left.

Then the city wall was broken through. All the soldiers ran away at night through the gate between the two walls, near the king's garden, even though the Babylonians were all around the city. The king ran toward the Jordan Valley.
But the Babylonian army chased King Zedekiah and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho. All his soldiers left him and scattered.
The Babylonians captured the king and took him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence was passed on him.
They killed Zedekiah's sons while he watched. Then they put out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him with bronze chains, and took him to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year that Nebuchadnezzar was king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem. He was the commander of the guard and an official of the king of Babylon.
He set fire to the LORD's temple, the palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned down every important building.
The whole Babylonian army under the commander of the guard tore down the walls around Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took away as prisoners the rest of the people left in the city, along with those who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the crowd.
But the commander of the guard left behind some of the poorest people of the land to work in the vineyards and fields.
The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, the bronze stands, and the huge bronze tank called the Sea, which were at the LORD's temple, and they carried the bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, spoons, and all the bronze objects used in the temple service.
The commander of the guard took away the fire pans and the sprinkling bowls, everything made of pure gold or pure silver.
The bronze from the two pillars, the Sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the LORD's temple was too heavy to weigh.

Each pillar was about eight metres high. The bronze top on each pillar was about one and a half metres high and was decorated all around with a network of bronze pomegranates. The second pillar, with its network, was just like the first.
The commander of the guard took as prisoners Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three doorkeepers.

From the people still in the city, he took the officer in charge of the soldiers, five of the king's advisers, the secretary of the army commander who called up the people of the land for war, and sixty of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took them all and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them put to death. So the people of Judah were taken away as prisoners from their land.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to be governor over the people he had left behind in Judah.

All the army officers and their men heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor. So they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They were Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth from Netophah, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, along with their men.
Gedaliah made a promise to them and their men. He said, "Do not be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Settle down in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for you."

But in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, who was from the royal family, came with ten men. They attacked Gedaliah and killed him, along with the people of Judah and the Babylonians who were with him at Mizpah.
Then all the people, from the least to the greatest, along with the army officers, ran away to Egypt, because they were afraid of the Babylonians.

In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah was taken prisoner, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach became king of Babylon. In that same year he set Jehoiachin king of Judah free from prison.
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honour higher than the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes. For the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king's table.
Every day the king gave him an allowance, for as long as he lived.

Pathrusites, Casluhites (the Philistines came from them), and the Caphtorites.

He was also the ancestor of the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites.
Shem's sons were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.
Arpachshad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber.
Eber had two sons. One was named Peleg, because in his time the earth was divided. His brother was named Joktan.
Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Ebal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were Joktan's sons.
The family line from Shem went: Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,
Eber, Peleg, Reu,
Serug, Nahor, Terah,
and Abram, who is also called Abraham.
Abraham's sons were Isaac and Ishmael.
These were their descendants. Ishmael's firstborn son was Nebaioth. Then came Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,
Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These were Ishmael's sons.
Keturah was Abraham's concubine. She gave birth to Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan's sons were Sheba and Dedan.
Midian's sons were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were Keturah's descendants.
Abraham was the father of Isaac. Isaac's sons were Esau and Israel.
Esau's sons were Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
Eliphaz's sons were Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek.
Reuel's sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
Seir's sons were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.
Lotan's sons were Hori and Homam. Lotan's sister was Timna.
Shobal's sons were Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. Zibeon's sons were Aiah and Anah.
Anah's son was Dishon. Dishon's sons were Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
Ezer's sons were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan. Dishan's sons were Uz and Aran.
These are the kings who ruled in the land of Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor, whose city was called Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah became king after him.
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king after him.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad became king after him. Hadad defeated the Midianites in the country of Moab. His city was called Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king after him.
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River became king after him.
When Shaul died, Baal-Hanan son of Achbor became king after him.
When Baal-Hanan died, Hadad became king after him. His city was called Pai. His wife was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.
Then Hadad died. The clan chiefs of Edom were: Timna, Aliah, Jetheth,
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
Magdiel, and Iram. These were the chiefs of Edom.
These were the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,
Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
Judah's sons were Er, Onan, and Shelah. These three were born to him by a Canaanite woman, the daughter of Shua. Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the LORD's eyes, so the LORD put him to death.
Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar gave birth to Perez and Zerah by him. Judah had five sons in all.
Perez's sons were Hezron and Hamul.
Zerah's sons were Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all.
Carmi's son was Achar, who brought trouble on Israel by stealing things that were set apart for God.
Ethan's son was Azariah.
The sons born to Hezron were Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb.
Ram was the father of Amminadab. Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, a leader of the people of Judah.
Nahshon was the father of Salma. Salma was the father of Boaz.
Boaz was the father of Obed. Obed was the father of Jesse.
Jesse's firstborn son was Eliab. His second son was Abinadab, his third was Shimea,
his fourth was Nethanel, his fifth was Raddai,
his sixth was Ozem, and his seventh was David.
Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah's three sons were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.
Abigail was the mother of Amasa. Amasa's father was Jether the Ishmaelite.
Hezron's son Caleb had children by his wife Azubah and by Jerioth. Azubah's sons were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.
When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, and she gave birth to Hur.
Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel.
Later, when Hezron was sixty years old, he married the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead. She gave birth to Segub.
Segub was the father of Jair, who ruled twenty-three towns in the land of Gilead.
But Geshur and Aram captured the towns of Jair, along with Kenath and its villages, sixty towns in all. All these people were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead.
After Hezron died in Caleb Ephrathah, his wife Abijah gave birth to Ashhur, who became the father of Tekoa.
The sons of Jerahmeel, Hezron's firstborn, were Ram his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.
Jerahmeel had another wife named Atarah. She was the mother of Onam.
The sons of Ram, Jerahmeel's firstborn, were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.
