All these men were under the direction of their fathers for the music in the LORD's temple. They played cymbals, lyres, and harps for the service of God's temple. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the king's direction.
They and their relatives were all trained and skilled in singing to the LORD. There were two hundred and eighty-eight of them.
They all drew lots for their duties, young and old alike, teacher and student alike.
The first lot, for Asaph, fell to Joseph. The second fell to Gedaliah, with his relatives and sons, twelve in all.
The third fell to Zaccur, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The fourth fell to Izri, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The fifth fell to Nethaniah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The sixth fell to Bukkiah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The seventh fell to Jesharelah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The eighth fell to Jeshaiah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The ninth fell to Mattaniah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The tenth fell to Shimei, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The eleventh fell to Azarel, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twelfth fell to Hashabiah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The thirteenth fell to Shubael, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The fourteenth fell to Mattithiah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The fifteenth fell to Jeremoth, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The sixteenth fell to Hananiah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The seventeenth fell to Joshbekashah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The eighteenth fell to Hanani, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The nineteenth fell to Mallothi, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twentieth fell to Eliathah, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twenty-first fell to Hothir, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twenty-second fell to Giddalti, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twenty-third fell to Mahazioth, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
The twenty-fourth fell to Romamti-Ezer, with his sons and relatives, twelve in all.
These were the groups of the gatekeepers. From the Korahites there was Meshelemiah son of Kore, one of the sons of Asaph.
Meshelemiah's sons were Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth,
Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, and Eliehoenai the seventh.
Obed-Edom's sons were Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sacar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,
Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peullethai the eighth. God had truly blessed Obed-Edom.
His son Shemaiah also had sons. They were leaders in their family, because they were very capable men.
Shemaiah's sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad. Their relatives Elihu and Semachiah were also capable men.
All these were descendants of Obed-Edom. They and their sons and relatives were capable men, strong enough for the work. There were sixty-two of them from Obed-Edom.
Meshelemiah had eighteen sons and relatives who were capable men.
Hosah, one of the Merarites, had sons. Shimri was the chief. He was not the firstborn, but his father made him the chief.
Hilkiah was second, Tebaliah third, and Zechariah fourth. Hosah had thirteen sons and relatives in all.
These groups of gatekeepers, led by their chief men, had duties for serving in the LORD's temple, just as their relatives did.
They drew lots for each gate, family by family, young and old alike.
The lot for the East Gate fell to Shelemiah. Then they drew lots for his son Zechariah, a wise adviser, and the North Gate fell to him.
The South Gate fell to Obed-Edom, and the storehouse fell to his sons.
The West Gate and the Shallecheth Gate on the upper road fell to Shuppim and Hosah. The guards stood side by side.
Six Levites stood guard each day at the east, four at the north, four at the south, and two at a time at the storehouse.
At the court on the west side, there were four at the road and two at the court itself.
These were the groups of gatekeepers from the descendants of Korah and Merari.
Their fellow Levites, led by Ahijah, were in charge of the treasuries of God's temple and the treasuries of the gifts set apart for God.
The descendants of Ladan, who were Gershonites through Ladan and heads of the families of Ladan the Gershonite, included Jehieli.
Jehieli's sons, Zetham and his brother Joel, were in charge of the treasuries of the LORD's temple.
From the clans of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel:
Shebuel, a descendant of Gershom son of Moses, was the chief officer in charge of the treasuries.
His relatives through Eliezer were Eliezer's son Rehabiah, Rehabiah's son Jeshaiah, Jeshaiah's son Joram, Joram's son Zichri, and Zichri's son Shelomoth.

Shelomoth and his relatives were in charge of all the treasuries of the gifts set apart for God. These gifts had been given by King David, by the heads of families, by the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and by the other army commanders.
They had given some of the goods taken in battle to repair the LORD's temple.

Everything that Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah had set apart for God, and everything anyone else had set apart, was in the care of Shelomoth and his relatives.
From the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were given work away from the temple. They served as officials and judges over Israel.

From the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his relatives, one thousand seven hundred capable men, were put in charge of Israel west of the Jordan River. They took care of all the LORD's work and the king's service.

From the Hebronites, Jerijah was the chief, according to the records of their families. In the fortieth year of David's rule, the records were searched, and capable warriors from this family were found at Jazer in Gilead.

Jerijah had two thousand seven hundred relatives who were capable men and heads of families. King David put them in charge of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, for everything that had to do with God and with the king.

This is the list of the Israelites who served the king: the heads of families, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and their officers. They served the king in all matters, in army groups that came on and went off duty month by month all through the year. Each group had twenty-four thousand men.
Jashobeam son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first group, for the first month. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
He was a descendant of Perez and the chief of all the army officers for the first month.
Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the group for the second month. Mikloth was the leader of his group. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The third army commander, for the third month, was Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
This was the Benaiah who was a mighty warrior among the Thirty and in charge of the Thirty. His son Ammizabad was in charge of his group.
The fourth, for the fourth month, was Asahel, Joab's brother. His son Zebadiah took his place after him. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The fifth, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, from the tribe of Ephraim. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, from the clan of Zerah. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer from Anathoth, from the tribe of Benjamin. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai from Netophah, from the clan of Zerah. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah from Pirathon, from the tribe of Ephraim. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
The twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai from Netophah, from the family of Othniel. There were twenty-four thousand men in his group.
These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel: over Reuben, Eliezer son of Zichri; over Simeon, Shephatiah son of Maacah;
over Levi, Hashabiah son of Kemuel; over the descendants of Aaron, Zadok;
over Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; over Issachar, Omri son of Michael;
over Zebulun, Ishmaiah son of Obadiah; over Naphtali, Jeremoth son of Azriel;
over Ephraim, Hoshea son of Azaziah; over the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel son of Pedaiah;
over the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo son of Zechariah; over Benjamin, Jaasiel son of Abner;
over Dan, Azarel son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.
David did not count the men who were twenty years old or younger, because the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars in the sky.
Joab son of Zeruiah began to count them but did not finish, because God's anger came on Israel because of the counting. So the total number was never written in the history book of King David.
Azmaveth son of Adiel was in charge of the king's storehouses. Jonathan son of Uzziah was in charge of the storehouses in the countryside, in the towns, in the villages, and in the towers.
Ezri son of Chelub was in charge of the farm workers who worked the land.
Shimei from Ramah was in charge of the vineyards. Zabdi the Shiphmite was in charge of storing the wine from the vineyards.
Baal-Hanan from Geder was in charge of the olive and fig trees in the western foothills. Joash was in charge of storing the olive oil.
Shitrai from Sharon was in charge of the cattle grazing in Sharon. Shaphat son of Adlai was in charge of the cattle in the valleys.
Obil the Ishmaelite was in charge of the camels. Jehdeiah from Meronoth was in charge of the donkeys. Jaziz the Hagrite was in charge of the flocks.
All these were the officials in charge of King David's property.
Jonathan, David's uncle, was an adviser, a wise man, and a scribe. Jehiel son of Hachmoni looked after the king's sons.
Ahithophel was the king's adviser. Hushai the Archite was the king's friend.
After Ahithophel came Jehoiada son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was the commander of the king's army.

David called all the leaders of Israel to meet in Jerusalem. He called the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of the army groups that served the king, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, the officials in charge of all the property and animals that belonged to the king and his sons, the palace officials, the mighty men, and all the brave warriors.

King David stood up and said, "Listen to me, my relatives and my people. I wanted to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the LORD's covenant, a footstool for our God, and I made plans to build it.
But God said to me, 'You will not build a house to honour my name, because you are a warrior and have spilled blood.'

Still, the LORD, the God of Israel, chose me from my whole family to be king over Israel forever. He chose the tribe of Judah to lead, and from Judah he chose my father's family. From my father's sons he was pleased to make me king over all Israel.
The LORD has given me many sons, and from all of them he has chosen my son Solomon to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom over Israel.
He said to me, 'Your son Solomon is the one who will build my house and my courtyards. I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.
I will make his kingdom last forever, if he keeps on obeying my commands and rules as he does now.'

So now, in front of all Israel, the LORD's assembly, and with our God listening, I tell you: Be careful to obey all the commands of the LORD your God. Then you will keep this good land and pass it on to your children after you forever.

And you, my son Solomon, know the God of your father. Serve him with all your heart and a willing mind, because the LORD looks into every heart and understands every plan and thought. If you look for him, you will find him. But if you turn away from him, he will reject you forever.
Remember this: the LORD has chosen you to build a house to be his holy place. Be strong and do the work."
Then David gave his son Solomon the plans for the porch of the temple, its buildings, its storerooms, its upstairs rooms, its inner rooms, and the room for the atonement cover.

He gave him the plans for everything the Spirit had put in his mind: the courtyards of the LORD's temple, all the rooms around it, the treasuries of God's temple, and the treasuries for the gifts set apart for God.
He gave him instructions for the groups of priests and Levites, for all the work of serving in the LORD's temple, and for all the objects to be used in its service.
He told him how much gold to use for all the gold objects used in each kind of service, and how much silver for all the silver objects used in each kind of service.

He told him how much gold to use for the gold lampstands and their lamps, by weight for each lampstand and its lamps. He also told him how much silver to use for each silver lampstand and its lamps, according to how each lampstand would be used.
He told him how much gold to use for each table for the holy bread, and how much silver for the silver tables.
He told him how much pure gold to use for the meat forks, the sprinkling bowls, and the pitchers, and how much gold and silver for each gold and silver dish.
He told him how much refined gold to use for the altar of incense. He also gave him the plan for the chariot, the gold cherubim that spread their wings over the ark of the LORD's covenant.
David said, "All this is written down from the LORD's own hand to me. He helped me understand all the details of the plan."

David also said to his son Solomon, "Be strong and brave, and do the work. Do not be afraid or lose heart, because the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or abandon you until all the work for the service of the LORD's temple is finished.

Look, the groups of priests and Levites are ready for all the service of God's temple. Every willing person with skill for any kind of work will help you. The leaders and all the people will do everything you command."

Then King David said to the whole assembly, "My son Solomon, the one God has chosen, is still young and has no experience. The work is great, because this palace is not for a human being. It is for the LORD God.

With all my strength I have provided for the house of my God: gold for the gold things, silver for the silver things, bronze for the bronze things, iron for the iron things, and wood for the wooden things. I have also provided onyx stones, stones for setting, shiny stones of many colours, all kinds of precious stones, and large amounts of marble.

Besides all this, because I love the house of my God, I am giving my own treasure of gold and silver to the house of my God. This is in addition to everything I have already provided for this holy house.
I am giving about one hundred tonnes of gold from Ophir and about two hundred and forty tonnes of refined silver to cover the walls of the buildings,
and for all the gold and silver work to be done by the craftsmen. Now, who else is willing to give himself to the LORD today?"
Then the leaders of the families, the leaders of the tribes of Israel, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officials in charge of the king's work gave willingly.

For the work on God's temple they gave about one hundred and seventy tonnes of gold and ten thousand gold coins, about three hundred and forty tonnes of silver, about six hundred and ten tonnes of bronze, and about three thousand four hundred tonnes of iron.
Anyone who had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the LORD's temple, which was in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.
The people were full of joy because their leaders had given so willingly. They had given to the LORD with all their hearts. King David was also very happy.
Then David praised the LORD in front of the whole assembly. He said, "Praise be to you, LORD, the God of our father Israel, forever and ever!
Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty. Everything in heaven and on earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD. You are honoured as the ruler over all.
Wealth and honour come from you, and you rule over everything. Power and strength are in your hands. You can make anyone great and give strength to all.
So now, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.
But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give so willingly like this? Everything comes from you, and we have only given you what came from your own hand.
We are like strangers and visitors in your sight, as all our ancestors were. Our days on earth are like a shadow, and they do not last.
LORD our God, all this wealth we have provided to build a house to honour your holy name comes from your hand. It all belongs to you.

I know, my God, that you test the heart and are pleased when people are honest. I have given all these things willingly and with an honest heart. And now I have seen with joy how your people here have given so willingly to you.
LORD, God of our ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, keep this desire in the hearts of your people forever, and keep their hearts loyal to you.
Give my son Solomon a heart that is completely true, so he will keep your commands, your teachings, and your laws, and do everything needed to build the palace I have provided for."
Then David said to the whole assembly, "Now praise the LORD your God!" So the whole assembly praised the LORD, the God of their ancestors. They bowed down low before the LORD and before the king.

The next day they offered sacrifices and burnt offerings to the LORD: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, along with their drink offerings, and many other sacrifices for all Israel.

That day they ate and drank with great joy in the LORD's presence. Then they made David's son Solomon king a second time. They anointed him before the LORD to be ruler, and they anointed Zadok to be priest.
So Solomon sat on the LORD's throne as king in place of his father David. He was successful, and all Israel obeyed him.
All the leaders, the mighty warriors, and all of King David's sons promised to be loyal to King Solomon.
The LORD made Solomon very great in the eyes of all Israel. He gave him royal majesty greater than any king of Israel before him.
David son of Jesse ruled over all Israel.
He ruled over Israel for forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
He died at a good old age, after a long life full of wealth and honour. His son Solomon became king after him.
Everything King David did, from beginning to end, is written in the records of Samuel the seer, the records of Nathan the prophet, and the records of Gad the seer.
These records tell about his whole rule, his power, and the things that happened to him, to Israel, and to all the kingdoms of the other lands.
2Chr: Solomon son of David took firm control of his kingdom. The LORD his God was with him and made him very great.
Solomon spoke to all Israel: to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders in Israel, the heads of families.
Then Solomon and the whole assembly with him went to the high place at Gibeon, because God's Tent of Meeting was there. It was the tent that Moses, the LORD's servant, had made in the desert.
David had already brought God's ark up from Kiriath Jearim to the place he had prepared for it. He had set up a tent for it in Jerusalem.
But the bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was there in Gibeon, in front of the LORD's tabernacle. So Solomon and the assembly went there to ask the LORD for guidance.
Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD at the Tent of Meeting, and he offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
That night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, "Ask for whatever you want me to give you."
Solomon answered God, "You showed great and faithful love to my father David, and you have made me king in his place.
Now, LORD God, let your promise to my father David come true, because you have made me king over a people as many as the dust of the earth.
Give me wisdom and knowledge, so I can lead these people. Who could ever rule this great people of yours?"

God said to Solomon, "This is what is in your heart. You did not ask for riches, wealth, or honour, or for the death of your enemies, or even for a long life. Instead, you asked for wisdom and knowledge so you can rule my people, over whom I have made you king.
So I will give you wisdom and knowledge. I will also give you riches, wealth, and honour, more than any king before you ever had, or any king after you will have."
Then Solomon left the high place at Gibeon, in front of the Tent of Meeting, and went back to Jerusalem. And he ruled over Israel.
Solomon gathered chariots and horses. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses. He kept some in the chariot cities and some with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar wood as common as the fig trees in the western foothills.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt and from Kue. The king's traders bought them in Kue.
They brought chariots from Egypt for six hundred pieces of silver each, and horses for one hundred and fifty each. They also sold them to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
Solomon decided to build a temple to honour the LORD's name, and a royal palace for himself.
He chose seventy thousand men to carry loads, eighty thousand men to cut stone in the hills, and three thousand six hundred men to be in charge of them.
Solomon sent this message to Huram king of Tyre: "Send me cedar logs, as you did for my father David when he built his palace to live in.

I am about to build a temple to honour the name of the LORD my God and to set it apart for him. There we will burn sweet-smelling incense before him, set out the holy bread regularly, and offer burnt offerings every morning and evening, on Sabbaths, at New Moon festivals, and at the appointed feasts of the LORD our God. This is a law for Israel forever.
The temple I am building will be great, because our God is greater than all gods.
But who is able to build a house for him, when even the highest heavens cannot hold him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to burn incense before him?

So send me a man who is skilled in working with gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and with purple, red, and blue cloth, and who knows how to carve designs. He will work with the skilled craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem whom my father David provided.
Also send me cedar, pine, and algum logs from Lebanon, because I know your workers are skilled at cutting trees there. My workers will work with yours
to prepare a large amount of wood for me, because the temple I am building will be great and wonderful.
I will give your workers who cut the trees twenty thousand measures of ground wheat, twenty thousand measures of barley, twenty thousand measures of wine, and twenty thousand measures of olive oil."
Huram king of Tyre answered Solomon in a letter: "Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you their king."

Huram went on, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth! He has given King David a wise son, full of good sense and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a palace for himself.
I am sending you a skilled man with great understanding named Huram-Abi.

His mother was from the tribe of Dan, and his father was from Tyre. He knows how to work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood, and with purple, blue, and red cloth and fine linen. He can carve any kind of design and make anything that is planned for him. He will work with your craftsmen and with those of my master, your father David.
Now let my master send his servants the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine he promised.
We will cut all the logs you need from Lebanon and float them as rafts by sea to Joppa. Then you can take them up to Jerusalem."
Solomon counted all the foreigners living in Israel, as his father David had done before. There were one hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred of them.
He made seventy thousand of them carry loads and eighty thousand cut stone in the hills. He put three thousand six hundred of them in charge, to keep the people working.

Then Solomon began to build the LORD's temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. It was on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, the place David had prepared.
He began building on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his rule.
These are the measurements Solomon used for the foundation of God's temple, using the old standard measure. It was about twenty-seven metres long and nine metres wide.
The porch at the front of the temple was nine metres wide, the same as the width of the temple, and fifty-four metres high. He covered the inside with pure gold.
He lined the main room with pine boards and covered them with fine gold. He decorated it with palm trees and chain designs.
He decorated the temple with precious stones to make it beautiful. The gold he used came from Parvaim.
He covered the ceiling beams, the doorframes, the walls, and the doors of the temple with gold, and he carved cherubim on the walls.
He built the Most Holy Place. It was nine metres long, the same as the width of the temple, and nine metres wide. He covered it with about twenty tonnes of fine gold.
The gold nails weighed about six hundred grams. He also covered the upper rooms with gold.
In the Most Holy Place he made two carved cherubim and covered them with gold.

The total length of the cherubim's wings was nine metres. One wing of the first cherub was over two metres long and touched the wall of the temple. Its other wing, also over two metres long, touched a wing of the second cherub.
One wing of the second cherub was over two metres long and touched the other wall of the temple. Its other wing, also over two metres long, touched the wing of the first cherub.
The wings of these cherubim stretched out nine metres in all. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the main room.
He made the curtain of blue, purple, and red yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it.
In front of the temple he made two pillars, about sixteen metres tall. Each had a top piece over two metres high.
He made chains like a necklace and put them on top of the pillars. He made a hundred pomegranates and attached them to the chains.
He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south side and one on the north. He named the one on the south Jakin and the one on the north Boaz.
He made a bronze altar nine metres long, nine metres wide, and four and a half metres high.
He also made the large round bronze tank called the Sea. It measured four and a half metres from rim to rim, was over two metres deep, and measured about thirteen and a half metres around.
Below the rim, all the way around, were figures of oxen, ten for every half metre or so, going around the Sea. The oxen were in two rows, cast in one piece with the Sea.
The Sea stood on twelve bronze oxen. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. The Sea rested on top of them, and their back parts faced the centre.
The Sea was about as thick as a hand is wide. Its rim was shaped like the rim of a cup, like a lily flower. It held about sixty-six thousand litres.
He also made ten basins for washing. He put five on the south side and five on the north. They were used to wash the things used for the burnt offerings. But the Sea was for the priests to wash in.
He made ten gold lampstands following the instructions for them, and put them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north.
He made ten tables and put them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. He also made a hundred gold bowls.
He made the courtyard of the priests and the large outer courtyard, with doors for the courtyard. He covered the doors with bronze.
He put the Sea on the south side, at the south-east corner of the temple.
Huram also made the pots, shovels, and bowls. So Huram finished the work he did for King Solomon on God's temple:
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped top pieces on the pillars; the two sets of net designs covering the two bowls of the top pieces on the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two sets of net designs, two rows of pomegranates for each net, covering the bowls of the top pieces on the pillars;
the stands, and the basins on the stands;
the Sea, and the twelve oxen under it;
and the pots, shovels, meat forks, and all the other tools. Huram-Abi made all these for King Solomon for the LORD's temple out of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay moulds on the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zeredah.
Solomon made so many of these things that no one could work out how much the bronze weighed.
Solomon also made all the things that were in God's temple: the gold altar; the tables for the holy bread;
the lampstands of pure gold with their lamps, to burn in front of the inner room as the law commanded;
the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs, made of the purest gold;
and the pure gold wick trimmers, bowls, dishes, and fire pans. The doors of the temple, both the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and the doors to the main hall, were made of gold.

When all the work Solomon did for the LORD's temple was finished, he brought in the things his father David had set apart for God: the silver, the gold, and all the objects. He put them in the treasure rooms of God's temple.

Then Solomon called together in Jerusalem the elders of Israel, all the heads of the tribes, and the leaders of the families of Israel. They came to bring up the ark of the LORD's covenant from the City of David, which is Zion.
All the men of Israel gathered before the king at the festival in the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had arrived, the Levites picked up the ark.
They brought up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy objects in it. The priests, who were Levites, carried them up.
King Solomon and the whole community of Israel gathered with him in front of the ark. They sacrificed so many sheep and cattle that no one could count them.
Then the priests brought the ark of the LORD's covenant to its place in the inner room of the temple, the Most Holy Place, and put it under the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark was, and they covered the ark and its carrying poles.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from in front of the inner room, but not from outside. They are still there today.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets Moses had put in it at Mount Horeb. That was where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel after they came out of Egypt.
Then the priests came out of the Holy Place. All the priests who were there had made themselves holy, no matter which group they belonged to.

All the Levites who were singers, Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and relatives, stood on the east side of the altar. They were dressed in fine linen and played cymbals, harps, and lyres. With them were one hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets.

The trumpeters and singers joined together as one voice to praise and thank the LORD. With trumpets, cymbals, and other instruments, they raised their voices and praised the LORD, singing, "He is good; his faithful love lasts forever!" Then a cloud filled the temple, the LORD's house.
The priests could not stay and do their work because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled God's temple.
Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would live in thick darkness.
But I have built a wonderful temple for you, a place for you to live forever."
Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel while they all stood there.
He said, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel! With his own mouth he made a promise to my father David, and with his own hands he has kept it. He said,

'Since the day I brought my people out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel to build a temple for my name to be there. And I have not chosen anyone to be the leader of my people Israel.
But now I have chosen Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I have chosen David to rule my people Israel.'
My father David wanted with all his heart to build a temple to honour the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to my father David, 'You wanted with all your heart to build a temple for my name. It was good that you wanted to do this.
But you will not build the temple. Your own son will build the temple for my name.'

Now the LORD has kept the promise he made. I have taken my father David's place, and I sit on the throne of Israel, just as the LORD promised. And I have built the temple for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
I have put the ark there. In it is the LORD's covenant that he made with the people of Israel."
Then Solomon stood before the LORD's altar in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

Solomon had made a bronze platform about two metres long, two metres wide, and over a metre high, and had put it in the middle of the courtyard. He stood on it, then knelt down in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven.
He prayed, "LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven or on earth. You keep your covenant and show faithful love to your servants who follow you with all their hearts.
You have kept your promise to your servant David, my father. With your mouth you promised, and with your hand you have done it, as we see today.

Now, LORD, God of Israel, keep the other promise you made to your servant David, my father. You said, 'You will always have a descendant to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your children are careful to live by my law as you have done.'
Now, LORD, God of Israel, let the promise you made to your servant David come true.
But will God really live on earth with people? Even the heavens, the highest heavens, cannot hold you. How much less this temple I have built!
Yet please listen to your servant's prayer and his request, LORD my God. Hear the cry and the prayer your servant is praying to you.
Watch over this temple day and night. This is the place where you said you would put your name. Hear the prayer your servant prays toward this place.
Listen to the requests of your servant and of your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, where you live, and when you hear, forgive.
If someone wrongs their neighbour and is made to swear an oath, and comes and swears before your altar in this temple,
then hear from heaven and act. Judge between your servants. Punish the guilty one as they deserve, and declare the innocent one innocent, rewarding them for doing right.
If your people Israel are beaten by an enemy because they have sinned against you, and then they turn back to you, praise your name, and pray and beg before you in this temple,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel. Bring them back to the land you gave to them and their ancestors.
When the sky is shut and there is no rain because your people have sinned against you, and they pray toward this place, praise your name, and turn from their sin because you have punished them,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Teach them the right way to live, and send rain on your land, the land you gave your people as their own.
If there is hunger in the land, or disease, or crops ruined by hot winds or mould, or locusts or grasshoppers; or if enemies surround any of their cities; whatever disaster or sickness comes,
and someone, or all your people Israel, prays and begs you for help, each one knowing their own trouble and pain, and spreads out their hands toward this temple,
then hear from heaven, where you live, and forgive. Give each person what they deserve for everything they do, since you know their hearts. Only you know what is in people's hearts.
Then they will respect you and follow your ways for as long as they live in the land you gave our ancestors.
Also, a foreigner who is not one of your people Israel may come from a far country because of your great name, your mighty hand, and your powerful arm. When they come and pray toward this temple,

then hear from heaven, where you live, and do whatever the foreigner asks of you. Then all the peoples of the earth will know your name and respect you, as your people Israel do. They will know that this temple I have built carries your name.
When your people go out to fight their enemies, wherever you send them, and they pray to you toward this city you have chosen and the temple I have built for your name,
then hear their prayer and their request from heaven, and help them win.
When they sin against you, for there is no one who does not sin, and you are angry with them and hand them over to their enemies, who take them away as prisoners to a land far away or near,
then if they change their hearts in the land where they are prisoners, and turn back and beg you there, saying, 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly,'

and if they return to you with all their heart and soul in the land where they were taken, and pray toward the land you gave their ancestors, toward the city you have chosen, and toward the temple I have built for your name,
then hear their prayer and requests from heaven, where you live. Help them, and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
Now, my God, please let your eyes be open and your ears listen to the prayers made in this place.
Now rise up, LORD God, and come to your resting place, you and the ark of your power. LORD God, let your priests be clothed with salvation, and let your faithful people rejoice in your goodness.
LORD God, do not turn away from your anointed king. Remember your faithful love for your servant David."
When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and burned up the burnt offering and the sacrifices. The glory of the LORD filled the temple.
The priests could not go into the LORD's temple, because the glory of the LORD filled it.

All the people of Israel watched the fire come down and saw the LORD's glory over the temple. They bowed down with their faces to the stone floor. They worshipped and thanked the LORD, singing, "He is good; his faithful love lasts forever!"
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before the LORD.
King Solomon sacrificed twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated God's temple.

The priests stood in their places. The Levites stood with the LORD's musical instruments that King David had made for praising the LORD, when David gave thanks through their service, singing, "His faithful love lasts forever." Facing the Levites, the priests blew trumpets, and all Israel stood.

Solomon made holy the middle part of the courtyard in front of the LORD's temple. There he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar he had made was too small to hold all the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and fat.
At that time Solomon and all Israel with him celebrated the festival for seven days. It was a very large crowd, people from Lebo Hamath in the north all the way to the Brook of Egypt in the south.
On the eighth day they held a special meeting. They had celebrated the dedication of the altar for seven days and the festival for seven days.

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people home. They were joyful and glad in their hearts for all the good things the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for his people Israel.
So Solomon finished the LORD's temple and the royal palace. He succeeded in doing everything he had planned for the LORD's temple and for his own palace.
Then the LORD appeared to Solomon at night and said to him, "I have heard your prayer, and I have chosen this place for myself as a temple for sacrifices.
When I shut the sky so there is no rain, or command locusts to eat up the land, or send disease among my people,
if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek me, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven. I will forgive their sin and heal their land.
Now my eyes will be open and my ears will listen to the prayers made in this place.
I have chosen this temple and made it holy, so that my name will be there forever. My eyes and my heart will always be there.
As for you, if you follow me as your father David did, and do everything I command, and obey my laws and rules,
then I will make your royal throne secure, as I promised your father David when I said, 'You will always have a descendant to rule over Israel.'
But if you turn away and abandon the laws and commands I have given you, and go and serve and worship other gods,
then I will pull Israel up by the roots from my land that I gave them. I will reject this temple I have made holy for my name. I will make it a joke and an insult among all the nations.
This temple is so impressive now, but everyone who passes by will be shocked and ask, 'Why has the LORD done this to this land and to this temple?'

People will answer, 'Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who brought them out of Egypt. They chose other gods, worshipping and serving them. That is why he has brought all this disaster on them.'"
It took Solomon twenty years to build the LORD's temple and his own palace.
Then Solomon rebuilt the towns Huram had given him, and he had Israelites settle in them.
Solomon went to Hamath Zobah and captured it.
He built Tadmor in the desert, and all the storage towns he built in Hamath.
He rebuilt Upper Beth Horon and Lower Beth Horon, strong cities with walls, gates, and bars.
He also built Baalath, all his storage towns, and all the towns for his chariots and horses. He built whatever he wanted in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout all the land he ruled.
There were still people left from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. These people were not Israelites.
They were descendants of those the Israelites had not destroyed in the land. Solomon forced them to be slave workers, as they still are today.
But Solomon did not make slaves of any Israelites for his work. They were his soldiers, the chiefs of his officers, and the commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
They were also King Solomon's chief officials, two hundred and fifty of them, who were in charge of the people.

Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the City of David to the palace he had built for her. He said, "My wife must not live in the palace of David king of Israel, because the places where the LORD's ark has been are holy."
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the LORD's altar he had built in front of the temple porch.

He did this according to what was required each day, following the commands of Moses for Sabbaths, New Moons, and the three yearly festivals: the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Festival of Weeks, and the Festival of Shelters.

Following the instructions of his father David, he appointed the groups of priests for their service, and the Levites for their duties of leading praise and helping the priests, as each day required. He also appointed the gatekeepers by their groups for each gate, because this is what David, the man of God, had commanded.
They did not turn away from anything the king commanded the priests and Levites, including the care of the treasuries.
So all of Solomon's work was carried out, from the day the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid until it was finished. So the LORD's temple was completed.
Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and Elath on the coast of Edom.
Huram sent him ships commanded by his own officers, men who knew the sea. They sailed with Solomon's men to Ophir and brought back about fifteen tonnes of gold, which they gave to King Solomon.

The queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's fame, and she came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions. She arrived with a very large group of servants and camels carrying spices, lots of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about everything on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. Nothing was too hard for him to explain to her.
The queen of Sheba saw Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built.

She saw the food on his table, the way his officials were seated, the service of his servants and their uniforms, his cupbearers and their uniforms, and the burnt offerings he offered at the LORD's temple. It took her breath away.
She said to the king, "What I heard in my own country about your achievements and your wisdom is true.
But I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes. They did not tell me even half of how great your wisdom is. You are far greater than what I heard!
How happy your people must be! How happy your officials must be, who always stand before you and hear your wisdom!

Praise the LORD your God, who was pleased with you and put you on his throne to rule for the LORD your God. Because your God loves Israel and wants to make them strong forever, he has made you their king, so you can do what is fair and right."
Then she gave the king about four tonnes of gold, a huge amount of spices, and precious stones. There had never been spices like the ones the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
Huram's men and Solomon's men, who brought gold from Ophir, also brought algum wood and precious stones.
The king used the algum wood to make steps for the LORD's temple and the royal palace, and to make harps and lyres for the musicians. Nothing like them had ever been seen in Judah.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she wanted and asked for, even more than she had brought to him. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
Each year Solomon received about twenty-three tonnes of gold.
This did not include the gold brought by traders and merchants. All the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land also brought gold and silver to Solomon.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold. Each shield used about seven kilograms of gold.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold, each using about three and a half kilograms of gold. The king put them in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king also made a great throne decorated with ivory and covered it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps and a gold footstool attached to it. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. Nothing like it had ever been made in any other kingdom.
All King Solomon's cups were made of gold, and all the dishes in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. Silver was not thought to be worth much in Solomon's time.
The king had ships that sailed to Tarshish with Huram's men. Once every three years the ships came back carrying gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon became greater in riches and wisdom than all the other kings of the earth.
All the kings of the earth wanted to meet Solomon and hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Every year each of them brought gifts: things made of silver and gold, clothes, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, and twelve thousand horses. He kept them in the chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem.
He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as the fig trees in the western foothills.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt and from all other countries.

Everything else Solomon did, from beginning to end, is written in the records of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah from Shiloh, and in the visions of Iddo the seer about Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Solomon ruled in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.
Then Solomon died and was buried in the City of David, his father. His son Rehoboam became king after him.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had come there to make him king.
Jeroboam son of Nebat was in Egypt, where he had run away from King Solomon. When he heard about this, he came back from Egypt.
The people sent for him, and Jeroboam and all Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam. They said,
"Your father made us work very hard, like a heavy load on our necks. Now make the hard work and the heavy load your father put on us lighter, and we will serve you."
He said to them, "Come back to me in three days." So the people went away.
King Rehoboam asked advice from the older men who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. He asked, "What do you advise me to answer these people?"
They said to him, "If you are kind to these people, please them, and speak good words to them, they will be your servants forever."
But he ignored the advice the older men gave him. Instead he asked advice from the young men who had grown up with him and who served him.
He asked them, "What do you advise? How should we answer these people who said to me, 'Make the load your father put on us lighter'?"

The young men who had grown up with him said, "Tell the people who said to you, 'Your father made our load heavy, but make it lighter for us,' tell them this: 'My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.
My father put a heavy load on you, but I will make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.'"
So on the third day Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam, just as the king had said, "Come back to me on the third day."
The king answered them harshly. King Rehoboam ignored the advice of the older men,
and spoke to them the way the young men had advised. He said, "My father made your load heavy, but I will make it heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions."
So the king did not listen to the people. God made this happen, so that the LORD would keep the promise he had spoken through Ahijah from Shiloh to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, they answered the king, "What share do we have in David? We have no part in the son of Jesse! Everyone go home, Israel! David, look after your own family now." So all Israel went home.
But Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah.
Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was in charge of the forced workers, and the Israelites threw stones at him until he died. King Rehoboam quickly got into his chariot and escaped to Jerusalem.
So Israel has rebelled against David's family to this day.
When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he gathered the people of Judah and Benjamin, one hundred eighty thousand chosen soldiers, to fight against Israel and win the kingdom back for Rehoboam.
But the LORD's message came to Shemaiah, the man of God. He said,
"Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the Israelites in Judah and Benjamin. Say,
'The LORD says: Do not go up and fight against your brothers! Everyone go back home, because I made this happen.'" So they obeyed the LORD's words and did not go to attack Jeroboam.
Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem and built towns in Judah for defense.
He built up Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,
Beth Zur, Soco, Adullam,
Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,
Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. These were strong, walled towns in Judah and Benjamin.
He made the forts strong and put commanders in them, with supplies of food, olive oil, and wine.
He put shields and spears in every town and made them very strong. So Judah and Benjamin belonged to him.
The priests and Levites from all over Israel came from their areas and stood with him.
The Levites left their pasture lands and their property and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons would not let them serve as priests of the LORD.
Jeroboam chose his own priests for the hilltop shrines and for the goat and calf idols he had made.
After the Levites, people from all the tribes of Israel who had set their hearts on seeking the LORD, the God of Israel, came to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
They made the kingdom of Judah strong and supported Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, because for three years they lived the way David and Solomon had lived.
Rehoboam married Mahalath. She was the daughter of Jerimoth son of David, and of Abihail, the daughter of Eliab son of Jesse.
She had sons for him: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
After her, he married Maacah, Absalom's granddaughter. She had Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith for him.
Rehoboam loved Maacah, Absalom's granddaughter, more than all his other wives and slave wives. He had eighteen wives and sixty slave wives, and he had twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam made Abijah son of Maacah the chief leader among his brothers, because he planned to make him king.
He acted wisely and spread some of his sons through all the areas of Judah and Benjamin, to every walled town. He gave them plenty of food and found many wives for them.
When Rehoboam's kingdom was firmly set up and he was strong, he turned away from the LORD's law, and all Israel did the same.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's rule, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem, because the people had been unfaithful to the LORD.
He came with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. With him came more soldiers from Egypt than anyone could count: Libyans, Sukkites, and Ethiopians.
He captured the walled towns of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.

Then the prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem because of Shishak. He said to them, "The LORD says, 'You have left me, so now I have left you in Shishak's hands.'"
Then the leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is right."

When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, his message came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them. I will soon rescue them, and I will not pour out my anger on Jerusalem through Shishak.
But they will become his servants, so they can learn the difference between serving me and serving the kings of other countries."
So Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the LORD's temple and the treasures of the king's palace. He took everything, including the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and gave them to the commanders of the guards who kept watch at the palace door.
Whenever the king went into the LORD's temple, the guards came and carried the shields, and then took them back to the guardroom.
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the LORD's anger turned away from him, and he was not completely destroyed. There were also some good things in Judah.

So King Rehoboam made himself strong in Jerusalem and ruled as king. He was forty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel as the place for his name. His mother was Naamah, from Ammon.
He did evil, because he did not set his heart on seeking the LORD.
Everything Rehoboam did, from beginning to end, is written in the records of the prophet Shemaiah and of Iddo the seer, in the family records. Rehoboam and Jeroboam were always at war.
Rehoboam died and was buried in the City of David. His son Abijah became king after him.
In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam's rule, Abijah became king of Judah.
He ruled for three years in Jerusalem. His mother was Micaiah, daughter of Uriel from Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.
Abijah went into battle with an army of four hundred thousand brave, chosen soldiers. Jeroboam lined up against him with eight hundred thousand chosen, strong, brave soldiers.
Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim, in the hill country of Ephraim, and shouted, "Listen to me, Jeroboam and all Israel!
Don't you know that the LORD, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom of Israel to David and his sons forever, by a covenant that cannot be broken, a covenant of salt?
But Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his master.
Worthless, wicked men gathered around him and stood against Rehoboam son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and timid and could not stand up to them.
Now you plan to fight against the LORD's kingdom, which is in the hands of David's sons. You are a huge crowd, and you have with you the gold calves that Jeroboam made to be your gods.

Didn't you drive out the LORD's priests, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites? Didn't you make your own priests like the peoples of other lands do? Anyone who comes with a young bull and seven rams to make himself holy can become a priest of gods that are not gods at all.
But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not left him. Our priests who serve the LORD are sons of Aaron, and the Levites help them in their work.

Every morning and every evening they burn offerings and sweet incense to the LORD. They put the holy bread on the pure table and take care of the gold lampstand and its lamps, to light them every evening. We obey the LORD our God, but you have left him.

Look, God is with us as our leader. His priests are here with trumpets to sound the battle call against you. People of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your ancestors, because you will not win."
But Jeroboam had sent soldiers around to hide behind Judah's army. So his main army was in front of Judah, and the hidden soldiers were behind them.
When the men of Judah looked around, they saw they were being attacked from the front and the back. They cried out to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets.
Then the men of Judah gave a battle shout. As they shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel in front of Abijah and Judah.
The Israelites ran away from Judah, and God handed them over to them.
Abijah and his army killed a great many of them. Five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell dead.
So the Israelites were defeated at that time, and the people of Judah won, because they trusted in the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Abijah chased Jeroboam and took towns from him: Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, with their villages.
Jeroboam never became strong again while Abijah was alive. The LORD struck him down, and he died.
But Abijah grew powerful. He married fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
Everything else Abijah did, how he lived and what he said, is written in the writings of the prophet Iddo.
Abijah died and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king after him. While Asa was king, the land had peace for ten years.
Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He removed the altars to foreign gods and the hilltop shrines. He smashed the stone pillars and cut down the Asherah poles.
He told the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and to obey his law and commands.
He also removed the hilltop shrines and the incense altars from all the towns of Judah. The kingdom had peace while he ruled.
He built walled towns in Judah, because the land was at peace. There was no war in those years, because the LORD gave him rest.

He said to the people of Judah, "Let's build up these towns and put walls around them, with towers, gates, and bars. The land is still ours, because we have looked to the LORD our God. We looked to him, and he has given us peace on every side." So they built and did well.

Asa had an army of three hundred thousand men from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and two hundred eighty thousand men from Benjamin, armed with small shields and bows. All of them were brave, strong soldiers.
Zerah from Ethiopia came out to fight them with an army of a million soldiers and three hundred chariots. He came as far as Mareshah.
Asa went out to meet him, and they lined up for battle in the Zephathah Valley near Mareshah.

Asa cried out to the LORD his God, "LORD, no one but you can help the weak against the strong. Help us, LORD our God, because we trust in you. In your name we have come against this huge army. LORD, you are our God. Do not let any man win against you."
So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians in front of Asa and Judah, and the Ethiopians ran away.
Asa and his army chased them as far as Gerar. So many Ethiopians fell that they could not recover. They were crushed by the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried off a huge amount of loot.
They destroyed all the towns around Gerar, because the fear of the LORD had fallen on them. They took everything of value from those towns, because there was a lot to take.
They also attacked the camps of the herders and took many sheep and camels. Then they went back to Jerusalem.
The Spirit of God came on Azariah son of Oded.

He went out to meet Asa and said to him, "Listen to me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin! The LORD is with you as long as you are with him. If you look for him, you will find him. But if you leave him, he will leave you.
For a long time Israel was without the true God, without a priest to teach them, and without the law.
But when they were in trouble and turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and looked for him, they found him.
In those days it was not safe for anyone to travel. Great trouble was on everyone who lived in those lands.
Nation fought against nation and town against town, because God troubled them with every kind of hardship.
But you, be strong! Do not give up, because your work will be rewarded."

When Asa heard these words, the message of Oded the prophet, he became brave. He removed the disgusting idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the towns he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim. He repaired the LORD's altar in front of the porch of the LORD's temple.

He gathered all the people of Judah and Benjamin, and the people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were living among them. Many people had come over to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.
They gathered in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa's rule.
That day they offered sacrifices to the LORD from the loot they had brought back: seven hundred cattle and seven thousand sheep.
They made a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, with all their heart and all their soul.
Anyone who would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, was to be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman.
They made a promise to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, and with trumpets and horns.
All Judah was happy about the promise, because they had promised with all their heart. They looked for the LORD with all their desire, and they found him. So the LORD gave them peace on every side.

King Asa also removed his grandmother Maacah from being queen mother, because she had made a disgusting idol for the goddess Asherah. Asa cut down the idol, crushed it to dust, and burned it at the Kidron Valley.
The hilltop shrines were not removed from Israel, but Asa's heart was fully faithful all his life.
He brought into God's temple the silver, gold, and other objects that he and his father had set apart for God.
There was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's rule.
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's rule, Baasha king of Israel attacked Judah. He built up the town of Ramah so that no one could go in or out to Asa king of Judah.
Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the LORD's temple and of the king's palace. He sent it to Ben Hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, with this message:

"Let's make a treaty between you and me, like there was between my father and your father. Look, I am sending you silver and gold. Go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so he will leave me alone."
Ben Hadad agreed with King Asa. He sent the commanders of his armies against the towns of Israel. They attacked Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage towns of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard about it, he stopped building Ramah and gave up the work.
Then King Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones and wood Baasha had been using to build Ramah. Asa used them to build up Geba and Mizpah.
At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, "You trusted the king of Syria and did not trust the LORD your God. So the army of the king of Syria has escaped from you.
Weren't the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army, with chariots and very many horsemen? But because you trusted the LORD, he handed them over to you.
The LORD's eyes search all over the earth to give strength to those whose hearts are fully faithful to him. You have acted foolishly in this. From now on you will have wars."
Asa was angry with the seer and put him in prison, because he was furious with him about this. At that time Asa also treated some of the people cruelly.
Everything Asa did, from beginning to end, is written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
In the thirty-ninth year of his rule, Asa got a disease in his feet. His disease was very bad, but even in his sickness he did not look to the LORD for help, only to doctors.
Asa died in the forty-first year of his rule.

They buried him in the tomb he had cut out for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bed covered with sweet-smelling spices and perfumes made by skilled perfume makers. And they made a very large fire to honor him.
Asa's son Jehoshaphat became king after him. He made his kingdom strong against Israel.
He put soldiers in all the walled towns of Judah. He also put army camps in the land of Judah and in the towns of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he lived the way his ancestor David had lived in his early years. He did not worship the Baal gods.
Instead he looked to the God of his father and obeyed his commands. He did not act like the people of Israel.
So the LORD made the kingdom strong under his control. All the people of Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat, and he had great wealth and honor.
His heart was proud to follow the LORD's ways. He also removed the hilltop shrines and the Asherah poles from Judah.
In the third year of his rule, he sent his officials Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the towns of Judah.
With them he sent some Levites: Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah. He also sent the priests Elishama and Jehoram with them.
They taught the people in Judah, and they had the book of the LORD's law with them. They went around to all the towns of Judah and taught the people.
The fear of the LORD fell on all the kingdoms around Judah, so they did not go to war against Jehoshaphat.
Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat gifts and silver as payment. The Arabs also brought him flocks: seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred male goats.
Jehoshaphat became more and more powerful. He built forts and storage towns in Judah.
He had a lot of supplies in the towns of Judah, and he kept brave, experienced soldiers in Jerusalem.
Here is the list of them by their families. From Judah, the commanders of thousands were: Adnah the commander, with three hundred thousand brave soldiers;
next, Jehohanan the commander, with two hundred eighty thousand;
next, Amasiah son of Zichri, who gladly offered himself to serve the LORD, with two hundred thousand brave soldiers.
From Benjamin: Eliada, a brave soldier, with two hundred thousand men armed with bows and shields;
next, Jehozabad, with one hundred eighty thousand men ready for war.
These were the men who served the king, besides the soldiers he put in the walled towns all over Judah.
Jehoshaphat had great wealth and honor. He made an alliance with Ahab by marriage.
Some years later, he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab killed many sheep and cattle for him and the people with him, and he talked him into going with him to attack Ramoth Gilead.

Ahab king of Israel asked Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me to attack Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat answered, "I am with you, and my people are like your people. We will join you in the war."
Then Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "But first, please ask what the LORD says."

So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, four hundred men, and asked them, "Should we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" They said, "Go, because God will hand it over to the king."
But Jehoshaphat asked, "Isn't there another prophet of the LORD here we can ask?"

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man we can ask the LORD through, but I hate him, because he never says anything good about me, only bad things. He is Micaiah son of Imla." Jehoshaphat said, "The king should not say that."
So the king of Israel called an officer and said, "Quickly, bring Micaiah son of Imla."

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, dressed in their royal robes. They were sitting in an open place at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying in front of them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made some iron horns and said, "The LORD says, 'With these you will push back the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"
All the prophets were saying the same thing: "Attack Ramoth Gilead and win, because the LORD will hand it over to the king."
The messenger who went to get Micaiah said to him, "Look, all the prophets are saying good things to the king with one voice. Please let your message agree with theirs, and say something good."
But Micaiah said, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will say what my God tells me."
When he came to the king, the king asked him, "Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" He answered, "Go and win. They will be handed over to you."
The king said to him, "How many times must I make you promise to tell me nothing but the truth in the LORD's name?"
Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These people have no master. Let each of them go home in peace.'"
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you he never says anything good about me, only bad?"
Micaiah said, "So listen to the LORD's message. I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, with all the armies of heaven standing on his right and on his left.
The LORD said, 'Who will trick Ahab king of Israel into attacking Ramoth Gilead so he will die there?' One said one thing, and another said something else.
Then a spirit came forward, stood in front of the LORD, and said, 'I will trick him.' The LORD asked him, 'How?'
He said, 'I will go and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' The LORD said, 'You will trick him and succeed. Go and do it.'
So now, look, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets of yours. The LORD has decided that disaster will come to you."
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up and slapped Micaiah on the face. He said, "Which way did the LORD's Spirit go when he left me to speak to you?"
Micaiah answered, "You will find out on the day you run into an inner room to hide."
The king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king's son.
Tell them, 'The king says: Put this man in prison. Give him nothing but a little bread and water until I come back safely.'"
Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, then the LORD has not spoken through me." Then he added, "Remember this, all you people!"
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went to attack Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will go into battle in disguise, but you wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.
The king of Syria had ordered his chariot commanders, "Do not fight anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel."
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "That is the king of Israel!" So they turned to attack him. But Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.

But a soldier shot an arrow without aiming, and it hit the king of Israel between the pieces of his armor. The king told his chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle, because I am badly wounded."
The battle grew fierce all that day. The king of Israel held himself up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. At sunset he died.
Jehoshaphat king of Judah came home safely to his palace in Jerusalem.
Jehu son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help wicked people and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, the LORD is angry with you.
But there is some good in you. You removed the Asherah poles from the land, and you have set your heart on seeking God."
Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. He went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
He chose judges in the land, in each of the walled towns of Judah.
He said to the judges, "Be careful what you do, because you are not judging for people but for the LORD. He is with you when you make a decision.
So let the fear of the LORD be on you. Be careful what you do, because the LORD our God is never unfair. He does not take sides or take bribes."
In Jerusalem too, Jehoshaphat chose some Levites, priests, and family leaders of Israel to judge for the LORD and settle arguments. They lived in Jerusalem.
He gave them these orders: "You must serve faithfully and with your whole heart, in the fear of the LORD.

Your relatives who live in the towns will bring you cases about murder, or about laws, commands, rules, and decisions. In every case, you must warn them not to sin against the LORD. Otherwise his anger will come on you and on your relatives. Do this, and you will not be guilty.

Amariah the chief priest will be over you in everything that has to do with the LORD. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of the tribe of Judah, will be over you in everything that has to do with the king. The Levites will serve you as officers. Be brave and do your work, and may the LORD be with those who do what is good."
After this, the people of Moab and Ammon, together with some of the Meunites, came to fight against Jehoshaphat.
Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A huge army is coming against you from Edom, from the other side of the Dead Sea. Look, they are already at Hazazon Tamar," which is En Gedi.
Jehoshaphat was afraid, and he decided to ask the LORD for help. He announced that everyone in Judah should go without food.
The people of Judah came together to ask the LORD for help. They came from every town in Judah to seek the LORD.
Jehoshaphat stood up in front of the people of Judah and Jerusalem at the LORD's temple, in front of the new courtyard.
He said, "LORD, God of our ancestors, aren't you the God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. You have power and strength, and no one can stand against you.
Our God, didn't you drive out the people who lived in this land ahead of your people Israel? Didn't you give it forever to the descendants of your friend Abraham?
They have lived in it and built a temple here to honor your name. They said,

'If trouble comes on us, whether war, punishment, disease, or famine, we will stand in front of this temple and in front of you, because your name is in this temple. We will cry out to you in our trouble, and you will hear us and save us.'
Now look at the people of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir. When Israel came out of Egypt, you did not let them invade these nations. So Israel turned away from them and did not destroy them.
Now look how they repay us! They are coming to drive us out of the land you gave us as our own.
Our God, won't you judge them? We have no power against this huge army that is attacking us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you."
All the men of Judah stood there in front of the LORD, with their babies, their wives, and their children.
Then the LORD's Spirit came on Jahaziel, there in the middle of the crowd. He was a Levite from the family of Asaph, the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah.
He said, "Listen, all Judah, people of Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat! The LORD says to you: 'Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this huge army. The battle is not yours, but God's.
Tomorrow, go down to meet them. They will be coming up the pass of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, facing the desert of Jeruel.

You will not need to fight this battle. Take your places, stand still, and watch the LORD save you, Judah and Jerusalem. Do not be afraid or discouraged. Go out to face them tomorrow, because the LORD is with you.'"
Jehoshaphat bowed down with his face to the ground. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem fell down in front of the LORD and worshiped him.
Then some Levites from the families of Kohath and Korah stood up and praised the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.

Early the next morning they went out into the desert of Tekoa. As they set out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Listen to me, Judah and people of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will stand firm. Believe his prophets, and you will succeed."
After talking with the people, he chose singers to go ahead of the army, praising the LORD for his holy beauty. They sang, "Give thanks to the LORD, because his love lasts forever."
As soon as they began to sing and praise, the LORD set ambushes against the people of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir who were attacking Judah, and they were defeated.
The armies of Ammon and Moab turned against the people of Mount Seir and destroyed them completely. When they had finished off the people of Seir, they turned and destroyed each other.
When the men of Judah came to the place that looks out over the desert, they looked toward the huge army. All they saw were dead bodies lying on the ground. No one had escaped.

Jehoshaphat and his people came to collect the loot. Among the bodies they found lots of goods, clothes, and valuable things. They took more than they could carry. There was so much that it took them three days to collect it all.
On the fourth day they gathered in the Valley of Beracah, where they praised the LORD. That is why it is still called the Valley of Beracah, which means Valley of Praise, to this day.
