Then all the men of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat leading them, went back to Jerusalem full of joy, because the LORD had given them joy over their enemies.
They came into Jerusalem and went to the LORD's temple with harps, lyres, and trumpets.
The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of those lands when they heard how the LORD had fought against Israel's enemies.
So Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, because his God gave him rest on every side.
So Jehoshaphat ruled over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the ways of his father Asa and did not turn away from them. He did what was right in the LORD's eyes.
But the hilltop shrines were not removed, and the people still had not set their hearts on the God of their ancestors.
Everything else Jehoshaphat did, from beginning to end, is written in the records of Jehu son of Hanani, which are part of the book of the kings of Israel.
Later, Jehoshaphat king of Judah made an agreement with Ahaziah king of Israel, who was very wicked.
They agreed to build ships to sail to Tarshish. They built the ships at Ezion Geber.

Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu from Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat. He said, "Because you joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." The ships were wrecked and could not sail to Tarshish.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram became king after him.
Jehoram had brothers, the other sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.
Their father had given them many gifts of silver, gold, and valuable things, and walled towns in Judah. But he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the oldest son.
When Jehoram had taken over his father's kingdom and made his power secure, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and some of the leaders of Israel too.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled for eight years in Jerusalem.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, just as Ahab's family had done, because he was married to Ahab's daughter. He did evil in the LORD's eyes.
But the LORD did not want to destroy David's family, because of the covenant he had made with David. He had promised to keep a lamp burning for David and his descendants forever.
While Jehoram was king, Edom rebelled against Judah and chose its own king.
So Jehoram went there with his commanders and all his chariots. The Edomites surrounded him, but he got up at night and attacked them and their chariot commanders.
So Edom has been free from Judah's rule to this day. At the same time the town of Libnah also rebelled against him, because he had left the LORD, the God of his ancestors.
He also built hilltop shrines in the hills of Judah. He led the people of Jerusalem to be unfaithful to God, like a woman selling her body, and he led Judah astray.
Then a letter came to Jehoram from the prophet Elijah. It said, "The LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says: 'You have not followed the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or of Asa king of Judah.

Instead you have followed the ways of the kings of Israel. You have led Judah and the people of Jerusalem to be unfaithful to me, just as Ahab's family did. You also murdered your own brothers, your father's sons, who were better than you.
So now the LORD is about to strike your people with a terrible disaster, including your children, your wives, and everything you own.
You yourself will become very sick with a disease of your bowels. Day after day it will get worse until your bowels come out.'"
The LORD stirred up the Philistines and the Arabs who lived near the Ethiopians to attack Jehoram.
They attacked Judah, broke in, and carried off everything they found in the king's palace, along with his sons and his wives. Only Jehoahaz, his youngest son, was left.
After all this, the LORD struck Jehoram with a disease of the bowels that could not be cured.
After about two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in terrible pain. His people did not light a fire to honor him, as they had done for his ancestors.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. No one was sad when he died. They buried him in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

The people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, Jehoram's youngest son, king after him. The raiders who came with the Arabs into the camp had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah became king.
Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled for one year in Jerusalem. His mother was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.
He also followed the ways of Ahab's family, because his mother gave him advice to do evil.
He did evil in the LORD's eyes, as Ahab's family had done. After his father died, they became his advisers, and that led to his ruin.
He followed their advice and went with Joram son of Ahab king of Israel to fight against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth Gilead. The Syrians wounded Joram.

Joram went back to Jezreel to heal from the wounds he got at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, because he was hurt.
God used this visit to Joram to bring about Ahaziah's downfall. When Ahaziah got there, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, the man the LORD had anointed to wipe out Ahab's family.
While Jehu was punishing Ahab's family, he found the leaders of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's relatives who were serving Ahaziah, and he killed them.

Then he went looking for Ahaziah. Jehu's men caught him hiding in Samaria. They brought him to Jehu and killed him. They buried him, because they said, "He was the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who looked to the LORD with all his heart." No one in Ahaziah's family was strong enough to rule the kingdom.
When Ahaziah's mother Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she set out to kill the whole royal family of Judah.

But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, secretly took Joash son of Ahaziah away from the king's sons who were about to be killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath, daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, was Ahaziah's sister. She hid the boy from Athaliah, so Athaliah did not kill him.
He stayed hidden with them in God's temple for six years, while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada found his courage. He made an agreement with the commanders of hundreds: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
They went all over Judah and gathered the Levites from all the towns, and the family leaders of Israel. Then they came to Jerusalem.
All the people gathered made an agreement with the king in God's temple. Jehoiada said to them, "Look, the king's son will rule, just as the LORD promised about David's descendants.
This is what you must do. One third of you priests and Levites who come on duty on the Sabbath will guard the doors.
One third will be at the king's palace, and one third at the Foundation Gate. All the other people will be in the courtyards of the LORD's temple.

Do not let anyone into the LORD's temple except the priests and the Levites who are serving. They may go in, because they are holy. But all the other people must obey the LORD's instructions and stay outside.
The Levites must stand around the king, every man with his weapon in his hand. Kill anyone who tries to enter the temple. Stay close to the king wherever he goes."

The Levites and all the men of Judah did everything Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each commander took his men, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty, because Jehoiada the priest had not let any group go home.
Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears and the large and small shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in God's temple.
He placed all the men, each with his weapon in his hand, around the king, from the right side of the temple to the left side, near the altar and the temple.
Then they brought out the king's son, put the crown on him, gave him a copy of the covenant law, and made him king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and shouted, "Long live the king!"
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and cheering for the king, she went to them at the LORD's temple.

She looked, and there was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, with the commanders and trumpet players beside him. All the people of the land were celebrating and blowing trumpets, and singers with musical instruments were leading the praise. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and shouted, "Traitors! Traitors!"

Jehoiada the priest sent out the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army. He told them, "Take her out between the rows of soldiers, and kill anyone who follows her." The priest had said, "Do not kill her in the LORD's temple."
So they grabbed her as she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate by the king's palace, and they killed her there.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they would be the LORD's people.
All the people went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed his altars and idols to pieces and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars.

Jehoiada put the work of the LORD's temple under the control of the Levitical priests, whom David had organized in groups in the LORD's temple. They were to offer burnt offerings to the LORD as the law of Moses says, with joy and singing, as David had ordered.
He put gatekeepers at the gates of the LORD's temple, so that no one who was unclean in any way could come in.

He took the commanders of hundreds, the important men, the rulers of the people, and all the people of the land, and they led the king down from the LORD's temple. They went through the Upper Gate to the king's palace and seated the king on the royal throne.
All the people of the land celebrated, and the city was calm, because Athaliah had been killed with the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he ruled for forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the LORD's eyes for as long as Jehoiada the priest was alive.
Jehoiada chose two wives for him, and he had sons and daughters.
Some time later, Joash decided to repair the LORD's temple.

He called the priests and Levites together and said to them, "Go out to the towns of Judah and collect money from all Israel every year to repair the temple of your God. Do it quickly." But the Levites did not hurry.

So the king called for Jehoiada, the chief priest, and asked him, "Why haven't you made the Levites bring in the tax from Judah and Jerusalem? Moses, the LORD's servant, and the people of Israel set this tax for the Tent of the Covenant."
The sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into God's temple and had used even the holy things of the LORD's temple for the Baal gods.
So at the king's order, they made a wooden box and put it outside, at the gate of the LORD's temple.
Then they announced all through Judah and Jerusalem that the people should bring to the LORD the tax that Moses, God's servant, had set for Israel in the desert.
All the leaders and all the people were happy to do it. They brought their money and dropped it into the box until it was full.

Whenever the Levites brought the box to the king's officials and they saw that there was a lot of money in it, the king's secretary and the chief priest's officer came and emptied it. Then they took the box back to its place. They did this day after day and collected a lot of money.

The king and Jehoiada gave the money to the men in charge of the work on the LORD's temple. They hired stoneworkers and carpenters to repair the LORD's temple, and workers in iron and bronze to fix it.
The workers worked hard, and the repairs went well. They rebuilt God's temple the way it was designed and made it strong.

When they had finished, they brought the money that was left to the king and Jehoiada. With it they made things for the LORD's temple: things for the temple service and for the offerings, including dishes and other objects of gold and silver. As long as Jehoiada lived, burnt offerings were offered in the LORD's temple all the time.
Jehoiada grew old and lived a long, full life. He died when he was one hundred thirty years old.
He was buried with the kings in the City of David, because he had done so much good in Israel for God and his temple.
After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah came and bowed down to the king, and the king listened to their advice.
They left the temple of the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and worshiped Asherah poles and idols. Because of this sin, God was angry with Judah and Jerusalem.
Still the LORD sent prophets to them to bring them back to him. The prophets warned them, but they would not listen.

Then the Spirit of God came on Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood up above the people and said to them, "God says: 'Why do you disobey the LORD's commands? You will not do well. Because you have left the LORD, he has left you.'"
But they plotted against him, and at the king's order they stoned him to death in the courtyard of the LORD's temple.
King Joash did not remember how kind Zechariah's father Jehoiada had been to him. Instead he killed his son. As Zechariah was dying, he said, "May the LORD see this and pay you back."
At the end of the year, the Syrian army came to attack Joash. They invaded Judah and Jerusalem, killed all the leaders of the people, and sent all the loot to their king in Damascus.
The Syrian army was only a small group of men, but the LORD handed a very large army over to them, because Judah had left the LORD, the God of their ancestors. In this way Joash was punished.

When the Syrians left, Joash was badly wounded. His own officials plotted against him because he had killed the son of Jehoiada the priest. They killed him in his bed, and he died. He was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
The men who plotted against him were Zabad, son of Shimeath, a woman from Ammon, and Jehozabad, son of Shimrith, a woman from Moab.
The story of his sons, the many prophecies against him, and the rebuilding of God's temple are written in the notes on the book of the kings. His son Amaziah became king after him.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jehoaddan from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, but not with his whole heart.
As soon as the kingdom was firmly under his control, he killed the officials who had murdered his father the king.

But he did not kill their children. He obeyed what is written in the law, in the book of Moses, where the LORD commanded: "Parents must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their parents. Each person must die for their own sin."

Amaziah gathered the people of Judah and organized them by families under commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, for all Judah and Benjamin. He counted the men twenty years old and older and found three hundred thousand chosen men ready for war, able to handle a spear and shield.
He also hired one hundred thousand brave soldiers from Israel for about three and a half tonnes of silver.
But a man of God came to him and said, "King, do not let the army of Israel go with you, because the LORD is not with Israel, with any of the people of Ephraim.
Even if you go and fight bravely, God will let the enemy defeat you. God has the power to help you or to make you fall."
Amaziah asked the man of God, "But what about all the silver I paid for the army of Israel?" The man of God answered, "The LORD can give you much more than that."
So Amaziah sent away the soldiers who had come to him from Ephraim and told them to go home. They were very angry with Judah and went home furious.
Then Amaziah became brave and led his army to the Valley of Salt. There he killed ten thousand men of Seir.
The army of Judah also captured ten thousand men alive. They took them to the top of a cliff and threw them off, and they were all smashed to pieces.
Meanwhile, the soldiers Amaziah had sent back and not allowed to fight attacked the towns of Judah, from Samaria to Beth Horon. They killed three thousand people and took a lot of loot.
After Amaziah came back from defeating the Edomites, he brought the gods of the people of Seir. He set them up as his own gods, bowed down to them, and burned incense to them.
So the LORD was angry with Amaziah. He sent a prophet to him, who said, "Why have you worshiped the gods of these people? They could not even save their own people from you!"

While the prophet was speaking, the king said to him, "Did we make you an adviser to the king? Stop! Why should you be killed?" So the prophet stopped, but said, "I know that God has decided to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my advice."
Then Amaziah king of Judah talked with his advisers. He sent a message to Joash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel: "Come, let's meet face to face in battle."

Joash king of Israel sent back this answer to Amaziah king of Judah: "A thorn bush in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar tree in Lebanon: 'Give your daughter to my son as his wife.' Then a wild animal in Lebanon came by and trampled the thorn bush.
You say you have defeated Edom, and now you are proud and boastful. Stay at home! Why ask for trouble that will make you fall, and Judah with you?"
But Amaziah would not listen. God made this happen so he could hand them over to their enemies, because they had worshiped the gods of Edom.
So Joash king of Israel attacked. He and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other in battle at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
Israel defeated Judah, and every man of Judah ran home.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, at Beth Shemesh. He brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, about one hundred eighty meters.

He took all the gold and silver and all the objects found in God's temple, which Obed-Edom looked after. He also took the treasures of the king's palace and some hostages. Then he went back to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for fifteen years after Joash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, died.
Everything else Amaziah did, from beginning to end, is written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, people in Jerusalem plotted against him. He ran away to Lachish, but they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there.
They carried his body back on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the City of Judah.
All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
Uzziah rebuilt the town of Elath and won it back for Judah after his father died.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he ruled for fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jecoliah from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his father Amaziah had done.
He looked to God while Zechariah was alive, a man who taught him to respect God. As long as he looked to the LORD, God made him successful.
He went to war against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He built towns near Ashdod and in other parts of Philistia.
God helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal, and against the Meunites.
The Ammonites paid Uzziah tribute money. He became famous as far as the border of Egypt, because he became very powerful.
Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate, and at the corner of the wall, and he made them strong.

He also built towers in the desert and dug many water wells, because he had many cattle in the foothills and on the plains. He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, because he loved farming.
Uzziah had a well-trained army ready for battle, organized in groups. They were counted by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer, under the command of Hananiah, one of the king's officials.
There were two thousand six hundred family leaders in charge of these brave soldiers.
Under them was an army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred men, trained to fight with great power to help the king against his enemies.
Uzziah gave the whole army shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and stones for slings.

In Jerusalem he had machines made by skilled men to put on the towers and corners of the walls, to shoot arrows and throw large stones. He became famous far and wide, because God helped him in amazing ways until he became powerful.
But when Uzziah became powerful, his pride led to his downfall. He was unfaithful to the LORD his God. He went into the LORD's temple to burn incense on the incense altar.
Azariah the priest went in after him with eighty other brave priests of the LORD.

They stood up to King Uzziah and said, "Uzziah, it is not your job to burn incense to the LORD. That is the job of the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who have been set apart to burn incense. Leave the holy place, because you have been unfaithful. The LORD God will not honor you for this."

Uzziah was holding a pan for burning incense, and he became angry. While he was raging at the priests in front of the incense altar in the LORD's temple, a skin disease broke out on his forehead right in front of them.

Azariah the chief priest and all the other priests looked at him and saw the skin disease on his forehead. They hurried him out of the temple. He himself was in a hurry to leave, because the LORD had struck him.

King Uzziah had the skin disease until the day he died. He lived in a separate house, because he had the disease and was not allowed in the LORD's temple. His son Jotham was in charge of the palace and ruled the people of the land.
The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz wrote down everything else Uzziah did, from beginning to end.
Uzziah died and was buried near his ancestors in a burial field that belonged to the kings, because people said, "He had a skin disease." His son Jotham became king after him.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jerushah, daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his father Uzziah had done. But he did not go into the LORD's temple as his father had. The people, however, kept on doing wrong.
Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the LORD's temple and did a lot of building on the wall at Ophel.
He built towns in the hill country of Judah, and forts and towers in the forest areas.

He fought against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them. That year the Ammonites paid him about three and a half tonnes of silver, ten thousand loads of wheat, and ten thousand loads of barley. They paid him the same amount in the second and third years.
Jotham became powerful because he lived carefully, obeying the LORD his God.
Everything else Jotham did, including all his wars and his ways, is written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for sixteen years in Jerusalem.
Jotham died and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz became king after him.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he ruled for sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the LORD's eyes, as his ancestor David had done.
Instead he followed the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made metal idols of the Baal gods.
He burned incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and burned his own sons as sacrifices in the fire. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the hilltop shrines, on the hills, and under every green tree.

So the LORD his God handed him over to the king of Syria. The Syrians defeated him and took many of his people as prisoners to Damascus. He was also handed over to the king of Israel, who killed a great many of his men.
In one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed one hundred twenty thousand brave soldiers in Judah, because they had left the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Zichri, a strong warrior from Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son, Azrikam the officer in charge of the palace, and Elkanah, the king's second in command.
The Israelites took two hundred thousand of their own relatives from Judah as prisoners: women, sons, and daughters. They also took a lot of loot and brought it to Samaria.

But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there. He went out to meet the army when it came to Samaria and said, "Look, the LORD, the God of your ancestors, was angry with Judah, so he handed them over to you. But you have killed them with a rage that reaches up to heaven.
Now you plan to make the people of Judah and Jerusalem your slaves, men and women. But aren't you also guilty of sins against the LORD your God?
Now listen to me! Send back the prisoners you have taken from your relatives, because the LORD's fierce anger is on you."

Then some of the leaders of Ephraim stood up against the men coming back from the war. They were Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai.
They said to them, "Do not bring the prisoners here! You want to add to our sin and guilt against the LORD. Our guilt is already great, and his fierce anger is on Israel."
So the soldiers left the prisoners and the loot in front of the leaders and all the people.

The men named above took charge of the prisoners. They used the loot to give clothes to everyone who was naked. They gave them clothes, sandals, food, and drink, and put healing oil on their wounds. They put all the weak ones on donkeys and took them to their relatives in Jericho, the City of Palm Trees. Then they went back to Samaria.
At that time King Ahaz asked the kings of Assyria for help.
The Edomites had come again, attacked Judah, and taken prisoners.

The Philistines had also raided the towns in the foothills and in the south of Judah. They captured and settled in Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, and Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo with their villages.
The LORD brought Judah down because of Ahaz king of Israel, who let Judah run wild and was very unfaithful to the LORD.
Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria came to him, but he caused him trouble instead of helping him.
Ahaz took some things from the LORD's temple, from the palace, and from the leaders, and gave them to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him.
Even in his time of trouble, King Ahaz was even more unfaithful to the LORD.

He offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, who had defeated him. He thought, "The gods of the kings of Syria helped them, so I will offer sacrifices to them so they will help me." But they caused his ruin and the ruin of all Israel.
Ahaz gathered the things from God's temple and cut them into pieces. He shut the doors of the LORD's temple and set up altars on every street corner in Jerusalem.
In every town in Judah he built hilltop shrines to burn incense to other gods. This made the LORD, the God of his ancestors, angry.
Everything else he did and all his ways, from beginning to end, are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz died and was buried in the city of Jerusalem, but not in the tombs of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah became king after him.
Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his ancestor David had done.
In the first month of the first year of his rule, he opened the doors of the LORD's temple and repaired them.
He brought in the priests and Levites and gathered them in the open square on the east side.
He said to them, "Listen to me, Levites! Make yourselves holy now, and make holy the temple of the LORD, the God of your ancestors. Take all the filth out of the holy place.
Our ancestors were unfaithful. They did evil in the eyes of the LORD our God and left him. They turned their faces away from the place where the LORD lives and turned their backs on him.
They shut the doors of the porch and put out the lamps. They did not burn incense or offer burnt offerings in the holy place to the God of Israel.
So the LORD has been angry with Judah and Jerusalem. He has made them something that frightens people, something they are shocked at and make fun of, as you can see with your own eyes.
That is why our fathers were killed in battle, and our sons, daughters, and wives have been taken as prisoners.
Now I have decided to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, so that his fierce anger will turn away from us.
My sons, do not be careless now. The LORD has chosen you to stand in front of him and serve him, to be his servants and to burn incense to him."

Then these Levites got ready to work. From the family of Kohath: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah. From the family of Merari: Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel. From the family of Gershon: Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah.
From the family of Elizaphan: Shimri and Jeuel. From the family of Asaph: Zechariah and Mattaniah.
From the family of Heman: Jehuel and Shimei. From the family of Jeduthun: Shemaiah and Uzziel.
They gathered their relatives, made themselves holy, and went in to clean the LORD's temple, as the king had ordered, following the LORD's words.

The priests went into the inner part of the LORD's temple to clean it. They brought out into the temple courtyard everything unclean they found in the LORD's temple. The Levites took it and carried it out to the Kidron Valley.

They began the work of making the temple holy on the first day of the first month. On the eighth day of the month they reached the LORD's porch. They spent eight more days making the LORD's temple holy, and they finished on the sixteenth day of the first month.

Then they went to King Hezekiah in the palace and said, "We have cleaned the whole temple of the LORD, the altar for burnt offerings with all its tools, and the table for the holy bread with all its things.
We have also prepared and made holy all the things King Ahaz threw away while he was king and unfaithful to God. Look, they are in front of the LORD's altar."
Early the next morning King Hezekiah gathered the city leaders and went up to the LORD's temple.

They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the temple, and for Judah. The king told the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to offer them on the LORD's altar.

So the priests killed the bulls, collected the blood, and sprinkled it on the altar. They killed the rams and sprinkled their blood on the altar. They killed the lambs and sprinkled their blood on the altar.
Then they brought the male goats for the sin offering to the king and the people, and they laid their hands on them.

The priests killed the goats and put their blood on the altar as a sin offering, to make all Israel right with God. The king had ordered that the burnt offering and the sin offering be made for all Israel.

Hezekiah placed the Levites in the LORD's temple with cymbals, harps, and lyres, as David, Gad the king's seer, and the prophet Nathan had commanded. This command came from the LORD through his prophets.
The Levites stood ready with David's instruments, and the priests with their trumpets.
Hezekiah ordered them to offer the burnt offering on the altar. As the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD also began, with trumpets and the instruments of David king of Israel.
All the people worshiped, the singers sang, and the trumpets played until the burnt offering was finished.
When the offerings were finished, the king and everyone with him bowed down and worshiped.
King Hezekiah and the leaders told the Levites to praise the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. So they sang praises with joy, and they bowed down and worshiped.

Then Hezekiah said, "Now you have given yourselves to the LORD. Come and bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the LORD's temple." So the people brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and everyone who wanted to brought burnt offerings.
The people brought seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. All these were burnt offerings to the LORD.
The other animals set apart as holy offerings were six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep.

But there were not enough priests to skin all the burnt offerings. So their relatives the Levites helped them until the work was done and until more priests had made themselves holy. The Levites had been more careful to make themselves holy than the priests.
There were many burnt offerings, along with the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings that went with each burnt offering. So the service of the LORD's temple was set up again.
Hezekiah and all the people were full of joy at what God had done for the people, because it had all happened so quickly.

Hezekiah sent messages to all Israel and Judah. He also wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting them to come to the LORD's temple in Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover for the LORD, the God of Israel.
The king, his leaders, and all the people in Jerusalem had agreed to celebrate the Passover in the second month.
They could not celebrate it at the normal time, because not enough priests had made themselves holy, and the people had not gathered in Jerusalem.
The plan seemed right to the king and to all the people.

So they decided to send an announcement all through Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, telling the people to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover for the LORD, the God of Israel. Many people had not celebrated it in the way the law says.

So messengers took letters from the king and his leaders all through Israel and Judah. As the king ordered, the letters said, "People of Israel, come back to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so he will come back to those of you who escaped from the kings of Assyria.
Do not be like your ancestors and your relatives, who were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their ancestors. He let them be destroyed, as you can see.
Do not be stubborn like your ancestors were. Give yourselves to the LORD. Come to his temple, which he has made holy forever. Serve the LORD your God, so his fierce anger will turn away from you.

If you come back to the LORD, the people who captured your relatives and children will show them mercy, and they will come back to this land. The LORD your God is kind and merciful. He will not turn his face away from you if you come back to him."
The messengers went from town to town through Ephraim and Manasseh, as far as Zebulun, but people laughed at them and made fun of them.
But some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
In Judah also, God's power made the people agree to obey what the king and leaders had ordered, following the LORD's word.
A very large crowd of people gathered in Jerusalem in the second month to celebrate the Festival of Bread Without Yeast.
They removed the altars in Jerusalem. They also took away all the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley.
They killed the Passover lambs on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and Levites were ashamed, so they made themselves holy and brought burnt offerings to the LORD's temple.
They took their places as the law of Moses, the man of God, required. The priests sprinkled the blood that the Levites handed to them.
Many people in the crowd had not made themselves holy. So the Levites killed the Passover lambs for everyone who was not clean, to make the lambs holy for the LORD.

Many of the people, especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not made themselves clean. Still they ate the Passover, which was not what the law says. But Hezekiah prayed for them: "May the good LORD forgive everyone
who sets their heart on seeking God, the LORD, the God of their ancestors, even if they are not clean by the rules of the temple."
The LORD listened to Hezekiah and healed the people.

The Israelites in Jerusalem celebrated the Festival of Bread Without Yeast for seven days with great joy. Every day the Levites and priests praised the LORD, singing with loud instruments to the LORD.

Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who understood well how to serve the LORD. For the seven days of the festival they ate their share, offered peace offerings, and gave thanks to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Then all the people agreed to celebrate for seven more days. So they celebrated another seven days with joy.
Hezekiah king of Judah gave the people one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for offerings. The leaders gave them one thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. Many priests made themselves holy.
All the people of Judah were full of joy, together with the priests and Levites, all the people who came from Israel, and the foreigners who came from Israel or lived in Judah.
There was great joy in Jerusalem. Nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the time of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.
Then the priests and Levites stood up and blessed the people. God heard them, and their prayer reached heaven, his holy home.

When all this was over, all the Israelites who were there went out to the towns of Judah. They smashed the stone pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and tore down the hilltop shrines and altars all through Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the Israelites went back to their own towns and their own land.

Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites into their groups, each with their own work. Some offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Others served, gave thanks, and sang praises at the gates of the LORD's temple.

The king gave animals from his own property for the burnt offerings: for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and for the burnt offerings on the Sabbaths, at the New Moon festivals, and at the other set festivals, as written in the LORD's law.
He also ordered the people living in Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their share, so they could give all their time to the LORD's law.

As soon as the order went out, the Israelites gave generously from the first part of their harvest: grain, new wine, olive oil, honey, and everything the fields produced. They brought a large amount, a tenth of everything.

The people of Israel and Judah who lived in the towns of Judah also brought a tenth of their cattle and sheep, and a tenth of the holy things set apart for the LORD their God. They piled them up in heaps.
They began making the heaps in the third month and finished in the seventh month.
When Hezekiah and the leaders came and saw the heaps, they praised the LORD and blessed his people Israel.
Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps.

Azariah the chief priest, from Zadok's family, answered, "Since the people began bringing their gifts to the LORD's temple, we have had enough to eat and plenty left over, because the LORD has blessed his people. This huge amount is what is left."
Then Hezekiah ordered them to prepare storerooms in the LORD's temple, and they did.
They faithfully brought in the gifts, the tenths, and the holy things. Conaniah the Levite was in charge of them, and his brother Shimei was second in charge.

Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were supervisors under Conaniah and his brother Shimei. King Hezekiah and Azariah, the official in charge of God's temple, appointed them.
Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the gatekeeper at the East Gate, was in charge of the gifts people chose to give to God. He handed out the gifts given to the LORD and the most holy things.
Under him were Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah. They worked faithfully in the towns of the priests, giving shares to their relatives by their groups, to old and young alike.
They also gave shares to the males three years old and older who were listed in the family records, everyone who went into the LORD's temple to do their daily work, by their groups and duties.
They gave shares to the priests listed by their families, and to the Levites twenty years old and older, by their duties and groups.
They also gave to the little children, wives, sons, and daughters listed in the family records of the whole community, because they had faithfully kept themselves holy.

For the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who lived in the farm lands around their towns, men were chosen by name in every town to give shares to every male among the priests and to everyone listed in the records of the Levites.
Hezekiah did this all through Judah. He did what was good, right, and faithful before the LORD his God.
Everything he started to do for the service of God's temple, and in obeying the law and commands, he did with all his heart to seek his God. And he was successful.
After Hezekiah had faithfully done all these things, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah. He camped outside the walled towns and planned to capture them.
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and planned to attack Jerusalem.
So he talked with his officials and military leaders about blocking off the water from the springs outside the city, and they helped him.
Many people gathered and blocked all the springs and the stream that flowed through the land. They said, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?"

Hezekiah worked hard to rebuild all the broken parts of the wall and built towers on it. He built another wall outside it and made the supporting terraces in the City of David stronger. He also made many weapons and shields.
He put army commanders over the people and gathered them in the open square at the city gate. He encouraged them, saying,
"Be strong and brave. Do not be afraid or discouraged because of the king of Assyria and the huge army with him. The one with us is greater than the one with him.
He only has human strength, but we have the LORD our God to help us and fight our battles." The people were encouraged by the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
Later, while Sennacherib king of Assyria and all his army were attacking Lachish, he sent his officers to Jerusalem with a message for Hezekiah king of Judah and all the people of Judah in Jerusalem.
It said, "Sennacherib king of Assyria says: What are you trusting in, that you stay in Jerusalem while it is surrounded?
Hezekiah is tricking you, so you will die of hunger and thirst. He says, 'The LORD our God will save us from the king of Assyria.'
Didn't Hezekiah himself remove the LORD's hilltop shrines and altars? Didn't he tell Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship at only one altar and burn incense on it'?
Don't you know what my ancestors and I have done to all the peoples of other lands? Were the gods of those nations able to save their land from me?
Not one of the gods of the nations my ancestors destroyed could save his people from me. So how could your God save you from me?

Don't let Hezekiah fool you or mislead you like this. Don't believe him. No god of any nation or kingdom has been able to save his people from me or my ancestors. How much less will your God save you from me!"
Sennacherib's officers said even more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah.

The king also wrote letters insulting the LORD, the God of Israel, and speaking against him. He wrote, "The gods of the other nations did not save their people from me, and the God of Hezekiah will not save his people from me either."
His officers shouted in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall. They wanted to scare them and frighten them so they could capture the city.
They talked about the God of Jerusalem as if he were like the gods of the other peoples of the world, which are only things made by human hands.
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed about this and cried out to heaven.

The LORD sent an angel who wiped out all the strong soldiers, the leaders, and the commanders in the camp of the king of Assyria. So Sennacherib went back to his own land in shame. When he went into the temple of his god, some of his own sons killed him there with a sword.
So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from Sennacherib king of Assyria and from all their other enemies. He gave them peace on every side.
Many people brought gifts to Jerusalem for the LORD, and valuable gifts for Hezekiah king of Judah. From then on, all the nations respected him greatly.
Around that time Hezekiah became sick and was about to die. He prayed to the LORD, and the LORD answered him and gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah was proud and did not show thanks for the kindness he had received. So the LORD was angry with him and with Judah and Jerusalem.
But then Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem humbled themselves and turned from their pride. So the LORD's anger did not come on them while Hezekiah was alive.
Hezekiah had great wealth and honor. He built treasure rooms for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuable things.
He also built storehouses for grain, new wine, and olive oil, stalls for all kinds of animals, and pens for flocks.
He built towns for himself and had huge numbers of flocks and herds, because God had made him very rich.
It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper spring of the Gihon and sent the water straight down to the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah was successful in everything he did.
But when the leaders of Babylon sent messengers to ask him about the amazing sign that had happened in the land, God left him alone to test him, to see everything that was in his heart.
Everything else Hezekiah did, and his acts of faithful love, are written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Hezekiah died and was buried on the hill where the tombs of David's descendants are. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem honored him when he died. His son Manasseh became king after him.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he ruled for fifty-five years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the LORD's eyes. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.
He rebuilt the hilltop shrines his father Hezekiah had torn down. He set up altars for the Baal gods and made Asherah poles. He bowed down to all the stars in the sky and worshiped them.
He built altars in the LORD's temple, the place the LORD had spoken about when he said, "My name will be in Jerusalem forever."
He built altars for all the stars in the sky in both courtyards of the LORD's temple.

He sacrificed his own sons in the fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. He practiced magic, fortune telling, and witchcraft, and he went to people who talk with the dead and with spirits. He did much evil in the LORD's eyes and made him angry.

He took the idol he had carved and put it in God's temple. God had said to David and his son Solomon about this temple, "In this temple, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever.

I will never again make the Israelites leave the land I gave their ancestors, if only they will be careful to obey everything I have commanded them, all the law, the rules, and the decisions given through Moses."
But Manasseh led the people of Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did even more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed ahead of the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen.
So the LORD brought the army commanders of the king of Assyria against them. They captured Manasseh, put a hook in his nose, bound him with bronze chains, and took him to Babylon.
In his trouble, Manasseh begged the LORD his God for help and humbled himself greatly before the God of his ancestors.
When he prayed, the LORD was moved by his prayer and listened to his request. He brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.

After this, Manasseh built an outer wall for the City of David, west of the Gihon spring in the valley, as far as the entrance of the Fish Gate. He built it around the hill of Ophel and made it very high. He also put army commanders in all the walled towns of Judah.
He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the LORD's temple. He also removed all the altars he had built on the temple hill and in Jerusalem, and threw them out of the city.
He rebuilt the LORD's altar and offered peace offerings and thank offerings on it. He told the people of Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.
The people still offered sacrifices at the hilltop shrines, but only to the LORD their God.
Everything else Manasseh did, his prayer to his God, and the words the seers spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, are written in the records of the kings of Israel.

His prayer and how God answered it, all his sins and unfaithfulness, and the places where he built hilltop shrines and set up Asherah poles and idols before he humbled himself, are all written in the records of the seers.
Manasseh died and was buried in his palace. His son Amon became king after him.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled for two years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the LORD's eyes, just as his father Manasseh had done. Amon offered sacrifices to all the idols his father Manasseh had made, and he worshiped them.
But he did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done. Instead, Amon sinned more and more.
His officials plotted against him and killed him in his palace.
But the people of the land killed everyone who had plotted against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah king after him.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he ruled for thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes. He followed the ways of his ancestor David and did not turn away from them to the right or to the left.

In the eighth year of his rule, while he was still young, he began to seek the God of his ancestor David. In the twelfth year he began to clean Judah and Jerusalem of the hilltop shrines, the Asherah poles, and the carved and metal idols.

While he watched, the people tore down the altars of the Baal gods. He cut down the incense altars above them. He smashed the Asherah poles and the carved and metal idols, crushed them to dust, and scattered the dust over the graves of those who had offered sacrifices to them.
He burned the bones of the priests on their own altars. In this way he made Judah and Jerusalem clean again.
He did the same in the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins around them.
He tore down the altars, crushed the Asherah poles and idols into powder, and cut down all the incense altars all over the land of Israel. Then he went back to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his rule, after he had cleaned the land and the temple, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city governor, and Joah son of Joahaz, the record keeper, to repair the temple of the LORD his God.

They went to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought to God's temple. The Levites who guarded the doors had collected it from the people of Manasseh, Ephraim, and the rest of Israel, and from all Judah, Benjamin, and the people of Jerusalem.
They gave it to the men in charge of the work on the LORD's temple. These men paid the workers who repaired and restored the temple.
They gave money to the carpenters and builders to buy cut stone, and wood for the supports and beams of the buildings the kings of Judah had let fall apart.

The men did the work faithfully. Their supervisors were Jahath and Obadiah, Levites from the family of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam from the family of Kohath. Other Levites, who were all skilled musicians,
were in charge of the workers who carried loads and directed all the workers in every job. Some Levites were secretaries, officials, and gatekeepers.
While they were bringing out the money that had been brought to the LORD's temple, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the LORD's law, given through Moses.
Hilkiah said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the book of the law in the LORD's temple." He gave the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan took the book to the king and reported to him: "Your officials are doing everything you told them to do.
They have emptied out the money that was in the LORD's temple and given it to the supervisors and the workers."
Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it to the king.
When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.
He gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah, the king's servant:

"Go and ask the LORD for me and for the people left in Israel and Judah about what is written in this book that was found. The LORD's anger against us is great, because our ancestors did not obey the LORD's word. They did not do everything written in this book."

So Hilkiah and the men the king had sent went to the prophet Huldah. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, who was in charge of the royal clothes. She lived in the newer part of Jerusalem. They told her what had happened.
She said to them, "The LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Tell the man who sent you to me,
"The LORD says: Look, I am going to bring disaster on this place and the people who live here, all the curses written in the book that was read to the king of Judah.

They have left me and burned incense to other gods. They have made me angry with all the idols they have made with their hands. So my anger will be poured out on this place, and it will not be put out."'
But tell the king of Judah, who sent you to ask the LORD, 'The LORD, the God of Israel, says this about the words you heard:

Your heart was soft, and you humbled yourself before God when you heard what he said against this place and its people. You humbled yourself before me, tore your clothes, and cried in front of me. So I have heard you, says the LORD.
Look, I will let you die in peace and be buried with your ancestors. You will not see all the disaster I am going to bring on this place and its people.'" So they took her answer back to the king.
Then the king called together all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem.

The king went up to the LORD's temple with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests, the Levites, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. He read aloud to them all the words of the book of the covenant that had been found in the LORD's temple.

The king stood in his place and made a covenant in front of the LORD. He promised to follow the LORD and to obey his commands, laws, and rules with all his heart and all his soul, and to do what the covenant written in this book said.
He made everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin promise to keep it too. So the people of Jerusalem obeyed the covenant of God, the God of their ancestors.

Josiah removed all the disgusting idols from all the lands that belonged to the Israelites. He made everyone in Israel serve the LORD their God. As long as he lived, they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Josiah celebrated the Passover for the LORD in Jerusalem. They killed the Passover lambs on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He gave the priests their duties and encouraged them in their work in the LORD's temple.

He said to the Levites, who taught all Israel and had been set apart for the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the temple that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built. You do not need to carry it on your shoulders any more. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.
Get ready by your families and groups, as David king of Israel and his son Solomon wrote down.
Stand in the holy place with a group of Levites for each family group of your relatives, the ordinary people.
Kill the Passover lambs, make yourselves holy, and prepare the lambs for your relatives, doing what the LORD commanded through Moses."

Josiah gave the people thirty thousand lambs and young goats from his own flocks for the Passover offerings, for everyone who was there. He also gave three thousand bulls. All these came from the king's own property.

His officials also gave freely to the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the officials in charge of God's temple, gave the priests two thousand six hundred lambs and goats and three hundred cattle for the Passover offerings.

Conaniah and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, and Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the leaders of the Levites, gave the Levites five thousand lambs and goats and five hundred cattle for the Passover offerings.
When everything was ready for the service, the priests stood in their places, and the Levites in their groups, as the king had ordered.
They killed the Passover lambs. The priests sprinkled the blood the Levites handed them, and the Levites skinned the animals.
They set aside the parts for burnt offerings to give to the people by their family groups, to offer to the LORD as written in the book of Moses. They did the same with the cattle.
They roasted the Passover lambs over the fire, as the law says. They boiled the holy offerings in pots, kettles, and pans, and quickly served them to all the people.

After that, the Levites prepared food for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the descendants of Aaron, were busy offering the burnt offerings and the fat until night. So the Levites prepared food for themselves and for the priests.

The singers, the descendants of Asaph, were in their places, as David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer had ordered. The gatekeepers stood at each gate. They did not need to leave their posts, because their relatives the Levites prepared food for them.
So on that day the whole service of the LORD was carried out, to celebrate the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the LORD's altar, as King Josiah had ordered.
The Israelites who were there celebrated the Passover at that time, and the Festival of Bread Without Yeast for seven days.

No Passover like this had been celebrated in Israel since the days of the prophet Samuel. None of the kings of Israel had ever celebrated a Passover like the one Josiah celebrated, with the priests, the Levites, all the people of Judah and Israel who were there, and the people of Jerusalem.
This Passover was celebrated in the eighteenth year of Josiah's rule.
After all this, when Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco king of Egypt went to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates River. Josiah went out to fight against him.

But Neco sent messengers to him, saying, "What do you have against me, king of Judah? I am not coming to attack you today, but the kingdom I am at war with. God has told me to hurry. Stop fighting against God, who is with me, or he will destroy you."
But Josiah would not turn back. He disguised himself to fight him. He did not listen to what Neco said, though the message came from God. He went to fight in the plain of Megiddo.
Archers shot King Josiah, and he told his officers, "Take me away. I am badly wounded!"

So his officers took him out of his chariot, put him in his other chariot, and brought him to Jerusalem. There he died and was buried in the tombs of his ancestors. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

Jeremiah wrote sad songs about Josiah. To this day, all the men and women singers still remember Josiah in their sad songs. These songs became a custom in Israel, and they are written in the book of Laments.
Everything else Josiah did, and his faithful acts in obeying what is written in the LORD's law,
all his acts from beginning to end, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
Then the people of the land took Josiah's son Jehoahaz and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he ruled for three months in Jerusalem.
The king of Egypt removed him from being king in Jerusalem. He made the land pay about three and a half tonnes of silver and thirty-four kilograms of gold.
The king of Egypt made Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim king over Judah and Jerusalem and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Neco took Jehoahaz, Eliakim's brother, to Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the eyes of the LORD his God.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon attacked him and bound him with bronze chains to take him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar also took some of the things from the LORD's temple to Babylon and put them in his temple there.
Everything else Jehoiakim did, the disgusting things he did, and all the evil found in him, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. His son Jehoiachin became king after him.
Jehoiachin was eight years old when he became king, and he ruled for three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did evil in the LORD's eyes.
In the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and brought him to Babylon, along with valuable things from the LORD's temple. He made Jehoiachin's relative Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke the LORD's words.
He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him promise in God's name to be loyal. He was stubborn and refused to turn back to the LORD, the God of Israel.

All the leaders of the priests and the people also became more and more unfaithful. They followed all the disgusting practices of the nations, and they made the LORD's temple unclean, the temple he had made holy in Jerusalem.
The LORD, the God of their ancestors, sent messages to them through his messengers again and again, because he had pity on his people and on the place where he lived.
But they made fun of God's messengers, hated his words, and laughed at his prophets. At last the LORD's anger rose against his people, and nothing could stop it.

So he brought the king of the Babylonians against them. He killed their young men with the sword in their holy temple. He had no pity on young men or young women, old people or the weak. God handed them all over to him.
He took to Babylon all the things from God's temple, large and small, the treasures of the LORD's temple, and the treasures of the king and his officials.
They burned God's temple and broke down the wall of Jerusalem. They burned all the palaces and destroyed everything of value.
He took the people who survived the sword away to Babylon. They became servants to him and his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power.
This made the LORD's word through Jeremiah come true. The land finally enjoyed its Sabbath rests. All the time it lay empty, it rested, until seventy years were complete.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD made the message he spoke through Jeremiah come true. The LORD moved the heart of Cyrus king of Persia to send out an announcement all through his kingdom, and to write it down. It said:

"Cyrus king of Persia says: 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has chosen me to build a temple for him in Jerusalem in Judah. Any of his people among you may go up there, and may the LORD their God be with them.'"
Ezra: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD made the message he spoke through Jeremiah come true. The LORD moved the heart of Cyrus king of Persia to send out an announcement all through his kingdom, and to write it down. It said:
"Cyrus king of Persia says: 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has chosen me to build a temple for him in Jerusalem in Judah.
Any of his people among you may go up to Jerusalem in Judah, and may their God be with them. Let them build the temple of the LORD, the God of Israel. He is the God who lives in Jerusalem.
Wherever any of his people are left living, the people of that place must help them with silver, gold, goods, and animals, as well as gifts they choose to give for God's temple in Jerusalem.'"
Then the family leaders of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites got ready to go up and build the LORD's temple in Jerusalem. They were everyone whose heart God had moved.
All their neighbors helped them by giving them things made of silver, gold, goods, animals, and valuable gifts, besides all the gifts people chose to give.
King Cyrus also brought out the things from the LORD's temple that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and put in the temple of his gods.
Cyrus king of Persia had Mithredath the treasurer bring them out. He counted them out to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah.
This is the list of them: thirty gold dishes, one thousand silver dishes, twenty-nine knives,
thirty gold bowls, four hundred ten matching silver bowls, and one thousand other items.
In all there were five thousand four hundred gold and silver items. Sheshbazzar brought all of them with him when the prisoners went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

These are the people of the province who came back from being prisoners. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken them away to Babylon. Now they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. This is the number of the men of Israel:
The descendants of Parosh, two thousand one hundred seventy-two.
The descendants of Shephatiah, three hundred seventy-two.
The descendants of Arah, seven hundred seventy-five.
The descendants of Pahath-Moab, through Jeshua and Joab, two thousand eight hundred twelve.
The descendants of Elam, one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
The descendants of Zattu, nine hundred forty-five.
The descendants of Zaccai, seven hundred sixty.
The descendants of Bani, six hundred forty-two.
The descendants of Bebai, six hundred twenty-three.
The descendants of Azgad, one thousand two hundred twenty-two.
The descendants of Adonikam, six hundred sixty-six.
The descendants of Bigvai, two thousand fifty-six.
The descendants of Adin, four hundred fifty-four.
The descendants of Ater, through Hezekiah, ninety-eight.
The descendants of Bezai, three hundred twenty-three.
The descendants of Jorah, one hundred twelve.
The descendants of Hashum, two hundred twenty-three.
The descendants of Gibbar, ninety-five.
The people of Bethlehem, one hundred twenty-three.
The men of Netophah, fifty-six.
The men of Anathoth, one hundred twenty-eight.
The descendants of Azmaveth, forty-two.
The people of Kiriath Arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, seven hundred forty-three.
The people of Ramah and Geba, six hundred twenty-one.
The men of Michmas, one hundred twenty-two.
The men of Bethel and Ai, two hundred twenty-three.
The people of Nebo, fifty-two.
The people of Magbish, one hundred fifty-six.
The descendants of the other Elam, one thousand two hundred fifty-four.
The descendants of Harim, three hundred twenty.
The people of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty-five.
The people of Jericho, three hundred forty-five.
The people of Senaah, three thousand six hundred thirty.
The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, from the family of Jeshua, nine hundred seventy-three.
The descendants of Immer, one thousand fifty-two.
The descendants of Pashhur, one thousand two hundred forty-seven.
The descendants of Harim, one thousand seventeen.
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, from the family of Hodaviah, seventy-four.
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, one hundred twenty-eight.
The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai, one hundred thirty-nine in all.
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
Keros, Siaha, Padon,
Lebanah, Hagabah, Akkub,
Hagab, Shamlai, Hanan,
Giddel, Gahar, Reaiah,
Rezin, Nekoda, Gazzam,
Uzza, Paseah, Besai,
Asnah, Meunim, Nephisim,
Bakbuk, Hakupha, Harhur,
Bazluth, Mehida, Harsha,
Barkos, Sisera, Temah,
Neziah, and Hatipha.
The descendants of Solomon's servants: the descendants of Sotai, Hassophereth, Peruda,
Jaalah, Darkon, Giddel,
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Ami.
All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants were three hundred ninety-two.
Some people came up from the towns of Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel.
They were the descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, six hundred fifty-two.
From the priests: the descendants of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai. This Barzillai had married a daughter of Barzillai from Gilead and took his family name.
They searched for their names in the family records, but they could not find them. So they were not allowed to serve as priests.
The governor told them not to eat the most holy food until there was a priest who could ask God using the Urim and Thummim.
The whole group together was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty people,
besides their seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven male and female servants. They also had two hundred men and women singers.
They had seven hundred thirty-six horses, two hundred forty-five mules,
four hundred thirty-five camels, and six thousand seven hundred twenty donkeys.
When they arrived at the LORD's temple in Jerusalem, some of the family leaders gave gifts to rebuild God's temple on its old site.
They gave as much as they could to the building fund: about five hundred kilograms of gold, about three tonnes of silver, and one hundred robes for the priests.
So the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants settled in their own towns, and all the rest of Israel lived in their towns.
When the seventh month came, the Israelites were living in their towns. Then all the people gathered together in Jerusalem as one.

Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his relatives, began to build the altar of the God of Israel. They wanted to offer burnt offerings on it, as written in the law of Moses, the man of God.
They were afraid of the people living in the lands around them, but they still built the altar on its old base. They offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD every morning and evening.
They celebrated the Festival of Shelters as the law says. Each day they offered the number of burnt offerings required for that day.
After that they offered the regular burnt offerings, the offerings for the New Moon festivals, and for all the LORD's holy festivals. They also offered the gifts people chose to give to the LORD.
They began offering burnt offerings to the LORD on the first day of the seventh month, even though the foundation of the LORD's temple had not yet been laid.

They gave money to the stoneworkers and carpenters. They gave food, drink, and olive oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre, so they would bring cedar logs by sea from Lebanon to Joppa. King Cyrus of Persia had given them permission for this.

In the second month of the second year after they arrived at God's temple site in Jerusalem, the work began. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, the rest of their fellow priests and Levites, and all who had come back to Jerusalem from being prisoners started the work. They chose Levites twenty years old and older to be in charge of the work on the LORD's temple.

Jeshua with his sons and relatives, and Kadmiel and his sons, descendants of Judah, joined together to be in charge of the workers on God's temple. The sons of Henadad and their sons and relatives, who were Levites, helped them.

When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD's temple, the priests stood in their robes with trumpets, and the Levites, the descendants of Asaph, stood with cymbals. They praised the LORD, as David king of Israel had directed.

They sang back and forth to each other, praising and thanking the LORD: "He is good. His love for Israel lasts forever." All the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the LORD's temple had been laid.
But many of the older priests, Levites, and family leaders who had seen the first temple cried out loud when they saw the foundation of this temple being laid. Many others shouted for joy.
No one could tell the difference between the shouts of joy and the sound of crying, because the people made so much noise. The sound was heard far away.
The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the people who had come back from being prisoners were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.

So they came to Zerubbabel and the family leaders and said, "Let us help you build, because we worship your God just as you do. We have been offering sacrifices to him since the time of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us here."

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other family leaders of Israel answered, "You have no part with us in building a temple for our God. We alone will build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus, the king of Persia, commanded us."
Then the people of the land tried to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.
They paid advisers to work against them and stop their plans. They did this the whole time Cyrus was king of Persia, until Darius became king of Persia.
At the beginning of the rule of Xerxes, they wrote an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
In the time of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their friends wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. It was written in Aramaic letters and in the Aramaic language.
Rehum the commanding officer and Shimshai the secretary wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes. It said this.
It was from Rehum the commanding officer, Shimshai the secretary, and their friends: the judges, officials, and leaders over the people from Erech, Babylon, Susa in Elam, and other places,
and the other peoples whom the great and famous Ashurbanipal moved and settled in the city of Samaria and in other places west of the Euphrates River.
This is a copy of the letter they sent: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the people west of the Euphrates River.
The king should know that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and evil city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.
The king should know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, they will stop paying taxes, payments, and fees, and the king's income will suffer.
Since we are loyal to the palace, we do not want to see the king dishonored. So we are sending to tell the king,

so that you can search the record books of your ancestors. In those books you will find that this city is a rebellious city that has caused trouble for kings and provinces. It has been a place of rebellion since long ago. That is why it was destroyed.
We are telling the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, you will have nothing left west of the Euphrates River."
Then the king sent this answer: "To Rehum the commanding officer, Shimshai the secretary, and their friends living in Samaria and in the rest of the land west of the Euphrates River: Greetings.
The letter you sent us has been translated and read to me.
I gave an order, and a search was made. It was found that this city has rebelled against kings since long ago. It has been a place of rebellion and revolt.
Powerful kings have ruled over Jerusalem and all the land west of the Euphrates River, and taxes, payments, and fees were paid to them.
So now give an order to make these men stop. This city must not be rebuilt until I give the order.
Be careful not to neglect this. Why let this danger grow and harm the kings?"
As soon as a copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the secretary, and their friends, they hurried to the Jews in Jerusalem and forced them to stop.
So the work on God's temple in Jerusalem stopped. It stayed stopped until the second year of the rule of Darius king of Persia.
Then the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo spoke God's messages to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. They spoke in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them.
So Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak started again to build God's temple in Jerusalem. The prophets of God were with them, helping them.

At that time Tattenai, the governor of the land west of the Euphrates River, Shethar-Bozenai, and their friends came to them and asked, "Who gave you permission to rebuild this temple and finish this wall?"
They also asked, "What are the names of the men working on this building?"
But God was watching over the leaders of the Jews. So the officials did not stop them until a report could be sent to Darius and an answer came back in a letter.
This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai, the governor of the land west of the Euphrates River, Shethar-Bozenai, and their friends, the officials west of the river, sent to King Darius.
The report they sent said: "To King Darius: Greetings and peace.

The king should know that we went to the province of Judah, to the temple of the great God. It is being built with large stones, and wooden beams are being put in the walls. The work is being done with great care and is going well.
We asked the leaders, 'Who gave you permission to rebuild this temple and finish this wall?'
We also asked their names, so that we could write down the names of their leaders for you.
This is the answer they gave us: 'We are servants of the God of heaven and earth. We are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago. A great king of Israel built it and finished it.
But our ancestors made the God of heaven angry, so he handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian, king of Babylon. He destroyed this temple and took the people away to Babylon.
But in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, King Cyrus gave an order to rebuild this temple of God.

King Cyrus also took out of the temple in Babylon the gold and silver things from God's temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to the temple in Babylon. He gave them to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor.
Cyrus told him, "Take these things and put them back in the temple in Jerusalem. Rebuild God's temple on its old site."
So Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of God's temple in Jerusalem. Since then it has been under construction, but it is not finished yet.'
