Esther still had not told anyone who her family or her people were, just as Mordecai had told her. She kept obeying Mordecai just as she had when he was raising her.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's officials who guarded the door, Bigthan and Teresh, became angry and planned to kill King Xerxes.
Mordecai found out about the plan and told Queen Esther. Esther told the king, and she said that Mordecai had found it out.
The report was checked and found to be true, so the two officials were hanged on a pole. All this was written down in the book of records in front of the king.
After these things, King Xerxes promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He gave him a higher position than all the other officials.
All the king's officials at the king's gate bowed down and honored Haman, because the king had ordered it. But Mordecai would not bow down or honor him.
The king's officials at the gate asked Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's order?"
Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen. So they told Haman about it, to see whether Mordecai's reason would be accepted, because he had told them he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or honor him, he was furious.
But he did not want to punish only Mordecai. He had been told who Mordecai's people were. So Haman looked for a way to destroy all of Mordecai's people, the Jews, all through the kingdom of Xerxes.

In the first month, the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Xerxes, they threw the pur, which means the lot, in front of Haman, to choose a day and a month. The lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

Then Haman said to King Xerxes, "There is a certain people scattered among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their customs are different from everyone else's, and they do not obey the king's laws. It is not good for the king to let them live.
If it pleases the king, let an order be written to destroy them. I will pay about three hundred forty tonnes of silver to the men in charge of the king's business, to put into the royal treasury."
So the king took his signet ring off his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "Keep the money, and do whatever you want with the people."

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's secretaries were called. They wrote down all of Haman's orders to the king's governors, to the rulers of each province, and to the officials of each people. They wrote to each province in its own writing and to each people in their own language. It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the king's ring.

Messengers took the letters to all the king's provinces. The orders were to destroy, kill, and wipe out all the Jews, young and old, little children and women, on a single day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, and to take everything they owned.
A copy of the order was to be made law in every province and announced to all the peoples, so they would be ready for that day.
At the king's command, the messengers hurried out, and the order was announced in the fortress city of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was confused and upset.
When Mordecai found out everything that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and covered himself with ashes. He went out into the city, crying loudly and bitterly.
He went only as far as the king's gate, because no one dressed in sackcloth was allowed to go through it.
In every province where the king's order arrived, the Jews mourned greatly. They went without food, cried, and wailed. Many of them lay on sackcloth and ashes.
Esther's servant girls and officials came and told her about Mordecai. The queen was very upset. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, but he would not take them.
Then Esther called Hathach, one of the king's officials whom the king had chosen to serve her. She told him to go to Mordecai and find out what was wrong and why.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king's gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened. He told him the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasury for killing the Jews.

He also gave him a copy of the order to destroy the Jews, which had been announced in Susa, to show to Esther and explain to her. He told Hathach to urge her to go to the king, to beg him for mercy, and to plead with him for her people.
Hathach went back and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther told Hathach to give Mordecai this message:

"All the king's officials and the people of the king's provinces know this law: anyone, man or woman, who goes to the king in the inner courtyard without being called must be put to death. The only exception is if the king holds out his gold scepter to that person. Then their life is spared. And I have not been called to go to the king for thirty days."
They told Mordecai what Esther had said.
Then Mordecai sent back this answer to Esther: "Do not think that because you are in the king's palace, you will escape when all the other Jews are killed.

If you keep quiet at a time like this, help and rescue for the Jews will come from somewhere else, but you and your father's family will die. Who knows? Maybe you became queen for a time just like this."
Then Esther sent this answer to Mordecai:

"Go and gather all the Jews in Susa. Go without food for me. Do not eat or drink anything for three days, night or day. My servant girls and I will also go without food. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I die, I die."
So Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had told him.
On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner courtyard of the palace, facing the king's hall. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the hall, facing the entrance.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the courtyard, he was pleased with her. He held out to her the gold scepter that was in his hand. So Esther came near and touched the tip of the scepter.
Then the king asked her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What do you want? I will give it to you, even up to half of my kingdom."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to a dinner I have prepared for the king."
The king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so we can do what Esther asks." So the king and Haman went to the dinner Esther had prepared.
While they were drinking wine, the king asked Esther again, "What do you want? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half of my kingdom, it will be done."
Esther answered, "This is what I want and what I ask.

If the king is pleased with me, and if it pleases the king to give me what I want and do what I ask, let the king and Haman come tomorrow to the dinner I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king's question."
Haman left that day happy and in high spirits. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, and Mordecai did not stand up or show any fear of him, Haman was filled with anger against Mordecai.
But Haman controlled himself and went home. He called together his friends and his wife Zeresh.

Haman bragged to them about how rich he was and how many sons he had. He told them all the ways the king had honored him and how he had been promoted above the other officials and servants of the king.
Haman added, "And that's not all. Queen Esther invited no one but me to come with the king to the dinner she gave. And she has invited me again tomorrow with the king.
But none of this makes me happy as long as I see that Jew Mordecai sitting at the king's gate."

Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Have a pole set up, twenty-three meters high. In the morning, ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the dinner and be happy." Haman liked the idea, and he had the pole set up.
That night the king could not sleep. So he ordered the book of records to be brought and read to him.
It was found written there how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's officials who guarded the door, who had planned to kill King Xerxes.
The king asked, "What honor and reward was given to Mordecai for this?" The king's servants who were with him answered, "Nothing has been done for him."
The king asked, "Who is in the courtyard?" Haman had just come into the outer courtyard of the palace to ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on the pole he had set up for him.
The king's servants told him, "Haman is standing in the courtyard." The king said, "Let him come in."
When Haman came in, the king asked him, "What should be done for the man the king wants to honor?" Haman thought to himself, "Who would the king want to honor more than me?"
So he answered the king, "For the man the king wants to honor,
let them bring a royal robe the king has worn, and a horse the king has ridden, with a royal crown on its head.

Let the robe and the horse be given to one of the king's most important officials. Let him dress the man the king wants to honor, lead him on the horse through the city square, and shout ahead of him, 'This is what is done for the man the king wants to honor!'"
The king said to Haman, "Hurry. Take the robe and the horse, just as you said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Do not leave out anything you have said."
So Haman took the robe and the horse. He dressed Mordecai and led him on the horse through the city square, shouting ahead of him, "This is what is done for the man the king wants to honor!"
Afterward Mordecai went back to the king's gate. But Haman hurried home, sad and covering his head in shame.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His wise advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, "You have started to fall before Mordecai. Since he is a Jew, you cannot win against him. You will surely be ruined."
While they were still talking with him, the king's officials arrived and hurried Haman off to the dinner Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman went to dinner with Queen Esther.

On this second day, while they were drinking wine, the king asked Esther again, "What do you want, Queen Esther? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half of my kingdom, it will be done."
Queen Esther answered, "My king, if you are pleased with me, and if it pleases you, please spare my life. This is what I want. And please spare my people. This is what I ask.

My people and I have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out. If we had only been sold as slaves, men and women, I would have kept quiet. But no enemy could ever make up for the loss this would bring to the king."
King Xerxes asked Queen Esther, "Who is he? Where is the man who dared to do such a thing?"
Esther said, "The enemy and attacker is this evil man Haman!" Then Haman was terrified in front of the king and queen.
The king got up from the wine in a rage and went out into the palace garden. But Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, because he saw that the king had already decided to punish him.

Just as the king came back from the palace garden into the dining hall, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was lying. The king shouted, "Will he even attack the queen while I am right here in the palace?" As soon as the king said this, servants covered Haman's face.

Then Harbonah, one of the officials serving the king, said, "Look, there is a pole twenty-three meters high standing at Haman's house. He set it up for Mordecai, the man who spoke up to save the king." The king said, "Hang him on it!"
So they hanged Haman on the pole he had set up for Mordecai. Then the king's anger calmed down.
That same day King Xerxes gave Queen Esther everything Haman, the enemy of the Jews, had owned. Mordecai came before the king, because Esther had told the king how he was related to her.
The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther put Mordecai in charge of everything Haman had owned.
Esther spoke to the king again. She fell at his feet and cried, begging him to stop the evil plan of Haman the Agagite, the plan he had made against the Jews.
The king held out the gold scepter to Esther. So she got up and stood in front of the king.

She said, "If it pleases the king, if he is pleased with me, if he thinks it is right, and if I please him, let an order be written to cancel the letters Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite wrote. He wrote them to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.
How can I bear to see disaster come on my people? How can I bear to see my family destroyed?"
King Xerxes said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Look, I have given Esther everything Haman owned, and they have hanged him on the pole because he attacked the Jews.
Now you write another order in the king's name about the Jews, whatever seems best to you. Seal it with the king's ring. No order written in the king's name and sealed with his ring can be canceled."

So right away the king's secretaries were called. It was the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan. They wrote down everything Mordecai ordered for the Jews. They wrote to the governors, rulers, and officials of the one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. They wrote to each province in its own writing and to each people in their own language, and to the Jews in their own writing and language.
Mordecai wrote in the name of King Xerxes and sealed the letters with the king's ring. He sent them by messengers riding fast horses bred for the king's service.

In these letters the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives. They could destroy, kill, and wipe out any armed force of any people or province that attacked them, their children, and their women. They could also take the property of their enemies.
This was to happen on one day in all the provinces of King Xerxes, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the order was to be made law in every province and announced to all the peoples, so the Jews would be ready on that day to fight back against their enemies.
The messengers rode out quickly on the royal horses, hurried by the king's command. The order was also announced in the fortress city of Susa.
Mordecai left the king's presence wearing royal clothes of blue and white, a large gold crown, and a purple robe of fine linen. The city of Susa shouted for joy.
For the Jews it was a time of light, happiness, joy, and honor.

In every province and every city where the king's order arrived, the Jews were happy and joyful. They held feasts and celebrated. Many people of other nations became Jews, because they were afraid of the Jews.

The king's order was to be carried out on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. On that day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to defeat them. But things turned around, and the Jews defeated those who hated them.
The Jews gathered in their cities in all the provinces of King Xerxes to attack those who wanted to harm them. No one could stand against them, because all the peoples were afraid of them.
All the officials of the provinces, the governors, the rulers, and the king's officers helped the Jews, because they were afraid of Mordecai.
Mordecai was very important in the palace. His fame spread all through the provinces, and he became more and more powerful.
The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did whatever they wanted to those who hated them.
In the fortress city of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not take any of their property.
That same day the number of people killed in the fortress city of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "The Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman in the fortress city of Susa. What must they have done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what do you want? It will be given to you. What else do you ask? It will be done."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa do again tomorrow what today's order allows. And let the bodies of Haman's ten sons be hanged on the pole."
So the king ordered it to be done. An order was announced in Susa, and they hanged the bodies of Haman's ten sons.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, and they killed three hundred men in Susa. But they did not take any of their property.

Meanwhile, the other Jews in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives and get rest from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not take any of their property.
This happened on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. On the fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews in Susa had gathered on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, so on the fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.

That is why the Jews who live in villages and towns without walls celebrate the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting. It is a holiday when they send gifts of food to each other.
Mordecai wrote down these events. He sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Xerxes, near and far.
He told them to celebrate the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar every year.

These were the days when the Jews got rest from their enemies. It was the month when their sadness turned into joy and their mourning into a holiday. He told them to celebrate these days with feasting and joy, sending gifts of food to each other and giving gifts to the poor.
So the Jews agreed to keep on doing what they had started, as Mordecai had written to them.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had made a plan to destroy the Jews. He had thrown the pur, which means the lot, to crush and destroy them.
But when the king found out about it, he sent out written orders that Haman's evil plan against the Jews should come back on his own head. So Haman and his sons were hanged on the pole.
That is why these days are called Purim, from the word pur. Because of everything written in Mordecai's letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them,

the Jews decided to make it a custom for themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them. Every year, without fail, they would celebrate these two days at the right time, in the way that was written.

These days were to be remembered and celebrated in every generation, by every family, in every province, and in every city. These days of Purim were never to stop being celebrated by the Jews, and their descendants were never to forget them.
Then Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Xerxes.

The letters confirmed the days of Purim at their set times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had ordered, and as the Jews had set for themselves and their descendants, including their times of going without food and mourning.
Esther's order confirmed these rules about Purim, and it was written down in the records.
King Xerxes made the people of the whole land and the islands of the sea pay taxes.
Everything he did by his power and strength, and the full story of how great Mordecai became when the king promoted him, are written in the book of the records of the kings of Media and Persia.

Mordecai the Jew was second in power only to King Xerxes. He was important among the Jews and well liked by all his fellow Jews, because he worked for the good of his people and spoke up for the peace and safety of all their descendants.
Job: There was a man named Job who lived in the land of Uz. He was a good man with no fault in him. He was honest, he respected God, and he stayed away from evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters.

He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred pairs of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys. He also had a very large number of servants. He was the greatest man among all the people of the East.
Job's sons took turns holding feasts in their homes, each on his special day. They would invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children and make them clean before God. He would get up early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each of them. Job thought, "Maybe my children have sinned and turned against God in their hearts." Job did this every time.
One day the angels came to stand before the LORD, and Satan, the accuser, came with them.
The LORD asked Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD, "From wandering around the earth, going back and forth across it."
Then the LORD said to Satan, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him. He is a good man with no fault in him. He is honest, he respects God, and he stays away from evil."
Satan answered the LORD, "Does Job respect God for no reason?
You have put a wall of protection around him, his family, and everything he owns. You have blessed everything he does, and his flocks and herds have spread all over the land.
But reach out your hand and take away everything he has, and he will curse you to your face."
The LORD said to Satan, "All right. Everything he has is in your power, but do not lay a finger on Job himself." Then Satan left the LORD's presence.
One day Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at the home of their oldest brother.
A messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were eating grass nearby.
Then the Sabeans attacked and took them away. They killed the servants with swords, and I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "Fire from God fell from the sky. It burned up the sheep and the servants. I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"

While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups, attacked the camels, and took them away. They killed the servants with swords, and I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine at their oldest brother's house.
Suddenly a strong wind blew in from the desert and hit the four corners of the house. It fell on the young people, and they are dead. I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"
Then Job got up and tore his robe and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped.
He said, "I had nothing when I was born, and I will have nothing when I die. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Praise the name of the LORD."
In all this, Job did not sin or blame God for doing wrong.
On another day the angels came to stand before the LORD, and Satan came with them to stand before the LORD too.
The LORD asked Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD, "From wandering around the earth, going back and forth across it."

Then the LORD said to Satan, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him. He is a good man with no fault in him. He is honest, he respects God, and he stays away from evil. He is still faithful, even though you talked me into letting you ruin him for no reason."
Satan answered the LORD, "Skin for skin! A man will give up everything he has to save his own life.
But reach out your hand and hurt his body, his bones and flesh, and he will curse you to your face."
The LORD said to Satan, "All right. He is in your power. But you must spare his life."
So Satan left the LORD's presence and struck Job with painful sores from the bottom of his feet to the top of his head.
Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself, and he sat among the ashes.
His wife said to him, "Are you still holding on to your faithfulness? Curse God and die!"
But Job answered, "You are talking like a foolish woman. Should we accept only good things from God and not trouble?" In all this, Job did not sin in anything he said.

Job had three friends: Eliphaz from Teman, Bildad from Shuah, and Zophar from Naamah. When they heard about all the trouble that had come to Job, each of them left his home. They agreed to meet together and go to show Job their sympathy and comfort him.
When they saw Job from far away, they could hardly recognize him. They began to cry out loud. They tore their robes and threw dust into the air and onto their heads.
Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.
After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day he was born.
Job said:
"Let the day I was born be wiped out, and the night that said, 'A boy is coming!'
Let that day turn into darkness. Let God above not care about it. Let no light shine on it.
Let darkness and deep shadow take it back. Let a cloud settle over it. Let blackness frighten it away.
Let thick darkness grab that night. Let it not be counted among the days of the year. Let it not be part of any month.
Let that night be empty. Let no shout of joy be heard in it.
Let those who curse days curse it, those who are ready to wake up the sea monster Leviathan.
Let its morning stars stay dark. Let it wait for light that never comes. Let it never see the first rays of dawn.
It did not close my mother's womb to keep me from being born, and it did not hide trouble from my eyes.
Why didn't I die at birth? Why didn't I die as I came from my mother's body?
Why was there a lap to hold me, and breasts to feed me?
If I had died then, I would be lying down in peace. I would be asleep and at rest,
with kings and their advisers, who built great buildings that are now ruins,
or with rulers who had gold and filled their houses with silver.
Why wasn't I buried like a baby born dead, like a baby that never saw the light?
In death the wicked stop causing trouble, and the tired find rest.
Prisoners rest together there. They no longer hear the shouts of the slave driver.
The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.
Why does God give light to those who suffer, and life to those whose hearts are bitter?
They long for death, but it does not come. They search for it more than for hidden treasure.
They would be filled with joy and glad to reach the grave.
Why give light to a man who cannot see where he is going, whom God has fenced in?
My sighs are my food, and my groans pour out like water.
What I was afraid of has come on me. What I dreaded has happened to me.
I have no peace, no quiet, and no rest. Only trouble comes."
Then Eliphaz from Teman answered:
"If someone tries to speak to you, will it upset you? But who can keep quiet?
Think how you have taught many people. You have made weak hands strong.
Your words have helped up those who were falling. You have made weak knees strong.
But now trouble has come to you, and you are discouraged. It touches you, and you are terrified.
Shouldn't your respect for God give you confidence? Shouldn't your honest life give you hope?
Think about it. Has an innocent person ever been destroyed? When have honest people ever been wiped out?
From what I have seen, those who plow evil and plant trouble harvest the same.
God breathes on them and they die. The blast of his anger wipes them out.
The lion may roar and the fierce lion may growl, but the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The old lion dies because it has nothing to hunt, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
A message was brought to me secretly. My ears heard a whisper of it.
It came in troubling dreams at night, when people are in a deep sleep.
Fear and trembling took hold of me, and all my bones shook.
A spirit passed in front of my face, and the hair on my body stood up.
It stopped, but I could not tell what it looked like. A shape stood in front of my eyes. There was silence, and then I heard a voice say,
'Can a human be more right than God? Can a person be more pure than the one who made him?
Look, God does not trust even his servants. He finds fault even with his angels.
How much more with people who live in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, who can be crushed like a moth!
Between morning and evening they are broken to pieces. They die forever, and no one even notices.
Their tent ropes are pulled up, and they die without ever gaining wisdom.'
Call out if you want, but who will answer you? Which of the holy angels will you turn to?
Anger kills a foolish person, and jealousy kills a simple one.
I have seen a foolish person putting down roots, but suddenly I saw his home cursed.
His children are far from safety. They are crushed in court, and no one rescues them.
Hungry people eat up his harvest, taking it even from among the thorns. Thirsty people long for his wealth.
Trouble does not grow out of the dust, and hardship does not sprout from the ground.
But people are born for trouble, as surely as sparks fly upward.
If I were you, I would turn to God. I would bring my case to him.
He does great things that no one can understand, more amazing things than anyone can count.
He sends rain on the earth and water on the fields.
He lifts up those who are low, and lifts those who mourn to safety.
He ruins the plans of tricky people, so their hands do not succeed.
He catches the wise in their own tricks, and the plans of clever people are quickly swept away.
They run into darkness in the daytime. At noon they feel their way as if it were night.
He saves the needy from the sword of their mouths and from the power of the strong.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
How happy is the person God corrects! So do not refuse the training of the Almighty.
He hurts, but he also bandages the wound. He injures, but his hands also heal.
He will rescue you from six troubles. Even in seven, no harm will touch you.
In a famine he will save you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be protected from the whip of the tongue. You will not be afraid when destruction comes.
You will laugh at destruction and hunger, and you will not be afraid of wild animals.
You will have an agreement with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
You will know that your home is safe. When you check your property, nothing will be missing.
You will know that you will have many children. Your descendants will be like the grass of the earth.
You will come to your grave at a ripe old age, like grain gathered in at harvest time.
Look, we have studied this, and it is true. So listen and learn it for your own good."
Then Job answered:
"If only my pain could be weighed, and all my troubles put on a scale!
They would be heavier than all the sand of the seas. That is why my words have been wild.
The arrows of the Almighty are stuck in me, and my spirit drinks their poison. God's terrors are lined up against me.
Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass? Does an ox moan when it has food?
Can you eat food that has no taste without salt? Is there any flavor in the white of an egg?
I refuse to touch such things. They make me sick.
If only I could have what I ask for! If only God would give me what I long for,
that God would be willing to crush me, that he would reach out his hand and cut off my life!
Then I would still have this comfort, and I would jump for joy even in unending pain: I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What strength do I have, that I should keep hoping? What future do I have, that I should be patient?
Am I as strong as stone? Is my body made of bronze?
I have no power to help myself, and any chance of success has been taken from me.
A person who is about to give up should get kindness from his friends, even if he stops respecting the Almighty.
But my brothers have been as untrustworthy as a stream, as streams that run dry.
In winter they are dark with ice and hidden under snow.
But in the dry season they disappear. When it is hot, they vanish from their beds.
Travelers turn aside from their paths to find them. They go out into the desert and die.
The travelers from Tema look for water. The traders from Sheba hope to find it.
They are disappointed because they trusted. They get there and are confused.
Now you are just like those streams. You see something terrible and become afraid.
Have I ever said, 'Give me something,' or 'Pay something for me from your wealth'?
Have I said, 'Rescue me from my enemy,' or 'Save me from cruel people'?
Teach me, and I will be quiet. Show me what I have done wrong.
Honest words are powerful! But what does your arguing prove?
Do you want to correct what I say, and treat the words of a hopeless man as wind?
You would even throw lots for orphans and sell your friend.
Now please look at me. I would not lie to your face.
Please stop. Do not be unfair. Think again, because my innocence is at stake.
Is there anything evil on my lips? Can't I taste what is wrong?
Isn't life on earth hard work for everyone? Aren't our days like the days of a hired worker?
Like a slave who longs for the evening shade, like a worker waiting for his pay,
I have been given months of misery and long nights of suffering.
When I lie down, I think, 'When will I get up? When will the night be over?' I toss and turn until dawn.
My body is covered with worms and scabs. My skin is cracked and oozing.
My days go by faster than a weaver's shuttle, and they come to an end without hope.
Remember, God, that my life is only a breath. I will never see happiness again.
Those who see me now will not see me again. You will look for me, but I will be gone.
As a cloud fades away and is gone, so a person who goes down to the grave does not come back up.
He will never come home again, and his own house will not know him any more.
So I will not keep quiet. I will speak out of the pain in my spirit. I will complain out of the bitterness in my soul.
Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you must put a guard over me?
When I think, 'My bed will comfort me, and my couch will ease my complaint,'
then you frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions.
I would rather be strangled. I would rather die than live in this body.
I hate my life. I do not want to live forever. Leave me alone, because my days are only a breath.
What are people that you make so much of them, that you pay so much attention to them?
You check on them every morning and test them every moment.
Will you never look away from me? Won't you leave me alone even long enough to swallow?
If I have sinned, what have I done to you, you who watch over people? Why have you made me your target? Why have I become a burden to you?
Why don't you forgive my wrongs and take away my sins? Soon I will lie down in the dust. You will search for me, but I will be gone."
Then Bildad from Shuah answered:
"How long will you go on talking like this? Your words are like a strong wind.
Does God twist what is fair? Does the Almighty twist what is right?
When your children sinned against him, he gave them the punishment their sin deserved.
But if you will look to God and beg the Almighty for mercy,
if you are pure and honest, he will surely get up to help you and give you back your rightful home.
Even though you started with little, you will end up with much more.
Ask the people who lived before us. Find out what their ancestors learned.
We were only born yesterday and know nothing. Our days on earth are like a shadow.
Won't they teach you and tell you? Won't they share the wisdom of their hearts?
Can papyrus grow tall where there is no marsh? Can reeds grow without water?
While they are still green and not yet cut, they dry up faster than any other plant.
That is what happens to everyone who forgets God. The hope of godless people dies.
What they trust in breaks apart. Their confidence is as weak as a spider's web.
They lean on their web, but it gives way. They hold on to it, but it does not last.
They are like a well-watered plant in the sunshine, spreading its shoots over the garden.
Its roots wrap around a pile of rocks and grip the stones.
But when it is torn from its place, that place denies it and says, 'I never saw you.'
That is the end of its joy, and other plants spring up from the ground in its place.
Look, God does not reject a person with no fault, and he does not help evil people.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be covered with shame, and the homes of the wicked will be gone."
Then Job answered:
"Yes, I know that this is true. But how can a person be right with God?
If someone wanted to argue with God, he could not answer God even once in a thousand times.
God is very wise and very strong. Who has ever fought against him and won?
He moves mountains before they know it, and turns them over in his anger.
He shakes the earth from its place and makes its pillars tremble.
He commands the sun, and it does not rise. He hides the light of the stars.
He alone spreads out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea.
He made the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades, and the star groups of the south.
He does great things no one can understand, more amazing things than anyone can count.
When he passes by me, I cannot see him. When he goes past, I do not notice him.
If he takes something away, who can stop him? Who can say to him, 'What are you doing?'
God does not hold back his anger. Even the helpers of the monster Rahab bow down under him.
So how could I answer him? How could I choose words to argue with him?
Even if I were in the right, I could not answer him. I could only beg my judge for mercy.
Even if I called and he answered me, I do not believe he would listen to me.
He crushes me with a storm and gives me more and more wounds for no reason.
He does not let me catch my breath, but fills me with bitterness.
If it is a question of strength, he is the strongest! If it is a question of justice, who can call him to court?
Even if I were innocent, my own mouth would prove me guilty. Even if I had no fault, it would prove me wrong.
I have no fault, but I do not care about myself. I hate my life.
It is all the same, so I say, 'He destroys both the innocent and the wicked.'
When disaster suddenly kills people, he laughs at the suffering of the innocent.
When a land falls into the hands of the wicked, he covers the eyes of its judges. If it is not God who does this, then who is it?
My days go by faster than a runner. They fly away without seeing any happiness.
They pass by like fast boats made of reeds, like an eagle swooping down on its prey.
If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, change my sad face, and smile,'
I still dread all my suffering, because I know you will not hold me innocent.
I will be found guilty anyway, so why should I struggle for nothing?
Even if I washed myself with snow and cleaned my hands with soap,
you would throw me into a muddy pit, and even my own clothes would hate me.
God is not a human like me, so I cannot answer him or meet him in court.
If only there were someone to judge between us, to put his hand on both of us.
If only someone would take God's rod away from me, so his terror would no longer frighten me.
Then I would speak without being afraid of him. But as things are, I cannot."
I am tired of living. I will let my complaint pour out. I will speak out of the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God, 'Do not just declare me guilty. Tell me what charges you have against me.
Does it please you to crush me, to reject me, the work of your own hands, while you smile on the plans of the wicked?
Do you have human eyes? Do you see things the way people do?
Is your life as short as a human life? Are your years like ours,
that you must search for my wrongs and hunt for my sins?
You know that I am not guilty, but no one can rescue me from your hand.
Your hands shaped me and made me. Will you now turn around and destroy me?
Please remember that you shaped me like clay. Will you now turn me back into dust?
You poured me out like milk and made me thick like cheese.
You dressed me with skin and flesh, and wove me together with bones and muscles.
You gave me life and showed me your faithful love. Your care has kept my spirit alive.
But you hid this plan in your heart. I know this was what you intended:
if I sinned, you would be watching me, and you would not let my sin go unpunished.
If I am guilty, how terrible for me! Even if I am innocent, I cannot lift my head, because I am full of shame and drowning in my suffering.
If I hold my head up, you hunt me like a lion. Again you show your amazing power against me.
You keep bringing new witnesses against me. Your anger against me grows. Your armies attack me wave after wave.
Why did you let me be born? I wish I had died before anyone saw me.
I wish I had never existed, but had been carried straight from the womb to the grave.
My life is almost over. So stop! Leave me alone, so I can have a little comfort
before I go to the place from which I will never come back, the land of darkness and deep shadow,
the land of deepest night, of deep shadow and confusion, where even the light is like darkness.'"
Then Zophar from Naamah answered:
"Shouldn't all these words be answered? Is someone who talks so much proved right?
Should your bragging make people keep quiet? When you make fun of God, shouldn't someone make you ashamed?
You say to God, 'What I believe is pure, and I am clean in your sight.'
But oh, how I wish God would speak and open his mouth against you!
I wish he would show you the secrets of wisdom, because true wisdom has two sides. Know this: God is punishing you less than your sin deserves.
Can you understand the deep things of God? Can you discover the limits of the Almighty?
They are higher than the heavens. What can you do? They are deeper than the grave. What can you know?
They are longer than the earth and wider than the sea.
If God comes along and puts someone in prison and calls him to court, who can stop him?
He knows who is false. When he sees evil, doesn't he take note of it?
A foolish person will become wise when a wild donkey gives birth to a human.
But if you give your heart to God and lift your hands to him in prayer,
if you put away the sin that is in your hand and do not let evil live in your home,
then you will be able to lift your face without shame. You will stand firm and not be afraid.
You will forget your trouble. You will remember it only like water that has flowed away.
Your life will be brighter than noon. Even darkness will be like morning.
You will feel safe, because there is hope. You will look around and rest in safety.
You will lie down, and no one will frighten you. Many people will want your favor.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail. They will have no way to escape. Their only hope will be death."
Then Job answered:
"No doubt you are the only wise people, and wisdom will die with you!
But I have a mind just as you do. I am not less than you. Who doesn't know all these things?
I have become a joke to my friends, I who called on God and was answered. I am a good man with no fault, and yet I am a joke.
People who are comfortable look down on those in trouble. They think trouble comes to those whose feet slip.
The tents of robbers are peaceful, and those who make God angry are safe, those who carry their god in their hands.
But ask the animals, and they will teach you. Ask the birds of the sky, and they will tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you. Let the fish of the sea tell you.
Which of all these does not know that the LORD's hand has done this?
The life of every living thing is in his hand, and the breath of every human being.
Doesn't the ear test words, just as the tongue tastes food?
Wisdom is found among older people, and understanding comes with a long life.
But true wisdom and power belong to God. Advice and understanding are his.
What he tears down cannot be rebuilt. When he puts someone in prison, no one can let him out.
If he holds back the rain, everything dries up. If he lets the waters loose, they flood the earth.
Strength and success belong to him. Both the one who is fooled and the one who fools others are under his control.
He leads advisers away stripped of everything, and he makes judges look like fools.
He takes away the power of kings and ties a rope around their waists.
He leads priests away stripped of everything, and overthrows those who have been in power a long time.
He silences trusted advisers and takes away the good sense of the elders.
He brings shame on rulers and takes away the strength of the powerful.
He shows the deep things hidden in darkness and brings deep shadows into the light.
He makes nations great, and then destroys them. He makes nations large, and then scatters them.
He takes away the understanding of the world's leaders and sends them wandering in a desert where there is no path.
They feel their way in the dark with no light. He makes them stagger like drunks."
Look, my eyes have seen all this. My ears have heard it and understood it.
What you know, I also know. I am not less than you.
But I want to speak to the Almighty. I want to argue my case with God.
As for you, you cover things up with lies. You are all worthless doctors.
If only you would keep completely quiet! That would be the wise thing for you to do.
Now listen to my argument. Pay attention to what I have to say.
Will you tell lies for God? Will you speak falsely for him?
Will you take his side? Will you argue his case for him?
Would it go well for you if he looked closely at you? Can you fool him the way you fool people?
He would surely correct you if you secretly took sides.
Wouldn't his greatness frighten you? Wouldn't the fear of him fall on you?
Your wise sayings are as useless as ashes. Your arguments are as weak as clay.
Be quiet and let me speak! Then let whatever happens to me happen.
Why should I put myself in danger and take my life in my own hands?
Even if he kills me, and I have no hope, I will still defend my ways in front of him.
This might even save me, because no godless person would dare to come before him.
Listen carefully to my words. Let what I say ring in your ears.
Look, I have prepared my case, and I know I will be proved right.
Can anyone bring charges against me? If so, I will be quiet and die.
God, grant me just two things, and then I will not hide from you:
take your hand away from me, and stop frightening me with your terrors.
Then call me, and I will answer. Or let me speak, and you answer me.
How many wrongs and sins have I done? Show me my rebellion and my sin.
Why do you hide your face from me and treat me like your enemy?
Will you frighten a leaf blown by the wind? Will you chase after dry straw?
You write down bitter charges against me and make me pay for the sins I did when I was young.
You put my feet in chains and watch every step I take. You draw a line around where my feet may go.
So I waste away like something rotten, like clothing eaten by moths.
Every person born of a woman lives only a short time, and life is full of trouble.
We grow up like a flower and then wither. We fade away like a shadow and do not last.
Do you really keep your eyes on someone like me? Will you bring me to court to be judged by you?
Who can bring something pure out of something unclean? No one!
You have decided how long a person will live. You have set the number of his months, and set limits he cannot go past.
So look away from him and let him rest, until he finishes his time like a hired worker.
There is hope for a tree. If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and new shoots will keep growing.
Its roots may grow old in the ground, and its stump may die in the soil,
but at the smell of water it will bud and put out new branches like a young plant.
But a person dies and is laid low. He breathes his last breath, and where is he?
As water disappears from a lake, and a river dries up and is gone,
so people lie down and do not rise again. Until the heavens are gone, they will not wake up or be woken from their sleep.
I wish you would hide me in the grave and keep me hidden until your anger has passed. I wish you would set a time to remember me!
If a person dies, will he live again? I would wait all the days of my hard service, until my release came.
You would call, and I would answer you. You would long for the creature your hands have made.
Then you would watch my steps, but you would not keep track of my sin.
My wrongs would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my sin.
But as a mountain wears away and crumbles, and a rock is moved from its place,
as water wears down stones and floods wash away the soil, so you destroy a person's hope.
You overpower him once and for all, and he is gone. You change his face and send him away.
If his sons are honored, he does not know it. If they are brought low, he does not see it.
He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
Then Eliphaz from Teman answered:
"Would a wise man answer with empty ideas, and fill himself with hot air?
Would he argue with useless words and speeches that do no good?
But you are even destroying respect for God, and stopping people from praying to him.
Your sin is teaching your mouth what to say. You choose to speak like a tricky person.
Your own mouth proves you guilty, not mine. Your own lips speak against you.
Are you the first person ever born? Were you made before the hills?
Do you listen in on God's secret meetings? Do you think you are the only wise one?
What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not?
Old men with gray hair are on our side, men even older than your father.
Are God's comforts not enough for you, the gentle words spoken to you?
Why has your heart carried you away? Why do your eyes flash with anger,
so that you turn your anger against God and pour out such words from your mouth?
What is a human, that he could be pure? What is anyone born of a woman, that he could be right before God?
Look, God does not trust even his holy angels. Even the heavens are not pure in his sight.
How much less a person who is disgusting and evil, who drinks up sin like water!
Listen to me, and I will explain. I will tell you what I have seen,
what wise men have taught, passed down from their ancestors without hiding anything.
The land was given to their ancestors alone, and no foreigner lived among them.
An evil person suffers pain all his life, all the years set aside for the cruel.
Terrible sounds fill his ears. When things seem peaceful, the destroyer attacks him.
He does not believe he will escape the darkness. A sword is waiting for him.
He wanders around looking for food, asking, 'Where is it?' He knows the day of darkness is near.
Trouble and suffering terrify him. They overpower him like a king ready to attack.
This is because he shook his fist at God and acted proudly against the Almighty.
He stubbornly charged at God with a thick, strong shield.
His face is covered with fat, and his waist is thick with it.
He will live in ruined towns, in houses where no one lives, houses about to fall into piles of rubble.
He will not stay rich. His wealth will not last, and his property will not spread over the land.
He will not escape the darkness. A flame will dry up his shoots, and the breath of God's mouth will carry him away.
Let him not fool himself by trusting in what is worthless, because he will get nothing worthwhile in return.
He will be paid in full before his time, and his branches will not stay green.
He will be like a vine that drops its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.
The company of godless people will have no children, and fire will burn up the homes of those who love bribes.
They plan trouble and give birth to evil. Their hearts are always planning lies."
Then Job answered:
"I have heard many things like this before. You are all terrible comforters!
Will your long-winded speeches never end? What is bothering you that you keep on arguing?
I could talk the way you do if you were in my place. I could make fine speeches against you and shake my head at you.
But I would use my words to encourage you. My comforting words would ease your pain.
If I speak, my pain does not go away. If I keep quiet, it does not leave me.
God, you have surely worn me out. You have taken away my whole family.
You have made me shrivel up, and that has become a witness against me. My thin body stands up and speaks against me.
In his anger God has torn me and attacked me. He grinds his teeth at me. My enemy stares at me with piercing eyes.
People open their mouths wide to mock me. They slap my face to shame me. They all gang up against me.
God has handed me over to evil people and thrown me into the hands of the wicked.
I was at peace, but he shattered me. He grabbed me by the neck and smashed me to pieces. He set me up as his target.
His archers surround me. Without pity he pierces my insides and spills my insides on the ground.
He breaks through my walls again and again. He charges at me like a warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin and buried my pride in the dust.
My face is red from crying, and dark shadows ring my eyes.
Yet my hands have never done violence, and my prayer is pure.
Earth, do not cover up my blood. Do not let my cry for justice be silenced.
Even now my witness is in heaven. The one who will speak for me is on high.
My friends make fun of me, while my eyes pour out tears to God.
I want someone to plead with God for me, as a person pleads for a friend.
In just a few years I will go on the road from which I will never come back.
My spirit is broken. My days are almost over, and the grave is waiting for me.
Mockers surround me. I have to watch them insult me.
God, please promise to help me yourself. Who else will make a promise for me?
You have closed their minds to understanding, so you will not let them win.
If someone turns against his friends for a reward, his children will suffer for it.
God has made me a joke among the people. They spit in my face.
My eyes have grown dim with sadness. My whole body is as thin as a shadow.
Honest people are shocked at this. The innocent are upset with the godless.
But good people keep going on the right way, and those with clean hands grow stronger and stronger.
But all of you, come back and try again! I will not find a wise man among you.
My days are over. My plans have been broken, and so have the desires of my heart.
These men turn night into day. They say, 'Light is near,' when it is dark.
If the only home I hope for is the grave, if I make my bed in the darkness,
if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'You are my mother' or 'my sister,'
then where is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?
Will my hope go down with me to the gates of the grave? Will we go down together into the dust?"
Then Bildad from Shuah answered:
"How long will you keep searching for words? Think first, and then we can talk.
Why do you treat us like animals? Why do you think we are stupid?
You tear yourself apart in your anger. Should the earth be left empty just for you? Should the rocks be moved from their places for you?
The light of the wicked will be put out. The flame of his fire will stop burning.
The light in his tent will become dark. The lamp beside him will go out.
His strong steps will become weak. His own plans will trip him up.
His own feet lead him into a net, and he walks right into its holes.
A trap grabs him by the heel. A snare holds him tight.
A rope is hidden on the ground for him, and a trap lies on his path.
Terrors frighten him on every side and chase him at every step.
He is weak from hunger, and disaster is ready for him when he falls.
Disease eats away his skin. Death's firstborn eats away his arms and legs.
He is torn from the safety of his tent and marched off to the king of terrors.
Strangers live in his tent, and burning sulfur is scattered over his home.
His roots dry up below, and his branches wither above.
No one on earth remembers him. No one in the land knows his name.
He is driven from light into darkness and chased out of the world.
He has no children or grandchildren among his people, and no one is left where he once lived.
People who come after him are shocked at what happened to him, just as those who lived before were terrified.
This is surely what happens to the homes of evil people. This is the fate of those who do not know God."
Then Job answered:
"How long will you keep hurting me and crushing me with your words?
Ten times now you have insulted me. You attack me without any shame.
Even if it is true that I have done wrong, my mistake is my own business.
If you really want to make yourselves look better than me and use my shame as proof against me,
then know that God has wronged me and caught me in his net.
I cry out, 'Help! I am being treated wrongly!' But I get no answer. I call for help, but there is no justice.
God has blocked my way so I cannot get through. He has covered my paths with darkness.
He has taken away my honor and removed the crown from my head.
He tears me down on every side until I am gone. He has pulled up my hope like a tree.
His anger burns against me. He thinks of me as one of his enemies.
His armies come together. They build ramps to attack me and camp around my tent.
He has driven my brothers far away from me. The people who knew me have turned away.
My relatives have gone away, and my close friends have forgotten me.
My guests and my servant girls treat me like a stranger. They look at me as if I were a foreigner.
I call my servant, but he does not answer, even when I beg him.
My breath disgusts my wife. My own brothers find me disgusting.
Even little children look down on me. When I get up, they make fun of me.
All my closest friends hate me. Those I love have turned against me.
I am nothing but skin and bones. I have escaped with only the skin of my teeth.
Have pity on me, my friends! Have pity on me, because God's hand has struck me.
Why do you chase me as God does? Haven't you hurt my body enough?
I wish my words were written down! I wish they were written in a book!
I wish they were carved in rock forever with an iron tool and filled with lead!
But I know that the one who will rescue me is alive. In the end, he will stand on the earth.
Even after my skin has been destroyed, I will see God with my own body.
I myself will see him on my side. I will see him with my own eyes, not as a stranger. How my heart longs for that day!
If you say, 'Let's keep after him, since the root of the trouble is in him,'
then you should be afraid of the sword yourselves. God's anger brings punishment by the sword, so that you will know there is a judgment."
Then Zophar from Naamah answered:
"My troubled thoughts make me answer, because I am very upset inside.
I have heard your insults, which put me to shame, and my understanding tells me how to answer.
Surely you know that ever since long ago, since people were first put on the earth,
the happiness of evil people is short, and the joy of godless people lasts only a moment.
Even if their pride reaches up to the heavens and their heads touch the clouds,
they will disappear forever, like their own dung. Those who knew them will ask, 'Where are they?'
They fly away like a dream and cannot be found. They are chased away like a vision in the night.
The eyes that saw them will not see them again. Their home will never see them again.
Their children will have to beg the poor for help. They will have to give back the wealth they took.
Their bodies were once full of youthful strength, but that strength will lie with them in the dust.
Evil tastes sweet in their mouths, so they hide it under their tongues.
They enjoy it and do not want to let it go. They keep it in their mouths.
But their food turns sour in their stomachs. It becomes like snake poison inside them.
They swallowed riches, but they will throw them up. God will make their stomachs give them back.
They will suck snake poison. A poisonous snake's fangs will kill them.
They will never enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream.
They will have to give back what they worked for without eating it. They will not enjoy the profits from their trading.
This is because they crushed the poor and left them with nothing. They took over houses they did not build.
Their greed was never satisfied, so they will not be able to save any of the things they loved.
Nothing was left after they had eaten it all, so their wealth will not last.
Even when they have plenty, trouble will catch up with them. The full force of misery will come on them.
When they have filled their stomachs, God will pour out his burning anger on them. It will rain down on them while they eat.
They may run from an iron weapon, but a bronze arrow will pierce them.
They pull it out of their backs, the shining point out of their liver. Terror comes over them.
Total darkness is waiting for their treasures. A fire no one has lit will burn them up and destroy everything left in their tents.
The heavens will show their guilt, and the earth will stand up against them.
A flood will carry away their houses, rushing waters on the day of God's anger.
This is what God has planned for evil people. This is what God has given them as their share."
Then Job answered:
"Listen carefully to what I say. Let that be the comfort you give me.
Be patient while I speak, and after I have spoken, you can go on mocking me.
Am I complaining to a human being? Why shouldn't I be impatient?
Look at me and be shocked. Put your hand over your mouth.
When I think about this, I am terrified, and my body shakes.
Why do evil people go on living? They grow old and become more and more powerful.
Their children grow up around them, and they see their grandchildren.
Their homes are safe and free from fear. God does not punish them.
Their bulls never fail to breed. Their cows give birth and do not lose their calves.
They send out their little ones like a flock of lambs. Their children dance around.
They sing to the music of tambourines and harps, and they have fun with the sound of the flute.
They spend their lives in wealth and go down to the grave in peace.
Yet they say to God, 'Leave us alone! We do not want to know your ways.
Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him? What would we gain by praying to him?'
But their success is not in their own hands. I want nothing to do with the plans of the wicked.
How often is the lamp of the wicked put out? How often does disaster come on them? How often does God punish them in his anger?
How often are they like straw blown by the wind, or chaff carried away by a storm?
You say, 'God saves up their punishment for their children.' Let God punish them themselves, so they will know it.
Let them see their own ruin with their own eyes. Let them drink the anger of the Almighty.
Why should they care what happens to their families after they are dead and their time is over?
Can anyone teach God anything, since he judges even those in heaven?
One person dies while he is still strong, completely comfortable and at ease.
His body is well fed, and his bones are strong and healthy.
Another person dies with a bitter heart, never having enjoyed anything good.
But both of them lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.
Look, I know what you are thinking, the plans you have to hurt me.
You say, 'Where is the great man's house now? Where are the tents where the wicked lived?'
Haven't you asked those who travel? Haven't you listened to their stories?
Evil people are spared on the day of disaster. They are rescued on the day of God's anger.
Who tells them to their faces what they have done wrong? Who pays them back for what they have done?
They are carried to the grave, and people keep watch over their tombs.
The soil of the valley feels soft to them. Everyone follows after them, just as countless people went before them.
So how can you comfort me with your empty words? Nothing is left of your answers but lies!"
Then Eliphaz from Teman answered:
"Can a person be of any use to God? Even a wise person is only useful to himself.
Does it give the Almighty any pleasure if you are right? Does he gain anything if your life has no fault?
Is it because you respect him that he corrects you and brings you to court?
No, it is because your evil is great, and your sins have no end.
You took things from your relatives as a guarantee for loans, for no good reason. You took the clothes off people's backs and left them naked.
You did not give water to tired people or food to the hungry.
You were a powerful man who owned land, an honored man who lived in it.
You sent widows away with nothing and crushed the strength of orphans.
That is why traps are all around you, and sudden fear frightens you.
That is why it is so dark you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
Isn't God in the highest heavens? Look how high the farthest stars are!
Yet you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through such deep darkness?
Thick clouds hide him, so he cannot see us as he walks around the dome of the sky.'
Will you keep to the old path that evil people have walked?
They were snatched away before their time. Their foundations were washed away by a flood.
They said to God, 'Leave us alone! What can the Almighty do to us?'
Yet it was God who filled their houses with good things. I want nothing to do with the plans of the wicked.
Good people see their ruin and are glad. The innocent laugh at them and say,
'Our enemies are destroyed, and fire has burned up what was left of their wealth.'
Get to know God and make peace with him. Then good things will come to you.
Accept the teaching from his mouth, and keep his words in your heart.
If you come back to the Almighty, you will be built up again. Remove evil far from your home.
Throw your gold into the dust, your best gold among the rocks in the streams.
Then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
Then you will find joy in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.
You will pray to him, and he will hear you, and you will keep your promises to him.
Whatever you decide to do will succeed, and light will shine on your path.
When people are brought low and you say, 'Lift them up,' God will save the humble.
He will even rescue someone who is guilty. He will be rescued because your hands are clean."
Then Job answered:
"Even today my complaint is bitter. God's hand is heavy on me, even though I groan.
If only I knew where to find him! If only I could go to where he sits!
I would lay out my case in front of him and fill my mouth with arguments.
I would find out how he would answer me, and understand what he would say to me.
Would he use his great power to argue against me? No, he would listen to me.
There an honest person could reason with him, and my judge would set me free forever.
But if I go east, he is not there. If I go west, I cannot find him.
When he is at work in the north, I do not see him. When he turns to the south, I cannot catch sight of him.
But he knows the way I take. When he has tested me, I will come out as pure as gold.
My feet have closely followed his steps. I have kept to his way and not turned aside.
I have not turned away from the commands of his lips. I have treasured his words more than my daily food.
But he alone is God, and who can stand against him? He does whatever he wants.
He will do to me what he has planned, and he has many more plans like it.
That is why I am terrified in front of him. When I think about it, I am afraid of him.
God has made my heart weak. The Almighty has terrified me.
Yet I have not been silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face.
Why doesn't the Almighty set times for judging? Why do those who know him never see those days?
Some people move boundary stones to steal land. They steal flocks and put them in their own pastures.
They drive away the orphan's donkey and take the widow's ox as a guarantee for a loan.
They push needy people off the road, and all the poor of the land have to hide.
Like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go out to work, searching for food. The desert gives them food for their children.
They gather grain in other people's fields and pick the leftover grapes in the vineyards of the wicked.
They spend the night naked, with no clothes, with nothing to cover them in the cold.
They are soaked by mountain rains and hug the rocks because they have no shelter.
Some people snatch babies from their mothers' breasts. They take the babies of the poor as a guarantee for loans.
So the poor go around naked, without clothes. They carry bundles of grain but are still hungry.
They press olives between the walls of the rich and crush grapes in the winepresses, but they are still thirsty.
People groan in the crowded city, and the wounded cry out for help. Yet God does not notice that anything is wrong.
Some people rebel against the light. They do not know its ways or stay on its paths.
The murderer gets up at dawn and kills the poor and needy. At night he acts like a thief.
The person who sleeps with someone else's wife waits for evening. He thinks, 'No one will see me,' and he covers his face.
In the dark, robbers break into houses. During the day they shut themselves in. They want nothing to do with light.
For all of them, morning is like deep darkness. They are friends with the terrors of the dark.
They are like foam floating on the water. Their part of the land is cursed, and no one goes to their vineyards.
As heat and dry weather melt away the snow, so the grave takes away those who have sinned.
Their own mothers forget them. Worms feast on them. No one remembers them any more. So evil is broken like a tree.
They take advantage of women who have no children, and they do not help widows.
But God drags away the powerful by his strength. Even when they seem strong, they cannot be sure of their lives.
God may let them feel safe and secure, but his eyes are watching their ways.
They are great for a little while, and then they are gone. They are brought low and gathered up like everyone else. They are cut off like the heads of grain.
If this is not so, who can prove me a liar and show that my words are worth nothing?"
Then Bildad from Shuah answered:
"God rules, and everyone should fear him. He makes peace in the high heavens.
Can anyone count his armies? Is there anyone his light does not shine on?
So how can a human be right before God? How can anyone born of a woman be pure?
If even the moon is not bright and the stars are not pure in his sight,
how much less a human, who is only a maggot, a human being, who is only a worm!"
Then Job answered:
"What a help you are to someone with no power! How you have saved the arm with no strength!
What great advice you have given to someone without wisdom! How much good sense you have shown!
Who helped you say these words? Whose spirit spoke through you?
The spirits of the dead tremble, those beneath the waters and all who live there.
The grave lies open before God. The place of destruction has no cover.
He spreads out the northern skies over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing.
He wraps up the waters in his thick clouds, and the clouds do not burst under their weight.
He covers the face of the full moon by spreading his clouds over it.
He draws the horizon on the face of the waters, the boundary between light and darkness.
The pillars of heaven shake and are amazed when he speaks sharply.
By his power he calmed the sea. By his wisdom he struck down the monster Rahab.
By his breath the skies became clear. His hand pierced the gliding snake.
And these are only the edges of what he does. We hear only a small whisper of him. Who could ever understand the thunder of his power?"
Job continued speaking:
"As surely as God lives, who has refused me justice, the Almighty, who has made my life bitter,
as long as I have life in me and the breath of God is in my nose,
my lips will not say anything evil, and my tongue will not tell lies.
I will never say that you are right. Until the day I die, I will not stop saying I am innocent.
I will hold on to my innocence and never let it go. My conscience will not blame me as long as I live.
Let my enemy be treated like the wicked. Let anyone who attacks me be treated like the evil.
What hope do godless people have when God cuts them off and takes away their lives?
Will God listen to their cry when trouble comes on them?
Will they find joy in the Almighty? Will they call on God all the time?
I will teach you about God's power. I will not hide what the Almighty does.
You have all seen it for yourselves. So why do you keep talking such nonsense?
This is what God has planned for evil people, what cruel people will receive from the Almighty:
They may have many children, but the sword will kill them. Their descendants will never have enough to eat.
Disease will kill those who survive, and their widows will not even cry for them.
They may pile up silver like dust and clothes like piles of clay.
But good people will wear those clothes, and innocent people will share the silver.
The houses they build are like a moth's cocoon, like a hut put up by a guard in a field.
They go to bed rich, but it will be for the last time. When they open their eyes, everything is gone.
Terrors flood over them. A storm snatches them away in the night.
The east wind carries them off, and they are gone. It sweeps them out of their place.
It blows against them without mercy as they try to escape its power.
It claps its hands at them and hisses at them as they leave their place."
There are mines where silver is found, and places where gold is refined.
Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is melted out of rock.
Miners bring light into the darkness. They search the deepest places for stones hidden in the dark.
They dig shafts far from where people live, in places no one walks. They hang far from other people and swing back and forth on ropes.
Food grows from the surface of the earth, but underneath it is turned over as if by fire.
Sapphires are found in its rocks, and its dust contains gold.
No bird of prey knows that hidden path. No falcon's eye has seen it.
No proud wild animal has walked on it. No lion has gone that way.
Miners attack the hardest rock and dig away the roots of mountains.
They cut tunnels through the rock, and their eyes see all its treasures.
They dam up the sources of rivers and bring hidden things into the light.
But where can wisdom be found? Where does understanding live?
No human knows its value. It cannot be found in the land of the living.
The deep ocean says, 'It is not in me.' The sea says, 'It is not with me.'
It cannot be bought with the finest gold. Its price cannot be paid in silver.
It cannot be bought with gold from Ophir, with valuable onyx, or with sapphires.
Gold and crystal cannot compare with it. It cannot be traded for jewels of gold.
Coral and jasper are not worth mentioning. The price of wisdom is higher than rubies.
The topaz of Ethiopia cannot compare with it. It cannot be bought with pure gold.
So where does wisdom come from? Where does understanding live?
It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing, even from the birds of the sky.
Destruction and Death say, 'We have only heard rumors about it.'
God understands the way to it. He alone knows where it lives.
He sees to the ends of the earth and everything under the heavens.
When he gave the wind its force and measured out the waters,
when he made a law for the rain and a path for the thunderstorm,
then he looked at wisdom and told about it. He set it up and tested it.
And he said to people, 'Look, respecting the Lord is wisdom, and staying away from evil is understanding.'"
Job continued speaking:
"How I long for the months that have passed, for the days when God watched over me,
when his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked through the darkness!
Those were the best days of my life, when God's friendship blessed my home,
when the Almighty was still with me and my children were all around me,
when my path was rich with cream, and the rocks poured out streams of olive oil for me.
When I went to the city gate and took my seat in the public square,
the young men saw me and stepped aside, and the old men stood up out of respect.
The leaders stopped talking and covered their mouths with their hands.
The voices of the important men became quiet, and their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths.
Everyone who heard me spoke well of me, and everyone who saw me praised me,
because I rescued the poor who cried for help, and the orphans who had no one to help them.
People who were dying blessed me, and I made widows' hearts sing for joy.
I wore goodness like clothing. Justice was my robe and my turban.
I was eyes for the blind and feet for those who could not walk.
I was a father to the needy, and I took up the case of strangers.
I broke the teeth of evil people and snatched their victims from their mouths.
I thought, 'I will die in my own home, after a life with days as many as the grains of sand.
My roots will reach down to the water, and the dew will lie on my branches all night.
I will always be honored, and my strength will always be new, like a bow that never weakens.'
People listened to me and waited quietly for my advice.
After I spoke, they had nothing more to say. My words fell gently on their ears.
They waited for me as people wait for rain. They drank in my words like spring rain.
When they were discouraged, I smiled at them, and my cheerful face encouraged them.
I chose the way for them and sat as their leader. I lived like a king among his troops, like someone who comforts those who mourn.
But now they make fun of me, men younger than I am, whose fathers I would not have put with my sheepdogs.
What use was their strength to me? Their strength was gone.
They were thin from hunger and want. They wandered the dry land at night, in empty and ruined places.
They picked salty plants among the bushes and ate the roots of broom trees.
They were driven away from other people, who shouted at them as if they were thieves.
They had to live in dry stream beds, in holes in the ground and among the rocks.
They howled like animals among the bushes and huddled together under the weeds.
They were worthless people, the children of nobodies, driven out of the land with whips.
And now they make fun of me in their songs. I have become a joke to them.
They hate me and stay away from me. They do not even hold back from spitting in my face.
Because God has cut my bowstring and made me suffer, they do whatever they want to me.
On my right side a mob attacks me. They trip me up and build ramps to attack me.
They block my path and try to destroy me, and no one stops them.
They come at me as if through a wide gap in a wall. They roll over me in the ruins.
Terrors overwhelm me. My honor is blown away like the wind, and my safety vanishes like a cloud.
Now my life is draining out of me. Days of suffering have taken hold of me.
At night my bones ache, and the gnawing pain never rests.
