Suddenly there was such a strong earthquake that the prison was shaken to its foundations. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he pulled out his sword to kill himself. He thought the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul shouted, "Do not harm yourself! We are all here!"
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them out and asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"
They answered, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."
Then they told the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds. Then right away he and all his family were baptised.
He brought them into his house and gave them a meal. He and his whole family were filled with joy, because they had come to believe in God.
When it was daylight, the city officials sent their officers to the jailer with the order: "Let those men go."
The jailer told Paul, "The officials have ordered that you and Silas be set free. Now you can leave. Go in peace."

But Paul said to the officers, "They beat us in public without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. And now they want to get rid of us secretly? No! Let them come themselves and lead us out."
The officers reported this to the city officials. When the officials heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were afraid.
So they came and said they were sorry. They led them out of the prison and asked them to leave the city.
After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia's house. There they met with the believers and encouraged them. Then they left.
Paul and Silas travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As he usually did, Paul went into the synagogue. On three Sabbath days he reasoned with the people from the Scriptures.
He explained and proved that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. "This Jesus I am telling you about is the Christ," he said.
Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas. So did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few important women.

But the other Jews became jealous. They got some evil men from the market place, formed a crowd, and started a riot in the city. They rushed to Jason's house, looking for Paul and Silas to bring them out to the crowd.
When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers to the city officials. They shouted, "These men who have caused trouble all over the world have now come here,
and Jason has welcomed them into his house. They are all going against Caesar's laws, saying there is another king, called Jesus."
When the crowd and the city officials heard this, they were upset.
Then they made Jason and the others pay money as a promise of good behaviour, and let them go.
As soon as it was night, the believers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. When they arrived there, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
The people of Berea were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica. They were very eager to receive the message, and every day they studied the Scriptures to see if what Paul said was true.
Many of them believed, along with quite a few important Greek women and many Greek men.
But when the Jews in Thessalonica learned that Paul was preaching God's word in Berea, they went there too, stirring up the crowds and making trouble.
The believers at once sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy stayed in Berea.
The men who went with Paul took him as far as Athens. Then they went back with orders for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply upset to see that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Greeks. He also spoke every day in the market place with anyone who happened to be there.

Some Epicurean and Stoic thinkers also began to argue with him. Some of them asked, "What is this babbler trying to say?" Others said, "He seems to be talking about foreign gods." They said this because Paul was preaching the good news about Jesus and his rising from the dead.
Then they took him to a meeting of the Areopagus, where they said to him, "May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
You are bringing some strange ideas to our ears, and we would like to know what they mean."
All the people of Athens and the foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing but talking about and listening to the latest ideas.
Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, "People of Athens! I see that in every way you are very religious.

As I walked around and looked carefully at the things you worship, I even found an altar with these words on it: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Now I am going to tell you about this God whom you worship without knowing him.
"The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth. He does not live in temples built by human hands.
He is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. He himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
From one man he made all the nations, so that they would live all over the earth. He decided the times set for them and the exact places where they would live.
God did this so that they would seek him, and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any of us.
'For in him we live and move and exist.' As some of your own poets have said, 'We are his children.'
"Since we are God's children, we should not think that God is like gold or silver or stone, an image made by human skill and ideas.
In the past God took no notice of such ignorance. But now he commands all people everywhere to turn away from their sins.
He has set a day when he will judge the world fairly, by the man he has chosen. He has proved this to everyone by raising him from the dead."
When they heard about the rising of the dead, some of them laughed at Paul. But others said, "We want to hear you speak about this again."
So Paul left the meeting.
Some people joined him and believed. Among them was Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and some others.
After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he met a Jew named Aquila, who was born in Pontus. He had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them,
and because he made tents for a living just as they did, he stayed and worked with them.
Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul gave all his time to preaching. He told the Jews clearly that Jesus was the Christ.

But when they turned against Paul and insulted him, he shook the dust from his clothes and said to them, "If you are lost, it is your own fault! I am not to blame. From now on I will go to the Gentiles."
Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titius Justus, a man who worshipped God.
Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, and everyone in his house believed in the Lord. Many of the people in Corinth who heard Paul also believed and were baptised.
One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: "Do not be afraid. Keep on speaking, and do not be silent.
I am with you, and no one is going to attack you or harm you, because I have many people in this city."
So Paul stayed there for a year and a half, teaching them God's word.
While Gallio was governor of Achaia, the Jews got together and attacked Paul. They brought him to the court.
They said, "This man is persuading people to worship God in ways that are against the law."
Paul was about to speak, but Gallio said to the Jews, "If you were complaining about some crime or serious wrong, it would be right for me to listen to you Jews.
But since this is about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I will not be a judge of such things."
And he sent them out of the court.
Then the crowd grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the court. But Gallio did not care at all.

Paul stayed on in Corinth for some time. Then he said goodbye to the believers and sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila. Before he sailed, he had his hair cut off at Cenchrea because of a promise he had made to God.
They arrived at Ephesus, where Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer, but he said no.
As he left, he promised, "I will come back if it is God's will." Then he sailed from Ephesus.
When he landed at Caesarea, he went up to Jerusalem and greeted the church. Then he went down to Antioch.
After spending some time in Antioch, Paul left and travelled from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, making all the followers stronger.
Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, who was born in Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a good speaker and knew the Scriptures very well.
He had been taught the way of the Lord, and he spoke with great excitement. He taught correctly about Jesus, though he knew only about John's baptism.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him to their home and explained the way of God to him more clearly.

When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him. They wrote to the followers there, asking them to welcome him. When he arrived, he was a great help to those who by God's grace had believed.
He strongly proved the Jews wrong in public debate, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul travelled through the inland country and arrived at Ephesus. There he found some followers.
He asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" They answered, "No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit."
So Paul asked, "Then what baptism did you receive?" They said, "John's baptism."
Paul said, "John's baptism was a baptism for turning away from sin. He told the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus."
When they heard this, they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in other languages and prophesied.
There were about twelve men in all.
Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months. He reasoned with the people and tried to persuade them about God's Kingdom.

But some of them became stubborn. They refused to believe and spoke evil of the Way in front of the crowd. So Paul left them. He took the followers with him and talked with people every day in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that all the Jews and Greeks who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord.
God did amazing miracles through Paul.
Even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick. Their sicknesses were healed, and evil spirits left them.

Some Jews who went around driving out evil spirits tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. They would say, "In the name of Jesus, whom Paul preaches, I order you to come out."
Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
One day the evil spirit answered them, "I know Jesus, and I know about Paul, but who are you?"
Then the man who had the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. He beat them so badly that they ran out of the house naked and bleeding.
When this became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus, they were all filled with fear, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honour.
Many of those who believed now came and openly confessed the evil things they had done.
A number of those who had practised magic brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. When they added up the value of the books, it came to fifty thousand silver coins.
In this way the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power.
After all this had happened, Paul decided by the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. "After I have been there," he said, "I must also visit Rome."
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he stayed in Asia a little longer.
About that time there was a great disturbance about the Way.
A silversmith named Demetrius made small silver models of the temple of the goddess Artemis. His business brought a lot of work to the craftsmen.
He called them together, along with other workers in the same trade, and said, "Men, you know that we earn a good living from this business.

And you see and hear what this man Paul has done. He has persuaded and led astray large numbers of people here in Ephesus and in almost the whole of Asia. He says that gods made by human hands are not gods at all.

There is a danger that our trade will lose its good name. And the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be thought of as nothing. She is worshipped in all of Asia and the whole world, but she will be robbed of her greatness."
When they heard this, they were furious and began shouting, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
Soon the whole city was in an uproar. The people grabbed Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's travelling companions from Macedonia, and all rushed together into the theatre.
Paul wanted to go in and speak to the crowd, but the followers would not let him.
Even some officials of the province, who were friends of Paul, sent him a message begging him not to go into the theatre.
The meeting was in confusion. Some people were shouting one thing and some another. Most of them did not even know why they were there.
The Jews in the crowd pushed Alexander to the front, and some of the crowd told him what to say. He waved his hand for silence because he wanted to defend himself before the people.
But when they realised he was a Jew, they all shouted together for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The city clerk calmed the crowd and said, "People of Ephesus, everyone knows that the city of Ephesus guards the temple of the great Artemis, and her image that fell from heaven.
No one can deny these facts. So you should calm down and not do anything foolish.
You have brought these men here, though they have not robbed temples or said evil things about our goddess.
If Demetrius and his craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and there are governors. They can bring charges there.
If there is anything more you want to bring up, it must be settled in a lawful meeting.
As it is, we are in danger of being charged with rioting because of what happened today. There is no reason for it, and we would not be able to explain this uproar."
After he had said this, he sent the crowd away.
When the uproar was over, Paul sent for the followers and encouraged them. Then he said goodbye and left for Macedonia.
He travelled through that area and encouraged the believers with many words. Then he came to Greece.
He stayed there three months. Some Jews made a plan against him as he was about to sail for Syria, so he decided to go back through Macedonia.
These men went with him as far as Asia: Sopater from Beroea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These men went ahead and waited for us at Troas.
After the days of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi. Five days later we joined them at Troas, and we stayed there seven days.
On the first day of the week, we met together to break bread. Paul talked with the people. He planned to leave the next day, so he kept on talking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were meeting.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window. He became very sleepy as Paul talked on and on. At last he fell fast asleep and fell from the third floor. When they picked him up, he was dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on the young man and put his arms around him. He said, "Do not be upset. He is alive!"
Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread and ate. He talked with them for a long time, until the sun came up. Then he left.
The people took the young man home alive, and they were greatly comforted.
We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos. We planned to take Paul on board there. He had arranged this, because he wanted to go there on foot.
When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went on to Mitylene.
The next day we sailed from there and arrived opposite Chios. The day after that we crossed over to Samos, and the next day we reached Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so he would not spend time in Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if he could, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus, Paul sent a message to Ephesus and asked the elders of the church to come to him.
When they arrived, he said to them, "You know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I came to Asia.
I served the Lord with all humility and with tears. I went through hard times because of the plans of the Jews against me.
You know I did not hold back anything that would help you. I taught you in public and from house to house.
I told both Jews and Greeks that they must turn away from sin, turn to God, and believe in our Lord Jesus.
And now the Spirit is pushing me to go to Jerusalem. I do not know what will happen to me there.
I only know that in every city the Holy Spirit warns me that prison and troubles are waiting for me.
But my life means nothing to me. I only want to finish my race with joy, and finish the work the Lord Jesus gave me. That work is to tell the good news of God's grace.
And now I know that none of you, among whom I went about preaching God's Kingdom, will ever see me again.
So I tell you today that I am not to blame if any of you are lost.
I did not hold back from telling you everything God wants.
Take care of yourselves and of all the flock. The Holy Spirit has made you leaders over it. Be shepherds of God's church, which he bought with his own blood.
I know that after I leave, fierce wolves will come in among you. They will not spare the flock.
Even some men from your own group will rise up and twist the truth. They will try to pull the followers away after them.
So watch out! Remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you, night and day, with tears.
Now, brothers, I give you to God and to the message of his grace. That message can build you up and give you a share among all God's holy people.
I have never wanted anyone's silver, gold or clothes.
You know that I worked with my own hands to provide for myself and for the people who were with me.
In everything I showed you that by working hard like this, we must help the weak. Remember the words the Lord Jesus himself said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
When Paul had finished speaking, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
They all cried a lot. They hugged Paul and kissed him.
What made them saddest was that he had said they would never see him again. Then they went with him to the ship.
After we said goodbye to them, we set sail and went straight to Cos. The next day we reached Rhodes, and from there we went to Patara.
We found a ship going over to Phoenicia, so we got on board and set sail.
We saw Cyprus and passed it on our left. We sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, because the ship had to unload its cargo there.
We found some followers there and stayed with them seven days. Through the Spirit, they told Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
When our time was over, we left and went on our way. All of them, with their wives and children, walked with us out of the city. There we knelt on the beach and prayed.
We said goodbye to each other. Then we got on the ship, and they went back home.
We continued our trip from Tyre and landed at Ptolemais. We greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and went to Caesarea. We stayed at the house of Philip, who told people the good news. He was one of the seven helpers.
He had four daughters who were not married, and they prophesied.
We stayed there several days. Then a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us and took Paul's belt. He tied up his own feet and hands with it and said, "The Holy Spirit says: 'This is how the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt. They will hand him over to the Gentiles.'"
When we heard this, we and the people there begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, "Why are you crying and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be tied up, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
He would not listen to us, so we stopped and said, "May the Lord's will be done."
After this, we got ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the followers from Caesarea went with us. They took us to the home of Mnason, where we would stay. He was from Cyprus, and he was one of the first followers.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the believers welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went with us to see James. All the elders were there.
Paul greeted them and told them, one by one, everything God had done among the Gentiles through his work.
When they heard this, they praised God. Then they said to Paul, "Brother, you see how many thousands of Jews have believed. They all follow the law very strictly.
They have been told that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses. They heard you tell them not to circumcise their children and not to follow our customs.
What should we do? They will surely hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men here who have made a promise to God.

Take these men and go through the cleansing ceremony with them. Pay their costs so they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they heard about you is not true. They will see that you yourself keep the law.

As for the Gentiles who believe, we have written to them with our decision. They must not eat food offered to idols, or blood, or the meat of strangled animals, and they must stay away from sexual sin."

So the next day Paul took the men and went through the cleansing ceremony with them. Then he went into the temple to tell when the days of cleansing would end, and when the offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and grabbed him.

They shouted, "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people, our law and this place. And now he has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean!"
They had seen Trophimus from Ephesus with Paul in the city, and they thought Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was in an uproar, and the people came running. They grabbed Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, news reached the commander of the Roman soldiers that all of Jerusalem was in an uproar.
At once he took some officers and soldiers and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came and arrested Paul. He ordered him to be tied with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some people in the crowd shouted one thing and some shouted another. The commander could not find out the truth because of all the noise, so he ordered Paul to be taken into the army building.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because the crowd was so violent.
The crowd kept following and shouting, "Kill him!"
As Paul was about to be taken into the army building, he said to the commander, "May I say something to you?" The commander said, "You speak Greek?
Then are you not the Egyptian who started a revolt some time ago? He led four thousand terrorists out into the desert."
Paul answered, "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia. I am a citizen of an important city. Please let me speak to the people."
The commander gave him permission. So Paul stood on the steps and raised his hand to quiet the people. When they were all silent, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language.
"Brothers and fathers, listen now while I defend myself."
When they heard him speak to them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. Then Paul said,

"I am a Jew. I was born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but I grew up here in this city. I studied under Gamaliel. He taught me very carefully the law of our ancestors. I was eager to serve God, just as all of you are today.
I attacked the people who followed the Way, even to the point of death. I arrested men and women and threw them into prison.

The high priest and all the council of elders can tell you this is true. They even gave me letters to the Jewish brothers in Damascus. So I went there to arrest the believers and bring them back to Jerusalem to be punished.
As I was on my way and came near Damascus, at about midday, a bright light from the sky suddenly flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you attacking me?'
I asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' He said to me, 'I am Jesus of Nazareth, the one you are attacking.'
The men with me saw the light and were afraid, but they did not understand the voice of the one speaking to me.
I asked, 'What should I do, Lord?' The Lord said, 'Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told everything you have been chosen to do.'
The bright light had made me blind, so the men with me led me by the hand into Damascus.
A man named Ananias came to see me. He was a godly man who obeyed the law, and all the Jews living in Damascus spoke well of him.
He stood beside me and said, 'Brother Saul, see again!' At that very moment I could see him.
Then he said, 'The God of our ancestors has chosen you to know his will. He chose you to see the Righteous One and to hear his voice.
You will tell everyone about what you have seen and heard.
So what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptised and wash your sins away, calling on his name.'
Later I went back to Jerusalem. While I was praying in the temple, I saw a vision.
I saw the Lord, and he said to me, 'Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept what you tell them about me.'
I said, 'Lord, they know that I went from one synagogue to another to put believers in prison and beat them.
And when Stephen, who spoke for you, was killed, I was standing there. I agreed with it, and I guarded the coats of the men who were killing him.'
Then the Lord said to me, 'Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.'"
The crowd listened to Paul until he said this. Then they shouted, "Get rid of him! He is not fit to live!"
They shouted, threw off their coats and threw dust into the air.
So the commander ordered Paul to be taken into the army building. He told his soldiers to whip Paul and question him, to find out why the people were shouting against him like this.
When they had tied him up to be whipped, Paul said to the officer standing there, "Is it legal for you to whip a Roman citizen who has not even been found guilty?"
When the officer heard this, he went to the commander and said, "Be careful what you do! This man is a Roman citizen."
The commander came and asked Paul, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" Paul answered, "Yes."
The commander said, "I had to pay a lot of money to become a citizen." Paul said, "But I was born a citizen."
At once the men who were about to question him moved away. The commander was afraid too, because he had put a Roman citizen in chains.

The next day the commander wanted to know exactly why the Jews were accusing Paul. So he set him free and ordered the leading priests and the whole council to meet. Then he brought Paul and made him stand in front of them.
Paul looked straight at the council and said, "Brothers, I have lived my whole life before God with a clear conscience, right up to today."
The high priest Ananias ordered the men standing near Paul to hit him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God will hit you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there to judge me by the law, yet you break the law by ordering them to hit me!"
The men standing near Paul said, "How dare you insult God's high priest!"
Paul said, "Brothers, I did not know he was the high priest. It is written, 'Do not speak evil about a ruler of your people.'"

Paul knew that some of them were Sadducees and some were Pharisees. So he called out in the council, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, and my father was a Pharisee. I am on trial because I hope that the dead will rise again!"
When he said this, the Pharisees and the Sadducees started to argue, and the group was divided.
The Sadducees say that the dead do not rise again, and that there are no angels or spirits. But the Pharisees believe in all of these.

There was a lot of shouting. Some of the teachers of the law who were Pharisees stood up and argued strongly. They said, "We find nothing wrong with this man. Maybe a spirit or an angel really did speak to him. Let us not fight against God!"

The argument became so violent that the commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered the soldiers to go down, take Paul away from them by force and bring him into the army building.
The next night the Lord stood beside Paul and said, "Be brave, Paul! You have told people about me in Jerusalem. You must do the same in Rome."
In the morning some of the Jews made a secret plan. They made a promise to God and said they would not eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty men were part of this plan.
They went to the leading priests and the elders and said, "We have made a solemn promise not to eat anything until we have killed Paul.

So now you and the council must send a message to the commander. Ask him to bring Paul down to you, as if you want to look into his case more closely. We will be ready to kill him before he gets here."
But Paul's nephew, his sister's son, heard about the plan. He went into the army building and told Paul.
Then Paul called one of the officers and said, "Take this young man to the commander. He has something to tell him."
So the officer took him to the commander and said, "The prisoner Paul called me. He asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to tell you."
The commander took the young man by the hand and led him aside. He asked him in private, "What do you want to tell me?"
The young man said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow. They will pretend they want to ask him more questions.

But do not believe them! More than forty men are hiding and waiting for him. They have promised not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now. They are only waiting for you to agree."
The commander sent the young man away and told him, "Do not tell anyone that you have told me this."
Then the commander called two of his officers and said, "Get two hundred soldiers ready to go to Caesarea at nine o'clock tonight. Also take seventy horsemen and two hundred men with spears.
Get some horses for Paul to ride, and take him safely to Felix the governor."
Then he wrote this letter:
"From Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix. Greetings.
The Jews grabbed this man and were about to kill him. But I learned that he is a Roman citizen, so I went with my soldiers and rescued him.
I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their council.
I found out that they were accusing him about questions of their own law. But there was nothing he deserved to die for or be put in prison for.
Then I was told that there was a plan to kill him. So I sent him to you at once. I have also told his accusers to bring their case against him to you. Goodbye."
So the soldiers did what they were ordered. They took Paul during the night and brought him as far as Antipatris.
The next day the horsemen went on with Paul, and the other soldiers went back to the army building.
When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they gave the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.
The governor read the letter and asked Paul what province he was from. When he learned that Paul was from Cilicia,
he said, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's palace.
Five days later, Ananias the high priest came down to Caesarea with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus. They brought their charges against Paul to the governor.
When Paul was called in, Tertullus began to accuse him. He said, "Because of you, we have enjoyed a long time of peace. Your wise plans have brought many good changes to this nation.
Most excellent Felix, we accept this everywhere and in every way, and we are very thankful.
But I do not want to take up too much of your time. So please be kind and listen to us for a short while.
We have found that this man is a troublemaker. He stirs up riots among the Jews all over the world. He is a leader of the group called the Nazarenes.
He even tried to make the temple unclean, so we arrested him.
If you question him yourself, you will find out that everything we say about him is true."
The other Jews joined in the attack and said that all this was true.
The governor waved his hand for Paul to speak. Paul answered, "I know that you have been a judge over this nation for many years. So I am glad to defend myself in front of you.
You can easily check that it was no more than twelve days ago that I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
My accusers did not find me arguing with anyone in the temple. They did not find me stirring up a crowd in the synagogues or anywhere else in the city.
And they cannot prove to you the things they are now saying against me.

But I do admit this to you. I worship the God of our ancestors as a follower of the Way, which they call a false group. I believe everything that agrees with the law and everything written in the Prophets.
I have the same hope in God that these men have. I hope that all people, good and bad, will rise from the dead.
So I always try my best to have a clear conscience before God and before people.
After being away for several years, I came to Jerusalem to bring gifts of money for the poor of my nation, and to offer sacrifices.
I was doing this when they found me in the temple. I had gone through the cleansing ceremony. There was no crowd with me, and no trouble.
But some Jews from Asia were there. They should be here in front of you to accuse me, if they have anything against me.
Or let these men here say what crime they found me guilty of when I stood before the council.
The only thing they could say is that I shouted this while standing among them: 'I am on trial before you today because I believe the dead will rise again!'"
Felix knew a lot about the Way. So he stopped the trial and said, "When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case."
He ordered the officer to keep Paul under guard, but to give him some freedom. He also said Paul's friends could take care of his needs and visit him.
Some days later, Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and listened to him talk about believing in Christ Jesus.
Paul talked about living right, about self-control, and about the judgment that is coming. This made Felix afraid, and he said, "Go away for now. When I have time, I will send for you again."
At the same time, he hoped that Paul would give him money to set him free. So he often sent for Paul and talked with him.
After two years, Porcius Festus took Felix's place as governor. Felix wanted to please the Jews, so he left Paul in prison.
Festus arrived in the province, and three days later he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
There the leading priests and the most important Jewish leaders brought their charges against Paul. They begged Festus
to do them a favour and send Paul to Jerusalem. They were planning to hide and kill him on the way.
But Festus answered that Paul would be kept in Caesarea, and that he himself was going back there soon.
He said, "Let some of your leaders come with me. If this man has done anything wrong, they can accuse him there."
Festus stayed with them for more than ten days, and then he went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat in the judge's seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When Paul came in, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him. They brought many serious charges against him, but they could not prove any of them.
Paul defended himself and said, "I have done nothing wrong against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar."
But Festus wanted to please the Jews. So he asked Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and let me judge you there about these charges?"
Paul said, "I am standing before Caesar's court, and this is where I should be judged. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you know very well.
If I have done wrong and deserve to die, I do not refuse to die. But if their charges against me are not true, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!"
Festus talked this over with his advisers. Then he said, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!"
A few days later, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to welcome Festus.
They stayed there many days, and Festus told the king about Paul's case. He said, "There is a man here whom Felix left in prison.
When I was in Jerusalem, the leading priests and the Jewish elders brought charges against him. They asked me to sentence him.
I told them that Romans do not hand over anyone before he has met his accusers face to face. He must have a chance to defend himself against their charges.
So when they came here, I did not waste any time. The next day I sat in the judge's seat and ordered the man to be brought in.
When his accusers stood up to speak, they did not accuse him of any of the crimes I expected.
Instead they argued with him about their own religion, and about a dead man named Jesus. Paul says that Jesus is alive.
I did not know how to look into these things. So I asked Paul if he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about these charges.
But Paul asked to be kept in prison until the emperor could decide his case. So I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar."
Agrippa said to Festus, "I would like to hear this man myself." Festus answered, "Tomorrow you will hear him."
The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great show. They went into the hall with the army commanders and the important men of the city. Then Festus ordered Paul to be brought in.
Festus said, "King Agrippa and everyone here with us, you see this man. All the Jews, here and in Jerusalem, have complained to me about him. They keep shouting that he should not live any longer.
But I found that he had done nothing that deserves death. And because he appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him.

But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. So I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa. After we question him, I hope I will have something to write.
It makes no sense to me to send a prisoner without saying what the charges against him are."
Agrippa said to Paul, "You may now speak for yourself." So Paul raised his hand and began to defend himself.
"King Agrippa, I am glad that I can stand before you today to answer all the charges the Jews have made against me.
I am especially glad because you know all about Jewish customs and the questions we argue about. So please listen to me patiently.
All the Jews know how I have lived since I was young. They know how I lived from the beginning among my own people and in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time. If they want to, they can tell you that I lived as a Pharisee. The Pharisees follow our religion more strictly than any other group.
And now I am on trial because I hope in the promise God made to our ancestors.
Our twelve tribes hope to see this promise come true. That is why they worship God day and night with all their hearts. King Agrippa, it is because of this hope that the Jews accuse me!
Why do any of you think it is impossible for God to raise the dead?
I too once thought that I should do all I could against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. The leading priests gave me power to put many of God's people in prison. When they were put to death, I voted against them.
I often punished them in all the synagogues and tried to force them to speak against God. I was so angry with them that I even went to cities in other countries to attack them.
Once I was on my way to Damascus with the power and orders of the leading priests.
At midday, King Agrippa, as I was on the road, I saw a light from the sky. It was brighter than the sun, and it shone all around me and the men travelling with me.

We all fell to the ground. Then I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language. It said, 'Saul, Saul, why are you attacking me? You are only hurting yourself by fighting me, like an ox kicking against a sharp stick.'
I asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' The Lord answered, 'I am Jesus, the one you are attacking.
Now get up and stand on your feet. I have come to you to choose you to be my servant. You will tell people what you have seen of me today, and what I will show you later.
I will keep you safe from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them

to open their eyes, so they will turn from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. Then their sins will be forgiven, and they will have a place among God's people, who are made holy by believing in me.'
So, King Agrippa, I obeyed the vision from heaven.

First I preached to the people in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and in all of Judea, and also to the Gentiles. I told them to turn away from their sins and turn to God. I told them to show by what they do that they have really changed.
That is why the Jews grabbed me in the temple and tried to kill me.

But God has helped me to this very day. So I stand here and tell everyone, both important people and ordinary people, what I know. I say nothing more than what the prophets and Moses said would happen.
They said that the Christ would suffer and be the first to rise from the dead. They said he would bring the light of God to the Jews and to the Gentiles."
While Paul was still defending himself, Festus shouted, "Paul, you are out of your mind! Too much study has made you crazy!"
Paul answered, "I am not crazy, most excellent Festus. What I am saying is true and makes sense.
The king knows about these things, and I can speak freely to him. I am sure that he knows all about them, because these things did not happen in secret.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do."
Agrippa said to Paul, "Do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly?"
Paul answered, "Whether quickly or slowly, I pray to God that not only you but everyone listening to me today could become like me, except for these chains."
Then the king stood up, and so did the governor, Bernice, and the people sitting with them.
They left the room and talked to each other. They said, "This man has done nothing that deserves death or prison."
Agrippa said to Festus, "This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar."
It was decided that we would sail to Italy. Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to an army officer named Julius. He belonged to the Emperor's Regiment.
We got on a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was kind to Paul and let him visit his friends, so they could give him what he needed.
From there we put out to sea again. The winds were against us, so we sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus.
We crossed the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, and landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the officer found a ship from Alexandria that was sailing to Italy, and he put us on board.
We sailed slowly for many days and had a hard time reaching Cnidus. The wind would not let us go on, so we sailed on the sheltered side of Crete, past Salmone.
We moved along the coast with difficulty and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
We had lost a lot of time, and sailing had become dangerous, because it was already after the Day of Fasting. So Paul warned them.
He said, "Men, I can see that this trip will be dangerous. We will lose the ship and its cargo, and we may even lose our lives."
But the officer listened to the pilot and the owner of the ship instead of listening to Paul.

The harbour was not a good place to stay for the winter. So most of the men decided to sail on and try to reach Phoenix, and stay there for the winter. Phoenix is a harbour in Crete that faces both southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, the men thought they could do what they had planned. So they pulled up the anchor and sailed along the coast of Crete, close to the shore.
But soon a very strong wind, called the Northeaster, came down from the island.
The ship was caught by the storm and could not sail into the wind. So we gave up and let the wind carry us along.
We passed the sheltered side of a small island called Clauda. With great difficulty we pulled in the lifeboat.

After the men had lifted it on board, they tied ropes around the ship to hold it together. They were afraid of hitting the sandbanks near Syrtis, so they lowered the sea anchor and let the ship be driven along.
The storm was beating so hard against us that the next day the men began throwing the cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship's equipment overboard with their own hands.
For many days we could not see the sun or the stars, and the storm kept raging. At last we gave up all hope of being saved.

The men had gone a long time without food. Then Paul stood up in front of them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then you would have avoided all this damage and loss.
But now I beg you to be brave. None of you will lose your life. Only the ship will be lost.
Last night an angel came and stood beside me. He was sent by the God I belong to and serve.
The angel said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. And God has given you the lives of everyone sailing with you.'
So be brave, men! I trust God that it will happen just as he told me.
But we will run aground on some island."
On the fourteenth night, we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea. At about midnight, the sailors felt that we were getting close to land.
They dropped a weighted line and found that the water was about thirty-seven metres deep. A little later they measured again and found it was about twenty-seven metres deep.
They were afraid we would hit the rocks. So they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship and prayed for daylight to come.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They lowered the lifeboat into the sea, pretending they were going to drop some anchors from the front of the ship.
But Paul said to the officer and the soldiers, "If these men do not stay on the ship, you cannot be saved."
So the soldiers cut the ropes that held the lifeboat and let it fall away.
Just before dawn, Paul begged everyone to eat something. He said, "For fourteen days you have been waiting and worrying, and you have not eaten anything.
So I beg you to eat some food. You need it to stay alive. Not one hair on your heads will be lost."
After he said this, Paul took some bread and thanked God for it in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
They all felt braver, and they ate some food too.
There were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When everyone had eaten enough, they made the ship lighter by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not know what land it was. But they saw a bay with a sandy beach, and they decided to run the ship onto the beach if they could.
So they cut the anchors loose and left them in the sea. At the same time they untied the ropes that held the steering oars. Then they raised the front sail to the wind and headed for the beach.
But the ship hit a sandbank where two currents met, and it ran aground. The front of the ship stuck fast and would not move, and the back of the ship was being broken to pieces by the pounding waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.
But the officer wanted to save Paul's life, so he stopped them. He ordered everyone who could swim to jump overboard first and swim to land.
The rest were to follow, holding on to planks or pieces of the ship. And so everyone reached land safely.
When we were safe on land, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The people who lived there were very kind to us. It was raining and cold, so they built a fire and welcomed us all.
Paul gathered a pile of sticks and was putting them on the fire. A poisonous snake came out because of the heat and bit him on the hand.
The people of the island saw the snake hanging from Paul's hand. They said to each other, "This man must be a murderer! He escaped from the sea, but Justice will not let him live."
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and was not hurt at all.
The people waited for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after waiting a long time, they saw that nothing bad happened to him. So they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Near that place there were fields that belonged to Publius, the most important man on the island. He welcomed us into his home and was very kind to us for three days.
Publius's father was in bed, sick with fever and a bad stomach illness. Paul went in to see him. He prayed, put his hands on him and healed him.
After this happened, all the other sick people on the island came to Paul, and they were healed too.
They gave us many gifts to honour us. When we were ready to sail, they put on the ship everything we needed.
After three months we set sail on a ship from Alexandria that had stayed at the island for the winter. The ship had the sign of the twin gods on its front.
We landed at Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we sailed around and came to Rhegium. The next day a south wind began to blow, and the day after that we reached Puteoli.
There we found some believers, and they asked us to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The believers in Rome heard that we were coming, and they came out to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Inns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and felt encouraged.
When we arrived in Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

Three days later Paul called together the Jewish leaders in Rome. When they had gathered, he said to them, "Brothers, I have done nothing against our people or against the customs of our ancestors. But I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
The Romans questioned me and wanted to set me free, because I had done nothing that deserved death.
But the Jews were against it, so I had to appeal to Caesar. I do not have any charge to bring against my own people.
That is why I asked to see you and talk with you. I am wearing this chain because of the hope of Israel."
They answered him, "We have not received any letters about you from Judea. And none of the brothers who came from there has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we want to hear what you think. We know that people everywhere are speaking against this group."

They agreed on a day to meet with Paul, and even more of them came to the house where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained God's Kingdom to them. He tried to convince them about Jesus from the law of Moses and from the Prophets.
Some of them believed what he said, but others did not.
They could not agree with each other, and they began to leave. Then Paul said one more thing: "The Holy Spirit was right when he spoke to your ancestors through Isaiah the prophet.
He said, 'Go to these people and say: You will listen and listen, but never understand. You will look and look, but never see.

These people's hearts have become hard. Their ears can hardly hear, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn to me, and I would heal them.'
So I want you to know that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!"
When he had said this, the Jews left, arguing strongly among themselves.
For two whole years Paul stayed there in a house he rented. He welcomed everyone who came to see him.
He boldly preached God's Kingdom and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ, and no one tried to stop him.
Rom: From Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ. God called me to be an apostle and set me apart for his good news.
God promised this good news long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures.
It is about his Son. As a man, he was born from the family of David.
But by the Holy Spirit, and by rising from the dead, he was shown with power to be the Son of God. He is Jesus Christ our Lord.
Through him we received grace and the work of an apostle. Our work is to call people from all nations to trust and obey him, for the honour of his name.
You too are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ.
I write to all of you in Rome who are loved by God and called to be his holy people. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because people everywhere are talking about your faith.
God is my witness. I serve him with my whole heart as I tell the good news about his Son. I never stop remembering you in my prayers.
In my prayers I ask that now at last, by God's will, I may be able to come to you.
I long to see you, so that I can share some spiritual gift with you to make you strong.
I mean that you and I may encourage each other. Your faith will help me, and my faith will help you.
I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you, but I have been stopped until now. I want to see some fruit among you, as I have among the other nations.
I owe a debt both to Greeks and to people who are not Greeks, both to the wise and to the unwise.
That is why I am so eager to tell the good news also to you who are in Rome.
I am not ashamed of the good news. It is the power of God that saves everyone who believes, first the Jew, and also the Greek.
In the good news, God shows how he makes people right with himself. It is by faith from start to finish. As the Scriptures say, "The person who is right with God will live by faith."
God's anger is being shown from heaven against all the godless and wrong things people do. They hold down the truth by the wrong things they do.
What can be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain.
Ever since the world was made, people have been able to see what God is like. His everlasting power and his nature as God are clear from the things he has made. So they have no excuse.
They knew God, but they did not honour him as God or give him thanks. Their thinking became empty, and their foolish hearts were darkened.
They claimed to be wise, but they became fools.
They traded the glory of the God who never dies for images that look like people who die, and like birds, animals and reptiles.
So God gave them over to the dirty desires of their hearts. They dishonoured their own bodies with one another.
They traded the truth about God for a lie. They worshipped and served what God created instead of the Creator himself, who is to be praised for ever. Amen.
Because of this, God gave them over to shameful desires. Their women traded natural sexual relations for unnatural ones.

In the same way, the men also left natural relations with women and burned with desire for one another. Men did shameful things with other men, and they received in themselves the due penalty for their wrong.
Since they did not think it worthwhile to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a worthless mind, to do what should not be done.
They are full of every kind of wrong: sexual sin, evil, greed and hate. They are full of envy, murder, fighting, lies and spite. They gossip
and speak badly of others. They hate God. They are rude, proud and boastful. They invent ways of doing evil. They disobey their parents.
They are foolish, they break their promises, they have no love and no mercy.
They know God's just rule, that people who do such things deserve death. Yet they not only do them, but also approve of others who do them.
So you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you judge someone else. When you judge another person, you condemn yourself, because you who judge do the same things.
We know that God's judgement against people who do such things is based on truth.
Do you think, you who judge people for doing these things while you do the same, that you will escape God's judgement?
Or do you look down on the riches of his kindness, patience and long-suffering? Do you not realise that God's kindness is meant to lead you to turn back to him?
But because you are stubborn and will not turn back, you are storing up anger for yourself on the day of God's anger, when his just judgement will be shown.
God "will pay back each person according to what they have done."
He will give eternal life to those who keep doing good and seek glory, honour and a life that never dies.
But for those who are selfish, who refuse the truth and follow what is wrong, there will be anger and fury.
There will be trouble and pain for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, and also for the Greek.
But glory, honour and peace will come to everyone who does good, first to the Jew, and also to the Greek.
For God does not favour one person over another.
All who sin without having the law will also die without the law. All who sin under the law will be judged by the law.
It is not those who hear the law who are right with God. It is those who do what the law says who will be declared right.
When people of the nations, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law for themselves, even though they do not have the law.
They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts. Their conscience also speaks up, and their thoughts sometimes accuse them and sometimes defend them.
This will happen on the day when God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ, as my good news declares.
Now you call yourself a Jew. You rely on the law and boast about your relationship with God.
You know his will and approve of what is right, because you are taught by the law.
You are sure that you are a guide for the blind and a light for those in the dark,
a corrector of the foolish and a teacher of little children, because you have in the law the full form of knowledge and truth.
You, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?
You who say people must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who hate idols, do you rob temples?
You who boast in the law, do you dishonour God by breaking the law?
As the Scriptures say, "God's name is spoken against among the nations because of you."
Circumcision has value if you obey the law. But if you break the law, your circumcision has become no circumcision at all.
So if a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will he not be regarded as if he were circumcised?
The man who is not circumcised physically, yet obeys the law, will judge you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
A person is not a true Jew if he is only one outwardly. True circumcision is not only something done to the body.
A person is a true Jew if he is one inwardly. True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a person's praise comes not from people, but from God.
So what advantage is there in being a Jew? What value is there in circumcision?
Much in every way! First of all, the Jews were trusted with the very words of God.
What if some of them were unfaithful? Does their unfaithfulness cancel God's faithfulness?
Not at all! Let God be true, even if every human being is a liar. As the Scriptures say, "So that you may be proved right when you speak, and win when you are judged."
But if our wrongdoing shows how right God is, what shall we say? That God is unfair to bring his anger on us? (I am using a human way of speaking.)
Certainly not! If that were so, how could God judge the world?
Someone might say, "If my lie makes God's truth stand out more and brings him glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?"
Why not say, as some people slanderously claim that we say, "Let us do evil so that good may come"? Their condemnation is deserved.
What then? Are we Jews any better? Not at all! We have already made the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under the power of sin.
As the Scriptures say, "There is no one who is right with God, not even one.
There is no one who understands. There is no one who seeks God.
All have turned away. Together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, not even one."
"Their throats are open graves. Their tongues practise deceit." "The poison of snakes is under their lips."
"Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness."
"Their feet are quick to shed blood.
Ruin and misery mark their ways,
and the way of peace they have not known."
"There is no fear of God before their eyes."
Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.
So no one will be declared right in God's sight by doing what the law commands. Through the law we become aware of our sin.
But now God has shown a way to be right with him that does not depend on the law. The Law and the Prophets testify to it.
God makes people right with himself through faith in Jesus Christ. This is for everyone who believes. There is no difference.
For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
They are made right with him freely by his grace, through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.

God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood, to be received by faith. He did this to show his justice, because in his patience he had left the sins committed beforehand unpunished.
He did it to show his justice at the present time, so as to be just and the one who makes right those who have faith in Jesus.
Where, then, is boasting? It is shut out. On what principle? On the principle of works? No, on the principle of faith.
For we maintain that a person is made right with God by faith, apart from doing what the law commands.
Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of the nations also? Yes, of the nations also,
since there is only one God. He will make the circumcised right with himself by faith, and the uncircumcised right through that same faith.
Do we then cancel the law by this faith? Not at all! Rather, we uphold the law.
What then shall we say that Abraham, our father according to the flesh, discovered about this?
If Abraham was made right with God by what he did, he would have something to boast about. But not before God.
What do the Scriptures say? "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness."
Now when a person works, their wages are not credited as a gift, but as something owed.
But to the person who does not work, but trusts God who makes the ungodly right with himself, their faith is credited as righteousness.
David says the same thing when he speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works.
"Blessed are those whose wrongs are forgiven, whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord will never count against them."
Is this blessedness only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham's faith was credited to him as righteousness.
Under what circumstances was it credited? Was it after he was circumcised, or before? It was not after, but before!

He received circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. So he is the father of all who believe but have not been circumcised, in order that righteousness might be credited to them.
And he is also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised but who also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
It was not through the law that Abraham and his offspring received the promise that he would be heir of the world, but through the righteousness that comes by faith.
For if those who depend on the law are heirs, faith means nothing and the promise is worthless.
Because the law brings anger. And where there is no law there is no breaking of the law.

Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may be by grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham's offspring, not only to those who are of the law but also to those who have the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all.
As it is written, "I have made you a father of many nations." He is our father in the sight of God, in whom he believed, the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that were not.
Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations, just as it had been said to him, "So shall your offspring be."
Without weakening in his faith, he faced the fact that his body was as good as dead, since he was about a hundred years old, and that Sarah's womb was also dead.
Yet he did not waver through unbelief regarding the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God,
being fully persuaded that God had power to do what he had promised.
That is why "it was credited to him as righteousness."
The words "it was credited to him" were written not for him alone,
but also for us, to whom God will credit righteousness, for us who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
He was delivered over to death for our sins and was raised to life for our being made right with God.
Therefore, since we have been made right with God through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Through him we have also gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand. And we boast in the hope of the glory of God.
Not only that, but we also boast in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance.
Perseverance produces character, and character produces hope.
And hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly.
Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die.
But God shows his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Since we have now been made right with God by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God's anger through him!
For if, while we were God's enemies, we were made friends with him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been made friends, shall we be saved through his life!
Not only is this so, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received friendship with God.
Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all people, because all sinned.
To be sure, sin was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not charged against anyone's account where there is no law.
Nevertheless, death reigned from the time of Adam to the time of Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command, as did Adam, who is a pattern of the one to come.

But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God's grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, overflow to the many!

Nor can the gift of God be compared with the result of one man's sin. The judgement followed one sin and brought condemnation, but the gift followed many trespasses and brought being made right with God.

For if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive God's abundant provision of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!
Consequently, just as one trespass resulted in condemnation for all people, so also one righteous act resulted in being made right with God and life for all people.
For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made right with God.
The law was brought in so that the trespass might increase. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
What shall we say then? Shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase?
Certainly not! We are those who have died to sin. How can we live in it any longer?
Or don't you know that all of us who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death?
We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.
For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly also be united with him in a resurrection like his.
For we know that our old self was crucified with him so that the body ruled by sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves to sin,
because anyone who has died has been set free from sin.
Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, he cannot die again. Death no longer has mastery over him.
The death he died, he died to sin once for all. But the life he lives, he lives to God.
In the same way, count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its evil desires.

Do not offer any part of yourself to sin as an instrument of wickedness, but rather offer yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life. And offer every part of yourself to him as an instrument of righteousness.
For sin shall no longer be your master, because you are not under the law, but under grace.
What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? Certainly not!

Don't you know that when you offer yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether you are slaves to sin, which leads to death, or to obedience, which leads to righteousness?
But thanks be to God that, though you used to be slaves to sin, you have come to obey from your heart the pattern of teaching that has now claimed your allegiance.
You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness.

I am using an example from everyday life because of your human limitations. Just as you used to offer yourselves as slaves to impurity and to ever-increasing wickedness, so now offer yourselves as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness.
When you were slaves to sin, you were free from the control of righteousness.
What benefit did you reap at that time from the things you are now ashamed of? Those things result in death!
But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the benefit you reap leads to holiness, and the result is eternal life.
For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Do you not know, brothers and sisters, for I am speaking to those who know the law, that the law has authority over someone only as long as that person lives?
For example, by law a married woman is bound to her husband as long as he is alive. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law that binds her to him.

So then, if she has sexual relations with another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress. But if her husband dies, she is released from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man.
So, my brothers and sisters, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the realm of the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in us, so that we bore fruit for death.
But now, by dying to what once bound us, we have been released from the law so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code.

What shall we say, then? Is the law sinful? Certainly not! Nevertheless, I would not have known what sin was had it not been for the law. For I would not have known what coveting really was if the law had not said, "You shall not covet."
But sin, seizing the opportunity afforded by the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from the law, sin was dead.
Once I was alive apart from the law. But when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died.
I found that the very commandment that was intended to bring life actually brought death.
For sin, seizing the opportunity afforded by the commandment, deceived me, and through the commandment put me to death.
So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous and good.

Did that which is good, then, become death to me? By no means! Nevertheless, in order that sin might be recognised as sin, it used what is good to bring about my death, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.
We know that the law is spiritual. But I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.
I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do.
And if I do what I do not want to do, I agree that the law is good.
As it is, it is no longer I myself who do it, but it is sin living in me.
For I know that good itself does not dwell in me, that is, in my sinful nature. For I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out.
For I do not do the good I want to do, but the evil I do not want to do, this I keep on doing.
Now if I do what I do not want to do, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.
So I find this law at work: although I want to do good, evil is right there with me.
For in my inner being I delight in God's law.
But I see another law at work in me, waging war against the law of my mind and making me a prisoner of the law of sin at work within me.
What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body that is subject to death?
Thanks be to God, who delivers me through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself in my mind am a slave to God's law, but in my sinful nature a slave to the law of sin.
So now there is no condemnation for those who belong to Christ Jesus. They do not live by their sinful human nature, but by the Spirit.
For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit, who gives life, has set me free from the law of sin and death.

The law of Moses could not save us, because our sinful human nature made it weak. But God did what the law could not do. He sent his own Son in a body like our sinful bodies, to be an offering for sin. In this way God passed judgement on sin in a human body.
He did this so that the right standard of the law would be fully met in us, who do not live by our sinful nature but by the Spirit.
People who live by their sinful nature set their minds on what that nature wants. But people who live by the Spirit set their minds on what the Spirit wants.
A mind controlled by the sinful nature leads to death. But a mind controlled by the Spirit leads to life and peace.
The sinful mind is an enemy of God. It does not obey God's law, and it cannot.
So those who are controlled by their sinful nature cannot please God.
But you are not controlled by your sinful nature. You are controlled by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.
But if Christ lives in you, your body will die because of sin, yet the Spirit gives you life because God has made you right with him.

The Spirit of God raised Jesus from the dead. If that same Spirit lives in you, then God, who raised Christ from the dead, will also give life to your bodies that die. He will do this through his Spirit, who lives in you.
So, my brothers and sisters, we have a duty, but it is not to our sinful nature. We do not have to live the way it wants.
If you live by your sinful nature, you will die. But if, through the Spirit, you put to death the sinful things you do, you will live.
All who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God.
The Spirit you received does not make you slaves who live in fear again. Instead, you received the Spirit who makes you God's own children. By him we cry out, "Abba, Father."
The Spirit himself joins with our spirit to assure us that we are God's children.
And if we are his children, then we will receive what God has promised to his children. We will share it with Christ. But if we share in his suffering, we will also share in his glory.
I am sure that what we suffer now is nothing compared with the glory that will be shown to us later.
All of creation is waiting with eager hope for the day when God will show who his children really are.
Creation was made subject to emptiness and decay. This was not its own choice. It was the will of God, who made it so, but there was hope.
The hope is that creation itself will be set free from its slavery to decay. It will share in the glorious freedom of God's children.
We know that the whole of creation has been groaning together, like a woman in the pains of giving birth, right up to now.

And not only creation. We too groan inside ourselves, even though we have the Spirit as the first part of God's gift. We are waiting eagerly for God to make us fully his children, which includes setting our bodies free.
We were saved with this hope in our hearts. But hope that can already be seen is not really hope. Who hopes for something they already have?
But if we hope for something we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.
In the same way, the Spirit helps us when we are weak. We do not know what we ought to pray for. But the Spirit himself prays for us with groans that words cannot express.
God, who searches our hearts, knows what the Spirit is thinking, because the Spirit prays for God's people in the way God wants.
And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love him, those he has called according to his plan.
God knew his people before they were born, and he chose them to become like his Son. In this way his Son would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
Those he chose, he also called. Those he called, he also made right with himself. And those he made right with himself, he also gave a share in his glory.
